His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

The estimated sense is: "but leave me for the one who is called: 'Go to the mare of Umm 'Amir.'"

The beginning of these surahs was revealed about them, up to some eighty-odd verses, until their affair ended with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) calling them to mubahalah (mutual imprecation).[...] Its explanation will come later.

(p. 149) The Seven Readers recited "Alamu Allah," with a fatha on the mim and the alif omitted. It is narrated from 'Asim that he pronounced the mim with sukun and then cut the alif. Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi and Abu Haywah recited "Alami" with a kasra on the mim, for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. This is weak, because the ya' prevents that. The correct form is the fatha, the reading of the majority of people. Abu 'Ali said: The letters of spelling (huruf al-tahajji) are built on pausal form, so the mim is quiescent and the lam is quiescent, and the mim was given a fatha, just as the nun is given a vowel in your saying: "min Allah" and "min al-Muslimin," and so on.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever says that the vowel of the hamza was transferred onto the mim is weak, because there is consensus that the connecting alif of the definite article drops in continuous speech, and what drops is not given the vowel of another. This is what Abu 'Ali said.

The majority of readers recited "al-Qayyum," whose form is fa'yul. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and 'Alqamah ibn Qays recited "al-Qayyam," whose form is fa'yal. It is also narrated from 'Alqamah that he recited "al-Qayyim," whose form is fa'yil. All of this derives from qama bi-al-amr, yaqumu bihi, when one takes responsibility for its preservation and for everything it needs in order to exist. So Allah, exalted is He, is the Qayyam over everything, in what befits Him, or in it, or upon it.

(p. 150) The sending down of the Book by Allah is through the angel Jibril, peace be upon him. "Al-Kitab" in this place is the Qur'an by agreement of the exegetes. There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ is an independent, separate sentence.

His saying "bi-al-haqq" (with truth) may have two meanings. The first: that the meaning is "among the realities, of His good news, His command, His prohibition and His admonitions," so the ba' is in its ordinary sense, as in your saying: "A book came to me with the news of such and such," meaning that this news is recounted in it. The second: that the meaning is that He sent down the Book in deserving to be sent down, because of the comprehensive benefit in it. This does not mean it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to do it; rather, He has the right to do it. So the ba' in this sense is in its ordinary sense as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to [say].﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the meaning of "bi-al-haqq" is: concerning what the People of the Book differed about and what these visiting Christians were confused about. This falls within the first meaning.

"Musaddiqan" (confirming) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah), a fixed one that does not change, because it is not possible for it to be other than confirming what is before it of the Book of Allah. It is like the saying of Ibn Darrah:

"I am the son of Darrah, known by it is my lineage, and is there, O people, any shame in Darrah?"

"What is before it" (ma bayna yadayhi) means the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the books of Allah that were received from our law, like the Psalms and the scrolls (p. 151). What is "before the hand" in these events is what is earlier in time.

"Al-Tawrat" and "al-Injil" are names whose origin is Hebrew, but the grammarians and the people of language treated them as if they were derived in Arabic. They said of al-Tawrah that it is from wary al-zand yari, when it is struck and its fire appears; it is said: awraytuhu fa-wariya. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "fa-al-muriyat" (the sparking ones), and His saying: ﴿Have you considered the fire which you ignite?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 71]. Abu 'Ali said: As for their saying: wariyat bika zanadi (my firestick has sparked because of you), on the pattern fa'ila, Abu 'Uthman claimed that it was used only in this expression and was not extended to other uses.

According to al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the rest of the Basrans, Tawrah is fawalah, like hawqalah, originally wawrayah, in which the first waw was changed to ta', just as it was changed in tawlaja, whose origin is wawlaja, from walajat. Al-Zajjaj related from some Kufans that Tawrah originally has the form taf'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn, from wariyat bika zanadi. The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It should rather be from awraytu, so it would be tawriyah. Some said: it may be tif'ilah with a kasra on the 'ayn, like tawsiyah, then it was returned to taf'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Zajjaj said, as if he permitted in tawsiyah "tawsi'ah," and that is not attested. In any case, the ya' was, when what preceded it was opened and it itself was vocalized, changed into an alif, so it was said Tawrah. Abu 'Ali preferred the opinion of the Basrans, and others weakened it.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited "al-Tawrata" with a fatha on the ra'. Hamzah and Nafi' used to pronounce the ra' between the two sounds, between fatha and kasra, and they did so likewise in His saying "ma'a al-abrar" (with the righteous), "min al-ashrar" (from the wicked) and "min qarar" (from a resting-place), when the letter is in the genitive. Al-Musayyabi narrated from Nafi' the fatha on the ra' of al-Tawrah, and Warsh narrated from him the kasra. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i used to pronounce the ra' of al-Tawrah with kasra (p. 152), and they inclined "min al-abrar" and others more than Hamzah and Nafi' inclined them.

Regarding al-Injil, they said: it is ifil, from al-najl, which is the water that seeps out of the earth. Al-Khalil said: the earth became najlah, and it has najal when water comes out of it. Al-najl also means offspring and progeny, as al-Khalil and others said, and najalahu abuhu means his father fathered him. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"He was the most excellent of the days his two parents had him, when they fathered him, and what a fine fathering it was!"

Ibn Sidah related from Abu 'Ali: the meaning of his saying "ayyama walidahu bihi" is like your saying: "I am with Allah and with you." Abu al-Fath said: the meaning of the verse is: his parents excelled by him on the days when they fathered him; it is like your saying "hina'idhin" and "yawma'idhin," but it is a state of the agent placed between the annexed noun, which is "ayyam," and the noun it is annexed to, which is "idh." This verse is also narrated as "anjaba ayyama walidayhi" (he excelled in the days of his parents).

Al-najl also means throwing something, and that too comes from the meaning of appearing and one thing parting from another. Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji related in his Nawadir that the father is called najl, and that the word is among the antonyms. As for the verse of Zuhayr, the correct narration in it is:

"....................... and every stallion has najl"

that is, a noble offspring and progeny. Al-Asma'i is related, as reported from him, to have narrated: "and every branch has najl," and this is not tenable except on the basis of calling the father najl. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Injil is derived from al-najl, which is the origin, so this inclines toward what Abu al-Qasim related.

Abu al-Fath said: So al-Tawrah is from wari al-zind when its fire appears, and al-Injil is from najala when its offspring appears, or from the appearance of water from the earth. So it is extracted either from the Preserved Tablet or from the Torah.

"Al-Furqan" (the Criterion) is from separating truth from falsehood. Its letters are different, but the meaning of each is close to the others, since all of them mean the manifestation of truth, the clarification of the law, and its separation from other falsehoods.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "al-Anjil" with a fatha on the hamza. That is not tenable in Arabic speech, but the eminence of al-Hasan in eloquence protects it, and the fact that he recites only what he has narrated. I think he went with it toward the way of foreign names.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿min qablu﴾ (before) means before the Qur'an.

His saying: "guidance for the people" means a call. The people here are the Children of Israel, because they are the ones addressed by these two alone. If it is meant that they are guidance in themselves, toward which Pharaoh and others are called, and it is an accusative of purpose for whoever is guided by it, then "the people" is general, including everyone who wishes at that point to seek insight.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Here He said "lil-nas" (for the people), and in the Qur'an He said "hudan lil-muttaqin" (guidance for the God-fearing). In my view, this is because this statement is a bare report, whereas "guidance for the God-fearing" is a report joined with a summons and a turning toward faith, so the description was made beautiful, so that the hearer would feel energy and eagerness. Here, He mentioned the guidance which is the call, whereas the guidance which is the creation of guidance in the heart is mentioned there. Here He mentioned only the guidance which is the call, and the guidance which is in itself prepared so that people are guided by it, so it was called guidance for that reason. Ibn Furak said: the estimate here is "guidance for the people who are God-fearing," and this brings the general back to that specific. There is room for scrutiny in this.

Al-Furqan: the Qur'an. It is so named because it distinguishes (faraqa) between truth and falsehood. Muhammad ibn Ja'far said: it distinguished between truth and falsehood regarding the matter of 'Isa, peace be upon him, about which the delegation argued. Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: it distinguished between truth and falsehood in the rulings of the sacred laws (shara'i') and in what is lawful (halal) and unlawful (haram) and the like, and al-Furqan encompasses all of this.

Some exegetes said: al-Furqan here means every matter that distinguished between truth and falsehood, in what came before and what occurred later. Included in this interpretation are the Flood of Noah, the parting of the sea for the drowning of Pharaoh, the Day of Badr, and all other acts of God Most High that separate truth from falsehood. It is as if God Most High mentioned the Mighty Book, then the Torah and the Gospel, then all His acts and created things which separated truth from falsehood, just as these Books did. Then God Most High threatened the disbelievers in general with severe punishment. This encompasses the punishment of this world by the sword and by conquest, and the punishment of the Hereafter by the Fire. The reference of this threat is to the Christians of Najran. al-Naqqash said: it refers to the Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, the two sons of Akhtab, and others.

"'Aziz" means: dominant (ghalib), to whom everything submits. Al-niqmah and al-intiqam: punishing the wrongdoer with intensity in that regard.

There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ is an independent, separate sentence.

The first: that the meaning is "among the realities, of His good news, His command, His prohibition and His admonitions," so the ba' is in its ordinary sense, as in your saying: "A book came to me with the news of such and such," meaning that this news is recounted in it. The second: that the meaning is that He sent down the Book in deserving to be sent down, because of the comprehensive benefit in it. This does not mean it is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to do it; rather, He has the right to do it. So the ba' in this sense is in its ordinary sense as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to [say].﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the meaning of "bi-al-haqq" is: concerning what the People of the Book differed about and what these visiting Christians were confused about. This falls within the first meaning.

"Musaddiqan" (confirming) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah), a fixed one that does not change, because it is not possible for it to be other than confirming what is before it of the Book of Allah. It is like the saying of Ibn Darrah:

"I am the son of Darrah, known by it is my lineage, and is there, O people, any shame in Darrah?"

"What is before it" (ma bayna yadayhi) means the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the books of Allah that were received from our law, like the Psalms and the scrolls (p. 151). What is "before the hand" in these events is what is earlier in time.

"Al-Tawrat" and "al-Injil" are names whose origin is Hebrew, but the grammarians and the people of language treated them as if they were derived in Arabic. They said of al-Tawrah that it is from wary al-zand yari, when it is struck and its fire appears; it is said: awraytuhu fa-wariya. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "fa-al-muriyat" (the sparking ones), and His saying: ﴿Have you considered the fire which you ignite?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 71]. Abu 'Ali said: As for their saying: wariyat bika zanadi (my firestick has sparked because of you), on the pattern fa'ila, Abu 'Uthman claimed that it was used only in this expression and was not extended to other uses.

According to al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the rest of the Basrans, Tawrah is fawalah, like hawqalah, originally wawrayah, in which the first waw was changed to ta', just as it was changed in tawlaja, whose origin is wawlaja, from walajat. Al-Zajjaj related from some Kufans that Tawrah originally has the form taf'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn, from wariyat bika zanadi. The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It should rather be from awraytu, so it would be tawriyah. Some said: it may be tif'ilah with a kasra on the 'ayn, like tawsiyah, then it was returned to taf'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn. Al-Zajjaj said, as if he permitted in tawsiyah "tawsi'ah," and that is not attested. In any case, the ya' was, when what preceded it was opened and it itself was vocalized, changed into an alif, so it was said Tawrah. Abu 'Ali preferred the opinion of the Basrans, and others weakened it.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited "al-Tawrata" with a fatha on the ra'. Hamzah and Nafi' used to pronounce the ra' between the two sounds, between fatha and kasra, and they did so likewise in His saying "ma'a al-abrar" (with the righteous), "min al-ashrar" (from the wicked) and "min qarar" (from a resting-place), when the letter is in the genitive. Al-Musayyabi narrated from Nafi' the fatha on the ra' of al-Tawrah, and Warsh narrated from him the kasra. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i used to pronounce the ra' of al-Tawrah with kasra (p. 152), and they inclined "min al-abrar" and others more than Hamzah and Nafi' inclined them.

Regarding al-Injil, they said: it is ifil, from al-najl, which is the water that seeps out of the earth. Al-Khalil said: the earth became najlah, and it has najal when water comes out of it. Al-najl also means offspring and progeny, as al-Khalil and others said, and najalahu abuhu means his father fathered him. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"He was the most excellent of the days his two parents had him, when they fathered him, and what a fine fathering it was!"

Ibn Sidah related from Abu 'Ali: the meaning of his saying "ayyama walidahu bihi" is like your saying: "I am with Allah and with you." Abu al-Fath said: the meaning of the verse is: his parents excelled by him on the days when they fathered him; it is like your saying "hina'idhin" and "yawma'idhin," but it is a state of the agent placed between the annexed noun, which is "ayyam," and the noun it is annexed to, which is "idh." This verse is also narrated as "anjaba ayyama walidayhi" (he excelled in the days of his parents).

Al-najl also means throwing something, and that too comes from the meaning of appearing and one thing parting from another. Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji related in his Nawadir that the father is called najl, and that the word is among the antonyms. As for the verse of Zuhayr, the correct narration in it is:

"....................... and every stallion has najl"

that is, a noble offspring and progeny. Al-Asma'i is related, as reported from him, to have narrated: "and every branch has najl," and this is not tenable except on the basis of calling the father najl. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Injil is derived from al-najl, which is the origin, so this inclines toward what Abu al-Qasim related.

Abu al-Fath said: So al-Tawrah is from wari al-zind when its fire appears, and al-Injil is from najala when its offspring appears, or from the appearance of water from the earth. So it is extracted either from the Preserved Tablet or from the Torah.

"Al-Furqan" (the Criterion) is from separating truth from falsehood. Its letters are different, but the meaning of each is close to the others, since all of them mean the manifestation of truth, the clarification of the law, and its separation from other falsehoods.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "al-Anjil" with a fatha on the hamza. That is not tenable in Arabic speech, but the eminence of al-Hasan in eloquence protects it, and the fact that he recites only what he has narrated. I think he went with it toward the way of foreign names.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿min qablu﴾ (before) means before the Qur'an.

His saying: "guidance for the people" means a call. The people here are the Children of Israel, because they are the ones addressed by these two alone. If it is meant that they are guidance in themselves, toward which Pharaoh and others are called, and it is an accusative of purpose for whoever is guided by it, then "the people" is general, including everyone who wishes at that point to seek insight.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Here He said "lil-nas" (for the people), and in the Qur'an He said "hudan lil-muttaqin" (guidance for the God-fearing). In my view, this is because this statement is a bare report, whereas "guidance for the God-fearing" is a report joined with a summons and a turning toward faith, so the description was made beautiful, so that the hearer would feel energy and eagerness. Here, He mentioned the guidance which is the call, whereas the guidance which is the creation of guidance in the heart is mentioned there. Here He mentioned only the guidance which is the call, and the guidance which is in itself prepared so that people are guided by it, so it was called guidance for that reason. Ibn Furak said: the estimate here is "guidance for the people who are God-fearing," and this brings the general back to that specific. There is room for scrutiny in this.

Al-Furqan: the Qur'an. It is so named because it distinguishes (faraqa) between truth and falsehood. Muhammad ibn Ja'far said: it distinguished between truth and falsehood regarding the matter of 'Isa, peace be upon him, about which the delegation argued. Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: it distinguished between truth and falsehood in the rulings of the sacred laws (shara'i') and in what is lawful (halal) and unlawful (haram) and the like, and al-Furqan encompasses all of this.

Some exegetes said: al-Furqan here means every matter that distinguished between truth and falsehood, in what came before and what occurred later. Included in this interpretation are the Flood of Noah, the parting of the sea for the drowning of Pharaoh, the Day of Badr, and all other acts of God Most High that separate truth from falsehood. It is as if God Most High mentioned the Mighty Book, then the Torah and the Gospel, then all His acts and created things which separated truth from falsehood, just as these Books did. Then God Most High threatened the disbelievers in general with severe punishment. This encompasses the punishment of this world by the sword and by conquest, and the punishment of the Hereafter by the Fire. The reference of this threat is to the Christians of Najran. al-Naqqash said: it refers to the Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, the two sons of Akhtab, and others.

"'Aziz" means: dominant (ghalib), to whom everything submits. Al-niqmah and al-intiqam: punishing the wrongdoer with intensity in that regard.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 5–7 (part 1 of 2):**

The words of the Most High:
﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat).﴾

This verse is an informing about Allah's knowledge of things in detail. This is an attribute that was not held by 'Isa (peace be upon him) or by any of the created beings. Then He informed of His forming of humans in the wombs of their mothers. No rational person denies this, and no one denies that 'Isa and all other humans are unable to do it. No one denies that 'Isa (peace be upon him) was among those formed in the wombs. Thus this verse is a magnification of Allah the Most High, and within it is a refutation of the Christians of Najran.

In His words ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Him﴾ there is a warning to them. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Rabi' interpreted it in this manner. In His words ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ there is a refutation of the people of nature (ahl al-tabi'a), who make nature an active agent acting independently. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the manner of the formation in the hadith narrated by Ibn Mas'ud and others: "Indeed, when the sperm drop enters the womb, it remains a drop for forty days, then becomes a clot ('alaqa) for forty days, then a lump of flesh (mudgha) of similar duration. Then Allah sends an angel to it, and he says: 'O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed?'" The hadith is given in full with variations in its wording. In the Musnad of Ibn Sanjar there is a hadith: "Indeed Allah creates the bones of the fetus and its cartilage from the man's semen, and its flesh, its fat, and all the rest from the woman's semen."

"Sawwara" (he formed) is an intensive form (ibna mubalagha) from "sara yasuru," meaning to incline and bend toward a certain state. Since forming (taswir) is inclining something toward a state and establishing it in that state, its pattern is that of intensification. The womb (rahm) is the place where the fetus develops.

"As He wills" means in respect of height and shortness, color, soundness or defect, and other differences. "Al-'Aziz" means the Dominant, and "al-Hakim" means the one possessed of wisdom, or the one who makes judgments regarding His creatures. This is more specific to what was mentioned of forming.

"Al-Kitab" in this verse is the Qur'an by the consensus of the exegetes (al-mu'awwilin). The muhkamat are those that are detailed, clear, and whose rulings are fixed. The mutashabihat are those that require reflection and need interpretation (ta'wil, explanation of meaning). What appears in them at first glance is either a contradiction with another verse or with reason, and other kinds of ambiguity. This resemblance, for which they are described as mutashabihat, is only between them and the corrupt meanings that the people of deviation (ahl al-zaygh) and those who do not reflect deeply suppose. This is like the authentic hadith from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are ambiguous matters (mutashabihat)." That is, a thing may be unlawful in itself, yet to one who does not reflect deeply it resembles something lawful. Likewise, a verse may have a sound meaning in itself, yet to one who does not reflect deeply, or to one who deviates, it resembles another corrupt meaning, so he may use it to object against the Book of Allah. This, in my view, is the meaning of muhkam and mutashabih in this verse. Do you not see that "the Christians of Najran said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'Do you not have in your Book that 'Isa is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Then that is enough for us.'" This is the ambiguity.

The exegetes differed in their expressions concerning the specification of the muhkam and mutashabih intended in this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: the muhkamat are His words in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ (Al-An'am 6:151) through three verses, and His words in Banu Isra'il: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:23). In my view this is an example he gave of the muhkamat. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the muhkamat are its abrogating verses (nasikh), its lawful and unlawful, and what is to be believed and acted upon; the mutashabihat are its abrogated verses (mansukh), its preceding and succeeding, its parables, its oaths, and what is to be believed but not acted upon. Ibn Mas'ud and others said: the muhkamat are the abrogating verses (al-nasikhat), and the mutashabihat are the abrogated verses (al-mansukhat). In my view this is by way of illustration, that is, muhkam is found in this and mutashabih is found in that, not that it is restricted to this kind of verse. Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak held this view. Mujahid and 'Ikrima said: the muhkamat are those containing the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever else is mutashabih, confirming one another, like His words: ﴿He leads astray thereby only the defiantly disobedient﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:26), and His words: ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ (Al-An'am 6:125). These statements and what resembles them are weakened by the fact that the people of deviation have no attachment to one type of what was mentioned to the exclusion of the others.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the muhkamat are those in which is the proof of the Lord, the protection of the servants, and the repelling of adversaries and falsehood; they admit no alteration (tasrif) or distortion (tahrif) from what they were established upon. The mutashabihat are those that admit alteration, distortion, and interpretation, through which Allah tests the servants. This is the best of the statements concerning this verse. Ibn Zayd said: the muhkam is that in which the stories of the prophets and the nations are made clear and explained to Muhammad and his community; the mutashabih is that in which the stories of those peoples, when repeated in the surahs, have wordings that resemble one another while their meanings differ, some of which are identical in wording and different in meaning, and some the reverse, such as His words "a moving snake" and "a manifest serpent," and "insert your hand" and "put your hand in."

A group of scholars, among them Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab, and what appears to be the position of al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri and others, said: the muhkamat of the verses of the Qur'an are those whose interpretation the scholars know, and whose meaning and explanation they understand; the mutashabih is that for which no one has any way to knowledge, of what Allah has kept the knowledge of to Himself apart from His creation. Some of them said: this is like the time of the Hour, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, and like the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs.

The judge Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq (may Allah be pleased with him) said:
As for the unseen matters that will come, they are among the muhkamat, because what humans know of them is limited, and what they do not know, namely the specification of the time, is also limited. As for the beginnings of surahs, they are among the mutashabih, because they are open to interpretation. For this reason the Jews followed them and wanted to derive from them the duration of the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Some of these statements that we mentioned from the scholars face objections, because the ambiguity in this verse is restricted to what the people of deviation have an attachment to, whereas some expressions of the exegetes present an ambiguity that does not give the people of deviation any attachment.

As for His words ﴿they are the foundation of the Book (umm al-kitab)﴾, its meaning is informing that they are the bulk of the Book and its core, since the muhkam in the verses of Allah is abundant, detailed, and nothing in it has been neglected. Yahya ibn Ya'mar said: this is like the saying about Makkah: "Umm al-Qura" (mother of the towns), and about Marw: "Umm Khurasan," and like the saying "Umm al-Ra's" (the crown of the head) for the gathering place of the faculties, since it is the most vital place. Al-Mahdawi and al-Naqqash said: every muhkam verse in the Book of Allah is called "umm al-kitab." This is rejected; rather, all of the muhkam is the umm al-kitab. Al-Naqqash said: this is like your saying: "All of you are against me a fierce lion," and this example is not muhkam. Ibn Zayd said: "umm al-kitab" means the totality (jima') of the Book. Al-Tabari related from Abu Fakhita that he said: "they are the umm al-kitab" is meant to refer to the openings of the surahs, since from them the Qur'an is derived: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:1), ﴿That is the Book﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:2), from it the surah of al-Baqara was derived; ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:1), ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Sustainer﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:2), from it the surah of Al 'Imran was derived. This is a statement that collapses under its own weight, confused, and its speaker did not consider the beginning of the verse, its end, and its purpose. Rather the meaning of the verse is a rebuke of the people of deviation, and the reference in it at first is to the Christians of Najran and to the Jews who were contemporaries of Muhammad (peace be upon him), since they used to object to the meanings of the Qur'an. Then it generalizes to every person of deviation after that. Allah the Most High mentioned that He sent down the Book to Muhammad as a bounty from Him and a blessing, that its muhkam and clear part, against which there is no objection, is its bulk and predominant portion, and that its mutashabih, which admits interpretation and requires understanding, is its smaller part. Then the people of deviation abandon the muhkam, in which lies their sufficiency, and follow the mutashabih, seeking discord and seeking to corrupt matters and to turn people back to their deviation. Thus blame is directed at them.

"Ukhar" is the plural of "ukhra," and it does not take nunation (la yansarif) because it is a descriptive adjective (sifa), and it has been deflected from the definite article "al-" in that it is made plural and dual. All comparative adjectives (sifat al-tafdil), when stripped of "al-," are not made dual or plural, like "afdal" (more excellent) and what follows its pattern. These attributes cannot be used to compare between two things except when they are indefinite. When the definite article enters upon them, the meaning of comparison between two things disappears. The deflection of "ukhar" from the definite article does not affect definiteness, as is the case with the deflection of "sahar" (in the sense of "at dawn," "sahar" with the definite article omitted). Rather "ukhar" is indefinite. As for "sahar," it was deflected in that the definite article was removed while it remained definite, as in the saying: "I came on Friday at dawn (sahar)." Al-Mahdawi confused this issue and corrupted the words of Sibawayh, so consider it carefully.

**

The words of the Most High:
﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But no one knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

His words ﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)﴾ encompass every group of disbelievers, heretics, ignorant people, and possessors of innovation (bid'a). Zaygh means inclination, and from it comes "the sun declined (zaghat al-shams)" and "the eyes swerved (zaghat al-absar)." The reference of the verse at that time was to the Christians of Najran, because of their challenging the Qur'an concerning the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), as al-Rabi' said, and to the Jews. Then it extends to every person of innovation or disbelief. The interpretation of zaygh as inclination away from guidance was given by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Mas'ud, a group of the Companions, Mujahid, and others.

﴿What is allegorical of it﴾ is the same as what was described just before as "mutashabihat." Qatada, commenting on His words ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, said: if they are not the Harurites and the kinds of Kharijites, then I do not know who they are. 'A'isha said: "When you see those who dispute about the Qur'an, they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." Al-Tabari said: the most likely view is that the verse concerns those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) about his lifespan and the lifespan of his community, on account of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, and these were the Jews.

"Ibtigha'" (seeking) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), and its meaning is the seeking of discord (fitna). Al-Rabi' said: fitna here means polytheism (shirk). Mujahid said: fitna means doubts and confusion upon the believers.

Then He said: "seeking its interpretation." Ta'wil (interpretation) is the return of speech and its reference, and the meaning at which it stops, and it derives from "ala ya'ul," meaning to return. So the meaning is: seeking its interpretation according to their corrupt dispositions. This applies to what has a sound interpretation. If it is something not subject to interpretation but rather is left unexplained, like the discussion of the meaning of the spirit (ruh) and similar matters, then the very seeking of its interpretation is the following of what is allegorical. Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought to know the lifespan of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community.

Then He said: ﴿But no one knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾ This is in the absolute and complete sense regarding what is not subject to interpretation and to which no one has any access, such as the matter of the spirit, knowing the time of the Hour, and all the events that the Law has warned of. And it is also regarding what the scholars may interpret and what is legitimate to approach. So the meaning of the verse is: no one knows its interpretation in its completeness except Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 5–7 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. One group held that the raf' (nominative case) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" (and those firmly rooted) is by way of conjunction (ʿatf) with the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and that they are included in the knowledge of the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses) in the Book of Allah, and that they, together with their knowledge of it, "say: We believe in it..." to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas held this view and said: "I am among those who know its ta'wil (interpretation)." Mujahid said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge know its ta'wil and say: We believe in it." This was also said by al-Rabiʿ, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, and others. On this interpretation, "yaqulna" (they say) is in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial clause).

Another group held that "wa-al-rasikhuna" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject) and is separated from the preceding speech, and its khabar (predicate) is "yaqulna" (they say). According to the literal wording of the verse, the one who alone knows the mutashabih is Allah alone, and the act of those firmly rooted is their saying "We believe in it," as ʿAʾisha and Ibn ʿAbbas also said. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: Those firmly rooted do not know its ta'wil, but they say: "We believe in it." Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: You join this verse [to what precedes], but it is cut off; the knowledge of those firmly rooted ends only at their saying: ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾. Similar was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, and al-Tabari related something similar from Yunus from Ashhab from Malik ibn Anas.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
When this question is carefully considered, the disagreement over it comes close to consensus. Allah, Exalted is He, divided the verses of the Book into two categories: muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous). The muhkam is that whose meaning is evident to everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs; it requires no reflection, and nothing attaches to it that would confuse; the firmly rooted and others are equal in knowing it. The mutashabih is of varied kinds: some of it cannot be known at all, such as the reality of the Spirit and the timing of the unseen matters whose occurrence Allah has informed of, and all that is similar. Some of it can be understood in various senses and in the modes of Arabic speech, so it is interpreted and its correct interpretation is known, and whatever might be attached to it of an incorrect interpretation is removed, such as His saying concerning ʿIsa: "and a Spirit from Him," and other such cases. No one is called "firmly rooted" unless he knows a great deal of this second kind according to what has been decreed for him; otherwise, whoever knows only the muhkam is not called firmly rooted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none knows its ta'wil except Allah﴾: the pronoun refers to all the mutashabih of the Qur'an, which is of two kinds as we have mentioned. His saying "except Allah" necessarily implies, by the immediate judgment of reason, that He knows it in full and completeness, knowing both kinds entirely. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a conjunction with the Name of Allah, Exalted is He, then the meaning is their inclusion in the knowledge of ta'wil, but not in completeness; rather, their knowledge is only of the second kind of the mutashabih, and the immediate judgment of reason requires this. The speech is correct according to the eloquence of the Arabs, as you say: "None stood up to support me except so-and-so and so-and-so," where one of them has truly supported you by fighting alongside you, and the other has only helped you with words; and many examples of this kind. So the meaning is: "None knows the ta'wil of the mutashabih except Allah, and those firmly rooted, each according to his capacity and what is suitable for him." The firmly rooted are in a state of saying, regarding all of it, "We believe in it." When they attain, concerning that which is not known and cannot be conceived as distinguished from other things, that is a measure of knowledge of its ta'wil. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a nominative beginning, separated from what precedes, then calling them "firmly rooted" implies that they know more than the muhkam, which everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs equally knows; and in what would their rusukh (firm rootedness) consist, if they knew only what everyone knows? Rusukh is nothing but knowledge of the variations of speech, the sources of rulings, the placement of admonitions, and all of that is through a prepared natural disposition. So the meaning is: none knows its ta'wil in full except Allah, and the people who know from it what can be known say, regarding all of it: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord." This is the measure that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, pursued, and he is the interpreter of the Qur'an; and it should not be interpreted as implying that he knew the time of the Hour, the matter of the Spirit, or what resembles them. So the i'rab (grammatical parsing) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" admits both possibilities, and that is why Ibn ʿAbbas held both views, and the meanings in both converge by this consideration which we have set down.

As for one who says that the mutashabih is only that for which there is no way for anyone to know, then on his view it is consistent to exclude those firmly rooted from knowledge of its ta'wil; but restricting the mutashabih to this kind alone is not correct. Rather, the correct view is that of the one who said: the muhkam is that which admits only one interpretation, and the mutashabih is that which admits several interpretations. This is the course of the people of deviation, and upon this the consideration I mentioned is built. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "None knows it except Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." Ibn Masʿud recited: "and seeking its ta'wil; but its ta'wil is only with Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: "They are those whose right hand is righteous, whose tongue is truthful, and whose heart is upright." Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding﴾, meaning: none says this, believes in it, stops where it stops, and leaves off following the mutashabih, except one who possesses lubb (intellect), which is reason; and "ulu" is the plural of "dhu" (possessor of).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 5–7 (part 1 of 2):**

The words of the Most High:
﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat).﴾

This verse is an informing about Allah's knowledge of things in detail. This is an attribute that was not held by 'Isa (peace be upon him) or by any of the created beings. Then He informed of His forming of humans in the wombs of their mothers. No rational person denies this, and no one denies that 'Isa and all other humans are unable to do it. No one denies that 'Isa (peace be upon him) was among those formed in the wombs. Thus this verse is a magnification of Allah the Most High, and within it is a refutation of the Christians of Najran.

In His words ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Him﴾ there is a warning to them. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Rabi' interpreted it in this manner. In His words ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ there is a refutation of the people of nature (ahl al-tabi'a), who make nature an active agent acting independently. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained the manner of the formation in the hadith narrated by Ibn Mas'ud and others: "Indeed, when the sperm drop enters the womb, it remains a drop for forty days, then becomes a clot ('alaqa) for forty days, then a lump of flesh (mudgha) of similar duration. Then Allah sends an angel to it, and he says: 'O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed?'" The hadith is given in full with variations in its wording. In the Musnad of Ibn Sanjar there is a hadith: "Indeed Allah creates the bones of the fetus and its cartilage from the man's semen, and its flesh, its fat, and all the rest from the woman's semen."

"Sawwara" (he formed) is an intensive form (ibna mubalagha) from "sara yasuru," meaning to incline and bend toward a certain state. Since forming (taswir) is inclining something toward a state and establishing it in that state, its pattern is that of intensification. The womb (rahm) is the place where the fetus develops.

"As He wills" means in respect of height and shortness, color, soundness or defect, and other differences. "Al-'Aziz" means the Dominant, and "al-Hakim" means the one possessed of wisdom, or the one who makes judgments regarding His creatures. This is more specific to what was mentioned of forming.

"Al-Kitab" in this verse is the Qur'an by the consensus of the exegetes (al-mu'awwilin). The muhkamat are those that are detailed, clear, and whose rulings are fixed. The mutashabihat are those that require reflection and need interpretation (ta'wil, explanation of meaning). What appears in them at first glance is either a contradiction with another verse or with reason, and other kinds of ambiguity. This resemblance, for which they are described as mutashabihat, is only between them and the corrupt meanings that the people of deviation (ahl al-zaygh) and those who do not reflect deeply suppose. This is like the authentic hadith from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are ambiguous matters (mutashabihat)." That is, a thing may be unlawful in itself, yet to one who does not reflect deeply it resembles something lawful. Likewise, a verse may have a sound meaning in itself, yet to one who does not reflect deeply, or to one who deviates, it resembles another corrupt meaning, so he may use it to object against the Book of Allah. This, in my view, is the meaning of muhkam and mutashabih in this verse. Do you not see that "the Christians of Najran said to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'Do you not have in your Book that 'Isa is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Then that is enough for us.'" This is the ambiguity.

The exegetes differed in their expressions concerning the specification of the muhkam and mutashabih intended in this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: the muhkamat are His words in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ (Al-An'am 6:151) through three verses, and His words in Banu Isra'il: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:23). In my view this is an example he gave of the muhkamat. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the muhkamat are its abrogating verses (nasikh), its lawful and unlawful, and what is to be believed and acted upon; the mutashabihat are its abrogated verses (mansukh), its preceding and succeeding, its parables, its oaths, and what is to be believed but not acted upon. Ibn Mas'ud and others said: the muhkamat are the abrogating verses (al-nasikhat), and the mutashabihat are the abrogated verses (al-mansukhat). In my view this is by way of illustration, that is, muhkam is found in this and mutashabih is found in that, not that it is restricted to this kind of verse. Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak held this view. Mujahid and 'Ikrima said: the muhkamat are those containing the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever else is mutashabih, confirming one another, like His words: ﴿He leads astray thereby only the defiantly disobedient﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:26), and His words: ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ (Al-An'am 6:125). These statements and what resembles them are weakened by the fact that the people of deviation have no attachment to one type of what was mentioned to the exclusion of the others.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the muhkamat are those in which is the proof of the Lord, the protection of the servants, and the repelling of adversaries and falsehood; they admit no alteration (tasrif) or distortion (tahrif) from what they were established upon. The mutashabihat are those that admit alteration, distortion, and interpretation, through which Allah tests the servants. This is the best of the statements concerning this verse. Ibn Zayd said: the muhkam is that in which the stories of the prophets and the nations are made clear and explained to Muhammad and his community; the mutashabih is that in which the stories of those peoples, when repeated in the surahs, have wordings that resemble one another while their meanings differ, some of which are identical in wording and different in meaning, and some the reverse, such as His words "a moving snake" and "a manifest serpent," and "insert your hand" and "put your hand in."

A group of scholars, among them Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab, and what appears to be the position of al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri and others, said: the muhkamat of the verses of the Qur'an are those whose interpretation the scholars know, and whose meaning and explanation they understand; the mutashabih is that for which no one has any way to knowledge, of what Allah has kept the knowledge of to Himself apart from His creation. Some of them said: this is like the time of the Hour, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, and like the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs.

The judge Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq (may Allah be pleased with him) said:
As for the unseen matters that will come, they are among the muhkamat, because what humans know of them is limited, and what they do not know, namely the specification of the time, is also limited. As for the beginnings of surahs, they are among the mutashabih, because they are open to interpretation. For this reason the Jews followed them and wanted to derive from them the duration of the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Some of these statements that we mentioned from the scholars face objections, because the ambiguity in this verse is restricted to what the people of deviation have an attachment to, whereas some expressions of the exegetes present an ambiguity that does not give the people of deviation any attachment.

As for His words ﴿they are the foundation of the Book (umm al-kitab)﴾, its meaning is informing that they are the bulk of the Book and its core, since the muhkam in the verses of Allah is abundant, detailed, and nothing in it has been neglected. Yahya ibn Ya'mar said: this is like the saying about Makkah: "Umm al-Qura" (mother of the towns), and about Marw: "Umm Khurasan," and like the saying "Umm al-Ra's" (the crown of the head) for the gathering place of the faculties, since it is the most vital place. Al-Mahdawi and al-Naqqash said: every muhkam verse in the Book of Allah is called "umm al-kitab." This is rejected; rather, all of the muhkam is the umm al-kitab. Al-Naqqash said: this is like your saying: "All of you are against me a fierce lion," and this example is not muhkam. Ibn Zayd said: "umm al-kitab" means the totality (jima') of the Book. Al-Tabari related from Abu Fakhita that he said: "they are the umm al-kitab" is meant to refer to the openings of the surahs, since from them the Qur'an is derived: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:1), ﴿That is the Book﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:2), from it the surah of al-Baqara was derived; ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:1), ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Sustainer﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:2), from it the surah of Al 'Imran was derived. This is a statement that collapses under its own weight, confused, and its speaker did not consider the beginning of the verse, its end, and its purpose. Rather the meaning of the verse is a rebuke of the people of deviation, and the reference in it at first is to the Christians of Najran and to the Jews who were contemporaries of Muhammad (peace be upon him), since they used to object to the meanings of the Qur'an. Then it generalizes to every person of deviation after that. Allah the Most High mentioned that He sent down the Book to Muhammad as a bounty from Him and a blessing, that its muhkam and clear part, against which there is no objection, is its bulk and predominant portion, and that its mutashabih, which admits interpretation and requires understanding, is its smaller part. Then the people of deviation abandon the muhkam, in which lies their sufficiency, and follow the mutashabih, seeking discord and seeking to corrupt matters and to turn people back to their deviation. Thus blame is directed at them.

"Ukhar" is the plural of "ukhra," and it does not take nunation (la yansarif) because it is a descriptive adjective (sifa), and it has been deflected from the definite article "al-" in that it is made plural and dual. All comparative adjectives (sifat al-tafdil), when stripped of "al-," are not made dual or plural, like "afdal" (more excellent) and what follows its pattern. These attributes cannot be used to compare between two things except when they are indefinite. When the definite article enters upon them, the meaning of comparison between two things disappears. The deflection of "ukhar" from the definite article does not affect definiteness, as is the case with the deflection of "sahar" (in the sense of "at dawn," "sahar" with the definite article omitted). Rather "ukhar" is indefinite. As for "sahar," it was deflected in that the definite article was removed while it remained definite, as in the saying: "I came on Friday at dawn (sahar)." Al-Mahdawi confused this issue and corrupted the words of Sibawayh, so consider it carefully.

**

The words of the Most High:
﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But no one knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

His words ﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)﴾ encompass every group of disbelievers, heretics, ignorant people, and possessors of innovation (bid'a). Zaygh means inclination, and from it comes "the sun declined (zaghat al-shams)" and "the eyes swerved (zaghat al-absar)." The reference of the verse at that time was to the Christians of Najran, because of their challenging the Qur'an concerning the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), as al-Rabi' said, and to the Jews. Then it extends to every person of innovation or disbelief. The interpretation of zaygh as inclination away from guidance was given by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Mas'ud, a group of the Companions, Mujahid, and others.

﴿What is allegorical of it﴾ is the same as what was described just before as "mutashabihat." Qatada, commenting on His words ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, said: if they are not the Harurites and the kinds of Kharijites, then I do not know who they are. 'A'isha said: "When you see those who dispute about the Qur'an, they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." Al-Tabari said: the most likely view is that the verse concerns those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) about his lifespan and the lifespan of his community, on account of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, and these were the Jews.

"Ibtigha'" (seeking) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), and its meaning is the seeking of discord (fitna). Al-Rabi' said: fitna here means polytheism (shirk). Mujahid said: fitna means doubts and confusion upon the believers.

Then He said: "seeking its interpretation." Ta'wil (interpretation) is the return of speech and its reference, and the meaning at which it stops, and it derives from "ala ya'ul," meaning to return. So the meaning is: seeking its interpretation according to their corrupt dispositions. This applies to what has a sound interpretation. If it is something not subject to interpretation but rather is left unexplained, like the discussion of the meaning of the spirit (ruh) and similar matters, then the very seeking of its interpretation is the following of what is allegorical. Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought to know the lifespan of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community.

Then He said: ﴿But no one knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾ This is in the absolute and complete sense regarding what is not subject to interpretation and to which no one has any access, such as the matter of the spirit, knowing the time of the Hour, and all the events that the Law has warned of. And it is also regarding what the scholars may interpret and what is legitimate to approach. So the meaning of the verse is: no one knows its interpretation in its completeness except Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 5–7 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. One group held that the raf' (nominative case) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" (and those firmly rooted) is by way of conjunction (ʿatf) with the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and that they are included in the knowledge of the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses) in the Book of Allah, and that they, together with their knowledge of it, "say: We believe in it..." to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas held this view and said: "I am among those who know its ta'wil (interpretation)." Mujahid said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge know its ta'wil and say: We believe in it." This was also said by al-Rabiʿ, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, and others. On this interpretation, "yaqulna" (they say) is in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial clause).

Another group held that "wa-al-rasikhuna" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject) and is separated from the preceding speech, and its khabar (predicate) is "yaqulna" (they say). According to the literal wording of the verse, the one who alone knows the mutashabih is Allah alone, and the act of those firmly rooted is their saying "We believe in it," as ʿAʾisha and Ibn ʿAbbas also said. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: Those firmly rooted do not know its ta'wil, but they say: "We believe in it." Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: You join this verse [to what precedes], but it is cut off; the knowledge of those firmly rooted ends only at their saying: ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾. Similar was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, and al-Tabari related something similar from Yunus from Ashhab from Malik ibn Anas.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
When this question is carefully considered, the disagreement over it comes close to consensus. Allah, Exalted is He, divided the verses of the Book into two categories: muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous). The muhkam is that whose meaning is evident to everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs; it requires no reflection, and nothing attaches to it that would confuse; the firmly rooted and others are equal in knowing it. The mutashabih is of varied kinds: some of it cannot be known at all, such as the reality of the Spirit and the timing of the unseen matters whose occurrence Allah has informed of, and all that is similar. Some of it can be understood in various senses and in the modes of Arabic speech, so it is interpreted and its correct interpretation is known, and whatever might be attached to it of an incorrect interpretation is removed, such as His saying concerning ʿIsa: "and a Spirit from Him," and other such cases. No one is called "firmly rooted" unless he knows a great deal of this second kind according to what has been decreed for him; otherwise, whoever knows only the muhkam is not called firmly rooted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none knows its ta'wil except Allah﴾: the pronoun refers to all the mutashabih of the Qur'an, which is of two kinds as we have mentioned. His saying "except Allah" necessarily implies, by the immediate judgment of reason, that He knows it in full and completeness, knowing both kinds entirely. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a conjunction with the Name of Allah, Exalted is He, then the meaning is their inclusion in the knowledge of ta'wil, but not in completeness; rather, their knowledge is only of the second kind of the mutashabih, and the immediate judgment of reason requires this. The speech is correct according to the eloquence of the Arabs, as you say: "None stood up to support me except so-and-so and so-and-so," where one of them has truly supported you by fighting alongside you, and the other has only helped you with words; and many examples of this kind. So the meaning is: "None knows the ta'wil of the mutashabih except Allah, and those firmly rooted, each according to his capacity and what is suitable for him." The firmly rooted are in a state of saying, regarding all of it, "We believe in it." When they attain, concerning that which is not known and cannot be conceived as distinguished from other things, that is a measure of knowledge of its ta'wil. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a nominative beginning, separated from what precedes, then calling them "firmly rooted" implies that they know more than the muhkam, which everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs equally knows; and in what would their rusukh (firm rootedness) consist, if they knew only what everyone knows? Rusukh is nothing but knowledge of the variations of speech, the sources of rulings, the placement of admonitions, and all of that is through a prepared natural disposition. So the meaning is: none knows its ta'wil in full except Allah, and the people who know from it what can be known say, regarding all of it: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord." This is the measure that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, pursued, and he is the interpreter of the Qur'an; and it should not be interpreted as implying that he knew the time of the Hour, the matter of the Spirit, or what resembles them. So the i'rab (grammatical parsing) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" admits both possibilities, and that is why Ibn ʿAbbas held both views, and the meanings in both converge by this consideration which we have set down.

As for one who says that the mutashabih is only that for which there is no way for anyone to know, then on his view it is consistent to exclude those firmly rooted from knowledge of its ta'wil; but restricting the mutashabih to this kind alone is not correct. Rather, the correct view is that of the one who said: the muhkam is that which admits only one interpretation, and the mutashabih is that which admits several interpretations. This is the course of the people of deviation, and upon this the consideration I mentioned is built. As for the scholars of sound judgment who said that the firmly rooted do not know the ta'wil of the mutashabih, they meant only this kind, fearing that someone might think Allah described the firmly rooted as having complete knowledge of ta'wil. Likewise al-Zajjaj went to the view that the reference in "what is mutashabih of it" is to the time of resurrection, which he denied, and he explained the rest of the verse accordingly; this too is a restriction for which there is no evidence. As for one who says that the mutashabih is the abrogated (mansukh), then on his view it is consistent to include those firmly rooted in knowledge of ta'wil; but restricting the mutashabih to this kind is not correct. Ibn Fawrak preferred that the firmly rooted know the ta'wil, and expounded at length on this.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "None knows it except Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." Ibn Masʿud recited: "and seeking its ta'wil; but its ta'wil is only with Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." Rusukh (firm rootedness) means steadfastness in a thing, and its original sense in physical things is that a mountain or a tree takes firm root in the earth. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: "They are those whose right hand is righteous, whose tongue is truthful, and whose heart is upright." His saying: ﴿all is from our Lord﴾ contains a pronoun referring to the Book of Allah, its muhkam and its mutashabih, and the implied meaning is: "all of it is from our Lord," and the pronoun is omitted because the word "kull" (all) indicates it, since it is a word that requires an annexed noun.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding﴾, meaning: none says this, believes in it, stops where it stops, and leaves off following the mutashabih, except one who possesses lubb (intellect), which is reason; and "ulu" is the plural of "dhu" (possessor of).
