Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: the muhkamat are those in which is the proof of the Lord, the protection of the servants, and the repelling of adversaries and falsehood; they admit no alteration (tasrif) or distortion (tahrif) from what they were established upon. The mutashabihat are those that admit alteration, distortion, and interpretation, through which Allah tests the servants. This is the best of the statements concerning this verse. Ibn Zayd said: the muhkam is that in which the stories of the prophets and the nations are made clear and explained to Muhammad and his community; the mutashabih is that in which the stories of those peoples, when repeated in the surahs, have wordings that resemble one another while their meanings differ, some of which are identical in wording and different in meaning, and some the reverse, such as His words "a moving snake" and "a manifest serpent," and "insert your hand" and "put your hand in."

A group of scholars, among them Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab, and what appears to be the position of al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri and others, said: the muhkamat of the verses of the Qur'an are those whose interpretation the scholars know, and whose meaning and explanation they understand; the mutashabih is that for which no one has any way to knowledge, of what Allah has kept the knowledge of to Himself apart from His creation. Some of them said: this is like the time of the Hour, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, and like the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs.

The judge Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq (may Allah be pleased with him) said:
As for the unseen matters that will come, they are among the muhkamat, because what humans know of them is limited, and what they do not know, namely the specification of the time, is also limited. As for the beginnings of surahs, they are among the mutashabih, because they are open to interpretation. For this reason the Jews followed them and wanted to derive from them the duration of the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Some of these statements that we mentioned from the scholars face objections, because the ambiguity in this verse is restricted to what the people of deviation have an attachment to, whereas some expressions of the exegetes present an ambiguity that does not give the people of deviation any attachment.

As for His words ﴿they are the foundation of the Book (umm al-kitab)﴾, its meaning is informing that they are the bulk of the Book and its core, since the muhkam in the verses of Allah is abundant, detailed, and nothing in it has been neglected. Yahya ibn Ya'mar said: this is like the saying about Makkah: "Umm al-Qura" (mother of the towns), and about Marw: "Umm Khurasan," and like the saying "Umm al-Ra's" (the crown of the head) for the gathering place of the faculties, since it is the most vital place. Al-Mahdawi and al-Naqqash said: every muhkam verse in the Book of Allah is called "umm al-kitab." This is rejected; rather, all of the muhkam is the umm al-kitab. Al-Naqqash said: this is like your saying: "All of you are against me a fierce lion," and this example is not muhkam. Ibn Zayd said: "umm al-kitab" means the totality (jima') of the Book. Al-Tabari related from Abu Fakhita that he said: "they are the umm al-kitab" is meant to refer to the openings of the surahs, since from them the Qur'an is derived: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:1), ﴿That is the Book﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:2), from it the surah of al-Baqara was derived; ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:1), ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Sustainer﴾ (Al-'Imran 3:2), from it the surah of Al 'Imran was derived. This is a statement that collapses under its own weight, confused, and its speaker did not consider the beginning of the verse, its end, and its purpose. Rather the meaning of the verse is a rebuke of the people of deviation, and the reference in it at first is to the Christians of Najran and to the Jews who were contemporaries of Muhammad (peace be upon him), since they used to object to the meanings of the Qur'an. Then it generalizes to every person of deviation after that. Allah the Most High mentioned that He sent down the Book to Muhammad as a bounty from Him and a blessing, that its muhkam and clear part, against which there is no objection, is its bulk and predominant portion, and that its mutashabih, which admits interpretation and requires understanding, is its smaller part. Then the people of deviation abandon the muhkam, in which lies their sufficiency, and follow the mutashabih, seeking discord and seeking to corrupt matters and to turn people back to their deviation. Thus blame is directed at them.

"Ukhar" is the plural of "ukhra," and it does not take nunation (la yansarif) because it is a descriptive adjective (sifa), and it has been deflected from the definite article "al-" in that it is made plural and dual. All comparative adjectives (sifat al-tafdil), when stripped of "al-," are not made dual or plural, like "afdal" (more excellent) and what follows its pattern. These attributes cannot be used to compare between two things except when they are indefinite. When the definite article enters upon them, the meaning of comparison between two things disappears. The deflection of "ukhar" from the definite article does not affect definiteness, as is the case with the deflection of "sahar" (in the sense of "at dawn," "sahar" with the definite article omitted). Rather "ukhar" is indefinite. As for "sahar," it was deflected in that the definite article was removed while it remained definite, as in the saying: "I came on Friday at dawn (sahar)." Al-Mahdawi confused this issue and corrupted the words of Sibawayh, so consider it carefully.

**

The words of the Most High:
﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But no one knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

His words ﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)﴾ encompass every group of disbelievers, heretics, ignorant people, and possessors of innovation (bid'a). Zaygh means inclination, and from it comes "the sun declined (zaghat al-shams)" and "the eyes swerved (zaghat al-absar)." The reference of the verse at that time was to the Christians of Najran, because of their challenging the Qur'an concerning the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), as al-Rabi' said, and to the Jews. Then it extends to every person of innovation or disbelief. The interpretation of zaygh as inclination away from guidance was given by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Mas'ud, a group of the Companions, Mujahid, and others.

﴿What is allegorical of it﴾ is the same as what was described just before as "mutashabihat." Qatada, commenting on His words ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, said: if they are not the Harurites and the kinds of Kharijites, then I do not know who they are. 'A'isha said: "When you see those who dispute about the Qur'an, they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." Al-Tabari said: the most likely view is that the verse concerns those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) about his lifespan and the lifespan of his community, on account of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, and these were the Jews.

"Ibtigha'" (seeking) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), and its meaning is the seeking of discord (fitna). Al-Rabi' said: fitna here means polytheism (shirk). Mujahid said: fitna means doubts and confusion upon the believers.

Then He said: "seeking its interpretation." Ta'wil (interpretation) is the return of speech and its reference, and the meaning at which it stops, and it derives from "ala ya'ul," meaning to return. So the meaning is: seeking its interpretation according to their corrupt dispositions. This applies to what has a sound interpretation. If it is something not subject to interpretation but rather is left unexplained, like the discussion of the meaning of the spirit (ruh) and similar matters, then the very seeking of its interpretation is the following of what is allegorical. Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought to know the lifespan of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community.

Then He said: ﴿But no one knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾ This is in the absolute and complete sense regarding what is not subject to interpretation and to which no one has any access, such as the matter of the spirit, knowing the time of the Hour, and all the events that the Law has warned of. And it is also regarding what the scholars may interpret and what is legitimate to approach. So the meaning of the verse is: no one knows its interpretation in its completeness except Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 5–7 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. One group held that the raf' (nominative case) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" (and those firmly rooted) is by way of conjunction (ʿatf) with the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and that they are included in the knowledge of the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses) in the Book of Allah, and that they, together with their knowledge of it, "say: We believe in it..." to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas held this view and said: "I am among those who know its ta'wil (interpretation)." Mujahid said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge know its ta'wil and say: We believe in it." This was also said by al-Rabiʿ, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, and others. On this interpretation, "yaqulna" (they say) is in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial clause).

Another group held that "wa-al-rasikhuna" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject) and is separated from the preceding speech, and its khabar (predicate) is "yaqulna" (they say). According to the literal wording of the verse, the one who alone knows the mutashabih is Allah alone, and the act of those firmly rooted is their saying "We believe in it," as ʿAʾisha and Ibn ʿAbbas also said. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: Those firmly rooted do not know its ta'wil, but they say: "We believe in it." Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: You join this verse [to what precedes], but it is cut off; the knowledge of those firmly rooted ends only at their saying: ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾. Similar was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, and al-Tabari related something similar from Yunus from Ashhab from Malik ibn Anas.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
When this question is carefully considered, the disagreement over it comes close to consensus. Allah, Exalted is He, divided the verses of the Book into two categories: muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous). The muhkam is that whose meaning is evident to everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs; it requires no reflection, and nothing attaches to it that would confuse; the firmly rooted and others are equal in knowing it. The mutashabih is of varied kinds: some of it cannot be known at all, such as the reality of the Spirit and the timing of the unseen matters whose occurrence Allah has informed of, and all that is similar. Some of it can be understood in various senses and in the modes of Arabic speech, so it is interpreted and its correct interpretation is known, and whatever might be attached to it of an incorrect interpretation is removed, such as His saying concerning ʿIsa: "and a Spirit from Him," and other such cases. No one is called "firmly rooted" unless he knows a great deal of this second kind according to what has been decreed for him; otherwise, whoever knows only the muhkam is not called firmly rooted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none knows its ta'wil except Allah﴾: the pronoun refers to all the mutashabih of the Qur'an, which is of two kinds as we have mentioned. His saying "except Allah" necessarily implies, by the immediate judgment of reason, that He knows it in full and completeness, knowing both kinds entirely. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a conjunction with the Name of Allah, Exalted is He, then the meaning is their inclusion in the knowledge of ta'wil, but not in completeness; rather, their knowledge is only of the second kind of the mutashabih, and the immediate judgment of reason requires this. The speech is correct according to the eloquence of the Arabs, as you say: "None stood up to support me except so-and-so and so-and-so," where one of them has truly supported you by fighting alongside you, and the other has only helped you with words; and many examples of this kind. So the meaning is: "None knows the ta'wil of the mutashabih except Allah, and those firmly rooted, each according to his capacity and what is suitable for him." The firmly rooted are in a state of saying, regarding all of it, "We believe in it." When they attain, concerning that which is not known and cannot be conceived as distinguished from other things, that is a measure of knowledge of its ta'wil. If we make His saying "and those firmly rooted" a nominative beginning, separated from what precedes, then calling them "firmly rooted" implies that they know more than the muhkam, which everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs equally knows; and in what would their rusukh (firm rootedness) consist, if they knew only what everyone knows? Rusukh is nothing but knowledge of the variations of speech, the sources of rulings, the placement of admonitions, and all of that is through a prepared natural disposition. So the meaning is: none knows its ta'wil in full except Allah, and the people who know from it what can be known say, regarding all of it: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord." This is the measure that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, pursued, and he is the interpreter of the Qur'an; and it should not be interpreted as implying that he knew the time of the Hour, the matter of the Spirit, or what resembles them. So the i'rab (grammatical parsing) of "wa-al-rasikhuna" admits both possibilities, and that is why Ibn ʿAbbas held both views, and the meanings in both converge by this consideration which we have set down.

As for one who says that the mutashabih is only that for which there is no way for anyone to know, then on his view it is consistent to exclude those firmly rooted from knowledge of its ta'wil; but restricting the mutashabih to this kind alone is not correct. Rather, the correct view is that of the one who said: the muhkam is that which admits only one interpretation, and the mutashabih is that which admits several interpretations. This is the course of the people of deviation, and upon this the consideration I mentioned is built. As for the scholars of sound judgment who said that the firmly rooted do not know the ta'wil of the mutashabih, they meant only this kind, fearing that someone might think Allah described the firmly rooted as having complete knowledge of ta'wil. Likewise al-Zajjaj went to the view that the reference in "what is mutashabih of it" is to the time of resurrection, which he denied, and he explained the rest of the verse accordingly; this too is a restriction for which there is no evidence. As for one who says that the mutashabih is the abrogated (mansukh), then on his view it is consistent to include those firmly rooted in knowledge of ta'wil; but restricting the mutashabih to this kind is not correct. Ibn Fawrak preferred that the firmly rooted know the ta'wil, and expounded at length on this.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "None knows it except Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." Ibn Masʿud recited: "and seeking its ta'wil; but its ta'wil is only with Allah, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." Rusukh (firm rootedness) means steadfastness in a thing, and its original sense in physical things is that a mountain or a tree takes firm root in the earth. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: "They are those whose right hand is righteous, whose tongue is truthful, and whose heart is upright." His saying: ﴿all is from our Lord﴾ contains a pronoun referring to the Book of Allah, its muhkam and its mutashabih, and the implied meaning is: "all of it is from our Lord," and the pronoun is omitted because the word "kull" (all) indicates it, since it is a word that requires an annexed noun.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding﴾, meaning: none says this, believes in it, stops where it stops, and leaves off following the mutashabih, except one who possesses lubb (intellect), which is reason; and "ulu" is the plural of "dhu" (possessor of).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 8–9:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are gathering the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾

It is possible that this verse is a report about those firm in knowledge (al-Rasikhun fi al-'Ilm), that they say this together with their saying "We believe in it." It is also possible that the meaning is disconnected from what came before: when He mentioned the people of deviation and mentioned their opposite, and the difference between the two states became clear, He followed that by teaching His servants to supplicate to Him that they not be among the blameworthy group that was mentioned, namely the people of deviation (ahl al-zaygh). This verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) in their saying that Allah does not lead the servants astray. Had deviation not come from Him, it would not have been permissible to ask Him to repel what is not permissible for Him to do.

Tuzigh means: incline our hearts away from guidance and truth. Abu Waqid and al-Jarrah read "la tazigh qulubuna" (lā tazigh qulūbunā), with the verb attributed to the hearts, and this is also a plea to Allah, the Exalted. Abu al-Fath said: the apparent sense of this and similar phrasings is a plea directed to the hearts, whereas the one being asked is Allah, the Exalted. [And his saying "a plea directed to the hearts" is not sound.] The meaning of the verse according to both readings is: let there not be the like of the creation of deviation, so that the hearts themselves deviate. Al-Zajjaj said: It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: do not burden us with a heavy worship from which our hearts would deviate. This is an opinion which contains a safeguarding against Allah's creating deviation and misguidance in the heart of any of the servants.

"Min ladunka" means: from Your presence and from Your side, that is, let it be a bounty not due to any cause from us nor due to any deed. In this there is submission and self-abasement. The intended meaning is: grant us a blessing issuing from mercy, because mercy pertains to the attributes of the Essence, so gifting (hibah) cannot be conceived in relation to it.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are gathering the people﴾ is an affirmation of resurrection for the Day of Judgment. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the interpretation that the firm in knowledge knew, so they affirmed it, while it opposed those who followed what was ambiguous to them of the matter of resurrection when they denied it. Al-raybu means doubt, and the meaning is that it is in itself true, with no doubt about it; and if doubt occurs regarding it among those who deny it, that is not taken into account, since it is an error on their part.

(p-165) His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ may be a report from Him to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, and it may be a quotation from the words of those who supplicate; in that is an affirmation of an attribute of the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Mi'ad is on the pattern of mif'al from the root of promise (al-wa'd).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. And they are the fuel of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them. They denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

The aspirations of the disbelievers, who do not affirm resurrection, are directed only toward this age (al-dahr) and until the Day of Resurrection, within the adornment of the world, which is wealth and children. Allah, exalted is He, informs us in this verse that what they aspire to does not avail its possessor anything, nor does it protect him from the punishment and retribution of Allah. The "min" in His saying "min Allah" (from Allah) denotes the starting point of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The reference of the verse is to the contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ, who used to boast of their wealth and their children, and it nonetheless encompasses every disbeliever.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "lan yughniya" with the ya', according to the masculine form of the verb (ʿalā tadhkīr al-ʿalāma).

Al-wuqud with a fatha on the waw is what burns in the fire of firewood and the like, and this is also the recitation of the majority of people. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and a group other than them recited "wuqud" with a damma on the waw. This is according to the omission of a modifier, whose estimate is "fuel (hatab) of the fire's fuel (wuqud al-nar)." Al-wuqud with a damma on the waw is the verbal noun (al-masdar), from "qadat al-nar taqidu" when the fire blazes.

Al-da'b and al-da'b, with the hamza sukun and with its fatha, are the verbal noun of "da'aba yad'abu," when one persists in doing a thing and continues upon it diligently. "Da'b" is also said of habit. So the meaning in the verse is: comparing these people, in their persistence in disbelief and their continuing upon it, with those earlier ones, and the end of the verse implies a threat that these shall be struck with the like of what befell those earlier ones of punishment.

The kaf in His saying "ka-da'bi" is in the place of nominative case (raf'), the estimate being: "their custom is like the custom of..." It is also valid that the kaf is in the place of accusative case (nasb). Al-Farra' said: it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "disbelief like the custom of..." so the governing element in it is "kafaru." Al-Zajjaj rejected this view on the ground that the kaf lies outside the relative clause, so what is in the relative clause cannot govern it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid that a verb estimated from the root of "wuqud" governs it, and the comparison is in the very act of burning. This meaning is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh an evil punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45] ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. The first view is the most preferred of the views: that the kaf is in the place of nominative case, and the ha' in "qablihim" refers to the people of Pharaoh. It is possible that it refers to the disbelieving contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His saying "bi-ayatina" may mean by the signs the recited revelations, and it may mean the placed indicators. The expressions of the exegetes differed in explaining al-da'b, and all of that returns to the meaning we have mentioned.

This meaning is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh an evil punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45] ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. The first view is the most preferred of the views: that the kaf is in the place of nominative case, and the ha' in "qablihim" refers to the people of Pharaoh. It is possible that it refers to the disbelieving contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

His saying "bi-ayatina" may mean by the signs the recited revelations, and it may mean the placed indicators. The expressions of the exegetes differed in explaining al-da'b, and all of that returns to the meaning we have mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 12–13:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting-place."﴾ ﴿There has already been a sign for you in two armies that met: one fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving, whom they saw as twice their number with their own eyes. And Allah strengthens with His help whom He wills. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have insight.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "sa-tughlabun wa-tuhsharun" with the ta' from above, and "yaruna-hum" with the ya' from below. Abban reported from 'Asim "taruna-hum" with the ta' from above. Nafi' read all three with the ta' from above, and Hamzah read all three with the ya' from below. Most scholars recited according to each of these readings. Ibn 'Abbas, Talhah ibn Musarrif and Abu Haywah read "yurawna-hum" with a ya' that is damma (vowelled with ḍamma). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read it with a ta' from above that is damma.

There is disagreement about who the disbelievers addressed by this command are. It has been said: they are all of his contemporaries among the disbelievers; he was commanded to say to them this statement, which contains a declaration of the unseen and a warning, that has been fulfilled, praise be to Allah: disbelief was overcome, and whoever died upon it went to Hell. Abu 'Ali inclined to this in al-Hujjah. Narrations abound that the intended people are the Jews of Medina. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ struck Quraysh on the day of Badr and came to Medina, he gathered the Jews in the market of Banu Qaynuqa' and said: 'O assembly of Jews, embrace Islam before there befalls you the like of what befell Quraysh.' They said: 'O Muhammad, do not let yourself deceive you that you killed a group of Quraysh who were inexperienced and did not know fighting. If you had fought us, you would have known that we are the people (the real men).' So Allah revealed this verse concerning their words." Another narration, mentioned by al-Naqqash, is: "When the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, overcame Quraysh at Badr, the Jews said: 'This is the Prophet who was sent, who is in our Book, and he is the one whose banner is never defeated.' Their temptation to the matter grew, and their leaders and devils said to them: 'Do not hasten; wait until we see his affair in another encounter.' When Uhud occurred, all of them disbelieved and remained upon their former state, and they said: 'Muhammad is not the victorious Prophet.' So the verse was revealed concerning that," meaning: say to these Jews. "They will be overcome" refers to Quraysh. This interpretation is only consistent with the reading "sa-yughlabun wa-yuhsharun" with the ya' from below. Whoever reads with the ta' from above, the meaning of the verse is: say to the disbelievers, all of them, these words. Whoever reads with the ya' from below, the meaning is: say to them a statement whose meaning is this. The reading with ta' admits the interpretation we mentioned just above, i.e., say to the Jews: Quraysh will be overcome. Abu 'Ali preferred the reading with ta' as direct address, and that "those who disbelieve" encompasses both groups, the polytheists and the Jews, and each of them has been overcome by the sword, by the jizyah and by humiliation. Al-hashr means gathering and bringing forth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾ means Hell. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Mujahid said: the meaning is "wretched is what they prepared for their own souls," so the meaning is as if: "and wretched is their deed which led them to Hell."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in two armies...﴾ The verse may be addressed to the believers, or to all the disbelievers, or to the Jews of Medina, and for each possibility some people have spoken. Whoever sees that the address is to the believers, the meaning of the verse is to firm up and encourage souls, because when he had said to the disbelievers what he was commanded, it was possible that the hypocrites and some weak believers would find this far-fetched, just as a speaker said on the day of the Trench: "Muhammad promises us the wealth of Kisra and Caesar, while we cannot feel safe for our own selves in going to relieve ourselves." And just as 'Adi ibn Hatim said when the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, informed him of the security that would come, and I said within myself: "Where are the brigands of Tayy who set the lands ablaze?"... the hadith in full. So the verse was revealed strengthening the souls of the believers and clarifying the truth of what he had reported through the actual example.

Whoever reads "taruna-hum" with the ta' from above, it is addressed to all the believers, since most of them saw that; the ha' and mim in "taruna-hum" refer to all the polytheists, and in "mithlayhim" to all the believers. Whoever reads with the ya' from below, the meaning is: the group of believers sees the group of disbelievers as twice the group of believers. Whoever holds that the address is to all disbelievers, and whoever holds that it is to the Jews, the verse for them falls within what Muhammad, upon him be peace, was commanded to say to them as an argument against them, and a clarification of the image of the threat mentioned earlier, that they will be overcome. Whoever reads "yaruna-hum" with the ya' from below, the meaning is: the group of believers sees the group of disbelievers as twice the group of believers. Whoever reads with the ta' from above, the meaning is: "if you had been present," or "if you indeed had been present." The expression is acceptable because the matter was clear in itself and certainty of it was held by every person in that era. Whoever reads with a damma on the ta' or the ya', the meaning is as if: the belief that the disbelievers were multiplied was only conjecture and supposition, not certainty, so a kind of doubt was left in the expression: "ará" with a damma on the hamzah you say of what remains for you to consider, and "arā" with a fatha on the hamzah you say of what your consideration has already verified. Abu al-Fath took this same line, and it is sound. Abu 'Ali said: the seeing in this verse is with the eyes, and for that reason it transitively takes one object, (p-169) and "mithlayhim" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the ha' and mim in "taruna-hum". People agreed that the agent of "taruna" is the believers, and the attached pronoun refers to the disbelievers, except what al-Tabari related from some people that they said: rather Allah multiplied the number of the believers in the eyes of the disbelievers until they seemed to them twice as many. Al-Tabari rejected this view, and it is rejected on several grounds. Rather, Allah made each group seem small in the eyes of the other, so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was already decreed. He made the disbelievers seem small in the eyes of the believers so that boldness would occur and the enemy would be despised. This is along with the belief and statement of the Prophet, and the belief of the people of understanding among his companions, that they were between nine hundred and a thousand; but Allah removed from them the splendour, the spread of the armies, and the grandeur of arrangement. So much so that Ibn Mas'ud said in some of what is reported from him: "I said to a man beside me: Do you see them as seventy?" He said: "I think them a hundred." Then when we took the captives, they informed us that they had been a thousand. Allah made the believers seem small in the eyes of the disbelievers so that they would be deceived and not take precautions. The narrations are widespread that the number of the disbelievers at Badr was about a thousand, more than nine hundred, and that the number of the believers was three hundred and fourteen men; it has also been said: thirteen. So the disbelievers were three times the believers. But the Banu Zuhrah returned with al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and Talib ibn Abi Talib and followers and many people returned, until there remained for the fighting those who approached twice (the number of the believers). Al-Naqqash also mentioned something similar to this. So Allah's mention of the two multiples, when He commanded them, is certain and no one has ever disputed it. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the polytheists at the battle of Badr were six hundred and twenty-six men. Al-Zajjaj and some exegetes went to the view that they were about a thousand, and Allah showed the believers only twice their number. He said: this is the minimizing in the other verse; then He gave them victory over them, while knowing that they were twice them in number, because He knew that a hundred of them would overcome two hundred of the disbelievers. (p-170) Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, transmitted from the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, that he said on the day of Badr: "The people are a thousand."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for you there is a sign﴾ means a marker, an indication and a lesson. "Fi'ah" means a group of people, so named because one turns to it (yufa'u ilayha), i.e., one returns to it in times of hardship. Al-Zajjaj said: "fi'ah" means a company, derived from "fa'tu ra'sahu bil-sayf" (I split his head with the sword), and it is said "fa'aytuhu" when I split it. There is no disagreement that the reference of these two groups is to the day of Badr.

Most people read "fi'atun tuqatilu" with "fi'atun" in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimated form being: one of them is a group. Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Humayd read "fi'atin" in the genitive by way of apposition. Some read "kafirah" in the nominative, and some put it in the genitive by way of coordination. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "fi'atan" in the accusative, and likewise "kafirah" in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: this is directed as a circumstantial state, as if he had said: they met, believing and disbelieving; and it may be directed as implying a verb such as "a'nee" (I mean) and the like. "Ra'y al-'ayn" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maṣdar). "Yu'ayyidu" means: strengthens, from "al-ayd," which is strength.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, livestock, and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of the life of this world, but with Allah is the best return.﴾

The majority of readers recited "zuyyina" (was made attractive) with the verb in the passive voice and "hubb" (love) in the nominative, as the deputy subject (naʾib al-fāʿil, the grammatical substitute for the agent). Al-Dahhak and Mujahid recited "zayyana" with the verb in the active voice and "hubba" in the accusative as the direct object. People differed over who the one who beautifies is. One group said: Allah beautified it. This is the apparent meaning of the words of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, for he said: "When this verse was revealed, I said: 'Now, O Lord, when You have beautified it for us!' Then ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 15] was revealed." Another group said: the one who beautifies is Satan. This is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, for he said: "Who beautified it? No one is more critical of it than its Creator."

(p-171) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: When it is said "Allah beautified," its meaning is by bringing into existence, by preparing it for benefit, and by creating a natural disposition (jibilla) inclined toward these things. When it is said "Satan beautified," its meaning is by whispering, deception, and making the taking of them appear good from illegitimate ways. The verse admits both kinds of beautification, and this view does not conflict with the other. On both readings, this verse is an opening exhortation to all people, and within it is a rebuke for the Jews and others contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ). Desires are blameworthy; following them is destructive and obeying them is ruinous. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The Fire is surrounded by desires, and Paradise is surrounded by things disliked." It is enough for you that the Fire is surrounded by them, so whoever falls into them reaches the Fire.

"Al-qanatir" is the plural of "qintar," which is a large bundle or sum of money. People differed in determining its exact amount. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "The qintar is one thousand two hundred ounces (ūqiyya)." Mu'adh ibn Jabal, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Abu Hurayra, Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, and a group of scholars also said this, and it is the most sound of the opinions. However, according to this view the qintar varies with the variation of the ounce's weight from region to region. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the qintar is one thousand two hundred mithqals (a unit of weight). Al-Hasan narrated this as a hadith traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him. Al-Dahhak said: in silver, it is one thousand two hundred mithqals. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the qintar of silver is twelve thousand dirhams, and of gold it is one thousand dinars. This was narrated from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak as well. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: the qintar is eighty thousand. Qatada said: the qintar is a hundred ratls (pounds) of gold or eighty thousand dirhams of silver. Al-Suddi said: the qintar is eight thousand mithqals, which is a hundred ratls. Mujahid said: the qintar is seventy thousand dinars, and this was narrated from Ibn ʿUmar. Abu Nadra said: the qintar is a bull's hide filled with gold. Ibn Sida said: this is how it is in Syriac. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the qintar is a great amount of wealth, piled one upon another. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn al-Kalbi that the qintar in the language of the Romans is a bull's hide filled with gold. Al-Naqqash said: the plural "qanatir" is three, and "muqantara" is nine, because it is a plural of a plural. This is weak reasoning and an incorrect statement. Makki related something similar from Ibn Kaysan, who said: "al-muqantara" is not less than nine. Al-Mahdawi related from him and from al-Farra': "al-muqantara" is not more than nine. All of this is arbitrary. Abu Hurayra said: the qintar is twelve thousand ounces. Makki related an opinion that the qintar is forty ounces of gold or silver, and Ibn Sida said this in al-Muhkam, and said: in the language of the Berbers the qintar is a thousand mithqals. Anas ibn Malik narrated "from the Prophet, peace be upon him, in explanation of His saying: ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], that he said: 'a thousand dinars.'" This is mentioned by al-Tabari. Al-Zajjaj related that it was said: the qintar is a ratl of gold or silver, and I think this is a mistake, and that the original statement was "a hundred ratls," and "hundred" fell out by the transmitter's error. The qintar is in fact the name of the measure by which something is weighed, just as the ratl and the rubʿ are. What reaches that weight is called "this is a qintar," meaning it equals a qintar. The Arabs say: "qantara" (he became possessed of a qintar) when a man's wealth reaches the point of being weighed by the qintar. Al-Zajjaj said: qintar is derived from tying (ʿaqd) a thing and fastening it, and the arched bridge (qantara maʿqūda) is named after it, so the qintar is a knot of wealth.

People differed about the meaning of His saying "al-muqantara." Al-Tabari said: its meaning is "doubled," as if the qanatir were three and the muqantara nine, and this view was already mentioned. Al-Rabi' said: its meaning is wealth in great quantity, one piled upon another. Al-Suddi said: the meaning of al-muqantara is what has been minted until it became dinars or dirhams. Makki said: al-muqantara is the complete (mukammala). What I say is that it points to the presence of wealth and its being ready at hand, and that is more appealing regarding it. For you say of a man rich in livestock and property: "So-and-so is the owner of qanatir of wealth," meaning if his properties were valued, what they add up to would equal qanatir. But of the owner of wealth that is present and ready, you say: "He is the owner of muqantara qanatir," meaning they have actually been accumulated in the form of qintars, so they are muqantara. This is more appealing to souls and closer to benefit and the attainment of hopes. Marwan ibn al-Hakam said: "Wealth is only what the saddlebags (ʿiyab) hold." If this is so, it makes no difference whether the wealth is minted or unminted, although minted wealth is more appealing for the reason we mentioned. But the word "muqantara" does not express this.

"Al-khayl" (horses) is, according to Abu ʿUbayda, the plural of "khāʾil," and the horse was named so because it struts (yakhtāl) in its walk. So it is like "ṭāʾir" and "ṭayr" (bird and birds). Others said it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) with no singular from its own form.

The exegetes differed about the meaning of "al-musawwama." Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abza, al-Hasan, al-Rabi', and Mujahid said: its meaning is grazing in the pastures and open ranges. One says: "the animal and the sheep grazed" (sāmat) when they went out to pasture and took their "sawm," meaning their full effort in grazing, not falling short of one state in favor of another. "Asamtuha" (I let them graze) means I left them out for that purpose. From this is the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "In grazing sheep (sāʾima al-ghanam) there is zakat." From this is also His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿in which you pasture your livestock﴾ [al-Nahl: 10]. It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "al-musawwama" means "al-mutahhama," the handsome ones. ʿIkrima said: "sawwamaha" means beauty made them marked. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "al-musawwama" means "al-muʿallama," that is, having distinguishing marks (shiyyat) of horses on their faces. Qatada also said this. Labid's verse supports this view:

"And at the dawn of Qaʿ al-Qarnatayn we came upon them, a clamour in which the marks (tasweem) gleamed among them."

As for the saying of al-Nabigha:

"With dark spears like arrows, marked (musawwamat), upon them a company like jinn."

It may mean the beautiful, handsome ones; it may mean distinguished by markings; and it may mean prepared. People have explained His saying, ﴿marked (musawwama) by your Lord﴾ [Hud: 83], with the meaning "prepared." Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, ﴿and the branded horses﴾: its meaning is "prepared for jihad."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His saying "for jihad" is not part of the explanation of the word.

"Al-anʿam" (livestock) are the four categories: camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. "Al-harth" (tilled land) here is a name for everything that is tilled, and it is a verbal noun used as a name. You say: "The man tilled (haratha) a tilling (harthan)" when he stirred the earth for the purpose of farming. So the name "harth" applies to the cultivation of grain, to gardens, and to other kinds of farming. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿when the two judged concerning the field (al-harth)﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78]. The majority of exegetes said: it was a vineyard.

"Al-mataʿ" is what is enjoyed and benefited from for a limited period of time. "Al-maʾab" is the place of return. You say: "āba al-rajul yaʾūbu" (the man returned), and from this is the poet's saying:

"...I am content with the return (al-iyab) from the spoils (ghanima)."

And another's saying:

"...when the Qarizi al-ʿAnzi returned (ābā)."

And ʿUbayd's saying:

"...and one absent by death does not return (yaʾūbu)."

The original form of "maʾab" is "maʾwab," the vowel of the waw was transferred to the hamza, and the waw became an alif, as in "maqal." So the meaning of the verse is the diminishing and belittling of the affair of this world, and encouragement toward a good return to Allah, may He be exalted, in the Hereafter.

In His saying "Beautified for people," the verse contains a lament similar to what is in the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "A woman is married for four things..." (the hadith). And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 15] is comparable to the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "So win the one with religion."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 15:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are mindful of God, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and pure spouses, and approval from God. And God is Seeing of the servants.﴾

In this verse there is consolation regarding the world and strengthening for the souls of those who abandon it. He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the world and how the adornment of its desires was established, then came the announcement of something better than that, stirring the souls and gathering them together, so that they might hear this unusual news, which is beneficial for whoever understands. "Unabbi'u" (I inform) means "ukhbiru" (I tell).

A group of people went to the view that the speech which the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say is complete at His saying, "with their Lord." On this view, "jannatun" (gardens) is in the nominative as a subject with an implied predicate, its estimation being: "that is, gardens." Others went to the view that the speech is complete at His saying, "than that," and that His saying "lilladhina" (for those) is a preceding predicate, and "jannatun" is nominative as a subject. On the first interpretation it is permissible for "jannatun" to be in the genitive as an apposition to "khayrin" (something better), but that is not permissible on the second interpretation, and both interpretations are possible.

His saying "min tahtiha" means: from beneath their trees, and their elevations from the upper chambers and the like. "Khalidina" (abiding) is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

His saying "wa-azwajun" (and spouses) is conjoined to "jannat" (gardens). It is the plural of "zawj," and it is the wife of a person; it may also be said "zawja," but it has not come in the Qur'an.

"Mutahhara" (purified), its meaning is from what is known in this world of filth, doubts, and everything that stains in creation and in character. It is possible that "azwaj" means types and kinds.

"Ridwan" is a verbal noun from "ridha" (approval). In a hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him: "When the people of Paradise have settled therein and each one of them has obtained what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human, God will say to them: Do you wish that I give you something better than this? They will say: O our Lord, what could be better than this? God, exalted is He, will say: I shall bestow upon you My approval, so I shall never be displeased with you ever." This is the wording of the hadith, and it may come with different wordings, and the meaning is close from one to another.

And in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾ there is both promise and warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 16–17:

And the Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ ﴿the patient, the truthful, the devout, the spenders, and those who seek forgiveness at the dawn hours﴾

"Alladhina" (those who) is a substitute (badal) for "alladhina ittaqaw" (those who have warded off evil). In this verse he explains the states of the God-fearing who were promised the gardens. It is possible that the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "alladhina" in this verse is nominative by severance (qat') and by omitting the subject (idmar al-ibtida'), and it would require severance and an omitted verb in "al-sabirin." The genitive case throughout all of that as a substitute is more correct. It is permissible for "alladhina" and what follows it to be in the accusative as an expression of praise (madh).

The patience (sabr) in this verse means: patience in obedience, patience in refraining from disobedience, and patience against desires. Truthfulness (sidq) means: truthfulness in words and deeds. Qunut means obedience and also supplication, and the God-fearing person is characterized by all of these. Spending (infaq) means: in the way of God and in places where reward is expected, such as maintaining ties of kinship and other things. This spending is not restricted to the obligatory zakat. Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) means: asking God, exalted is He, for forgiveness. God specified the pre-dawn hours (sahar) because of what the Prophet ﷺ explained in his saying: "Our Lord, may He be exalted and glorified, descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: Who calls upon Me, that I may respond to him? Who asks of Me, that I may give him? And he continues so until the dawn breaks."

It is narrated in the interpretation of the words of Ya'qub, peace be upon him: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you" (Qur'an 12:98), that he postponed the matter until the pre-dawn hours. Ibrahim ibn Hatib narrated from his father, who said: "I heard a man in the pre-dawn hours in a corner of the mosque saying: 'My Lord, You commanded me and I obeyed You, and this is the pre-dawn, so forgive me.' I looked and it was Ibn Mas'ud." Anas ibn Malik said: "We were commanded to seek forgiveness at the pre-dawn seventy times." Nafi' said: "Ibn 'Umar would spend the night in prayer, then say: 'O Nafi', has dawn come?' I would say: 'No.' He would return to prayer, then ask again. When I said 'Yes,' he would sit and seek forgiveness." The wording of the verse only indicates the request for forgiveness, and this is how the Companions whom we have mentioned interpreted it. Qatada said: "The intended meaning of the verse is those who pray at the pre-dawn." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The intended meaning is those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation." All of this is accompanied by seeking forgiveness.

As for sahar (pre-dawn), with a fatha or sukun on the ha': it is the last part of the night. Al-Zajjaj and others said: it is before the rising of dawn (fajr), and this is correct, because what comes after dawn belongs to the day, not to the night. Some lexicographers said: sahar is from the last third of the night until dawn. The hadith about the descent and this verse about seeking forgiveness both support this. There may come in the poetry of the Arabs something that implies that the ruling of sahar continues after dawn, such as the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Its cold of teeth is cooled by it, when the bird that sings at dawn sings."

It is said: "asḥara" and "istaḥara" when one enters the sahar. Similarly, the expression "the breeze of the sahar" applies to what comes after dawn. Likewise the saying of the poet:

"He finds the women bare-headed wailing over him... they have risen before the breaking of the pre-dawn hours."

This indicates that sahar breaks forth at the rising of dawn. However, the true meaning of sahar in these legal rulings, such as praiseworthy seeking of forgiveness, the pre-dawn meal of the fasting person, and an oath if one is made, is only from the remaining third of the night until dawn.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge, standing firm in justice. There is no god but Him, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The original meaning of *shahida* (bore witness) in the speech of the Arabs is "was present," and from it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Whoever of you is present in the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Then the word was inflected until it was said of the rendering of what its knowledge has been established in the self, in whatever manner it has been established, whether by presence or otherwise: *shahida yashhadu*. So the meaning of "Allah bore witness" is that He informed His servants of this true matter and made it clear. Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "Allah bore witness" is "Allah decreed," but this is rejected on several grounds.

All the reciters read *anna-hu la ilaha* with a fathah on the alif of *anna-hu*, and with a kasrah on the alif of *inna* in His saying *inna al-dina* ("indeed the religion"), resuming the speech. Al-Kisa'i alone read *anna al-dina* with a fathah on the alif. Abu 'Ali said: *anna* is a *badal* (substitution, i.e., apposition replacing) of the first *anna-hu*. If you wish, you may make it a *badal* of the thing from the thing, where it is the same thing, because Islam is monotheism and justice. If you wish, you may make it a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), because Islam encompasses monotheism and justice. And if you wish, you may make *inna al-dina* a substitution for *al-qist* (justice), because it is the same in meaning. Al-Tabari gave this reading the interpretation that he assumed in the speech a conjunctive *waw* that was then elided while still intended, as if he had said: "wa-inna al-dina" (and indeed the religion). This is weak.

Abdullah ibn al-Abbas read *inna-hu la ilaha illa Hu* with a kasrah on the alif of *inna-hu*, and read *anna al-dina* with a fathah on the alif. So he made *shahida* govern *anna al-dina*, and His saying *inna-hu la ilaha illa Hu* came as a beautiful parenthetical insertion within the connected speech. Al-Suddi interpreted the verse in accordance with the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, saying: Allah, His angels and the scholars bear witness: "that the religion with Allah is Islam."

Abu al-Muhallab, the paternal uncle of Muharib ibn Dithar, read *shuhada'a Allah* on the pattern of *fu'ala'* and with the idafa (genitive construction) to *al-maktuba*. Abu al-Fath said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in *al-mustaghfirin*, and it is the plural of *shahid* or the plural of *shahid* in the manner of *'alim* and *'ulama'*. It is reported from Abu al-Muhallab that he read *shuhada'u Allah* with the *shuhada'* in the nominative. It is also reported from him that he read *shuhuda Allah* on the pattern of *fu'ul*, with a damma on the fa' and the 'ayn, and *shuhada'a* in the accusative as a state. Al-Naqqash related that it was read *shuhudu Allah* with a damma on the shin and the ha', and with the idafa to *al-maktuba*, and he said: some of them put the accusative on the dal and some put the nominative on it.

The most correct of these readings is the reading of the majority, and the attribution of the witnessing to the unity (of God). His saying *wa-al-mala'ikatu wa-ulu al-'ilm* (and the angels and those of knowledge) is conjoined to the name of Allah, the Exalted. On some of what we have mentioned of the readings, His saying *wa-al-mala'ikatu wa-ulu al-'ilm* comes as a new beginning (*ibtida'*), and its predicate is elided, as if He said: *wa-al-mala'ikatu wa-ulu al-'ilm yashhadun* (the angels and those of knowledge bear witness). *Qa'iman* is in the accusative as a state (*hal*) from His name, the Exalted, in His saying *shahida Allah*, or from His saying *illa Hu*. Ibn Mas'ud read *al-qa'imu bi-al-qist* (the one standing in justice), and *al-qist* means justice.

(p-179)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 19:

(p-180) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envious animosity among themselves. And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

The disagreement of the reciters concerning the kasra of the alif in "inna" (Indeed) in ﴿inna al-dina﴾ and its fatha has already been mentioned. As for "al-din" (religion) in this verse, it means obedience and the creed (milla). The meaning is that the religion which is accepted, or beneficial, or established.

"Al-Islam" in this verse is faith and obedience. This was said by Abu al-'Aliya, and the majority of the theologians (mutakallimun) hold it. Qatada and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr expressed it as faith (iman), and their intention is that it is together with the deeds.

Islam is what Jibril (Gabriel) asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about when he came to teach the people their religion... the hadith. The Prophet's answer to him concerning faith (iman) and Islam explains this, and likewise his explanation of his saying (peace be upon him): "Islam is built upon five..." the hadith. Every believer in his Prophet who is committed to the obedience of his law falls under this description. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "Inna al-dina 'inda Allahi la-l-Islam" with the lam.

Then He, the Exalted, informed about the disagreement of the People of the Book, that it was with knowledge from them of the realities, and that it was out of envious animosity and seeking of worldly gain. This was said by Ibn 'Umar and others.

(p-181) "Those who were given the Scripture" is a term that includes the Jews and the Christians. However, al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "The intended meaning of this verse is the Jews." That is because Musa (peace be upon him), when death approached him, called seventy rabbis of the rabbis of the Children of Israel and entrusted them with the Torah, with a portion with each rabbi, and he appointed Yusha' ibn Nun as successor. When three centuries had passed, division occurred among them. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: "The intended meaning of this verse is the Christians, and it is a rebuke to the Christians of Najran."

"Baghyan" (out of envious animosity) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "alladhina." Then the Mighty and Majestic threatened the disbelievers.

The swiftness of reckoning may be understood as the swiftness of the coming of the Resurrection and the reckoning, since it is certain to occur, so everything that is coming is near. It may also be understood that the swiftness of reckoning means that Allah, the Exalted, by His encompassing knowledge of everything, does not need counting or deliberation. This was said by Mujahid.

"Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary" is not the right frame here, so I'll translate the passage as given.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, verse 20:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then if they argue with you, say: "I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me. And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered: 'Have you submitted?' If they submit, then they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, then your duty is only to convey (the message), and God is Seeing of the servants."﴾

"Ḥājjūka" is a verb of the form *fāʿalūka*, from *al-ḥujjah* (proof, argument). The pronoun in "ḥājjūka" refers to the Jews and the Christians of Najrān. The meaning is: if they dispute with you and persist in obstinacy with fabricated statements and sophistries, then rely on what you have been charged with of faith and conveying (the message), and God is your helper.

As for his saying "wajhī" (my face), it may be intended to mean purpose, as you say: "So-and-so set out in the direction (*wajh*) of such-and-such," so the meaning of the verse would be: I have made my purpose for God. It may also be that the meaning of the verse is: I have submitted my person, my self and my whole being, and I have made that for God. He expressed it by "the face" because the face is the most noble of a person's limbs and the most comprehensive of the senses. The masters among the theologians have said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 27], that it is an expression for the Essence.

"Aslamtu" in this place means "I delivered and I surrendered," and it does not mean "I entered into peace (*salm*)," because that does not take an object. His saying ﴿and whoever follows me﴾ is in the nominative position, conjoined to the pronoun in "aslamtu," and it may be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), meaning: and whoever follows me has submitted his face. Some have said: it may be in the genitive position, conjoined to the name of God, exalted is He, as if he says: I have made my purpose for God through faith in Him and obedience to Him, and for whoever follows me through guarding Him and being devoted to His teaching and companionship.

In "ittabaʿanī" you have the option of omitting the *yāʾ* and affirming it; omitting it is better, in following the orthography of the Muṣḥaf. This *nūn* is only so that the fatḥah of the verb's final radical is preserved; with the kasrah it stands in place of the *yāʾ*, especially when it is the end of a verse, for it is likened to the rhymes of poetry, as al-Aʿshā said:

*Wa-hal yamnaʿanna irtiyādī al-bilād* ∗∗∗ *min ḥadhari al-mawti an yaʾtiyan*

Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord has honored me﴾ [al-Fajr: 15]. When there is no *nūn*, affirming the *yāʾ* is better; but they have said: "Hadhā ghulāmī qad jāʾa," and they were content with the kasrah as an indication of the *yāʾ*.

"Those who were given the Book" in this place includes the Jews and the Christians by consensus. "Al-ummiyyūn" are those who do not write, and they are the Arabs in this verse. This attribution is either to *al-umm* (the mother) or to *al-ummah* (the nation), meaning as the mother is (i.e., in the state of their mothers' birth), or in the state of a person who has come out of his mother's womb, or in the state of the simple nation before learning and becoming skilled.

His saying "a-aslamtum" is a affirmation which implies a command, so said al-Ṭabarī and others, "and that is clear." Al-Zajjāj said: "a-aslamtum" is a threat, and this is good, because the meaning is: "Have you submitted or not?"

His saying ﴿then they are rightly guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137] came in the past tense, as an intensification in reporting the occurrence and attainment of guidance for them.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then your duty is only to convey﴾, some people have mentioned that it is a verse of conciliation (*muwādaʿah*), and that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword. This requires that knowledge of the date of its revelation be joined with it. But according to the apparent revelation of this verse at the time of the delegation of Najrān, the meaning is: "then your duty is only to convey," regarding what involves fighting and other things. "Al-balāgh" is a verbal noun of *balagha* with the middle radical lightened. In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and God is Seeing of the servants﴾ there is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 21–22:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who enjoin justice from among the people — give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and others said: This verse concerns the Jews and the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It encompasses everyone who is in this condition. The verse is a rebuke to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the evil deeds of their forebears, and for their own persistence in doing what they were able to do of those same evil deeds, because they were eager to kill Muhammad, upon him be peace. It is related that the Children of Israel killed seventy prophets in a single day, and after that the vegetable market was set up. Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah narrated from the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "They killed forty-three prophets, and then a hundred and twenty of their best and their rabbis gathered to change things and to denounce, and they were all killed, all of that in a single day;" and this is the meaning of His, the Exalted, saying: (p-184) ﴿and kill those who enjoin justice﴾. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿without right﴾ is an intensification in declaring the sin, since it is possible that this would be required by a command of Allah, the Exalted, in some respect, such as honouring the Prophet or other than that. On this meaning comes the form "afal min kadha" (a comparative form), when it contains commonality, like: ahabb (more beloved), khayr (better) and afdal (more excellent) and the like, said between two things whose apparent meaning is that they share it.

The reciters of the community largely read: "wa-yaqtulūna alladhīna" (and they kill those who). Hamza and a group outside the seven read: "wa-yuqatilūna alladhīna" (and they fight those who), and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-qatilū alladhīna" (and fight those who). al-A'mash read it so, and all of them are valid, and the clearest of them is the reading of the majority.

Al-qist: justice. The good tidings of punishment came in a way that explicitly states it, and when good tidings come unrestricted, their general sense is in what is considered praiseworthy.

The fa' entered into His saying "fa-bashshirhum" (so give them tidings) because of the meaning of the conditional in "alladhī" in this context. This is like your saying: "Whoever does such-and-such, for him is such-and-such," when you intend that this comes to him only because of his doing the other thing. The verb is in its relative clause, and it is in a position where no governing particle has entered upon it that changes its meaning, such as laita and la'alla. This meaning is explicitly stated in the book of Sibawayh, in a chapter whose title is: "This is the chapter of the particles that take the place of command and prohibition, because they carry the meaning of command and prohibition."

"Ḥabiṭat" means: became void and its ruling ceased. Its voiding in this world is the persistence of blame and curse upon them (p-185), and its voiding in the Hereafter is that they become scattered dust and that they are punished for them. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi read: "ḥabaṭat" with a fatḥa on the ba', and this is a dialect. Then He negated help for them in both states.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 21–22:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who enjoin justice from among the people — give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and others said: This verse concerns the Jews and the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It encompasses everyone who is in this condition. The verse is a rebuke to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the evil deeds of their forebears, and for their own persistence in doing what they were able to do of those same evil deeds, because they were eager to kill Muhammad, upon him be peace. It is related that the Children of Israel killed seventy prophets in a single day, and after that the vegetable market was set up. Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah narrated from the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "They killed forty-three prophets, and then a hundred and twenty of their best and their rabbis gathered to change things and to denounce, and they were all killed, all of that in a single day;" and this is the meaning of His, the Exalted, saying: (p-184) ﴿and kill those who enjoin justice﴾. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿without right﴾ is an intensification in declaring the sin, since it is possible that this would be required by a command of Allah, the Exalted, in some respect, such as honouring the Prophet or other than that. On this meaning comes the form "afal min kadha" (a comparative form), when it contains commonality, like: ahabb (more beloved), khayr (better) and afdal (more excellent) and the like, said between two things whose apparent meaning is that they share it.

The reciters of the community largely read: "wa-yaqtulūna alladhīna" (and they kill those who). Hamza and a group outside the seven read: "wa-yuqatilūna alladhīna" (and they fight those who), and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-qatilū alladhīna" (and fight those who). al-A'mash read it so, and all of them are valid, and the clearest of them is the reading of the majority.

Al-qist: justice. The good tidings of punishment came in a way that explicitly states it, and when good tidings come unrestricted, their general sense is in what is considered praiseworthy.

The fa' entered into His saying "fa-bashshirhum" (so give them tidings) because of the meaning of the conditional in "alladhī" in this context. This is like your saying: "Whoever does such-and-such, for him is such-and-such," when you intend that this comes to him only because of his doing the other thing. This meaning is explicitly stated in the book of Sibawayh, in a chapter whose title is: "This is the chapter of the particles that take the place of command and prohibition, because they carry the meaning of command and prohibition."

Its voiding in this world is the persistence of blame and curse upon them (p-185), and its voiding in the Hereafter is that they become scattered dust and that they are punished for them. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi read: "ḥabaṭat" with a fatḥa on the ba', and this is a dialect. Then He negated help for them in both states.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Book? They are invited to the Book of Allah so that it may judge between them; then a faction of them turns away, while they are averse.﴾ ﴿That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days," and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion.﴾ ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul is paid in full what it has earned, while they are not wronged?﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: This verse was revealed on the occasion when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the House of Learning (Bayt al-Madaris) upon a group of Jews and invited them to Allah. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "Upon what religion are you, O Muhammad?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am upon the creed (millah) of Ibrahim." They said: "But Ibrahim was a Jew." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to them: "Come to the Torah, for it is between us and you." They refused it, and so the verse was revealed.

al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed because a group of Jews denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to them: "Come to the Torah, for in it is my description." They refused.

So "the Book" in His saying "a portion of the Book" is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and "the Book" in His saying ﴿to the Book of Allah﴾ is the Torah. Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: "the Book" in His saying ﴿to the Book of Allah﴾ is the Qur'an; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was inviting them to it, and they would turn away. al-Tabari preferred the first opinion. (p-186) Makki said: the first "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and the second is the Torah.

The majority of reciters read "liyahkuma" with a fatha on the ya', meaning "so that the Book may judge." al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and 'Asim al-Jahdari read "liyuhkama" with a damma on the ya' and the verb in the passive voice. Allah the Exalted specified only a faction for turning away, not all of them, because among them were those who did not turn away, such as Ibn Salam and others.

His Exalted saying ﴿That is because they said﴾: the reference of "that" is to the turning away and aversion; that is, they turned away and became averse only because of their being deluded by these sayings and the fabrications they had, such as their saying, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," and other meanings of this kind. Among the statements of the Children of Israel was that the Fire would touch them only for forty days, the number of days during which they worshipped the calf; this was said by al-Rabi' and Qatada. al-Tabari related that they said: Allah promised their father Ya'qub that He would not cause any of his offspring to enter the Fire except for the fulfilment of an oath (tahillat al-qasam). In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the Jews: 'Who will be the first to enter the Fire?' They said: 'We, for a brief period, then you will succeed us in it.' He said: 'You have lied...'" The hadith in its entirety. And "yaftaruna" means: they invent and fabricate, from the reports in praise of their religion and themselves, and claim virtues for it.

Then He, the Exalted, said, addressing Muhammad and his community in the manner of questioning and wonder: How then will be the state of these who were deluded by falsehoods when they are gathered on the Day of Resurrection, and those adornments that they claimed in this world have vanished, and they are recompensed for what they earned of their disbelief and their ugly deeds? al-Naqqash said: "al-yawm" means "the time." Likewise His saying ﴿in six days﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] and ﴿in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9] and ﴿four days﴾ [Fussilat: 10] are expressions for periods of time, for days and nights are only with reference to us. The correct view regarding the Day of Resurrection is that it is a day, because before it there is a night and in it there is a sun. The lam in His saying "liyawmin" (for a day) requires an omitted element; al-Tabari said: its estimate is: "for what occurs on a day..."
