Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 26–27:

(p-187) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You honour whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things capable."﴾ ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night. You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living. And You provide for whom You will without account.﴾

Some scholars said: This verse refutes the falsehood of the Christians of Najran in their saying that 'Isa is Allah, because these attributes make clear to everyone of sound nature that 'Isa, peace be upon him, has no share in any of them. Qatada said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, asked his Lord that the kingdom of Persia and Rome be granted to his community, and so the verse was revealed concerning that." Mujahid said: The "sovereignty" in this verse is prophethood. The correct view is that He is the absolute Owner of all sovereignty in all its kinds, and the most noble sovereignty He gives is the happiness of the Hereafter. It is also narrated that the verse was revealed because the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, gave his community the good news of the conquest of the kingdom of Persia and others, and the Jews and the hypocrites said: "Far-fetched! Indeed, they lie about that."

The grammarians differed over the construction of the word "Allahumma" (O Allah), after they agreed that its *ha'* is pronounced with a *damma* (u), its *mim* is doubled and has a *fatha* (a), and that it is a vocative (munada, a called-upon noun). The evidence for this is that it is never used in the sense of a statement (khabar). The view of al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad), Sibawayh and the Basrans is that the original form was "ya Allah" (O Allah). When the word was used without the vocative particle which is "ya", they replaced the vocative particle with this doubled *mim*. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of a singular vocative noun, and two letters were dropped, so it was compensated with two letters. The view of al-Farra' and the Kufans is that the original of "Allahumma" is "ya Allah, umma", meaning "umma bi-khayr" (may He bring goodness), and that the *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of the hamza that was in "umma", which was transferred. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: It is impossible that the *damma* which is the evidence of the vocative of a singular noun be left, and that the *damma* of "umma" be placed on the name of Allah; this is a deviation (ilhad) regarding the name of Allah, the Exalted. This is an exaggeration by al-Zajjaj. He also said: This hamza which is dropped in speech, its custom is that it is sometimes pronounced, as they said "wailummihi" for "wail ummihi" (woe to his mother). The more common usage is to keep the hamza, and it was never heard at all as "ya Allah umma" in this expression. He also said: The Arabs do not say "ya Allahumma". The Kufans said: The vocative particle may indeed enter upon "Allahumma", and they cited as evidence:

(verse) "What harm is it to you that you say, whenever you glorify or utter the tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah): 'O Allahumma'?"

(verse) "Return to us our shaykh, greeted (with peace)."

They said: If the *mim* were a replacement for the vocative particle, the two would not be combined. Al-Zajjaj said: This is an anomaly whose speaker is unknown, and what is in the Book of Allah and in the whole collection of Arabic poetry cannot be abandoned for it. The Kufans said: The *mim* is only added in a light form in "fam" and "ibnam" and similar words, but a doubled *mim* is not added. The Basrans said: When two letters were dropped, two letters were given as compensation. "Malika" is in the accusative as a vocative; Sibawayh explicitly stated this in the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "O Allahumma, Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Zumar: 46]. He said: "Allahumma" is not described by an adjective, because the *mim* has been attached to it. Al-Zajjaj said: In my view "malika" is an adjective of the name of Allah, the Exalted, and likewise "fatiri al-samawati" (Originator of the heavens). Abu 'Ali said: This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas, but what Sibawayh said is more correct, because there is nothing among described nouns that is like "Allahumma", since it is a single noun to which a sound has been added, and sounds are not described, like "ghaq" and what resembles it. It seems that the ruling for a single noun is that it is not described, although they have described it in some places. So when something that is not described was added here to what was analogically not to be described, it became like a sound added to a sound, such as "hay-hala", so it is not described. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: Whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah by all of His names. Al-Hasan said: "Allahumma" is the gathering of supplication.

Allah, the Exalted, specified "the good" for mention, although everything is in His hand, because the verse has the meaning of supplication (du'a') and desire. So it is as if the meaning is: "In Your hand is the good, so increase my share of it." It was said: The intended meaning is "In Your hand is the good and the evil," and one of them was omitted because the other indicates it, as He said: ﴿It protects you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. Al-Naqqash said: "In Your hand is the good," that is, victory and spoils, and it was omitted because one of them indicates the other.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said regarding the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾... the verse: It means that what is taken from the day is added to the night, and what is taken from the night is added to the day, in a constant pattern in every season of the year. The wording of the verse may include the alternation of night and day, as if the departure of one of them is an entering into the other.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾... the verse. Al-Hasan said: Its meaning is that You bring the believer out of the disbeliever and the disbeliever out of the believer. A similar report is narrated from Salman al-Farisi. Al-Zuhri narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ entered upon one of his wives and found there a woman with a beautiful voice. He said: 'Who is this?' She said: 'One of your maternal aunts.' He said: 'My maternal aunts in this town are strangers. Which of my aunts is she?' She said: 'Khalida bint al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Glory be to the One who brings the living out of the dead.'" She was a righteous woman, and her father was a disbeliever and was one of the mockers whom the Prophet ﷺ was sufficed against, peace be upon him. According to this view, the intended meaning is the death of the heart of the disbeliever and the life of the heart of the believer, and "life" and "death" are used metaphorically.

But a large majority of the scholars held that life and death in the verse are literally life and literally death, not by metaphor. Then they differed about the examples by which they explained it. 'Ikrima said: It is the bringing out of a living hen from an egg, which is dead, and the bringing out of a dead egg from a living hen. The word "bringing out" in this example and what fits it is a term established in its customary usage.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said in explaining the verse: It is the drop of semen that comes out of a man, which is dead, while he is alive, and a man comes out of it, while it is dead. The word "bringing out" in the transformation of the drop until it becomes a man is only an expression for a change of state, as you say of a well-built child: "A strong man will come out of this." This meaning is called by Ibn Jinni "al-tajrid" (stripping), that is, the stripping of a thing from one state to another, which is an "exit". His saying, the Exalted: ("And You bring the dead out of the living") may be understood to mean that every animal causes it to die, and this is the very meaning of "tajrid". Ibn Jinni cited as evidence:

(verse) "The sons of Marwan have wrongfully spilled our blood, and in Allah, if they do not do justice, is a just judge."

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik, who said in explaining the verse: It is the grain that comes out of the ear of grain, and the ear of grain that comes out of the grain; the date-pit that comes out of the date-palm, and the date-palm that comes out of the date-pit. And the life in the date-palm and the ear of grain is a comparison.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without account﴾, it was said that its meaning is: without account from you, because He, the Exalted, does not fear that His treasuries will be diminished. This is the saying of al-Rabi' and others. It was also said: The meaning of "without account" is: "from no one to you," because He, the Exalted, has no one to repel His command. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "al-mayta" with a sukun on the ya' throughout the Qur'an. Hafs narrated from 'Asim "min al-mayyiti" with a shadda on the ya'. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-mayyiti" with a shadda on the ya' in this verse, and in His saying "to a dead land" and "to a dead land," and Hamza and al-Kisa'i lightened other than these letters. Abu 'Ali said: "Mayyit" is the original, and the waw which is the 'ayn of the root was changed to a ya' by assimilating the ya' into it; and "mayt" with light pronunciation has its 'ayn dropped, the word being made defective by deletion just as it was made defective by conversion. Deletion is good and full form is good, and "mata" (he died) and "lam yamut" (he did not die) are equivalent in usage in this category.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A group held that "mayt" with light pronunciation is used only of what has already died, while "mayyit" with a shadda is used of what has died and of what has not yet died.

The grammarians differed over the construction of the word "Allahumma" (O Allah), after they agreed that its *ha'* is pronounced with a *damma* (u), its *mim* is doubled and has a *fatha* (a), and that it is a vocative (munada, a called-upon noun). The evidence for this is that it is never used in the sense of a statement (khabar). The view of al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad), Sibawayh and the Basrans is that the original form was "ya Allah" (O Allah). When the word was used without the vocative particle which is "ya", they replaced the vocative particle with this doubled *mim*. The *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of a singular vocative noun, and two letters were dropped, so it was compensated with two letters. The view of al-Farra' and the Kufans is that the original of "Allahumma" is "ya Allah, umma", meaning "umma bi-khayr" (may He bring goodness), and that the *damma* on the *ha'* is the *damma* of the hamza that was in "umma", which was transferred. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: It is impossible that the *damma* which is the evidence of the vocative of a singular noun be left, and that the *damma* of "umma" be placed on the name of Allah; this is a deviation (ilhad) regarding the name of Allah, the Exalted. This is an exaggeration by al-Zajjaj. He also said: This hamza which is dropped in speech, its custom is that it is sometimes pronounced, as they said "wailummihi" for "wail ummihi" (woe to his mother). The more common usage is to keep the hamza, and it was never heard at all as "ya Allah umma" in this expression. He also said: The Arabs do not say "ya Allahumma". The Kufans said: The vocative particle may indeed enter upon "Allahumma", and they cited as evidence:

(verse) "What harm is it to you that you say, whenever you glorify or utter the tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah): 'O Allahumma'?"

(verse) "Return to us our shaykh, greeted (with peace)."

They said: If the *mim* were a replacement for the vocative particle, the two would not be combined. Al-Zajjaj said: This is an anomaly whose speaker is unknown, and what is in the Book of Allah and in the whole collection of Arabic poetry cannot be abandoned for it. The Kufans said: The *mim* is only added in a light form in "fam" and "ibnam" and similar words, but a doubled *mim* is not added. The Basrans said: When two letters were dropped, two letters were given as compensation. "Malika" is in the accusative as a vocative; Sibawayh explicitly stated this in the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "O Allahumma, Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Zumar: 46]. He said: "Allahumma" is not described by an adjective, because the *mim* has been attached to it. Al-Zajjaj said: In my view "malika" is an adjective of the name of Allah, the Exalted, and likewise "fatiri al-samawati" (Originator of the heavens). Abu 'Ali said: This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas, but what Sibawayh said is more correct, because there is nothing among described nouns that is like "Allahumma", since it is a single noun to which a sound has been added, and sounds are not described, like "ghaq" and what resembles it. It seems that the ruling for a single noun is that it is not described, although they have described it in some places. So when something that is not described was added here to what was analogically not to be described, it became like a sound added to a sound, such as "hay-hala", so it is not described. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: Whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah by all of His names. Al-Hasan said: "Allahumma" is the gathering of supplication.

Allah, the Exalted, specified "the good" for mention, although everything is in His hand, because the verse has the meaning of supplication (du'a') and desire. So it is as if the meaning is: "In Your hand is the good, so increase my share of it." It was said: The intended meaning is "In Your hand is the good and the evil," and one of them was omitted because the other indicates it, as He said: ﴿It protects you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. Al-Naqqash said: "In Your hand is the good," that is, victory and spoils, and it was omitted because one of them indicates the other.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said regarding the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾... the verse: It means that what is taken from the day is added to the night, and what is taken from the night is added to the day, in a constant pattern in every season of the year. The wording of the verse may include the alternation of night and day, as if the departure of one of them is an entering into the other.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾... the verse. Al-Hasan said: Its meaning is that You bring the believer out of the disbeliever and the disbeliever out of the believer. A similar report is narrated from Salman al-Farisi. Al-Zuhri narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ entered upon one of his wives and found there a woman with a beautiful voice. He said: 'Who is this?' She said: 'One of your maternal aunts.' He said: 'My maternal aunts in this town are strangers. Which of my aunts is she?' She said: 'Khalida bint al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Glory be to the One who brings the living out of the dead.'" She was a righteous woman, and her father was a disbeliever and was one of the mockers whom the Prophet ﷺ was sufficed against, peace be upon him. According to this view, the intended meaning is the death of the heart of the disbeliever and the life of the heart of the believer, and "life" and "death" are used metaphorically.

But a large majority of the scholars held that life and death in the verse are literally life and literally death, not by metaphor. Then they differed about the examples by which they explained it. 'Ikrima said: It is the bringing out of a living hen from an egg, which is dead, and the bringing out of a dead egg from a living hen. The word "bringing out" in this example and what fits it is a term established in its customary usage.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said in explaining the verse: It is the drop of semen that comes out of a man, which is dead, while he is alive, and a man comes out of it, while it is dead. The word "bringing out" in the transformation of the drop until it becomes a man is only an expression for a change of state, as you say of a well-built child: "A strong man will come out of this." This meaning is called by Ibn Jinni "al-tajrid" (stripping), that is, the stripping of a thing from one state to another, which is an "exit". His saying, the Exalted: ("And You bring the dead out of the living") may be understood to mean that every animal causes it to die, and this is the very meaning of "tajrid". Ibn Jinni cited as evidence:

(verse) "The sons of Marwan have wrongfully spilled our blood, and in Allah, if they do not do justice, is a just judge."

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik, who said in explaining the verse: It is the grain that comes out of the ear of grain, and the ear of grain that comes out of the grain; the date-pit that comes out of the date-palm, and the date-palm that comes out of the date-pit. And the life in the date-palm and the ear of grain is a comparison.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without account﴾, it was said that its meaning is: without account from you, because He, the Exalted, does not fear that His treasuries will be diminished. This is the saying of al-Rabi' and others. It was also said: The meaning of "without account" is: "from no one to you," because He, the Exalted, has no one to repel His command. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "al-mayta" with a sukun on the ya' throughout the Qur'an. Hafs narrated from 'Asim "min al-mayyiti" with a shadda on the ya'. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-mayyiti" with a shadda on the ya' in this verse, and in His saying "to a dead land" and "to a dead land," and Hamza and al-Kisa'i lightened other than these letters. Abu 'Ali said: "Mayyit" is the original, and the waw which is the 'ayn of the root was changed to a ya' by assimilating the ya' into it; and "mayt" with light pronunciation has its 'ayn dropped, the word being made defective by deletion just as it was made defective by conversion. Deletion is good and full form is good, and "mata" (he died) and "lam yamut" (he did not die) are equivalent in usage in this category.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A group held that "mayt" with light pronunciation is used only of what has already died, while "mayyit" with a shadda is used of what has died and of what has not yet died.

[p. 191] The Almighty's words:

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Whoever does that has nothing to do with God, unless you are protecting yourselves against them out of caution. God warns you about Himself, and to God is the final return.﴾

This prohibition on taking allies applies to what a person displays outwardly. As for taking someone as an ally in one's heart and intention, no believer does that. The people addressed here have already been granted faith, so the prohibition is an expression of forbidding the display of affection and inclination toward the disbelievers. The wording of the verse is general and applies to all ages.

People differed about the occasion of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ibn Abi al-Huqayq and Qays ibn Zayd had made secret alliances with a group of the Ansar in order to seduce them from their religion. Rifa'a ibn al-Mundhir ibn Zabir, 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr and Sa'd ibn Khaythama said to those men: "Avoid these Jews and beware of their secret dealings." But those men insisted on allying themselves with the Jews, so the verse was revealed concerning that. Others said: the verse was revealed concerning the story of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a and his letter to the people of Makkah. The verse is general and includes all of this. It also includes the action of Abu Lubaba, when he gestured to his throat, at the time the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to persuade the Banu Qurayza to come down. As for the torture of Ammar by the Banu al-Mughira, it was revealed regarding what the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted for Ammar: ﴿Except one who is compelled while his heart is firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106].

The Almighty's words ﴿min dun﴾ ("instead of") express that the thing to which "dun" is added is absent and set aside, having nothing to do with the first matter. In the proverb: "Wadhdham is a thing that is sour, instead of ('Ubayda)," as if it did not reach the level of the thing to which it is added. Al-Zajjaj arranged it as: the opposite of honour in something lowly. There is room for scrutiny in what he said.

His words ﴿so he has nothing to do with God﴾ mean: nothing that is pleasing to God in its completeness and correctness. This is like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever deceives us is not one of us." The sentence contains an elided noun, and its implied meaning is: "so he has no share in drawing near to God, or seeking favour with Him, and similar things."

His words "in anything" are in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, "state") of the pronoun in His words ("has nothing to do with God"). Then God permitted the outward display of taking them as allies on condition of taqiyya (protective caution, dissimulation). As for inwardly taking them as allies, it is not valid for a believer to be described by this in any state.

The majority of readers recited "tuqatan" (ﵟ ﵞ), whose original form was wuqayatun, on the pattern fu'alatun, with a dammah on the fa' and a fatḥah on the 'ayn. They changed the waw into a tā' as in tujāh and tuka'a, so it became tuqayatun. Then the yā' was changed to an alif because it was vowelled and preceded by an open vowel, so it became tuqātun. Abu 'Ali said: it may be that tuqātun, like rummāt, is a circumstantial qualifier of "tattaqū", and it is the plural of fā'il, even though fā'il was not used from it. It may also be the plural of taqiyy, with fa'īl treated as the equivalent of fā'il.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Humayd ibn Qays, Ya'qub al-Hadrami, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari and Abu Haywa read "taqiyyatan" (with a fatḥah on the tā' and a shaddah on the yā'), on the pattern fa'īlah. Al-Mufaddal related this same reading from Asim. Al-Kisa'i inclined the qāf in "tuqātan" in both places. Hamza inclined it in this verse but did not incline it in His words ﴿true piety due to Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. All the other readers pronounced the qāf with a fatḥah, except that Nafi' used to read it between the fatḥah and the kasrah.

Qatada held that the meaning of the verse, ﴿except that you protect yourselves against them out of caution﴾, concerns maintaining family ties, namely blame. So in his view the verse permits kindness to relatives among the disbelievers. The majority of commentators held that the meaning of the verse is: "except that you fear them with a fear," and this is the meaning of taqiyya. Scholars differed about taqiyya: from whom does it come? With what does it occur? And what does it permit? As for the one from whom taqiyya comes, it is every powerful, dominant person who coerces with injustice. This includes disbelievers when they dominate, unjust rulers, robbers, and people of influence in the cities. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: the husband of a woman may also coerce her.

As for what causes taqiyya and what ruling follows from it: it arises from fear of death, from fear for one's limbs, from being beaten with a whip, and from all other forms of torture. If something of this sort is done to a person, or he fears it with a firmly established fear, then he is one who is coerced and he has the ruling of taqiyya. Imprisonment is coercion, shackling is coercion, threat and warning are coercion, and hostility from influential unjust people is taqiyya. All of these depend on the condition of the one who is coerced and on the matter to which he is coerced. Many people are not affected by imprisonment as coercion. Likewise, a great man may be coerced by imprisonment and by beating that does not destroy him, to make him disbelieve. Such a person's taqiyya cannot be imagined, because of the magnitude of what is demanded of him. Matters of coercion belong to the kind that falls under the jurisprudence of the particular situation.

As for what taqiyya permits: the scholars agreed that it permits verbal statements, including disbelief and what is less than it, sale, gift and divorce, and speaking freely about all of these, as well as flattery and courteous accommodation. Ibn Mas'ud said: "No speech that averts from me two lashes from a holder of authority is something I would not say." People differed about actions. A group of scholars, among them al-Hasan, Makhul and Masruq, said: the coerced person does whatever he is compelled to do of what God has forbidden, and by that he saves himself. Masruq said: if he does not do it until he dies, he enters the Fire. Many scholars, among them Sahnun, said: rather, if he does not do it until he dies, he is rewarded, and abandoning that permitted act is better than doing it. It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said concerning a man called Nuhayt ibn al-Harith, whom the Persians had taken captive, and to whom drinking wine and eating pork were offered, and who was threatened with the Fire but did not comply, so they threw him into it: when this reached 'Umar, he said: "Was it upon Nuhayt to eat?" A large group of scholars said: taqiyya permits only verbal statements; as for actions, it does not. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak, and it was related from Sahnun. Al-Hasan, concerning a man who was told: "Prostrate to an idol, or we will kill you," said: if the idol is opposite the qiblah, he should prostrate and make his intention for God; but if it is not in the direction of the qiblah, then no, even if they kill him. Ibn Habib said: this is a good opinion.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Nothing prevents him from making his intention for God even if the idol is not in the direction of the qiblah. In the Book of God: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. And in the Shari'ah it is permitted for a traveller to perform voluntary prayer facing a direction other than the qiblah. These are the principles of the question of taqiyya. As for its many branches, they are numerous, and brevity does not call for gathering them.

His words, the Almighty: ﴿God warns you about Himself﴾... to the end of the verse, are a threat, an admonition, an exhortation and a reminder of the Hereafter. His words "Himself" ("nafsahu") stand in place of "iyyāhu" (Him). This is an address in terms of what humans commonly understand, and "self" in such a context refers to the essence. The sentence contains an elided noun, because warning is only of punishment, retribution and the like. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "God warns you of His punishment."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 29–30:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. And Allah is over all things Competent.﴾ ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between itself and that were a great distance. And Allah warns you of Himself, and Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾

The pronoun in "tukhfū" (you conceal) refers to the believers who were forbidden to take the disbelievers as allies (awliyā'). The meaning is: if you harbour eagerness to display your allegiance to them, Allah knows that and dislikes it from you. His saying, "and He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," means: in detail. His saying, "over all things Competent," is general, and "shay'" (thing) in the speech of the Arabs means that which exists.

"Yawma" (on the day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and scholars differed concerning its governing element (ʿāmil). Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: its governing element is "Competent" (qadīr). Al-Ṭabarī said: its governing element is His saying, "and to Allah is the final return" (Āl ʿImrān: 28), and this is also the view of al-Zajjāj, who further said: its governing element is (and Allah warns you of Himself on the day), and he preferred this. Makkī related: its governing element is an implied verb, its estimate being "remember the day." And "mā" means "that which."

"Muḥḍaran" (present): Qatādah said its meaning is "fully given" (muwaffaran). This is an explanation by meaning, and "ḥuḍūr" (presence) is clearer than being explained by another word.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "and what it has done of evil," "mā" may be conjoined to the first "mā," so it is in the accusative position, and "tawaddu" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). To this conjunction Al-Ṭabarī and others went. It may also be in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "tawaddu" and what follows it, as if he said: its evil deed is rejected by it, [namely] that between it and that there is a great distance.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd, "min sū' waddat" (of evil it wished), and Ibn Abī 'Abla read likewise. Upon this reading "mā" may be conditional. That is not permissible upon the reading "tawaddu," because the verb is a present tense marked with ḍamma, and the conditional requires it to be jussive, unless one estimates an elided "fa-hiya tawaddu" (then it wishes) in the speech, and that is weak.

"Amad" (distance): the specified limit of place or time. An-Nābighah said:

"... the lead of the steed when it has reached the limit (amad)"

So this is a limit in place. And aṭ-Ṭirimmāḥ said:

"Every living being completes the count of life, and is gone when its term (amad) has ended"

So this is a limit in time.

Al-Ḥasan said in explaining this verse: a person would be pleased that he never meets that deed of his at all; that is his wish. As for in this world, his sin was something he took pleasure in.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "and Allah is Kind to the servants": it may be an allusion to the warning, since His warning and alerting them to salvation is a mercy from Him to His servants. It may also be the beginning of informing them of this attribute, and its implication is reassurance, lest the threat fall too heavily upon the soul of a believer. The verse comes in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed your Lord is severe in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful," because His saying, "And Allah warns you of Himself," means: Allah is the One whose punishment is to be feared.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 31–32:

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger. But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers.﴾

The exegetes differed concerning those to whom Muhammad (ﷺ) was commanded to say this statement. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: "Some people during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Muhammad, we love our Lord.' So this verse was revealed concerning their saying," and Allah made following Muhammad a sign of His love. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say this statement to the Christians of Najran, meaning: if your saying about 'Isa and your exaggeration regarding his matter is out of love for Allah, then follow me. It is possible that the verse is general to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, because they used to claim that they love Allah and that He loves them. Do you not see that all of them said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]? The word "beloved ones" (ahibba'uhu) only indicates that Allah loves them, but He knows that their intention was "and those who love Him" (muhibbuhu), so it is fitting to say to them: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah﴾.

Al-Zuhri read "fa-ittabi'uni" with a shaddah on the nun. Abu Raja' read "yuhbibkum" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the first ba', from "habba" (to be loved), and this is a dialect. Al-Zajjaj said: "habbuba" is rare in the language, and al-Kisa'i claimed that it is a dialect that has died out, and upon it the word "mahbub" (beloved) is used.

Love (al-mahabbah) is a will accompanied by an inclination of the soul and a leaning of the belief. The bare will may concern what the one who wills dislikes, and Allah the Exalted wills the occurrence of disbelief but does not love it. The servant's love for Allah the Exalted necessarily results in obeying Him, and his actions are according to the soul's inclination. Some scholars, when they saw the Ka'bah, took the example and recited:

"This is His house, and you are one who loves Him, *** what remains of tears in the eyelids?"

The sign of Allah's love for the servant is, for the one who reflects, that he sees the servant guided, made firm, and accepted on earth. So Allah's gentleness toward the servant and His mercy to him are the fruit of His love, and by this understanding the term "love" is explained wherever it occurs in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zajjaj mentioned that Abu 'Amr read "wa-yaghfir lakum" with the idgham (assimilation) of the ra' into the lam, and he considered the readers (in error), and I think he wrongly attributed it to those who narrated it from Abu 'Amr.

Al-Tabari held that His saying: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ is addressed to the Christians of Najran, and His saying: ﴿indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾ is a threat. It is possible that this was after the declaration of fighting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 31–32:

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger. But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers.﴾

The exegetes differed concerning those to whom Muhammad (ﷺ) was commanded to say this statement. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: "Some people during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Muhammad, we love our Lord.' So this verse was revealed concerning their saying," and Allah made following Muhammad a sign of His love. Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say this statement to the Christians of Najran, meaning: if your saying about 'Isa and your exaggeration regarding his matter is out of love for Allah, then follow me. It is possible that the verse is general to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, because they used to claim that they love Allah and that He loves them. Do you not see that all of them said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]? The word "beloved ones" (ahibba'uhu) only indicates that Allah loves them, but He knows that their intention was "and those who love Him" (muhibbuhu), so it is fitting to say to them: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah﴾.

Al-Zuhri read "fa-ittabi'uni" with a shaddah on the nun. Abu Raja' read "yuhbibkum" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the first ba', from "habba" (to be loved), and this is a dialect. Al-Zajjaj said: "habbuba" is rare in the language, and al-Kisa'i claimed that it is a dialect that has died out, and upon it the word "mahbub" (beloved) is used.

Love (al-mahabbah) is a will accompanied by an inclination of the soul and a leaning of the belief. The bare will may concern what the one who wills dislikes, and Allah the Exalted wills the occurrence of disbelief but does not love it. The servant's love for Allah the Exalted necessarily results in obeying Him, and his actions are according to the soul's inclination. Some scholars, when they saw the Ka'bah, took the example and recited:

"This is His house, and you are one who loves Him, *** what remains of tears in the eyelids?"

The sign of Allah's love for the servant is, for the one who reflects, that he sees the servant guided, made firm, and accepted on earth. So Allah's gentleness toward the servant and His mercy to him are the fruit of His love, and by this understanding the term "love" is explained wherever it occurs in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zajjaj mentioned that Abu 'Amr read "wa-yaghfir lakum" with the idgham (assimilation) of the ra' into the lam, and he considered the readers (in error), and I think he wrongly attributed it to those who narrated it from Abu 'Amr.

Al-Tabari held that His saying: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ is addressed to the Christians of Najran, and His saying: ﴿indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾ is a threat. It is possible that this was after the declaration of fighting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 33–35:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of 'Imran over the worlds.﴾ ﴿Offspring, some of them from others. And Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated (to Your service). So accept it from me. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing."﴾

When a section of the disputation with the Christians of Najran, the refutation of them, and the clarification of the corruption of what they were upon had passed, this verse came, informing of the form of the matter in which they had gone astray and reporting its true nature as it was. He, exalted is He, began by mentioning His favour upon this group, from among them the family of 'Imran. Then He singled out the wife of 'Imran for mention, because the aim is to describe the story of these people, until the matter of 'Isa, peace be upon him, becomes clear and how it was.

"Istafa" (chose) means: he chose the pure (ṣafw) of the people. So these mentioned persons were that, and the disbelievers remained turbid (p-198). "Adam" is our father, peace be upon him. Allah chose him by creating him, by messengership to his offspring, by prophethood, and by direct speech, as is recorded in the ḥadīth. Al-Zajjaj related from a group that Allah chose Adam, peace be upon him, by messengership to the angels, in His saying: ﴿Inform them of their names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33]. This is weak. Noah, peace be upon him, is, according to the majority, our youngest father, and he was the first prophet sent to the disbelievers. Noah is used without the foreign form and without the definite article because the name is light, like Hud and Lut.

"And the family of Abraham" means Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him. In the language, "āl" means family and kin, and it is also said of followers and the people of obedience. From it comes "the family of Pharaoh." From it also is the saying of the poet, Arakah al-Thaqafi, in lamenting the Prophet ﷺ while consoling himself for his brother 'Amr:

"So do not weep for a dead man after a dead man whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr have buried."

He meant all the believers. The word "āl" in this verse admits both meanings. If we say that by "āl" is meant kin and lineage, then the sense is: Allah chose these over the scholars of their own time, or over the worlds generally, by having Muhammad, peace be upon him, descend from the family of Abraham. If we say that by "āl" is meant followers, then it is consistent for the community of Muhammad to enter into "āl," because they follow the creed (millah) of Abraham.

Mundhir ibn Sa'id and others held that the mention of Adam includes an indication to the believers among his offspring, and likewise the mention of Noah, peace be upon him, and that "āl" means followers. Thus the verse encompasses all believers in the world. The meaning is that Allah chose the believers over the disbelievers, and He singled out these for mention as an honour to them, and because the discourse concerns the story of some of them.

"And the family of 'Imran" also admits the same interpretation (ta'wil) as was mentioned for "the family of Abraham." 'Imran is a man from the Children of Israel, from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, according to what al-Tabari related. Makki said: he is 'Imran ibn Mathan (p-199). Qatadah said in the explanation of this verse: God, exalted is He, mentioned two righteous households and two righteous men, and He preferred them over the worlds. Muhammad was from the family of Abraham. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah chose this group with religion, prophethood, and obedience to Him.

His, exalted is He, saying: "Dhurriyyatan" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal). It was said it is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl), because the meaning of ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾ is that they are alike in religion and condition. This is more apparent than the substitution. In common usage, "dhurriyyah" applies to the offspring that descend from one below. In linguistic derivation, the word gives that it may apply to all people, meaning every person is an offspring (dhurriyyah) of another. Thus all people are offspring, some of them of others. The word "dhurriyyah" is used this way in His saying: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Yasin: 41], meaning the offspring of this species. It is not proper to say of a parent: "this is an offspring for his child." The word derives from "dharra," meaning to scatter, and its meaning comes accordingly. Likewise if we make it from "dharā," and likewise if it is made from "dhara'a," or from "dharr," which is the small ants. Abu al-Fath said: "dhurriyyah" may be derived from these four roots. Then Abu al-Fath lengthened his discussion of its pattern (wazn) on each derivation from these four letters, at a length this brevity does not require mentioning. Abu 'Ali mentioned it in al-A'raf, in the commentary on ﴿from their backs their offspring﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. Al-Zajjaj said: its origin is fu'liyyah, from "dharr," because Allah brought forth creation from the loins of Adam like ants (dharr). Abu al-Fath said: this is a nisba to "dharr," whose first letter was changed, as they said regarding the nisba to "al-Haram": "Hirmi," with a kasra on the ḥa', and other changes of the nisba. Al-Zajjaj said: it was also said that the origin of "dhurriyyatan" is "dhurrurah," with the pattern fu'lulah. When the rā's multiplied, they replaced the last one with a yā', so it became "dhurruwiyyah," then the wāw was assimilated into the yā', and it came out as "dhurriyyah."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a derivation from "dharra yadhurru," or from "dhara." If it is from "dhara'a," its pattern is fa'ilah, like "mariqah," (p-200) its origin being "dhari'ah," and then the substitution and lightening were obligatory, as they did with "al-bariyyah" according to the view of one who derives it from "bara'a Allah al-khalq," and with "kawkabun durriyyun" according to the view of one who derives it from "dara'a," because it repels darkness with its light.

Most people read "dhurriyyatan" with a ḍammah on the dhāl. Zayd ibn Thabit and al-Dahhak read "dhirriyyatan" with a kasra on the dhāl. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿some of them from others﴾ means in faith and obedience, and in Allah's bestowal of prophethood upon them.

People differed about the governing element (al-'amil) of His saying: "idh qalat" (when she said). Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar said: "idh" is superfluous, and this is a rejected view. Al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said: the governing element is a hidden verb, its estimate being "remember when." Al-Zajjaj said: the governing element is the meaning of choosing (al-istifa'), the estimate being: "and He chose the family of 'Imran when."

According to this view, 'Imran is excluded from the choosing. Al-Tabari said something whose meaning is: the governing element of "idh" is His saying "Hearing" (samī').

The name of the wife of 'Imran was Hannah daughter of Qadhudh, according to what al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn Ishaq. She is the mother of Maryam daughter of 'Imran.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated﴾ is: I have made a vow that this child in my womb be confined to the service of Your House, freed (muharraran) from every service and every occupation of worldly affairs; that is, emancipated from that. It is from the word "ḥurriyyah" (freedom), and its accusative is as a state (ḥāl). Makki said: whoever puts it in the accusative as a qualifier of an omitted object, estimating "a freed boy," there is consideration in this. The house she vowed it to is the Bayt al-Maqdis.

Ibn Ishaq said: the cause of Hannah's vow was that she had been without a child until she grew old. Then, while she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and her soul was moved toward having a child. So she called upon Allah to grant her a child, and she conceived Maryam. 'Imran died. When she knew there was a fetus (janin) in her womb, she dedicated it as a votive offering to Allah, to serve the church, without benefiting from it in anything of worldly affairs.

Mujahid said: "muharraran" means serving the church. Al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. This meaning of dedicating (taḥrīr) to churches was a custom specifically for males, and it was an obligation upon sons to undertake that. So she said: "what is in my womb," and she did not specify its maleness, because of the difficulty involved. Yet she firmly made the supplication, hoping it would be a male. The acceptance (taqabbul) of a thing and its acceptance: taking it in a manner in which taking and being pleased with it can be conceived in every condition. So the meaning of her saying "so accept it from me" is: be pleased with me in that, and make it an accepted act, rewarded for. "The Hearing" refers to her supplication, and "the Knowing" refers to her intention.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated﴾ is: I have made a vow that this child in my womb be confined to the service of Your House, freed (muharraran) from every service and every occupation of worldly affairs; that is, emancipated from that. It is from the word "ḥurriyyah" (freedom), and its accusative is as a state (ḥāl). Makki said: whoever puts it in the accusative as a qualifier of an omitted object, estimating "a freed boy," there is consideration in this. The house she vowed it to is the Bayt al-Maqdis.

Ibn Ishaq said: the cause of Hannah's vow was that she had been without a child until she grew old. Then, while she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and her soul was moved toward having a child. So she called upon Allah to grant her a child, and she conceived Maryam. 'Imran died. When she knew there was a fetus (janin) in her womb, she dedicated it as a votive offering to Allah, to serve the church, without benefiting from it in anything of worldly affairs.

Mujahid said: "muharraran" means serving the church. Al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same. This meaning of dedicating (taḥrīr) to churches was a custom specifically for males, and it was an obligation upon sons to undertake that. So she said: "what is in my womb," and she did not specify its maleness, because of the difficulty involved. Yet she firmly made the supplication, hoping it would be a male. The acceptance (taqabbul) of a thing and its acceptance: taking it in a manner in which taking and being pleased with it can be conceived in every condition. So the meaning of her saying "so accept it from me" is: be pleased with me in that, and make it an accepted act, rewarded for. "The Hearing" refers to her supplication, and "the Knowing" refers to her intention.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 36–37:

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿So when she gave birth to her, she said, "My Lord, I have given birth to a female," and Allah knew best what she had given birth to, "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan."﴾ ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth, and Zakariyya took charge of her. Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab (prayer niche), he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾

This verse is an address from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-wad' means giving birth. The pronoun in "wada'atha" is feminine, in accordance with the thing that was present, and in keeping with the word "ma" in her saying: ﴿What is in my womb﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 35]. Her saying, "My Lord, I have given birth to a female," is a statement in form, but it contains regret and grief, and Allah clarified this by His saying: ﴿And Allah knew best what she had given birth to﴾.

The majority of people read "wada'at" with a fatha on the 'ayn and a sukun on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "wada'tu" with a damma on the ta' and a sukun on the 'ayn. This also is the way her saying "My Lord, I have given birth to a female" moves from the meaning of a statement to the meaning of grief. She grieved because they did not free females for the service of the churches, and this was not permitted by them. She had hoped that what was in her womb would be a male. When she gave birth to a female, she grieved over the loss of her hope, and it frightened her that she had made a vow of something that was not permissible to vow. Ibn 'Abbas read "wada'at" with a kasra on the ta', in address from Allah to her.

Her saying, "and the male is not like the female," means: in the permissibility of vowing him (to the service of the sanctuary), because the female menstruates and is not fit for companionship with the monks. This was said by Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, 'Ikrima and others. She began with mention of what was most important to her. Otherwise the context of her story would require her to say, "The female is not like the male," placing the negation particle with the thing she possessed, from which the attributes of perfection were negated, for the intended purpose.

In her saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ there is the practice of naming children close to birth. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A child was born to me tonight, and I named him after my father Ibrahim." It has also been narrated from him (peace be upon him) that "on the seventh day, the newborn is to have an 'aqiqah (ritual sacrifice) and be named." Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Whoever's child dies before the seventh day, there is no 'aqiqah upon him, nor naming." Ibn Habib said: "It is more beloved to me that he be named, and that the miscarried fetus be named, because of what has been narrated about the hope of its intercession."

Maryam is not declined (in Arabic grammar, it is diptote) because of its foreignness, its definiteness, and its femininity. The rest of the verse is a repetition. There is a report from the Prophet (peace be upon him) through Abu Hurayra, who said: "Every child of the children of Adam is touched by a jab from Satan, and by it he cries out, except Maryam, daughter of 'Imran, and her son. For her mother said when she gave birth to her: ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan﴾. So a veil was placed between them, and Satan struck the veil." The wordings of the hadith differ through various chains, but the meaning is one, as I have mentioned.

His saying the Exalted, ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾, is an announcement to Muhammad (ﷺ) that Allah was pleased with Maryam for the service of the sanctuary, as her mother had vowed, and He made her hope for that. The meaning requires that Allah revealed to Zakariyya and whoever was there that He had accepted her, and therefore they made her as she had vowed.

His saying "with a good acceptance" is a verbal noun that came in a form other than the usual verbal noun. Similarly His saying "growth" after "anbata" (He caused to grow). His saying ﴿and caused her to grow in a good growth﴾ is an expression for a good upbringing and rapid excellence in her, in form and in character.

His saying the Exalted, ﴿and Zakariyya took charge of her﴾, means: he included her in his support and custody. The kafil (guardian, one who takes charge) is the one who raises and nurtures. Ibn Ishaq said: Zakariyya was the husband of her maternal aunt, because he and 'Imran were in-laws through two sisters. The wife of Zakariyya bore Yahya, and the wife of 'Imran bore Maryam. Al-Suddi and others said: Zakariyya was the husband of another daughter of 'Imran. This view is strengthened by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Yahya and 'Isa: "The two sons of the maternal aunt." Makki said: "He is Zakariyya ibn Adhan."

Qatada and more than one of the people of knowledge mentioned that in that time they used to compete over the one freed (for service) — who would be among those responsible for the affairs of the sanctuary — and they would draw lots for it. They did this with Maryam. It is narrated that they cast their pens, with which they used to write the Torah, into the river. It was also said: they were pens they had cut from wood like arrows and arrow-shafts. It was also said: they were their staffs, and all of these are cut. It is narrated that they cast these into the river Jordan. It is narrated that they cast them into a spring. It is narrated that the pen of Zakariyya rose up against the current, while the pens of the others went along with the water in its flow. It is narrated that the pens of the people floated upon the water laid out, as sticks do, while the pen of Zakariyya remained standing firm, as if it had been fixed in mud. So Zakariyya took charge of her, by this drawing of lots, peace be upon him.

Al-Tabari related from Ibn Ishaq that when she grew up, the Children of Israel were struck by famine. Zakariyya said to them: "I have become unable to support Maryam, so draw lots among yourselves as to who shall take charge of her." They did so, and the lot fell upon a man called Jurayj, who began to spend on her. At that time Zakariyya would enter upon her in the mihrab, with Jurayj, and find provision with her. This drawing of lots is different from the first: this one was for the purpose of assigning her, and the first was for the purpose of taking her. The implication of this report is that Zakariyya took charge of her from her childhood without drawing lots. But because her mother had died, and her father had died while she was in her mother's womb, Zakariyya took her into his own care due to her kinship with his wife. This is what Ibn Ishaq said. What the people hold to is that Zakariyya took charge of her by drawing lots, due to their competition at that time over who would take charge of the one freed (for service).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-kafalaha," with the fa' open and light, and "Zakariyya'" in the nominative, extended. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "wa-kaffalaha" with the fa' doubled, and "Zakariyya'a" in the accusative, extended, throughout the Qur'an. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read "wa-kaffalaha" with the fa' doubled and open, and "Zakariyya" shortened throughout the Qur'an. In the narration of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "wa-akfalaha Zakariyya'a," with the fa' open, by transitivity through the hamza. Mujahid read "fa-taqabbalha" with a sukun on the lam, as a supplication, "rabbaha" with a fatha on the ba' as a vocative, "anbitha" with a kasra on the ba' as a supplication, and "kaffilha" with a kasra on the fa' and doubled, as a supplication, "Zakariyya'a" in the accusative, extended. It is narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Kathir and Abu 'Abdullah al-Muzani: "wa-kafilaha," with a kasra on the fa' and light. This is a dialect; it is said: kafila yakfulu (with a damma on the 'ayn in the imperfect), and kafila (with a kasra on the 'ayn) yakfalu (with a fatha in the imperfect).

"Zakariyya": is a non-Arabic name, which may be extended or shortened. Abu 'Ali said: when it was Arabicized, it coincided with Arabic in its pattern, so it is like "al-Haypa'" which is extended and shortened. Al-Zajjaj said: as for its not being declined, it is because in the extended form it has two feminine alifs, and in the shortened form one feminine alif. Abu 'Ali said: the alif of Zakariyya is a feminine alif; it cannot be an alif of augmentation (ilhaq), because there is nothing in the roots of this pattern, nor can it be a changed letter. It is said in one dialect: "Zakariyy," declined and Arabicized. Abu 'Ali said: these two are the ya' of relation (nisba), and if they were the two that are in Zakariyya, the name would have to be undeclined because of foreignness and definiteness; but that (the feminine alif) was removed and the ya' of relation was brought in. Abu Hatim reported "Zakariyyu" without tanwin (nunation), and this is an error according to the grammarians; Makki mentioned it.

His saying the Exalted, ﴿kullama﴾ (whenever), is an adverb of time, and the governing verb of it is "wajada" (he found). The mihrab is a well-built structure, like the upper rooms and high chambers and the like. The mihrab of a palace is the most noble part of it. For this reason, the most noble part of a place of prayer, which is the place where the imam stands, is called a mihrab. A poet said:

"The lady of a mihrab, when I come to her,
I do not reach her except by climbing a ladder."

And like the saying of another:

"Like idols of ivory in the mihrabs, or like the white (flowers) in the meadow, whose blossoms shine."

His saying the Exalted, ﴿he found with her provision﴾, means: food by which she nourished herself, which he had not known and did not know how it was brought to her. She was, as al-Rabi' mentioned, under seven locked doors. Makki related that she was in an upper room that was reached by a ladder. Ibn 'Abbas said: he found with her grapes in a basket out of season. Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said the same. Al-Dahhak, Mujahid also, and Qatada said: he would find with her winter fruit in summer, and summer fruit in winter. Ibn 'Abbas said: he would find with her fruits of Paradise: summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. Al-Hasan said: he would find with her a provision from heaven that was not with other people; and if he had known that this provision was from Allah, he would not have asked her about it. Ibn Ishaq said: this entering which Allah the Exalted mentioned in His saying ﴿whenever he entered upon her﴾ is only Zakariyya's entering upon her while she was in the custody of Jurayj, at the end. That is because Jurayj used to bring her food, and Allah would make it grow and multiply. Then when Zakariyya entered upon her, he marveled at its abundance, and said: ﴿O Maryam, from where is this for you?﴾. What the people hold to is stronger than what Ibn Ishaq mentioned.

His saying "anna" means: how? and from where? Her saying ﴿It is from Allah﴾ is evidence that it was not brought by a human. Thus Zakariyya understood the meaning; otherwise he would not have been content with this answer.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is from the sign of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya: 91]. It is narrated that she never took a breast at all.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾ is an affirmation that this provision is from Allah. Al-Tabari held that this is not the saying of Maryam, but is an announcement from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah's treasuries are not diminished, so He does not reckon what goes out of them. This expression is sometimes used of the wealthy among people, that they spend without account, but that is a metaphor and a comparison. The reality is in what comes out of the treasuries of Allah the Exalted.

*Hunaka* (there) in the speech of the Arabs is a pointer to a place that is distant, or to a time. *Hunalika*, with the *lam*, is more emphatic in indicating distance. *Hunalika* is indeclinable (la yu'rab) because it is a demonstrative, so it resembles the particles that have meaning.

The meaning of this verse is that at the time when Zakariyya saw God's provision to Maryam and her standing with Him, and considered that she had come to have [a fruit of summer in winter] (or: that she had been given provision) after her mother had grown old, and that God had accepted her and made her among the righteous women, his hope was stirred to ask for a child, and his expectation grew strong. This was while he was in a state of old age, weakness of bone, and his hair had turned white with fire-like brightness. He was also fearful of his kinsmen (al-mawali) after him, as will be explained in Surat Maryam, God willing. So he called upon his Lord to grant him good offspring.

*Dhurriyya* (offspring) is a collective noun (ism jins) that applies to one or more, just as *walī* (guardian/heir) is a collective noun of the same kind. He made *ṭayyiba* (good) feminine in agreement with the word *dhurriyya*, as the poet said:

*Abūka khalīfatun waladathu ukhrā*
*wa-anta khalīfatun dhāka al-kamālu*

[Your father is a caliph whom another woman bore, and you are a caliph, that is perfection.]

And as another poet said:

*Fa-mā tazdarī min ḥayyatin jabaliyyatin*
*sukātin idhā mā ʿaḍḍa laysa bi-adradā*

[So do not scorn a mountain snake, silent when it bites, which is not toothless.]

There is a criticism of what al-Tabari said. Rather, *dhurriyya* and *walī* are collective nouns that apply to one or more, and this was indeed Zakariyya's request, peace be upon him. *Ṭayyiba* means sound in character and religion, pure. *Samī'* (Hearer) in this verse is an active participle pattern (ism fā'il).

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾. Many elements are omitted, which what has been mentioned indicates. Its implied sense is: God accepted his supplication, granted him Yahya, and sent an angel or angels with this news to him, and they called out to him. It is mentioned that between his supplication and the response of the good news there were forty years. Most of the exegetes mention that the one who called out and gave the news was Jibril alone, and this is the customary form of revelation to the prophets. Others said: rather, many angels called out, as the wording of the verse requires. We have found that God sent angels to Lut and to Ibrahim, peace be upon them, in more than one story.

In the codex (mushaf) of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud and in his recitation: "Then Jibril called out to him while he was standing in prayer." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read *fa-nādat-hu* with a *tā'* (feminine verb) followed by *al-malā'ika*. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-nādā-hu al-malā'ika*, with *alif* and imala of the *dal*. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with the *tā'* does so because of the sense of the group (al-jama'a), and a broken plural (jam' taksir) of rational beings is treated like non-rational things. Do you not see that you say *hiya al-rijāl* just as you say *hiya al-judhū'* and *hiya al-jimāl*? Similar to this is *qālati al-a'rābu* [the Bedouins said]. So Abu 'Ali interpreted the caller as many angels. The reading with *tā'* according to the view of one who says the caller was Jibril alone is directed toward the consideration of the wording "malā'ika", and he expressed Jibril with "angels" because he is one of them, so he mentioned the collective noun, as God, exalted, said: ﴿those to whom people said﴾. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads *fa-nādā-hu al-malā'ika* is like His saying: ﴿and women said in the city﴾.

[p-208] The judge (al-Qadi) said: This is on the basis that the caller was many. As for whoever says it was Jibril alone, like al-Suddi and others, he used the singular verb in consideration of the meaning, and he expressed Jibril, peace be upon him, with "angels" since it is the name of his kind.

God's saying *fa-nādat-hu* is an expression used for giving good news, and for what should be hastened and conveyed to the hearer's soul so that he may be gladdened. So this was not, from the angels, a report in the customary manner of revelation, but a call, as a man from the Ansar called Ka'b ibn Malik from the top of a mountain.

God's saying ﴿he was standing﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 33] is a clause in place of the circumstantial state (hal). *Yuṣallī* (praying) is a qualifier of *qā'im* (standing), and *al-miḥrāb* in this place is the place where the imam stands in the mosque.

Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read *innā Allāh* with a kasra on the *alif*. Abu 'Ali said: this is by implying a verb of saying, as if he said: "the angels called to him" and then "they said". This is like His saying: ﴿so he called upon his Lord: "Indeed I am overcome"﴾ according to the reading of one who kasrah the *alif*. Some grammarians said: it was given a kasra after a call and a supplication because calling and supplicating are sayings.

The rest read *anna Allāha yubashshiruka* with a fatha on the *alif*. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is: "they called to him with [the message] that God..." When the preposition was omitted, the verb reached it and governed it in the accusative, so *anna* is in the accusative position, and according to al-Khalil's analogy, in the genitive position. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "in the sanctuary, O Zakariyyā'u, indeed God..." Abu 'Ali said: *Zakariyyā'u* is in the accusative position by being the object of the call. It is not permitted to put a fatha on the *alif* of *inna* in this reading because *nādat-hu* has already completed its two objects: one is the pronoun and the other is the one called. If you put a fatha on *inna*, nothing would remain to govern it. Abu 'Ali said: all of them read *fi al-miḥrābi* with a fatha on the *rā'*, except Ibn 'Amir, who made it imala. Ibn Mujahid made a general statement about Ibn 'Amir's imala of the *alif* in *miḥrāb*, and did not restrict it to the genitive case. Other than Ibn Mujahid said: we only pronounce it with imala in the genitive case.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *yubashshiruka* with a damma on the *yā'*, a fatha on the *bā'* and shadda, in the whole Qur'an except in *ʿSq*, for in that they both read *dhālika alladhī yabshuru Allāhu ʿibādahu* with a fatha on the *yā'*, a sukun on the *bā'* and a damma on the *shīn*. Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read *yubashshiruka* with a shadda on the kasra *shīn* in the whole Qur'an. Hamza read *yabshuru* lightly with a damma on the *shīn* in the whole Qur'an, except God's saying: ﴿So with what do you give good news?﴾. Al-Kisa'i read *yabshuru* with lightness in five places: in Al 'Imran in the story of Zakariyya and the story of Maryam, in Surat Bani Isra'il and al-Kahf: *wa-yabshuru al-mu'minīn*, and in ʿSq: *yabshuru Allāhu ʿibādahu*.

Several lexicographers said: this word has three forms: *bashshara* with shadda on the *shīn*, *basara* with lightness, and *abshara yubshiru ibshāran*. All these readings are correct, eloquent and transmitted. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud: *yubshiruka*, with a damma on the *yā'* and lightness on the kasra *shīn*, from *abshara*. And he read this way in the whole Qur'an.

*Yaḥyā* is a name that God gave him before he was born. Abu 'Ali said: it is a name in Hebrew that happened to match this pattern, and its meaning is from Arabic. Al-Zajjaj said: it is not declined (la yanṣarif) because if it is foreign, it has definiteness and foreignness, and if it is Arabic, it has definiteness and the verbal pattern. Qatada said: God named him Yahya because He gave him life through faith.

*Muṣaddiqan* (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and it is emphatic according to the state of these prophets, peace be upon them.

God's saying ﴿a word from God﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others said: the "word" here means ʿĪsā son of Maryam. God called ʿĪsā a "word" because he came from a word of His, exalted, not through a human cause as is the custom of mankind. Ibn 'Abbas related that the wife of Zakariyya said to Maryam while both were pregnant: "I find that what is in my belly moves toward what is in your belly." In some reports: "prostrates to what is in your belly." He said: that is its confirmation, meaning: the first of the confirmation. Some people said: "a word from God" means: a book from God, the Gospel and other books of God. So the singular was used in the place of the plural, and *kalima* is a collective noun. On this view the Arabs called a long poem a *kalima*.

God's saying ﴿and a noble master (sayyidan)﴾: Qatada said regarding it: that is, by God, a master in forbearance, worship and piety. At another time he said: its meaning is: in knowledge and worship. Ibn Jubayr said: "sayyidan" means forbearing. At another time he said: the *sayyid* is the pious one. Al-Dahhak said: "sayyidan" means pious and forbearing. Ibn Zayd said: the *sayyid* is the noble one. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the *sayyid* is the jurist, the learned one. Ibn 'Abbas said: "sayyidan" means, he says, pious and forbearing. ʿIkrima said: the *sayyid* is the one whom anger does not overcome.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Whoever among these scholars mentioned explained *su'dud* (nobility) by forbearance, has obtained most of the meaning of nobility. Whoever restricted its explanation to knowledge and piety and the like has not explained it according to the speech of the Arabs. Knowledge was attained by Yahya, peace be upon him, through God's saying, exalted: ﴿confirming a word from God﴾, and piety was attained through the rest of the verse. God specified for him the mention of nobility, which is the effort to win the pleasure of people in the noblest ways without falling into falsehood. This is a term that encompasses nobility. Its detail is that it is said: giving generously, and this is generosity; withholding harm, and here is chastity of the private parts, hand and tongue; and bearing great burdens, and here is forbearance and other things, such as bearing debts, mending the broken, benefiting the one who seeks help, and rescuing from ruin. Note that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the master of the sons of Adam, and there is no boasting, [on the Day] when God gathers the first and the last," and he mentioned the hadith of intercession at the general standing (al-mawqif). That is from him a bearing of [the burden for] the pleasure of the sons of Adam, so he is their master by that. Among the trustworthy scholars there may be one who does not stand out in these qualities, and there may be one who stands out in these and so is called a master, even if he falls short in many obligations, meaning the obligations of recommended acts and of standing firm for the truth, and indifference to blame. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "I have never seen anyone blacker than Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan." It was said to him: "And Abu Bakr and ʿUmar?" He said: "They are better than Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya is blacker than them." [p-211] So this is an indication that Mu'awiya excelled in these qualities without committing a forbidden act; and that Abu Bakr and ʿUmar were, in their diligence in the obligations and in tracing these out in themselves and establishing the realities among the people, such that they were better than Mu'awiya. And with tracing out the realities, and guiding people to the right path, and indifference to their pleasure, and weighing by the scale of the Shari'a with precise accuracy, many of these qualities that constitute nobility are undermined and time occupies itself away from them. Piety, knowledge and taking the more stringent course are more binding and higher than nobility. As for the pious scholar, it is good for him to take from nobility whatever does not harm his knowledge and piety, and so was Yahya, peace be upon him. This is not something that is obligatory necessarily, just as tracing out and strictness in severity are not obligatory necessarily. Both are two good extremes that the Shari'a has encompassed. So some go to this and some go to that. An example of this is a stern, frowning, harsh ruler toward whoever has the slightest crookedness, who does not attend to people's needs; and another who has an open, smiling face, who attends to what is permissible, does not pursue what is not brought before him, and executes the judgment with gentleness toward the one judged against. These are two good ways.

His saying: *wa-ḥaṣūran* (and chaste). The root of this word is confinement and prevention. From it comes *ḥaṣīr* (mat), because it confines whoever sits on it. From it the prison is called *ḥaṣīr*, and Hell is called *ḥaṣīr*. From it comes *ḥaṣr al-ʿadūw* (besieging the enemy) and *iḥṣār* (being prevented by illness or excuse). From it it is said of one who does not spend with his drinking companions: *ḥaṣūr*. Al-Akhtal said:

*Wa-shāribin murbiḥin bi-al-kasi nādamanī*
*lā bi-al-ḥaṣūri wa-lā fīhā bi-sawwāri*

[And a drinker who profited by the cup kept company with me, not one who is stingy, nor one who in it is a squanderer.]

And it is said of one who keeps a secret: *ḥaṣūr* and *ḥaṣir*. Jarir said:

*Wa-laqad tasāqaṭanī al-wushātu fa-ṣādafū*
*ḥaṣiran bi-sirrika yā Umayma ḍanīnā*

[The informers have indeed hounded me, and they found me a keeper of your secret, O Umaymah, guarding it closely.]

Ibn 'Atiyya, *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*, commentary on Surah 3, verses 38–39 (part 2 of 2):

The commentators whose opinions are considered unanimously agree that this attribute of Yahya (peace be upon him) is only abstention from sexual intercourse with women. The exception is what Makki (Makki ibn Abi Talib) relates from someone who said that *al-ḥaṣūr* (one who restrains himself) means one who abstains from sins, that is, who does not commit them (p. 212). Ibn al-Musayyib narrated from Ibn al-'Ass, either 'Abdullah or his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every child of Adam will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." He said: Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his hand to the ground, took a small stick, and said: "That is because he had nothing of what men have except like this stick. For this reason God named him *sayyid* (noble leader) and *ḥaṣūr*."

Ibn Mas'ud said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is *al-'innīn* (impotent). Mujahid and Qatada said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is the one who does not have intercourse with women. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is the one who does not emit semen.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some scholars held that Yahya's (peace be upon him) being *ḥaṣūr* was because he had only something like a small hair-tuft (*hudba*). Others held that his being *ḥaṣūr* was because he was impotent, unable to have intercourse with women, although his physical make-up was not defective. Others held that his being *ḥaṣūr* was because he restrained himself, out of piety and steadfastness in obedience to God, while he had the capacity for sexual intercourse. They said: This is more praiseworthy for him, and in the first two interpretations there is no praise for him, except that God made something easy for him in which he had no personal effort. The rest of the verse is clear. It is also related of his righteousness (peace be upon him) that he used to live on plants, and that he wept much out of fear of God, to the point that tears left channels and furrows on his face.

﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, grant me from You good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication."﴾ ﴿So the angels called out to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary (al-mihrab): "Indeed, God gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from God, and a noble master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."﴾

*Hunaka* (there) in the speech of the Arabs is a pointer to a place that is distant, or to a time. *Hunalika*, with the *lam*, is more emphatic in indicating distance. *Hunalika* is indeclinable (la yu'rab) because it is a demonstrative, so it resembles the particles that have meaning.

The meaning of this verse is that at the time when Zakariyya saw God's provision to Maryam and her standing with Him, and considered that she had come to have [a fruit of summer in winter] (or: that she had been given provision) after her mother had grown old, and that God had accepted her and made her among the righteous women, his hope was stirred to ask for a child, and his expectation grew strong. This was while he was in a state of old age, weakness of bone, and his hair had turned white with fire-like brightness. He was also fearful of his kinsmen (al-mawali) after him, as will be explained in Surat Maryam, God willing. So he called upon his Lord to grant him good offspring.

*Dhurriyya* (offspring) is a collective noun (ism jins) that applies to one or more, just as *walī* (guardian/heir) is a collective noun of the same kind. Al-Tabari said that by *dhurriyya* here he meant only one person, and the proof of this is that he asked for a *walī* (singular) and did not ask for *awliya'* (plural). He made *ṭayyiba* (good) feminine in agreement with the word *dhurriyya*, as the poet said:

*Abūka khalīfatun waladathu ukhrā*
*wa-anta khalīfatun dhāka al-kamālu*

[Your father is a caliph whom another woman bore, and you are a caliph, that is perfection.]

And as another poet said:

*Fa-mā tazdarī min ḥayyatin jabaliyyatin*

Ibn Jubayr said: "sayyidan" means forbearing. At another time he said: the *sayyid* is the pious one. Al-Dahhak said: "sayyidan" means pious and forbearing.
