It was said to him: "And Abu Bakr and ʿUmar?" He said: "They are better than Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya is blacker than them." [p-211] So this is an indication that Mu'awiya excelled in these qualities without committing a forbidden act; and that Abu Bakr and ʿUmar were, in their diligence in the obligations and in tracing these out in themselves and establishing the realities among the people, such that they were better than Mu'awiya. And with tracing out the realities, and guiding people to the right path, and indifference to their pleasure, and weighing by the scale of the Shari'a with precise accuracy, many of these qualities that constitute nobility are undermined and time occupies itself away from them. Piety, knowledge and taking the more stringent course are more binding and higher than nobility. As for the pious scholar, it is good for him to take from nobility whatever does not harm his knowledge and piety, and so was Yahya, peace be upon him. This is not something that is obligatory necessarily, just as tracing out and strictness in severity are not obligatory necessarily. Both are two good extremes that the Shari'a has encompassed. So some go to this and some go to that. An example of this is a stern, frowning, harsh ruler toward whoever has the slightest crookedness, who does not attend to people's needs; and another who has an open, smiling face, who attends to what is permissible, does not pursue what is not brought before him, and executes the judgment with gentleness toward the one judged against. These are two good ways.

His saying: *wa-ḥaṣūran* (and chaste). The root of this word is confinement and prevention. From it comes *ḥaṣīr* (mat), because it confines whoever sits on it. From it the prison is called *ḥaṣīr*, and Hell is called *ḥaṣīr*. From it comes *ḥaṣr al-ʿadūw* (besieging the enemy) and *iḥṣār* (being prevented by illness or excuse). From it it is said of one who does not spend with his drinking companions: *ḥaṣūr*. Al-Akhtal said:

*Wa-shāribin murbiḥin bi-al-kasi nādamanī*
*lā bi-al-ḥaṣūri wa-lā fīhā bi-sawwāri*

[And a drinker who profited by the cup kept company with me, not one who is stingy, nor one who in it is a squanderer.]

And it is said of one who keeps a secret: *ḥaṣūr* and *ḥaṣir*. Jarir said:

*Wa-laqad tasāqaṭanī al-wushātu fa-ṣādafū*
*ḥaṣiran bi-sirrika yā Umayma ḍanīnā*

[The informers have indeed hounded me, and they found me a keeper of your secret, O Umaymah, guarding it closely.]

Ibn 'Atiyya, *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*, commentary on Surah 3, verses 38–39 (part 2 of 2):

The commentators whose opinions are considered unanimously agree that this attribute of Yahya (peace be upon him) is only abstention from sexual intercourse with women. The exception is what Makki (Makki ibn Abi Talib) relates from someone who said that *al-ḥaṣūr* (one who restrains himself) means one who abstains from sins, that is, who does not commit them (p. 212). Ibn al-Musayyib narrated from Ibn al-'Ass, either 'Abdullah or his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every child of Adam will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." He said: Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his hand to the ground, took a small stick, and said: "That is because he had nothing of what men have except like this stick. For this reason God named him *sayyid* (noble leader) and *ḥaṣūr*."

Ibn Mas'ud said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is *al-'innīn* (impotent). Mujahid and Qatada said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is the one who does not have intercourse with women. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: *al-ḥaṣūr* is the one who does not emit semen.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some scholars held that Yahya's (peace be upon him) being *ḥaṣūr* was because he had only something like a small hair-tuft (*hudba*). Others held that his being *ḥaṣūr* was because he was impotent, unable to have intercourse with women, although his physical make-up was not defective. Others held that his being *ḥaṣūr* was because he restrained himself, out of piety and steadfastness in obedience to God, while he had the capacity for sexual intercourse. They said: This is more praiseworthy for him, and in the first two interpretations there is no praise for him, except that God made something easy for him in which he had no personal effort. The rest of the verse is clear. It is also related of his righteousness (peace be upon him) that he used to live on plants, and that he wept much out of fear of God, to the point that tears left channels and furrows on his face.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 40:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when old age has already overtaken me and my wife is barren?" He said, "Thus does Allah do what He wills."﴾

The exegetes differed as to why Zakariyya said, ﴿My Lord, how will I have a boy?﴾ 'Ikrima and al-Suddi said: he was called to this glad tidings, but Satan came to cloud over for him the blessing of his Lord, and said: "Do you know who called you?" He said: "The angels of my Lord called me." He said: "No, it was that Satan. Had this been from your Lord, He would have concealed it from you, just as you concealed your calling." So a whisper entered his heart and doubt took its place, and he said: ﴿How will I have a boy?﴾

al-Tabari and others went to the view that when Zakariyya saw the state of himself and the state of his wife, and that she was not in a condition for offspring, he asked about the manner in which the boy would come to be: would the woman's createdness be changed, or how would it happen?

This is a good interpretation, fitting for Zakariyya, peace be upon him. Makki said: it was also said that he only asked because he had forgotten his supplication, owing to the long period between the supplication and the glad tidings, which was forty years. This is a view weak in meaning.

"Anna" means: how? and from where? His saying ﴿old age has already overtaken me﴾ is a metaphor: as if time is a road and events follow one another along it; when two events meet, each of them has reached the other. The real sense of "reaching" in bodies is that the one who reaches moves to the place reached. In the verse, ﴿old age has already overtaken me﴾ is apt because it expresses a weak, acted-upon state, whereas "I have reached" expresses an active, dominant state, so reflect on it. This is not objected to by his saying: ﴿And I have indeed reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam: 8], because he has made clear the weakness of his condition by mentioning ʿitiyy (extreme decrepitude).

"Al-ʿaqir" (the barren): the person who does not bear children; this is said of a woman and of a man. ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl said:

"Wretched is the youth if I am one-eyed, barren, ∗∗∗ a coward; what excuse have I before every assembly?"

ʿAqir is of the pattern fāʿil and is in the sense of attribution (nisba), and is not derived in the manner of a verb.

The demonstrative "dhalika" in His saying, ﴿Thus Allah...﴾ may refer to this strange thing with which he was given glad tidings, meaning: like this astonishing power is the power of Allah; so there is an elided modifier in the speech, and the speech is complete at ﴿Thus Allah﴾, and His saying ﴿does what He wills﴾ explains the ambiguity in that. It is also possible that the demonstrative "dhalika" refers to the state of Zakariyya and the state of his wife, as if he said: "My Lord, in what manner will we have a boy when we are in such and such a state?" So He said to him: "As you both are, a boy will be yours." On this interpretation the speech is complete at "thus," and His saying ﴿Allah does what He wills﴾ is a clarifying sentence establishing in the soul the occurrence of this strange matter.

(p-214) His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture. And remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and the morning."﴾

Al-'āya (the sign) means the indication. Al-Rabī' (ibn Anas), al-Suddī and others said: Zakariyyā said, "My Lord, if that speech was from You and the glad tidings are true, then appoint for me a sign by which I may know its soundness." He was therefore punished for this doubt about God's command, by being prevented from speaking with the people for three days.

A group of exegetes (tafsīr) said: Zakariyyā never doubted at all. He only asked about the means by which the child would come to be and the glad tidings would be completed. When it was said to him, ﴿Thus God does what He wills﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 40], he asked for a sign for the time of conception, so that he would know when Yaḥyā would be conceived.

The exegetes differed over whether his inability to speak was caused by an affliction that befell him or not. Jubayr ibn Nufayr said: his tongue swelled in his mouth until it filled it, then God released him after three days. Al-Rabī' and others said: he was punished because the angels had spoken the glad tidings to him directly, and after that he asked for a sign, so God seized his tongue, and he was unable to speak. A group of exegetes said: it was not an affliction; rather, he was prevented from conversing with people and was unable to do so, but he could remember God. This was reported by al-Ṭabarī, and something similar is reported from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

Then He excepted the ramz (gesture), and this is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it). The jurists (fuqahāʾ) held that gesture and the like have the ruling of speech in matters of oaths and similar cases. On this view the exception is connected (muttaṣil). But the speech meant by the sign is only vocal utterance by the tongue, not conveying what is in the self, so the true nature of this exception is that it is disjunctive.

The majority of readers read "ramzan" with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and sukūn on the mīm. ʿAlqama ibn Qays read "rumuzan" with ḍammah on both. Al-Aʿmash read "ramazan" with fatḥah on both. In the language, ar-ramz is a movement that makes known what is in the mind of the one who gestures, whatever the movement may be: with the eye, the eyebrow, the lip, the hand, a stick, or other things. It has been said that words deviated from their apparent meaning are called rumūz, because they are signs without the word that is laid down for the intended meaning. It may also be said of an audible sound that indicates a meaning that it is a ramz. From this is the saying of Juʾayya ibn ʿĀʾid:

"And the speech of the heroes was signs (ramzan), and murmuring among them like the roaring."

As for the exegetes, each of them specified a type of ramz in his explanation of this verse. Mujāhid said: "illā ramzan" means: except moving the lips. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means: except a sign with the hand and head. Al-Suddī and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr said the same. Al-Ḥasan said: his tongue was held back, so he began to indicate with his hand to his people. Qatāda said: "illā ramzan" means: except by signalling (īmāʾ).

The majority of readers read "allā tukallima an-nāsa" with the verb in the subjunctive after "an". Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "allā tukallimu" with ḍammah on the mīm. This is on the basis that "an" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna", with the pronoun of the matter and affair in it, and the implied meaning is: "your sign is that he will not speak to the people." The claim that this verse was abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "There is no silence (ṣamt) for a day until night" is a claim that is clearly false in several respects.

God commanded him to remember his Lord much, because nothing came between him and the remembrance of God. This indicates that no affliction or illness had reached his tongue. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: If God had granted anyone permission to leave off remembrance, He would have granted it to Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, when He said, ﴿your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾, but He said to him, ﴿and remember your Lord much﴾.

His, the Exalted's, saying "wa-sabbiḥ" (and glorify) means: say "Subḥān Allāh" (Glory be to God). Some people said it means: pray. The first view is more correct, because it fits with remembrance, and it is more fitting given the impossibility of speaking with people.

Al-ʿashiyy in the language means from the decline of the sun until its setting. From this is the saying of al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad: "I did not meet people except that they were praying Ẓuhr in the ʿashiyy." And al-ʿashiyy is from the time the shade (fayʾ) begins to return. From this is the saying of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr:

"So you cannot endure the shade of the cold of the forenoon, nor do you taste the shade of the chill of the evening."

Al-ʿashiyy is, according to some, a singular noun, and according to others it is the plural of ʿashiyya, like safīna and safīn (ship and ships). Al-Ibkār is the verbal noun of abkara ar-rajul, when a man hastens to his affair from the rising of the sun, and the early morning continues somewhat after sunrise. One says abkara ar-rajul and bakkara. From the first is the saying of Ibn Abī Rabīʿa:

"Are you setting off in the morning from the household of Nuʿmā, or going early...?"

From the second is the saying of Jarīr:

"Has Salmā departed early, so that her departure was hastened, and she split the staff after its leader had united them?"

Mujāhid said, explaining al-ibkār: it is the beginning of dawn. And al-ʿashiyy: the sun's inclination until it sets.

(p-٢١٧) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow."﴾

Al-Tabari said: The governing element (al-'amil) in "idh" is His saying "Sami'" (Hearing), so it is coordinated with His saying: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]. Many of the grammarians (al-nuhat) said: the governing element in "idh" in this verse is a hidden verb whose estimated form is "wa-udhkur" (and mention). This is the preferred view, because these verses are all reports of the unseen which point to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the purpose of mentioning them is most evident in preserving the splendor of the speech (ruwnaq al-kalam).

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa-idh qala al-malaikatu" (and the angel said).

The commentators differed as to whether "al-mala'ika" here refers to Jibril alone or to a group of angels. The discussion of a similar expression was given earlier, in His saying: ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39].

"Istafaka" is derived from "safa, yasfu" and its form is "ifta'ala," with the "ta'" changed to "ta'" (ṭa') to harmonize with the "sad." The meaning is: He selected you for His obedience.

His saying, "wa-tahharaka" (and purified you), means: from everything that defames women, whether in creation, character, or religion. This was said by Mujahid and others. Al-Zajjaj said: It has come in the tafsir that it means purification from menstruation and postnatal bleeding; but this requires a strong chain of transmission, and I do not know of one.

His saying, ﴿and chosen you above the women of the worlds﴾: If we take "al-'alamin" as general, encompassing those who came before and after, then we take the choosing as specific to the matter of 'Isa, peace be upon him, and that she was chosen to bear a child without a male. If we take the choosing as general, then we take His saying "al-'alamin" as specific to the world of that time. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and others. It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of the women of Paradise is Maryam bint 'Imran; the best of the women of Paradise is Khadija bint Khuwaylid." It is also narrated from him that he said: "The best of its women is Maryam bint 'Imran, and the best of its women is Khadija bint Khuwaylid." Al-Tabari and others held that the pronoun in His saying "khayru nisa'iha" (the best of its women) refers to Paradise. Others held that it refers to this world, i.e., each woman in her own time. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The best of women who rode camels are the righteous women of Quraysh: the most compassionate of them toward a child in its infancy, and the most attentive to a husband in what is in her possession." Abu Hurayra, the narrator of the hadith, said: "Maryam bint 'Imran never rode a camel at all." This addition involves the unseen, so it cannot be interpreted as something Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said except from hearing it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of the women of the worlds are four: Maryam bint 'Imran, Asiya bint Muzahim the wife of Pharaoh, Khadija bint Khuwaylid, and Fatima bint Muhammad." Al-Tabari also transmitted a report that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to his daughter Fatima: "You are the mistress of the women of the people of Paradise, except Maryam bint 'Imran the virgin (al-batul)." And he said: "Khadija has been preferred over the women of my community, just as Maryam has been preferred over the women of the worlds."

When you reflect on these hadiths and others like them in meaning, you find that Maryam is placed first in them. It is therefore permissible to interpret the generality of the choosing over "the worlds" as general as well. Some people have said that Maryam was a prophetess. Ibn Ishaq said: The angels would approach Maryam and say: ﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you﴾, to the end of the verse, and Zakariyya would hear that and say: "Indeed Maryam has a great matter." From the angels' address to her, this speaker made her a prophetess. But the majority of people hold that no woman was made a prophetess.

"Iqnuti" means: worship and obey. This was said by Qatada and al-Hasan. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Every qunut in the Qur'an means obedience to Allah." It may also mean: prolong standing in prayer. This is the view of the majority, and it fits the meaning of His saying ﴿and prostrate and bow﴾. Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi' said this. Mujahid narrated that when she was addressed with this, she stood until her feet swelled. al-Awza'i narrated that she stood until blood and pus flowed from her feet. It is also reported that birds would land on her head, thinking her an object because of her stillness through her long standing.

(p-٢١٩) Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Iqnuti li-Rabbiki" means: devote yourself sincerely to your Lord.

The interpreters differed on why prostration was mentioned before bowing. Some said that this was the law of Zakariyya and others before him. Others said: the particle "wa" (and) does not indicate order; the meaning is: do this and do that, and the sequence of bowing is already known. This verse presents more difficulty than our saying "Zayd and 'Amr stood," because the standing of Zayd and 'Amr has no known order, whereas in this verse it is known that prostration comes after bowing, so how did the "wa" come in reverse? My view on this is that Maryam was commanded with two components and two landmarks of prayer, namely prolonged standing and prostration. They were singled out for mention because of their nobility among the pillars of prayer, since the servant draws near to Allah, the Exalted, at the time of prostration. These two belong specifically to her solitary prayer. Otherwise, whoever prays behind an imam is not told: "Prolong your standing." Then she was afterwards commanded to pray in congregation, and it was said to her: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾. Here a landmark of prayer is intended, so that a word is not repeated. The verse does not mean the prostration and bowing that are contained within a single rak'a. And Allah knows best.

﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow."﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 44–45:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿That is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they cast their pens (arqam), to see which of them would take charge (yakfulu) of Mary. Nor were you with them when they disputed.﴾ ﴿When the angels said: "O Mary, indeed God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, honoured in this world and the Hereafter and one of those brought near.﴾

This address is to Muhammad, peace be upon him. The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the stories mentioned before. Al-anba' means the reports, and "al-ghayb" means what is hidden from human perception. "Nuhihi" means: We place it in your soul in secrecy. The definition of wahy (revelation) is the placing of a meaning in the soul in secrecy. Its forms vary: it may come through an angel, through inspiration (ilham), through a sign (isharah), or through a book, as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*They reached the non-Arabs and the horizons with his poems,*
*Remaining as the revelation (wahy) remains on the hard, solid rock.*

The Arabs say both "awha" and "wahaa." In this verse there is a proof of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, since he brought unseen matters that no one knows except one who witnessed them, and he was not present among them. Either he learned them from reading the books of the People of the Book, while Muhammad, peace be upon him, was an unlettered man from an unlettered people, or God informed him of them, and he is that, may God bless him and grant him peace. "Ladayhim" means: with them and in their company. The discussion of the pens (aqlam) and the guardianship (kafl) has already been given. Most scholars hold that it was a drawing of lots (istihamun) to take them and a competition for them. Ibn Ishaq said: their casting of lots happened when famine struck them, so that each sought to lift the burden of her maintenance.

"Yakhtasimun" means: they exchange loud words about her matter. In this verse there is the use of lots (qur'ah), and the lot is a sunnah. "When the Prophet, peace be upon him, travelled, he drew lots among his wives." He, peace be upon him, also said: "If people knew what is in the first row, they would cast lots for it." Most of the community permit the lot, except one who deviated and thought it was gambling. All of this concerns matters in which mutual consent can be reached without a lot, so the lot here serves to make that allocation acceptable. As for cases where mutual consent is not permitted, such as freeing slaves from a dead person's one-third, the majority permitted the lot, while Abu Hanifa prohibited it. In a hadith: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, drew lots among six slaves, freed two, and kept four in bondage."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ayyuhum yakfulu Maryam﴾ (which of them would take charge of Mary) is a subject and predicate in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by a verb whose implied form is "they look at": ﴿which of them would take charge of Mary﴾. The governing element of His saying ﴿When the angels said﴾ is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember ﴿when the angels said﴾." Thus the description of the verse proceeds in order, and these unseen matters follow one another. Al-Zajjaj said: the governing element of it is "yakhtasimun," and it may be connected to His saying ﴿You were not with them﴾. All of this is refuted by the meaning, because the disputing did not occur at the time of the angels' saying.

Ibn Mas'ud and Abdullah ibn Umar read: "Idh qala al-malaikatu" (when the angel said, singular). The interpreters differed over whether "al-malaikah" here refers to Gabriel alone or to a group of angels. The meaning of this entire matter has already been given in His saying earlier: ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾ [3:39], so reflect on it. The readings of "yubashshiruki" have already been mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 46–47:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle (al-mahd) and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous.﴾ ﴿She said, "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said, "Thus Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾

His saying "wa-yukallimu" (and he will speak) is a substitute for a circumstantial clause (hal), whose estimated form is "wa-mukallliman" (and speaking). It is coordinated with His saying "wajihan" (honored). The coordination of the imperfect verb with the active participle is due to the resemblance between them (al-mudara'a), just as it is permissible to coordinate an active participle with an imperfect verb, as in the words of the poet:

*I spent the night feeding them with a sharp, cutting sword,*
*aiming at their shanks and their... (the rest of the line)*

His saying "fi al-mahd" (in the cradle) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yukallimu." "Kahlan" (in maturity) is a circumstantial clause coordinated with His saying "fi al-mahd." His saying "min al-salihin" (among the righteous) is a circumstantial clause coordinated with His saying "wa-yukallimu."

This verse is a report from Allah, the Exalted, to Mary, that her son will speak with people while in the cradle, as a sign indicating the innocence of his mother from what a suspicious slanderer might accuse her of. The mahd (cradle) is the place where the infant lies during the period of his upbringing.

He, the Exalted, informed that he would also speak to people in maturity (kahl). The benefit of this, since speech in maturity is already known, is that it is a report to her about his life extending to the age of maturity. This is the statement of al-Rabi' and a group of exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: the benefit of His saying "wa-kahlan" is the report of his descent at the time he kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist) in maturity. The majority of people said: the kahl is one who has reached the age of maturity. Mujahid said: the kahl is the forbearing (halim). This is an explanation of maturity by an attribute that usually accompanies it.

People differed over the limit of maturity. It was said: the kahl is one who is forty years old. It was said: thirty-five. It was said: thirty-three. It was said: thirty-two, and this is the beginning limit. As for its end, it is fifty-two, after which one enters the age of old age (shaykhukha).

Mary's saying, "My Lord, how can I have a child?" is a question about the manner of her conception and an expression of astonishment at conception in the state of her virginity (bakara). "Yamsasni" means: he would have intercourse with her and have sexual relations with her. Al-masis is intercourse. Mary did not deny the touching of hands.

The indication in His, the Exalted, saying "Thus" (kadhalika) may refer to this power contained in the glad tidings of the Word, and it may refer to the state of Mary and her virginity. The explanation of these two interpretations has already been given in the matter of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. In Zakariyya's matter the expression was "yaf'alu" (He does), while here it is "yakhluqu" (He creates). Since the matter of Zakariyya falls within what is possible and familiar, though rare, while the story of Mary is not familiar at all, the word "khalq" (creation) is closer to innovation (al-ikhtira') and more indicative of it.

It is narrated that 'Isa, peace be upon him, was born after eight months, and for this reason one born in other than this way does not live for such a period.

His, the Exalted, saying "idha qada" (when He decrees) means: when He wills its existence. "Al-amr" (the matter) is the singular of "al-umur" (affairs), and it is a verbal noun that has been named by it. The pronoun in "lahu" (to it) refers to the matter, and the saying is in the manner of direct address. Makki said: it was said that the meaning is "He says for its sake," and this leans toward what we will mention later from Abu 'Ali.

The majority of the Seven Readers recited "fayakunu" with a nominative vowel (ar-raf'), while Ibn 'Amir alone recited "fayakuna" with an accusative vowel (an-nasb). The reason for the nominative is coordination with "yaqulu" (He says), or the estimate: "fahuwa yakunu" (so He is). As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir, it is not well-directed, because the earlier command is an address to the one decreed, while His saying "fayakuna" is an address to the one informed. So it is not like His saying "qum fa-uhsin ilayka" (Stand up and do good to yourself). However, its justification is that he observed the verbal resemblance in that a command-form word is placed earlier in the speech, as Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said regarding His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed that they should establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], that it follows the course of the answer to a command even though it is not truly an answer. Likewise, according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir, His saying "fayakuna" takes the place of the answer to a command even though it is not an answer.

Abu 'Ali, in this issue, went to the view that the saying here is not pure direct address, but is a figurative saying, as in the words of the poet:

*The basin became full and said, "Enough for me!"...*

and other examples. He said: because the non-existent is not a thing that exists, it is not addressed, just as it is not commanded. The meaning is: "When He wills it, it is (kawnuhu), so it is." This is a Mu'tazili tendency. May God have mercy on him and forgive him.

The Qur'anic verses are in the Qur'an, so they appear in the Qur'anic (Arabic) order as given.

(p-225) His the Exalted, the Majestic, said:
﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom, and the Torah and the Injil﴾ ﴿and [make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: that I create for you from clay the likeness of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by the permission of Allah."﴾

Nafi' and 'Asim read "wa-yu'allimuhu" with the yā' (ي), and this is a conjunction with "yubashshiruki bi-kalimah" (He gives you good tidings of a word from Him). So said Abu 'Ali. It is also possible that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), conjoined with "wa-yukallimu" (and he speaks). The rest read "nu'allimuhu" with the nūn, which in meaning is like the yā' reading, but comes with the nūn of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah). Al-Ṭabarī said: the reading with yā' is a conjunction with His saying "yakhluqu mā yashā'" (He creates what He wills), and the reading with nūn is a conjunction with His saying "nūḥīhi ilayka" (We reveal it to you).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
What he said is an error in both readings, and it corrupts the meaning. "Al-Kitāb" is writing with the hand; it is a verbal noun of kataba, yaktubu. This is the statement of Ibn Jurayj and the group of exegetes. Some of them said that it refers to a revealed Book that is not specified, but this is a claim for which there is no proof. As for "al-ḥikmah" (wisdom), it is the Sunnah which the prophets speak in matters of law, admonitions and the like, of what was not revealed to them in a book or through an angel; rather they are inspired to it and their natural dispositions are strengthened toward it. Some scholars have described wisdom as being correctness in speech and action. Allah the Exalted mentions in this verse that He teaches ʿIsā, peace be upon him, wisdom. Teaching is firmly established regarding what is of wisdom by revelation, or transmitted from those who preceded ʿIsā among prophets and scholars. As for what was of ʿIsā's own particular wisdom, it is said regarding it "nu'allimuhu" in the sense of: We prepare his natural disposition for it, we equip him, and we make him train in extracting it, and his mind moves toward that.

"Al-Tawrāh" is what was revealed to Mūsā, peace be upon him. It is narrated that ʿIsā, peace be upon him, used to memorize the Torah, and was the most knowledgeable of people about it and the most active in acting upon it. Al-Naqqāsh related an opinion that al-akmah is the mute who neither understands nor is understood, dead of heart. Ibn ʿAbbās also said, and Qatādah: al-akmah is one born blind with closed eyes.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
ʿIsā, peace be upon him, used to heal every ailment by his supplication and the wiping of his hand, and it would be cured. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 50–51:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And confirming what was before me of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of that which was forbidden to you. I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear Allah and obey me. Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾

His saying "muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) conjoined to His saying: ﴿that I have come to you with a sign﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 49], because that saying occupies the position of a ḥāl. ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, was confirming the Torah, following it and acting by what is in it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he used to observe the Sabbath and face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

Qatādah said, in explaining His saying: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of that which was forbidden to you﴾, that what ʿĪsā brought was gentler than what Mūsā brought. Ibn Jurayj said: he made lawful for them the flesh of camels and fats. Al-Rabīʿ said: and some things from fish, and birds that have no ṣiṣiyah (talon-like toe/claw on the hind foot). In the Torah there were prohibitions which the law of ʿĪsā left in their state, so the word "some" (baʿḍ) on this view is well-founded. Abū ʿUbaydah said: "baʿḍ" in this verse means "kull" (all), and people criticized him for this statement. Abū ʿUbaydah cited as evidence for his view a verse of Labīd:

؎ Tarrāku amkinatin idhā lam yarḍahā aw yakhtarim baʿḍa al-nufūsi ḥimāmuhā

(p-232) But the verse contains no proof for him, because Labīd meant himself, so it is a valid partitive usage. Some exegetes held that His saying: ﴿was forbidden to you﴾ refers to what the rabbis after Mūsā forbade and legislated, as if ʿĪsā returned the rulings of the Torah to their true realities which were sent down from Allah the Exalted.

ʿIkrimah recited "ḥarrama ʿalaykum" with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and a shaddah on the rāʾ, attributing the verb to Allah the Exalted or to Mūsā, peace be upon him. The majority recited "wa-jiʾtukum bi-āyatin", and in the muṣḥaf of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd: "wa-jiʾtukum bi-āyātin min rabbikum". His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿so fear Allah and obey me﴾ is a warning and a call to Allah the Exalted.

The majority of readers recited ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a resumption of the statement. Some people recited "anna Allāha rabbī wa-rabbukum" with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Al-Ṭabarī said: "inna" is a substitute (badal) for "āyah" in His saying: ﴿I have come to you with a sign﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 49]. In this there is weakness; rather the implied sense is: "Obey me, because Allah is my Lord and your Lord," or the meaning is: "Because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him."

His saying ﴿This is a straight path﴾ refers to His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾, because its words gather faith and acts of obedience. The ṣirāṭ (path) is the road, and the mustaqīm (straight) is that in which there is no crookedness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 52–54:

(p-233) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, "We are the helpers of Allah. We have believed in Allah, so bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and have followed the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed. And Allah is the best of schemers.﴾

Before this verse there is an omitted part, by which the coherence of the verses is completed. Its estimated meaning: Jesus, peace be upon him, came as Allah had announced, and he said to the Children of Israel all that was mentioned. ﴿So when he sensed﴾: the meaning of "sensed" (ahassa) is that he knew through the senses what he heard of their statements denying him, and saw from the indicators of circumstances and the intensity of enmity and aversion. It is said: "I sensed (ahsastu) the thing" and "I perceived it (hassaytu bihi)"; its origin is hassastu, and one of the two sins was replaced by a yā'. "Disbelief" (al-kufr) here is denial of him. It is related that he saw from them an intention to kill him, and then he sought help. The pronoun in "from them" refers to the Children of Israel.

And His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾ is an expression of Jesus' condition in seeking one who will stand up for the religion, believe in the Sharia and protect it, just as Muhammad ﷺ used to present himself to the tribes and approach the clans during the seasons. All these actions, and what they contain of statements, are expressed by ﴿"Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾. There is no doubt that these words were among his sayings to the people. "Al-Anṣār" is the plural of naṣīr, like shahīd and ashhād and other such forms; and it was said: it is the plural of nāṣir, like ṣāḥib and aṣḥāb. His saying "ilā Allāh" (for Allah) may carry two meanings. One: "Who will help me in the way to Allah?" Then "ilā" indicates the end-point clearly, in its proper sense. The second meaning: the sense is "Who will add his support to the support of Allah for me?" It then has the function of His saying: ﴿And do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa': 2]. When you reflect on it, you find in it the meaning of the end-point, because it includes the addition of one thing to another.

(p-234) Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi have expressed it as meaning "ma'a" (with). Indeed "ma'a" can take the place of "ilā" in these meanings, but it is not permissible from this to say that "ilā" means "ma'a", to the point that some jurists erred in interpreting His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. He said: "ilā" means "ma'a", and this is a barbarism. Rather, "ilā" in this verse is a bare end-point, and one examines whether what follows "ilā" enters what precedes it by another means.

"Al-Hawariyyun" are a people whom Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by, and he invited them to support him and follow his religion, and they answered him and carried this out in the best manner, and they were patient in the cause of Allah. It is related that he passed by them while they were fishing. People differed over why they were called al-Hawariyyun. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they were named so for the whiteness and cleanness of their garments. Abu Arta'ah said: they were named so because they were fullers (qassarin) who whiten clothes, i.e. they bleach them. Qatadah said: al-Hawariyyun are the chosen ones of the prophets, those fit for the caliphate; al-Dahhak said something similar. This describes their condition and is not an explanation of the word. On this same basis the Prophet ﷺ likened his cousin to them in his saying: "And the disciple (hawari) of al-Zubayr." The first statements are the explanation of the word, since it derives from al-hawar, which is whiteness; one says "I whitened the garment (hawwartu al-thawb)", meaning I made it white, and from it comes "hawari". The Arabs also call the women who dwell in the cities "al-hawariyyat", because whiteness predominates over them. From this is the saying of Abu Jildah al-Yashkuri:

(p-235)
"So say to the hawariyyat, let them weep for others than us,
And let none weep for us except the barking dogs."

Makki mentioned that Mary nursed Jesus, peace be upon him, in his childhood in various tasks, and the last thing she entrusted him to was the disciples, who were the ones who shorten garments and then dye them. He showed them signs, and he dyed for them various colours from one water.

Most people recited "al-Hawariyyun" with a shadda on the yā', its singular being "hawariyy"; it is not a yā' of nisba but like the yā' of kursiyy. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Bakr al-Thaqafi recited "al-Hawariyun" with a light yā' throughout the Qur'an. Abu al-Fath said: the Arabs dislike the damma on a light yā' preceded by a kasra, and avoid it; when it occurs in forms like their saying al-'adiyun, al-qadiyun, and al-sa'iyun, they treat it as defective by finding the damma heavy, so they make the yā' quiescent, transfer its vowel, then delete it for its quiescence and the quiescence of the wāw after it, so one gets al-'adun and similar. According to this, it should have been said "al-hawarun". But the basis of the recitation, though weak, is that the yā' was lightened because of the difficulty of doubling it, and the damma was retained to indicate that the doubling is intended, since doubling can bear the damma. This is like what Abu al-Hasan did in lightening yastahziyun, where he made the hamza purely a yā', and kept the damma as a reminder of the state of the hamza intended in it.

The disciples' saying "and bear witness" (wash-had) may be an address to Jesus, peace be upon him, meaning: bear witness for us before Allah. It may also be an address to Allah, the Exalted, as when you say: "I call Allah to witness for such and such" when you resolve and emphasise commitment. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "O Allah, bear witness." Al-Tabari said: in this verse there is a rebuke to the Christians of Najran, i.e. this is the statement of the earlier believers in Jesus, not what you say, O you who claim divinity for him.

His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down"﴾ means the Gospel and the signs of Jesus. "The Messenger" is Jesus, peace be upon him. Their saying: ﴿"so record us among the witnesses"﴾ is an expression of the desire to be, in His sight, among those of the believing nations who bore witness to the truth. Since people record what they need to know and verify at a later stage in writing, they expressed Allah's act toward them in these terms. Ibn 'Abbas said: their saying "among the witnesses" means: make us of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, in being among those who bear witness over the people.

Then the Exalted informed about the Children of Israel who disbelieved in Jesus, saying: "And they schemed" — meaning their contriving to seize Jesus for killing, in their own claim. It is related that they plotted against him and set spies upon him until he and the disciples entered a house, and they seized them therein. This is the scheming of the Children of Israel. Allah, the Exalted, requited them by casting the likeness of Jesus upon one of the disciples and raising Jesus, and He brought upon the Children of Israel humiliation and disgrace in this world and the Hereafter. This punishment is what Allah called a scheme in His saying ﴿and Allah schemed﴾, and it is the established practice to name a punishment by the name of the sin even if it is not of its meaning. On this basis the majority of exegetes explained the verse. And it is also said: Jesus said to the disciples, "Who will be patient, so that my likeness is cast upon him and he is killed, and he will have Paradise?" One of them said: "I," and that happened. Others related that the Children of Israel sent a Jewish spy to Jesus until he accompanied him and guided them to him, and he entered the house with him; when they were surrounded, Allah cast the likeness of Jesus upon that Jewish man, and he was seized and crucified. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they schemed and Allah schemed﴾, and this too is naming a punishment by the name of the sin. Scheming in the language is pursuing a person without that being apparent to him, rather the schemer conceals the opposite of what he shows.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾ means: in that He is the doer of truth in that matter, whereas the schemer among humans is mostly a doer of falsehood, because in falsehoods one needs trickery; and Allah, glorified is He, is mightier in seizing and more effective in His will. So He is better in countless respects; there is no god but Him. The mention of Jesus' being besieged, the number of his companions, the matter of the likeness and other aspects of his affair will come in its place, God willing.

Qatadah said: al-Hawariyyun are the chosen ones of the prophets, those fit for the caliphate; al-Dahhak said something similar. This describes their condition and is not an explanation of the word. On this same basis the Prophet ﷺ likened his cousin to them in his saying: "And the disciple (hawari) of al-Zubayr." The first statements are the explanation of the word, since it derives from al-hawar, which is whiteness; one says "I whitened the garment (hawwartu al-thawb)", meaning I made it white, and from it comes "hawari". The Arabs also call the women who dwell in the cities "al-hawariyyat", because whiteness predominates over them. From this is the saying of Abu Jildah al-Yashkuri:

(p-235)
"So say to the hawariyyat, let them weep for others than us,
And let none weep for us except the barking dogs."

Makki mentioned that Mary nursed Jesus, peace be upon him, in his childhood in various tasks, and the last thing she entrusted him to was the disciples, who were the ones who shorten garments and then dye them. He showed them signs, and he dyed for them various colours from one water.

Most people recited "al-Hawariyyun" with a shadda on the yā', its singular being "hawariyy"; it is not a yā' of nisba but like the yā' of kursiyy. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Bakr al-Thaqafi recited "al-Hawariyun" with a light yā' throughout the Qur'an. Abu al-Fath said: the Arabs dislike the damma on a light yā' preceded by a kasra, and avoid it; when it occurs in forms like their saying al-'adiyun, al-qadiyun, and al-sa'iyun, they treat it as defective by finding the damma heavy, so they make the yā' quiescent, transfer its vowel, then delete it for its quiescence and the quiescence of the wāw after it, so one gets al-'adun and similar. According to this, it should have been said "al-hawarun". But the basis of the recitation, though weak, is that the yā' was lightened because of the difficulty of doubling it, and the damma was retained to indicate that the doubling is intended, since doubling can bear the damma. This is like what Abu al-Hasan did in lightening yastahziyun, where he made the hamza purely a yā', and kept the damma as a reminder of the state of the hamza intended in it.

The disciples' saying "and bear witness" (wash-had) may be an address to Jesus, peace be upon him, meaning: bear witness for us before Allah. It may also be an address to Allah, the Exalted, as when you say: "I call Allah to witness for such and such" when you resolve and emphasise commitment. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "O Allah, bear witness." Al-Tabari said: in this verse there is a rebuke to the Christians of Najran, i.e. this is the statement of the earlier believers in Jesus, not what you say, O you who claim divinity for him.

His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down"﴾ means the Gospel and the signs of Jesus. "The Messenger" is Jesus, peace be upon him. Their saying: ﴿"so record us among the witnesses"﴾ is an expression of the desire to be, in His sight, among those of the believing nations who bore witness to the truth. Since people record what they need to know and verify at a later stage in writing, they expressed Allah's act toward them in these terms. Ibn 'Abbas said: their saying "among the witnesses" means: make us of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, in being among those who bear witness over the people.

Then the Exalted informed about the Children of Israel who disbelieved in Jesus, saying: "And they schemed" — meaning their contriving to seize Jesus for killing, in their own claim. It is related that they plotted against him and set spies upon him until he and the disciples entered a house, and they seized them therein. This is the scheming of the Children of Israel. Allah, the Exalted, requited them by casting the likeness of Jesus upon one of the disciples and raising Jesus, and He brought upon the Children of Israel humiliation and disgrace in this world and the Hereafter. This punishment is what Allah called a scheme in His saying ﴿and Allah schemed﴾, and it is the established practice to name a punishment by the name of the sin even if it is not of its meaning. On this basis the majority of exegetes explained the verse. And it is also said: Jesus said to the disciples, "Who will be patient, so that my likeness is cast upon him and he is killed, and he will have Paradise?" One of them said: "I," and that happened. Others related that the Children of Israel sent a Jewish spy to Jesus until he accompanied him and guided them to him, and he entered the house with him; when they were surrounded, Allah cast the likeness of Jesus upon that Jewish man, and he was seized and crucified. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they schemed and Allah schemed﴾, and this too is naming a punishment by the name of the sin. Scheming in the language is pursuing a person without that being apparent to him, rather the schemer conceals the opposite of what he shows.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾ means: in that He is the doer of truth in that matter, whereas the schemer among humans is mostly a doer of falsehood, because in falsehoods one needs trickery; and Allah, glorified is He, is mightier in seizing and more effective in His will. So He is better in countless respects; there is no god but Him. The mention of Jesus' being besieged, the number of his companions, the matter of the likeness and other aspects of his affair will come in its place, God willing.

(p-٢٣٧) His saying, mighty and majestic:

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, I will take you in death and raise you to Me, and purify you from those who disbelieve, and I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ."﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And God does not love the wrongdoers.﴾

Al-Ṭabarī said: The governing element of "إذْ" (idh, "when") is His saying, ﴿and God planned﴾ [3:54]. Other grammarians said: the governing element is a hidden verb whose estimate is "اذْكُرْ" (udhkur, "remember"), and this is the more correct view. This statement was conveyed through the mediation of an angel, because Jesus was not directly addressed.

"عِيسى" (ʿĪsā) is a non-Arabic proper noun that is definite, and therefore it is not declined (لا يَنْصَرِفُ). In Syriac it is "إيسُوعُ" (Īsūʿ), and the Arabs modified it into "عِيسى" (ʿĪsā).

The exegetes differed concerning this "تَوَفِّي" (tawaffī). Al-Rabīʿ said: it is the death of sleep; God raised him during his sleep. Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jurayj, Maṭar al-Warrāq, Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr and a group of scholars said: the meaning is, "I will seize you (قابِضُكَ) from the earth and gather you (مُحَصِّلُكَ) in heaven," so it is a "تَوَفِّي" of seizing and gathering. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the death of dying, meaning, "I will cause you to die (مُمِيتُكَ)." This is the wording of Ibn ʿAbbās, and he did not elaborate. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God caused him to die for three hours and raised him during them, then God revived him after that with Him in heaven. In some books it is given as seven hours. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is the death of dying, but the meaning is, "I will cause you to die (مُتَوَفِّيكَ) at the end of your affair, at your descent and your killing of the Dajjal," so there is inversion (تَقْدِيمٌ وتَأْخِيرٌ) in the speech. Mālik, in the Jāmiʿ al-ʿUtbiyya, said: Jesus died at the age of thirty-three years. In the book of Makkī, it occurred on the authority of some people that the meaning of "مُتَوَفِّيكَ" is "مُتَقَبِّلٌ عَمَلَكَ" (accepting your deed), and this is weak from the standpoint of the wording.

The Ummah (community) agreed upon what is contained in the mutawātir (widely transmitted) hadith: that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, is alive in heaven, and that he will descend at the end of time, kill the swine, break the cross, kill the Dajjal, spread justice, establish this religion, the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), perform the Ḥajj to the House and the ʿUmrah, and remain on earth for twenty-four years, and it was said forty years. Then God will cause him to die.

Abū Muḥammad the judge (may God have mercy on him) said: The statement of Ibn ʿAbbās (may God be pleased with him), "it is the death of dying," must come to pass, either according to the statement of Wahb ibn Munabbih or according to the statement of al-Farrāʾ. His saying, ﴿and raise you to Me﴾, is an expression for transferring him from a low place to a high place. His saying, "إلَيَّ" (ilayya, "to Me"), is an idāfa of honour (إضافَةُ تَشْرِيفٍ) to what was his heaven, the honoured, glorified, and desired direction. Otherwise, it is known that God the Exalted is not confined to a direction. His saying, ﴿and purify you﴾: the true meaning of tathhīr (purification) is only from filth and the like. It is used for abuse, false claims, sins, and association with the wicked and keeping their company, by comparing all of that to filth. So God the Mighty purified Jesus from the claims of the disbelievers and their vile company with him.

His saying, "وَجاعِلُ" (wa-jāʿil, "and making"), is an active participle (اسْمُ فاعِلٍ) for the future (لِلِاسْتِقْبالِ), and its tanwīn is dropped for lightness. It is transitive to two objects, because it means "مُصَيِّرٌ" (making into). One of them is "الَّذِينَ" (alladhīna, "those who"), and the other is in His saying, ﴿above those who disbelieve﴾. Ibn Zayd said: those who followed him are the Christians, and those who disbelieved are the Jews. The verse informs of the humiliation and punishment of the Jews: the Christians are above them in all regions of the earth until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd restricted the followers and the disbelievers, and made it a worldly ruling with no virtue in it for the disbelieving followers. Rather, their being above the Jews is a punishment for the Jews only. The majority of exegetes said: the wording regarding the followers is general, so the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) enters into it, because it follows Jesus. Qatādah and others stated this. Likewise, they said the wording regarding the disbelievers is general. So the requirement of the verse is informing Jesus, peace be upon him, that those who believe in him, as is obligatory, are above those who disbelieved by proof and evidence, and by might and dominance. It appears from the statement of Ibn Jurayj and others that what is meant are those who followed him at the time of his seeking help, and they are the Ḥawāriyyūn (the disciples). God placed them above the disbelievers because He honoured them and left for them a remembrance among the righteous. So they are above them by proof and evidence, and by the signs of God's good pleasure that appeared upon them.

His saying, ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾: the address is to Jesus, and what is meant is informing of the Resurrection and the Gathering. Therefore the wording came general in terms of the matter itself, not specific to Jesus alone. It is as if He said to him, "Then to Me, that is, to My judgment and My justice, people return," and He addressed him as one addresses a group, since he is one of them, and since they are intended in meaning. As for His saying, "فَأحْكُمُ" (fa-aḥkum, "so I will judge") to the end of the verse, it is a promise to Jesus and the believers, and a warning to the disbelievers.

His saying, ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾ and the rest of the verse, informs of what their condition will be made upon from the beginning of their affair. It is not informing of what will be done after the Day of Resurrection, because He mentioned "الدُّنْيا" (the world), which comes before it. The meaning is: as for the disbelievers, the treatment of them is that they will be punished with a severe punishment in this world by captivity, killing, the jizyah (poll tax, جِزْيَةٌ), and humiliation. Whoever among them is not reached by it lives under its fear, as he knows that the law of Islam demands it from him, and existence has made this manifest. In the Hereafter, its meaning is the punishment of the Fire. Then He mentioned the category of faith and joined to it the righteous deeds, as an alert to the degree of perfection and an invitation to it.

Ḥafṣ reported from ʿĀṣim: "فَيُوَفِّيهِمْ" (fa-yuwaffīhim) with the yāʾ, in the third person, the verb attributed to God the Exalted. The rest, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, read "فَنُوَفِّيهِمْ" (fa-nuwaffīhim) with the nūn, which is the nūn of majesty (نُونُ العَظَمَةِ). The giving of the rewards in full is the apportioning of the abodes in Paradise, and that is according to the deeds. But entering Paradise itself is by God's mercy and His grace. A parallel to His saying, ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾, has preceded in His saying earlier: ﴿But if they turn away, then God does not love the disbelievers﴾ [3:32].

It appears from the statement of Ibn Jurayj and others that what is meant are those who followed him at the time of his seeking help, and they are the Ḥawāriyyūn (the disciples). God placed them above the disbelievers because He honoured them and left for them a remembrance among the righteous. So they are above them by proof and evidence, and by the signs of God's good pleasure that appeared upon them.

His saying, ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾: the address is to Jesus, and what is meant is informing of the Resurrection and the Gathering. Therefore the wording came general in terms of the matter itself, not specific to Jesus alone. It is as if He said to him, "Then to Me, that is, to My judgment and My justice, people return," and He addressed him as one addresses a group, since he is one of them, and since they are intended in meaning. As for His saying, "فَأحْكُمُ" (fa-aḥkum, "so I will judge") to the end of the verse, it is a promise to Jesus and the believers, and a warning to the disbelievers.

His saying, ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾ and the rest of the verse, informs of what their condition will be made upon from the beginning of their affair. It is not informing of what will be done after the Day of Resurrection, because He mentioned "الدُّنْيا" (the world), which comes before it. The meaning is: as for the disbelievers, the treatment of them is that they will be punished with a severe punishment in this world by captivity, killing, the jizyah (poll tax, جِزْيَةٌ), and humiliation. Whoever among them is not reached by it lives under its fear, as he knows that the law of Islam demands it from him, and existence has made this manifest. In the Hereafter, its meaning is the punishment of the Fire. Then He mentioned the category of faith and joined to it the righteous deeds, as an alert to the degree of perfection and an invitation to it.

Ḥafṣ reported from ʿĀṣim: "فَيُوَفِّيهِمْ" (fa-yuwaffīhim) with the yāʾ, in the third person, the verb attributed to God the Exalted. The rest, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, read "فَنُوَفِّيهِمْ" (fa-nuwaffīhim) with the nūn, which is the nūn of majesty (نُونُ العَظَمَةِ). The giving of the rewards in full is the apportioning of the abodes in Paradise, and that is according to the deeds. But entering Paradise itself is by God's mercy and His grace. A parallel to His saying, ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾, has preceded in His saying earlier: ﴿But if they turn away, then God does not love the disbelievers﴾ [3:32].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 58–61:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿That is what We recite to you of the signs and the wise Reminder.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾ ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿Whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you, say, "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us invoke [the curse of] Allah upon the liars."﴾

"Dhalika" (that) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and the reference of "bihi" (by it) is to what preceded of the news. And ﴿natlūhu ʿalayka﴾ (We recite it to you) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. His saying ﴿min al-āyāt﴾ (of the signs) is for specifying the genus (li-bayān al-jins), and it is permissible that it be partitive (lil-tab'īd). It is also valid that ﴿natlūhu ʿalayka﴾ be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the predicate then is in his saying ﴿min al-āyāt﴾. According to the view of the Kufans, his saying "natluhu" is a relative clause (ṣila) for "dhalika", in the manner of their saying in the verse of Ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

؎ ................ and this you carry, free [one]

And the predicate is in his saying ﴿min al-āyāt﴾. The view of the Basrans on the verse is that "taḥmilīn" is a circumstantial clause, the meaning being: "and this being carried." "Natluhu" means: we narrate it in sequence (nasruduhu). The apparent meaning of ﴿min al-āyāt﴾ is the verses of the Qur'an. It is possible that by his saying ﴿min al-āyāt﴾ he means from the miracles and the wondrous matters, that they come to you with these unseen matters from Us, and through Our recitation, while you are unlettered and do not read, and you are not one who accompanied the People of the Book. So the meaning is: they are signs of your prophethood. This possibility is only fully established when "natluhu" is a circumstantial clause. "Al-Dhikr" (the Reminder) is what descends from Allah. "Al-Ḥakīm" (the wise) may be interpreted in the sense of "muḥkam" (perfected, firm), so it is a form (fa'īl) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl); and it is valid to interpret it in the sense of one who clearly expresses wisdom, so it is then in the form of an active participle (ism fā'il). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Al-Dhikr" is the Qur'an, and "al-Ḥakīm" is the one whose wisdom is perfect.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and others mentioned, they said: the occasion of revelation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah﴾ ... the verse was: "The delegation of Christians of Najran disputed with the Prophet ﷺ about the matter of Jesus, and they said: 'It has reached us that you revile our companion and say that he is a servant.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'What harm does that do to Jesus? Yes, he is the servant of Allah, and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him.' They said: 'Have you ever seen a human who came without a male, or have you heard of such?' And they left the Prophet, and Allah revealed this verse to him."

As for the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, the likeness﴾ (mathal), some people interpreted it as meaning the attribute (ṣifa) of Jesus, and they connected this to the words of the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of Paradise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35]. They said: its meaning is "the attribute of Paradise." This, in my view, is a weakness in understanding the meaning of the speech. Rather, the meaning is: the likeness that the souls and minds conceive of Jesus is like what is conceived of Adam, since all people agree that Allah the Exalted created him from dust without a male. Likewise, "the likeness of Paradise" is an expression for what is conceived of it. In this verse is the validity of analogy (qiyas), that is: when the matter of Adam is conceived, the permissibility of the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, is analogized upon it. The "kāf" in his saying "kamathali" (like the likeness of) is a noun (ism) according to the meaning we have mentioned. His saying "ʿinda Allah" (before Allah) is an expression for the truth in itself, that is: thus is the matter in what is hidden from you. His saying ﴿He created him from dust﴾ is an explanation of the likeness of Adam which should be conceived. "Mathal" and "mithāl" have one meaning. It is not permissible that "khalaqahu" be a relative clause for Adam nor a circumstantial clause from him. Al-Zajjaj said: since the past tense cannot be a circumstantial clause "you are in it," rather it is a separate statement (kalām maqṭūʿ) from it, whose implication is the explanation of the likeness.

And the words of the Exalted and Majestic:

"Thumma qāla" (then He said) is a sequential ordering (tartīb) of the reports to Muhammad ﷺ. The meaning: He created him from dust, then there was, in His eternal decree, that He said to him: "Be" at such a time. And according to the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, that speech is figurative, like "wa qāla qaṭnī" (and the earth said: "Enough for me"), and that this verse is an expression for creating (takwīn), then "thumma" is in its original sense of ordering the two mentioned matters. The reading of the majority is "fayakūnu" with a nominative ending (raf'), in the sense of: "so he is (and) becomes." Ibn 'Amir read "fayakūna" with an accusative ending (naṣb), and this reading is weak in its grammatical basis, and its explanation has already preceded just now in the address to Maryam.

And his saying the Exalted: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate in what is related to it is his saying "min rabbika" (from your Lord), or "al-ḥaqq dhālika" (the truth is that), or "mā qulnā laka" (what We have said to you). It is also permissible that it be the predicate of a subject, its estimate being: "this is the truth." "Al-mumtarīn" (the doubters) are those who are in doubt, and "al-miryah" is doubt. The Prophet ﷺ was prohibited in an expression that implied the blame of the doubters, and this indicates that what is intended by "imtirā'" (doubting) is other than him. If it had been said: "so do not be a doubter," this implication would have been weaker; if it had been said: "so do not doubt," it would have been weaker still. The prohibition of the Prophet, peace be upon him, from doubting, despite his distance from it, is in the manner of confirmation and perseverance in his state.

And his saying the Exalted: ﴿Whoever argues with you about it﴾ means: disputes with you and contends with you in argument (ḥujja). The pronoun in his saying the Exalted "fīhi" (about it) may refer to Jesus, and it may refer to the truth. The "knowledge" (ʿilm) which is referred to by "coming" is what these preceding verses included of the matter of Jesus. [p-242] And his saying the Exalted: "Fa qul ta'ālaw" ... the verse: is the invitation to mubāhala (mutual invocation of curse), and "ta'ālaw" (come) is a form of "tafā'alū" from "al-ʿulūw" (height), and it is a word which was first intended for the goodness of manners with the one invited, then it became common until a person says it to his enemy, to an animal, and the like. And "nabtahil" means: we invoke the curse (nalta'in), and it is said "ʿalayhim bahlat Allāh" meaning the curse of Allah, and "al-ibtihāl" is earnestness in supplication with the "bahla" (curse).

It is related in the accounts of this verse that it was revealed on account of the disputation of the Christians of Najran about Jesus, peace be upon him, and their saying: "He is Allah," and they used to argue much. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Juz' al-Sawa'i related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "I wish there were a barrier between me and the people of Najran, so that I would not see them and they would not see me," because of how much they disputed. When the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse, he invited them to that. Al-Sha'bi and others related that: "They promised him for the next day that they would invoke the curse upon him. They set out to al-Sayyid and al-'Aqib, and they both agreed with them to invoke the curse. They went to another man among them, a wise man, and they told him what they had done. He blamed them and said to them: 'If he is a prophet and then invokes against you, you will be destroyed. And if he is a king and prevails, he will not spare you.' They said: 'So what shall we do, when we have promised him?' He said: 'When you go out in the morning and he invites you to that, seek refuge in Allah from it, for perhaps he will excuse you.' When the next day came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out embracing Husayn and holding the hand of Hasan, with Fatima walking behind him. He invited them to the appointment, and they said: 'We seek refuge in Allah.' He repeated, and they repeated the seeking of refuge. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If you refuse, then embrace Islam. If you refuse, then pay the jizya (poll tax) with humility, while you are humbled. If you refuse, then I will declare war upon you on equal terms.' They said: 'We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will pay the jizya.' He said: So he imposed upon them each year two thousand robes, a thousand in Rajab and a thousand in Safar, and they requested from him a trustworthy man to judge between them, so he sent with them Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'The one who brings good news has come to me about the destruction of the people of Najran, had they completed the mutual cursing.'"

And Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and others related: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them, they said: 'Leave us to look into our affair, then we will come to you with what we will do.' They went to al-'Aqib, who was their man of counsel, and they said: 'O Abd al-Masih, what do you think?' He said: 'O company of Christians, by Allah, you know that Muhammad is a prophet sent, and he has brought you the decisive account of your companion Jesus. You know that no people have ever invoked a curse upon a prophet and then their elder remained, nor did their young grow up. If you do it, it will be total destruction. If you refuse except to hold to your religion and what you are upon regarding your companion, then make peace with the man and return to your lands until time shows you his judgment.' They came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, we have decided not to invoke the curse upon you, and to remain upon our religion.' They reconciled with him for wealth, and they said to him: 'Send with us a man from your companions whom you approve for us, who will judge in matters about which we have disagreed concerning our wealth, for you are trusted by us.'" Al-Suddi and others related that the Prophet, peace be upon him, came himself with 'Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn, and invited them, but they refused and became anxious. Their rabbis said to them: "If you do it, the valley will be set ablaze with fire upon you." So they reconciled with the Prophet ﷺ for eighty thousand dirhams a year. Whatever the dirhams could not cover was made up in goods: a robe for forty, and upon them thirty-three coats of mail, thirty-three camels, and thirty-four horses lent every year, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as guarantor for this until he delivers them to them. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If they had invoked the curse, they would have been uprooted from the face of the earth." And he also said: "If they had done it, the valley would have been set ablaze with fire upon them." 'Ilba' ibn Ahmar al-Yashkuri related, saying: "When this verse was revealed, Muhammad ﷺ sent for 'Ali, Fatima, and their two sons Hasan and Husayn, and invited the Jews to mutually curse them. A young Jew said: 'Woe to you! Is not your covenant with yesterday's brethren, those who were transformed into monkeys and pigs? So do not mutually curse them.' And they desisted." In this account there are differences among the narrators and expressions, all of which run in the meaning of what we have mentioned, but we intended brevity.

[p-244] The abstention of the Christians from mutual cursing, because of their knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad, is a great proof of the validity of his prophethood ﷺ. What has been related about this is better than what al-Sha'bi related about that wise man among them dividing the matter of Muhammad into that he is either a prophet or a king, because this is a worldly view. And what the narrators related about their abandoning the mutual cursing due to their knowledge of his prophethood is a stronger proof for us against all the disbelievers, and more fitting to the status of Muhammad ﷺ. The invoking of women and children for the mutual cursing is more stirring to souls and more conducive to the mercy of Allah, or to His wrath upon the falsifiers. The apparent matter is that the Prophet ﷺ brought them what is specific to him, and if they had resolved, he would have summoned the believers with their children and women. It is possible that he would have been content with himself and his close family alone.

The Prophet ﷺ was prohibited in an expression that implied the blame of the doubters, and this indicates that what is intended by "imtirā'" (doubting) is other than him. If it had been said: "so do not be a doubter," this implication would have been weaker; if it had been said: "so do not doubt," it would have been weaker still. The prohibition of the Prophet, peace be upon him, from doubting, despite his distance from it, is in the manner of confirmation and perseverance in his state.

And his saying the Exalted: ﴿Whoever argues with you about it﴾ means: disputes with you and contends with you in argument (ḥujja). When the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse, he invited them to that. Al-Sha'bi and others related that: "They promised him for the next day that they would invoke the curse upon him. They set out to al-Sayyid and al-'Aqib, and they both agreed with them to invoke the curse. They went to another man among them, a wise man, and they told him what they had done. He blamed them and said to them: 'If he is a prophet and then invokes against you, you will be destroyed. And if he is a king and prevails, he will not spare you.' They said: 'So what shall we do, when we have promised him?' He said: 'When you go out in the morning and he invites you to that, seek refuge in Allah from it, for perhaps he will excuse you.' When the next day came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out embracing Husayn and holding the hand of Hasan, with Fatima walking behind him. He invited them to the appointment, and they said: 'We seek refuge in Allah.' He repeated, and they repeated the seeking of refuge. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If you refuse, then embrace Islam. If you refuse, then pay the jizya (poll tax) with humility, while you are humbled. If you refuse, then I will declare war upon you on equal terms.' They said: 'We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will pay the jizya.' He said: 'O company of Christians, by Allah, you know that Muhammad is a prophet sent, and he has brought you the decisive account of your companion Jesus. You know that no people have ever invoked a curse upon a prophet and then their elder remained, nor did their young grow up. If you do it, it will be total destruction. If you refuse except to hold to your religion and what you are upon regarding your companion, then make peace with the man and return to your lands until time shows you his judgment.' They came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, we have decided not to invoke the curse upon you, and to remain upon our religion.' And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If they had invoked the curse, they would have been uprooted from the face of the earth." And he also said: "If they had done it, the valley would have been set ablaze with fire upon them." His saying "lahuwa" may be a separator (faṣl, the pronoun that separates the predicate from the subject) and may be the start of a sentence (ibtidāʾ).
