Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 65–66:

(p-247) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not reason?﴾ ﴿Here you are, you are those who argued about that of which you have knowledge; so why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾

The exegetes differed concerning who this verse was revealed about. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Christians of Najran and the rabbis of the Jews gathered before the Prophet, peace be upon him, and they disputed in his presence. The rabbis said: Abraham was none but a Jew, and the Christians said: Abraham was none but a Christian. So Allah revealed the verse." As-Suddi and Qatadah said, and at-Tabari related from Mujahid and Qatadah as well, that they both said: the verse was revealed because of the claim of the Jews that he was of them and that he died a Jew. He placed this statement under a separate heading of its own.

The correct view is that all the interpreters went in one direction, and that the verse concerns the Jews and the Christians. The wording of the verse indicates this, so how could anyone defend one of the two groups in this? This verse clarifies the corruption of these claims, which are not even worth considering given the presence of a decisive proof of their falsity, because they claimed for Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil) creeds that did not arise on earth and did not exist until a long time after his death. And since the proof is rational, Allah, the Exalted, said to them, rebuking them: "Will you not reason?"

The readers differed concerning His saying "ha antum" in terms of the elongation (madd), the hamza, and its omission. Ibn Kathir read "ha'antum" in the pattern of "ha'antum" (with a hamza, short), Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "hantum" as an interrogative without a hamza, and the rest read "ha antum" elongated and with a hamza. They did not differ on the elongation of "ha'ulaa'" and "ulaa'". The basis of Ibn Kathir's reading is that he replaced the hamza of interrogation with the ha', intending "a-antum". The basis of the reading of Nafi' and Abu 'Amr is one of two matters: it is permissible that the ha of exhortation (al-tanbih) entered upon "antum", and the exhortation applies to the whole sentence, as it entered upon their saying "halumma", and as "ya" of exhortation entered in His saying "alla ya-sjudu", and in the words of the poet:

"O slayer of Allah's creatures, the children that Umm al-Hunaydh brings with her from a fire of hers that is kindled"

And in the words of another:

"O curse of Allah and of all the peoples, and of the righteous, upon Sam'an from Jar"

The hamza of "antum" was lightened and was not fully articulated after the alif, as they said of "habā'ah": "habāh". It is also permissible that the ha in "hantum" be a replacement for the hamza of interrogation, as in the basis of Ibn Kathir's reading, and that the alif be what enters between the two hamzas to separate them. The basis of the reading of the rest, "ha antum" with a hamza and elongation, admits both of the two bases of the reading of Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, and they realized the hamza that follows the alif and did not lighten it as Abu 'Amr and Nafi' lightened it. As for one who does not hold that the alif is added to separate the two hamzas, as Abu 'Amr holds, then the ha in His saying should be for exhortation and not a replacement for the hamza of interrogation. As for "ha'ulaa'", it has two dialects, the elongated and the shortened, and the verse of al-A'sha combines both in some transmissions:

"These, then these, I have given sandals studded with sandals"

As for the grammatical analysis of "ha antum ha'ulaa'": it is a subject and predicate (ibtida' wa khabar), and "hajajtum" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) which cannot be dispensed with, and it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then you are these who kill﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. It is also possible that "ha'ulaa'" is an appositive (badal) or an adjective (sifah), and the predicate is "hajajtum", and according to the school of the Kufans, "hajajtum" is a relative clause (silah) for "ulaa'", and the predicate is in His saying: "fa-lima tuhajjuna".

As for the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿concerning that of which you have knowledge﴾, it means: according to your claim. What is meant is: concerning that about which your claim is made doubtful, and the rational proof does not refute you. At-Tabari explained this position as meaning: concerning that of which they have knowledge through their books and their reports, of what they have become certain of and whose authenticity is established for them. But he, may Allah have mercy on him, overlooked that what is of this kind does not require argument with them about it, because they find it with Muhammad ﷺ as it was there in its reality. The rest of the verse is clear.

(p-٢٤٩) His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf (upright in faith), a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who believe, and Allah is the Protector of the believers.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, informs in this verse about the true reality of Abraham's affair. He negates from him Judaism, Christianity, and polytheism, which is the worship of idols, and the polytheism that is contained within Judaism and Christianity is included in that. The ordering of the negation is in the highest eloquence: He first negates the religions themselves and establishes the good state, then He negates in a way that makes clear that those religions contain this corruption, which is shirk. This is like when you say: "I did not take money for you, rather I safeguarded it, and I was not a thief," so you have negated the worst possible form of taking.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informs with emphatic affirmation that the people most worthy of Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him, are the people who followed him in his ḥanīfiyyah religion. Here enters everyone who followed the ḥanīfiyyah during the intervals between prophets. "This Prophet" refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ), because he was sent with the easy (samḥah) ḥanīfiyyah. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 69–71:

The words of the Most High:

﴿A party of the People of the Book wish they could lead you astray, but they lead astray none but themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾ ﴿O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you bear witness?﴾ ﴿O People of the Book, why do you confuse the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾

God Most High informs us about a party that wishes and desires to lead the Muslims astray, meaning to destroy them in their religion and place them in error. Then He explained the "party" with His words ﴿from the People of the Book﴾. The particle "min" (from) may be partitive (lil-tab'id), so that the party would be the leaders and rabbis to whose words people incline. It may also be explanatory of the genus (li-bayan al-jins), so that the party would be all of the People of the Book.

Al-Tabari said: "yudillunakum" means "yuhlikunakum" (they destroy you), and he cited the verse of Jarir:

؎ You were a speck in a green, foaming wave, / which the flood cast about, so it strayed astray (ḍalla ḍalālā).

And the verse of al-Nabigha:

؎ Then his worshippers returned with a clear eye... ***

[the verse continues]

(p-251) This is an explanation that is not specific to the word itself; rather, this meaning of "strayed" (ḍalāl) is applied to it in the verse and in the two lines, where it is accompanied by destruction. As for explaining the word "ḍalāl" as "destruction," that is not sound (ghayr qawīm).

His words, Most High: ﴿and they lead astray none but themselves﴾ inform us that the evil of their deeds returns upon them, and that by their distance from Islam they are the ones who are astray. Then He informed us that they do not perceive this, meaning they are not alert to it. The word (yash'urūn, "perceive") is derived from "shi'ār" (the undergarment), which is derived from "sha'r" (hair/feeling). It has been said that the meaning is: "and they do not perceive that they cannot reach leading you astray."

Then God Most High, through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ), rebuked them by putting a question to them. The meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad: for what reason do you disbelieve in the signs of God, which is the sign of the Qur'an, while you bear witness that its matter and the description of Muhammad, who brings it, are in your Book? This meaning was stated by Qatada, Ibn Juraij and al-Suddi. The verse may also mean by "the signs" what appeared at the hands of Muhammad (peace be upon him), such as the challenge to the Arabs (ta'jīz al-'Arab), the announcement of unseen matters, the speech of groups, and other things. On this reading, "tash-hadūn" (you witness) means "tahḍarūn" (you are present) and "tu'āyinūn" (you see directly). The first interpretation is stronger, because it has been narrated that the People of the Book, before the appearance of Muhammad (ﷺ), used to report the description of the Prophet who would come and his condition; when he appeared they disbelieved in him out of envy. So their earlier report of his coming is the testimony to which they were witnesses. Makki said: It has also been said that these verses refer to the Qurayza, the Nadir, the Banu Qaynuqa', and the Christians of Najran.

His words, Most High: ﴿why do you confuse the truth﴾ mean: you mix (takhlitūn). You say: "labastu al-amr" (with the vowel of the ba' being fatha), meaning "I mixed it." From this is His words, Most High: ﴿And We would have confused for them what they confuse﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. You also say: "labistu al-thawb" (with the vowel of the ba' being kasra), meaning "I wore the garment." Ibn Zayd said: the truth they confused is the revealed Torah, and the falsehood with which they confused it is what they wrote with their own hands and attributed to the Torah. Ibn 'Abbas said: the truth is their Islam at the beginning of the day, and the falsehood is their disbelief at its end. The verse was revealed concerning the statement of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sayf, 'Adi ibn Zayd, and al-Harith ibn 'Awf: "Come, let us believe in what was revealed to Muhammad at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end; perhaps we may confuse the Muslims regarding their affair." Qatada and Ibn Juraij said: "why do you confuse the truth with falsehood" means: why do you mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, when you know that the religion of God which is not accepted other than it is Islam?

So the meaning according to this is: why do you keep these religions and sustain them, so that there is confusion for all the people? Some of the exegetes said: the truth they confused is their statement that Muhammad is a prophet sent, and the falsehood with which they confused it is the statement of their rabbis: "But it is not for us; rather, the religion of Moses is perpetual."

His words, Most High: ﴿and conceal the truth while you know﴾ mean the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus said al-Rabi', Ibn Juraij, Qatada and others. In His words ﴿while you know﴾ there is a clear rebuke for obstinacy. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: If it had been said "wa-taktumū al-ḥaqq" (and that you conceal the truth, in the subjunctive), it would be permissible according to your saying: "why do you combine this and that?" But "taktumū" is in a position of nasb (accusative) as an adverbial of time (ẓarf) according to the Kufans, and with an implied "an" (that) according to our companions (the Basrans). Abu 'Ali said: the adverbial reading is ugly here, and likewise the implied "an," because "taktumūn" is coordinated with an affirmed statement (mūjab muqarrar), and it is not the subject of a question. He only asked about the cause of the confusion, and the confusion is an affirmed fact. So the verse is not like the saying: "Do you eat fish and drink milk?" nor like your saying: "Do you stand so that I stand?" Coordinating with an affirmed statement is ugly when put in the accusative, except in a poetic necessity, as is narrated:

؎ .............. / "and I join with the Hijaz, so I may rest."

Sibawayh said regarding your saying: "Did you travel until you enter the city?" that only the accusative is permissible for "tadkhula" (enter), because the travelling is what is questioned about and is not affirmed. But if you say: "Which of them travelled until he enters it?" you put it in the nominative, because the travelling is affirmed and the question has fallen upon something other than it.

(p-253) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may return."﴾ ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion. Say: "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God—that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you before your Lord."﴾

In this verse God informs us that a group of the Jews, from among their rabbis, resorted to this scheme to deceive the Muslims. Al-Hasan said: "The Jews of Khaybar said this to the Jews of Madina." Qatada, Abu Malik, al-Suddi and others said: "Some of the rabbis said: Let us show belief in Muhammad at the beginning of the day, then let us disbelieve in him at the end of the day. Then the Muslims will say at that point: What is the matter with these people? They were with us, then they turned away from us. This can only be because a truth about the matter has been revealed to them, so they are in doubt, and perhaps they will return from belief in Muhammad ﷺ." Since the rabbis were presumed to have knowledge, sound judgment and familiarity with the ancient Scripture, they hoped that the Arabs would be deceived by this stratagem, so they did it: they came to the Prophet ﷺ early in the day and said: "O Muhammad, you are the one described in our Book, but give us time until the evening so that we may consider our affair." Then they returned in the evening and said: "We have considered, and you are not him."

"Wajh" (face, front) in this interpretation is in the accusative, governed by "āminū" (believe), and the meaning is: show belief at the front of the day. The pronoun in "ākhirahu" (its end) refers to the day.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: the verse was revealed because the Jews resorted to plotting against the believers: they prayed the dawn prayer with the Prophet ﷺ, then they returned at the end of the day and prayed their own prayer, so that people would see that some misguidance had appeared to them from him after they had followed him. This view is close to the first view.

A group of the exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning the matter of the qibla. The Messenger of God ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer facing Syria as he used to pray, then the qibla was changed, and he prayed the noon prayer—and it was said the afternoon prayer—facing Mecca. The rabbis then said to their followers and to the Arabs: "Believe in what was revealed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve in this last qibla."

According to this interpretation, the governing element of "wajh al-nahār" is the verb "unzila" (was revealed), and the pronoun in "ākhirahu" may refer either to the day or to "alladhī unzila" (that which was revealed). "Yarji'ūn" (that they may return), on this interpretation, means: from Mecca to our qibla, which is Syria; so said the proponent of this interpretation.

"Wajh al-nahār" means its first part, the part one faces, by analogy with the face of a person. Likewise one says: ṣadr al-nahār (the start of the day) and ghurrat al-ʿām and al-shahr (the first of the year and the month). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Did you kill him in the first of Islam?" From this also is the verse of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād al-ʿAbsī:

"Whoever was glad at the killing of Mālik,
let him come to our women at the face of day;
he will find the women bareheaded, lamenting him,
having risen before the dawn broke."

He says this about Mālik ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhayma al-ʿAbsī, and they had already taken vengeance for him. Among them the slain was not mourned or lamented until his blood-debt had been exacted.

The meaning is: whoever was pleased by our calamity in him, let him look at what shows that we have overtaken his vengeance, and so let him be grieved and distressed by that. From the figurative use of "wajh" is the saying: "I did such-and-such ʿalā wajh al-dahr," meaning in the distant past.

God, exalted, mentioned about this group of the People of the Book that they said: "And do not believe except in one who follows your religion." There is no disagreement among the people of interpretation that this statement is from the words of the group. People differed concerning His saying, exalted: "that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you." Mujahid and others among the people of interpretation said: the whole utterance is from the words of the group to their followers, and His saying, exalted, "Say: indeed, guidance is the guidance of God," is a parenthetical interjection between the two statements.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation the speech may bear several meanings. One of them: "Do not affirm with genuine affirmation and believe except in one who came with the like of your religion, out of aversion, or fear, or caution, that anyone should be given prophethood and honour the like of what you were given, and out of caution that they should argue with you by your affirmation of them before your Lord if you do not persevere in it." This view, on this meaning, is the fruit of envy and disbelief, together with knowledge of the soundness of Muhammad's prophethood ﷺ.

It may also be that the sense is "that no one be given," with "lā" omitted because the context indicates it. The speech may also mean: "Do not affirm and believe, regarding the bestowal of the like of what you were given on anyone, except in one who follows your religion and comes with its like and supports it, for that is not granted to anyone other than you," and "or they should argue with you before your Lord" means: "unless they argue with you," as one says: "I will not leave you unless you pay me my due." This view, on this meaning, is the fruit of denying Muhammad ﷺ, from a belief held by them that prophethood is only among the Children of Israel.

The speech may also mean: "Do not believe in Muhammad and acknowledge his prophethood, though you know its soundness, except for the Jews who are of you; and 'that anyone should be given the like of what you were given' is a description of Muhammad's condition." The meaning is: you conceal, by your acknowledgement, that someone has been given the like of what you were given, or: they—meaning the Arabs—will argue with you by acknowledgement before your Lord.

Abu ʿAlī said: "tu'minū" is transitive through the implied preposition "bi" in "an yu'tā," just as it is transitive at the beginning of the verse in "bi-alladhī unzila." The "lām" in "li-man tabiʿa" cannot easily be attached to "tu'minū," since you have already connected it with "bi," so that it would govern two prepositional complements, just as one cannot make it govern two objects when it is transitive to only one. The matter of this "lām" is rather understood by sense: the meaning is "do not acknowledge that God gives anyone the like of what you were given, except to one who..." This is like saying: "I acknowledged to Zayd a thousand," where the "lām" is connected by meaning, not superfluous in the manner of "in kuntum lil-ru'yā taʿburūn" (Yusuf 43), nor connected as a direct object. Abu ʿAlī said: "āmana" is also transitive with "lām" in His saying: "But none believed in Mūsā except a few of his people" (Yunus 83); and His saying: "Do you believe him?" and His saying: "He believes in God and believes for the believers" (al-Tawba 61). "Aḥad" entered this speech only because of the negation occurring in "wa-lā tu'minū," just as "min" entered in His saying: "Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish that any good be sent down upon you from your Lord" (al-Baqara 105). Just as "min" entered the complement of "an yunazzala" because it is the object of the negation that follows the beginning of the speech, so "aḥad" entered the complement of "an" in "an yu'tā aḥad," because the negation entered at the beginning of the speech.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is because "aḥad," which carries the sense of generality, does not occur in an affirmative sentence, since it conveys no meaning there. Ibn Kathir alone among the seven readers recited "ā'an yu'tā" with a long vowel, in the form of an interrogative expressing affirmation. Abu ʿAlī explained Ibn Kathir's reading as follows: the whole speech is from the words of the group, except the interjection "Say: indeed, guidance is the guidance of God," which is undisputedly from God, exalted, to Muhammad ﷺ. He said: with the interrogative, "an yu'tā" cannot be taken as governed by the verb preceding it, because the interrogative is decisive. It is therefore permissible for "an" to be in the nominative position as the subject of an inceptive sentence, with an omitted predicate whose estimate is: "you affirm it, or you acknowledge it, or you mention it to others," and similar expressions indicated by the context; and "yuḥājjūkum" would then be coordinated with "an yu'tā." Abu ʿAlī said: it is also permissible for the position of "an" to be accusative, so the meaning would be: "Do you spread it abroad, or do you mention it: that anyone should be given the like of what you were given?" This would be in the sense of His saying about them: "Do you tell them what God has opened to you?" (al-Baqara 76). Thus on both readings the meaning of the verse is a rebuke from the rabbis to the followers for their affirmation that Muhammad is a sent prophet; and His saying, exalted, "or they should argue with you" would be in the sense of the accusative "an," i.e., "or do you wish that they should argue with you?" Abu ʿAlī said: this is a place where the reading of someone other than Ibn Kathir should be preferred over Ibn Kathir's reading, because singular nouns do not necessarily denote plurality.

Yet "aḥad" in reference to the like of prophethood indicates it, insofar as it implies followers.

Al-Aʿmash and Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamza read "in yu'tā" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning: no one has been given the like of the honour you have been given. This reading may be understood as a speech from the group that spoke, and their saying "or they should argue with you" would mean "or let them argue with you." This is on the firm insistence that no one will be given the like of what was given; it may also mean "unless they argue with you," which allows that someone may be given that if the proof is established for him. This is the arrangement of the explanation and the readings according to the view of those who say the whole speech is from the words of the group.

It is also related from some grammarians that the meaning is: "that He not give anyone," with "lā" omitted because the speech indicates it, as in His saying, exalted: "God makes clear to you lest you go astray" (al-Nisa' 176), meaning "lest you not go astray." And his saying "aw yuhajjukum" (or they dispute with you) would mean "or let them dispute with you," for they will overcome you.

This view explains its meanings, and what came before in the words of others of the division (of meanings). And God is the One sought for help.

He attributed that to the Lord as an honour. It is as if the meaning were: "or they dispute with you by the truth."

The meaning is: the bounty of God is not resembled by the bounty of any of His creatures. The most apparent thing in this recitation is that it is an address from Muhammad (peace be upon him) to his community, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: "If anyone gives anyone (anything)."

﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may return."﴾ ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion. Say: "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God—that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you before your Lord."﴾

Qatada, Abu Malik, al-Suddi and others said: "Some of the rabbis said: Let us show belief in Muhammad at the beginning of the day, then let us disbelieve in him at the end of the day. Then the Muslims will say at that point: What is the matter with these people? They were with us, then they turned away from us. This can only be because a truth about the matter has been revealed to them, so they are in doubt, and perhaps they will return from belief in Muhammad ﷺ." Since the rabbis were presumed to have knowledge, sound judgment and familiarity with the ancient Scripture, they hoped that the Arabs would be deceived by this stratagem, so they did it: they came to the Prophet ﷺ early in the day and said: "O Muhammad, you are the one described in our Book, but give us time until the evening so that we may consider our affair." Then they returned in the evening and said: "We have considered, and you are not him."

This view is close to the first view.

The most apparent thing in this recitation is that it is an address from Muhammad (peace be upon him) to his community, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: "If anyone gives anyone (anything)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 74–75:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Say, "Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He grants it to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing."﴾ [Al-Imran: 73] ﴿He specifies for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿And among the People of the Scripture is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you remain standing over him.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say, indeed bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ [Al-Imran: 73] up to His saying "the Great" is a refutation of the Jews in their claim: "The prophethood of Musa is perpetual, and Allah will never give anyone what He gave the Children of Israel of prophethood and nobility." The rest of the verse, including the word "wasi'" (All-Encompassing) and other matters, has had its parallels discussed earlier.

Then the Most High informed us that the People of the Scripture are of two categories with regard to trustworthiness. The purpose of the verse is to censure the treacherous among them, and to refute their opinion and their lying against Allah in regarding the wealth of the Arabs as lawful for them. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it is "tiyamnahu" with a ta' and a ya' in both places, and likewise "tiyamnan" in Surah Yusuf. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: "This is the dialect of Tamim."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I do not regard it as anything but a Qurashi dialect, which is the kasra on the nun of the plural, as in "nasta'in" (we seek help), and on the alif of the first person, as in the saying of Ibn 'Umar, "la ikhaluhu" (I do not think it), and on the ta' of the second person, as in this verse. They do not give the ya' of the third person a kasra. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "tiyamnan" with it, as did Ibn Mas'ud, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Ibn Thabbab. The discussion of "qintar" has already been given at the beginning of the surah.

Most of the people read "yu'addihi ilayk" with a kasra on the ha' which is the pronoun referring to the qintar, and likewise in the other instance, which is the pronoun referring to the dinar. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, 'Asim and al-A'mash agreed on sukun (silencing) of the ha', and likewise every similar form in the Qur'an, such as "nusliHi jahannam" (We will burn him in Hell), "nu'tihi" (We will give him), and "nuwalliHi" (We will turn him), except for one word that is reported from Abu 'Amr as having a kasra, namely His saying, ﴿Throw it to them﴾ [An-Naml: 28], "fa-alqih ilayhim." Abu Ishaq said: "This sukun reported from these men is a clear error, because the ha' should not be jussified (given a jazm), and when it is not jussified, it is not permissible to make it sakin in connected speech. As for Abu 'Amr, I think he used to pronounce the kasra in a brief, slurred manner, and so it was misattributed to him, just as he was misattributed in 'bari'ikum' (your Creator). Sibawayh, who is an authority on the like of this, reported from him that he gave it a light kasra."

The qintar in this verse is an example of a large amount of wealth, which includes more than a qintar and less. As for the dinar, it may be the same, an example of what is small, and it may be intended to refer to a class that is treacherous only in a dinar or more. The treacherous are not mentioned in relation to less, because they are a rabble and a worthless residue.

Most of the people read "dumta" with a damma on the dal. Ibn Thabbab, al-A'mash, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan and others read "dimta" and "dumtum" with a kasra on the dal throughout the Qur'an. Abu Ishaq said: from their saying "dimta, tadamu," like "nimta, tanamu" (you slept, you sleep), and it is a dialect. "Dama" means: to remain upon a certain state. "Tadwim" upon a thing is circling around the thing, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

...........................and the sun bewildered, for it in the air is a circling.

"Dawam" is dizziness that seizes a person's head, so he sees things spinning for him. The "tadawwur" of a bird in the sky is its remaining steady when it spreads its wings and circles, and stagnant water and the like is that which seems to revolve around its center.

His saying "qa'iman" (standing) may have two meanings. Al-Zajjaj, Qatadah and Mujahid said: its meaning is: standing over the collection of your debt. They mean by the various kinds of collection: pressing and litigation before the judges. According to this interpretation, the form of this continual standing is not observed, rather the word is from a person's standing over his affairs, that is, his diligence in them. Al-Suddi and others said: "qa'iman" in this verse means: standing over his head, in the well-known posture. That is the extreme of pressing, because it means that he is busy with another matter which he intends to attend to. A group of jurists took this interpretation and derived from the verses the permissibility of imprisonment, because the one over whom his creditor stands prevents him from his disposals outside of judicial process, and there is no difference between preventing dispositions and imprisonment.

This verse and what follows were revealed, as it is reported, because a group of Arabs had debts owed to them by some people among the People of the Scripture. When those Arabs embraced Islam, the Jews said to them: "We will not pay you anything, since you have left the religion you were upon." So the verse was revealed concerning that. It is also reported that the Children of Israel used to believe in the lawfulness of the wealth of the Arabs because they were people of idols. When Islam came and some Arabs embraced it, the Jews remained upon that belief, so the verse was revealed to protect against that.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, every matter of the Jahiliyyah is under my feet, except trust, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked."

(p-262) The words of the Exalted: ﴿That is because they say, "There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered (al-ummiyyin)," and they tell lies against God while they know it.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75] ﴿Yes! Whoever fulfils his covenant and is mindful of God, then God loves those who are mindful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price, those will have no share in the Hereafter, and God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾

The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to their not returning the trust (al-amanah) for a dinar or more, according to one of the two interpretations. The pronoun in "they say" refers to the mass of the Children of Israel, because they used to say: "We are the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and the Arabs are unlettered (ummiyyun), idol-worshippers. Their wealth is lawful to us whenever we gain control over any of it. There is no proof against us in that, and no path (sabil) for any objector or critic to reach us regarding it." The unlettered (al-ummiyyun) are the people who do not write, because they do not know how to write. The derivation of the word has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The metaphorical use of "path" (sabil) here, meaning proof, is in the manner of the words of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"And am I, if I console myself with a grove
of the acacia trees, one upon whom a path is open?"

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Against such there is no path (sabil)﴾ [al-Shura: 41] are of this meaning. It is common in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. It is related that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "We pass, in military campaigns, by the property of the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah), and we take from it a sheep, a hen, and the like." He said: "And what do you say?" He said: "We say: there is no harm upon us." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is just as the People of the Book said: ﴿There is no path against us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]. Indeed, when they pay the poll-tax (jizyah), their property is not lawful to you except with their willing consent."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and they tell lies against God while they know it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75] are a censure of the Children of Israel, that they lie against God the Exalted about things without any basis, while they are knowledgeable of the places of truth, had they intended them. Among the gravest of these is the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of a group of the interpreters. It is related from al-Suddi (p-263) and Ibn Jurayj and others that a group of the People of the Book claimed that the Torah contains God's permission for them to take the property of the unlettered. This was a lie of theirs, and they knew that it was a lie in this matter. The two said: the reference of this verse is to that specific lie in this section.

Then God, the Exalted, at the beginning of their statement "there is no blame on us," refuted it with His words "Yes" (bala), meaning: rather, there is a path against them, and a proof, and a reckoning. Then He informed, in the form of a conditional, that whoever fulfils the covenant and is mindful of God's punishment for breaking it, then indeed he is beloved to God. The Arabs say "wafa bi-l-'ahd" and "awfa bihi" with the same meaning, and "awfa" is the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-Tabari and others interpreted the pronoun in His words "His covenant" as referring to God, the Exalted. Some of the exegetes said: it refers to "whoever" (man). The two views return to one meaning, because God's command to fulfil is connected to the covenant of every person. Ibn 'Abbas said: "ittaqa" (is mindful) in this verse means: is mindful of shirk (associating partners with God). Then the response to the conditional came in a general form, "the mindful" (al-muttaqin), as an honouring of piety and an urging towards it.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who sell the covenant of God﴾ ... the verse is a threat to whoever does these deeds until the Day of Resurrection. It is a verse that includes disbelief and what is below it, such as denying rights and breaking pledges. Each person takes from the threat of the verse according to the measure of his offence.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of its revelation. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews: Abu Rafi', Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who abandoned the covenant of God in the Torah for the gains and leadership they were pursuing. It is related that it was revealed because of a dispute between al-Ash'ath ibn Qays and a man from the Jews over land. The oath became obligatory upon the Jew, and al-Ash'ath said: "Then he will swear, O Messenger of God, and take my property." So the verse was revealed. It is related that (p-264) al-Ash'ath ibn Qays disputed over land with a man of his kin, and the oath became obligatory upon al-Ash'ath, while in reality he was in the wrong, having seized that land in his time of ignorance (jahiliyyah). So the verse was revealed, and al-Ash'ath refrained from the oath, was scrupulous, gave up the land, and added another land from his own.

It is related that the verse was revealed because of a dispute involving someone other than al-Ash'ath ibn Qays. Al-Sha'bi said: the verse was revealed concerning a man who displayed a commodity in the market from the beginning of the day. When it was the end of the day, a man came to him and bargained with him, and he swore, lying: "He withheld it at the start of the day for such and such, and were it not for the evening, he would not have sold it." So the verse was revealed concerning him. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "The false oath (al-yamin al-fajirah) is among the major sins," then he recited this verse. Ibn Mas'ud said: "We used to consider, while we were with our Prophet, that among the sins that are not forgiven is the oath of patience (yamin al-sabr), if its swearer commits perjury in it." God has made oaths in these expressions a purchase, so they are also a price. "Khalaq" means portion, share, and due measure, and it is used for what is desired (mustahabbat).

Al-Tabari said: "And God will not speak to them" means: with what would please them. Others said: God, the Exalted, negated that He would speak to them at all, because He speaks to His believing and mindful servants. Some scholars said: it is an expression for anger. The meaning is: He does not give them any concern and does not be pleased with them. "And He will not purify them" (wa la yuzakkihim) may have two meanings: one, that He cleanses them from sins and their defilements; the other, that He increases their deeds, so it is an increase for them. Both meanings are negated for them in the Hereafter. "Painful" (alim) is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of the active participle (mu'lim), so the meaning is: causing pain.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 78–79:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And indeed, among them is a party who distort their tongues with the Book, so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah. And they speak a lie against Allah while they know.﴾ ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment, and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants to me rather than to Allah."﴾

The pronoun in "minhum" refers to the People of the Book. And the firq (party) is a group of people, derived from faraqa, meaning to separate and make one thing distinct from another. And "yalwūna" means: they distort and devise by altering meanings, through the resemblance of words, their shared usage, and the diversity of interpretations they admit. An example of this is their saying: ﴿We have heard and disobeyed, and hear without being made to hear﴾ [al-Nisa: 46] and the like. Mere substitution is not called layy (twisting), while the real meaning of layy in garments, ropes and the like is twisting and bending them. From it comes laywu al-'unuq (twisting of the neck). Then this was used for proofs, disputes and arguments, by analogy with that bending found in bodies. From it comes their saying: khasm alwā (a disputant who twists his argument). From it is the saying of the poet:

"If there were in Layla any fragrance of dispute, I would twist the necks of the disputants, the stubborn ones."

And another said:

"You found me twisting far from the path."

The majority of readers recited "yalwūna," the present tense of lawā, on the pattern fa'ala with the 'ayn lightened. Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shayba ibn Nisāh recited "yulawwūna" with the waw doubled and the lam fathah from lawwā, on the pattern fa''ala with the 'ayn doubled, and this is doubling for intensity, not doubling for transitivity. Ḥumayd recited "yalūna" with the lam dammah and the waw sukūn; in origin it is "yalwūna" like the recitation of the majority, but the dammah on the waw was turned into a hamzah because that is its form in some dialects, so it became "yalʾūna," then the dammah of the hamzah was transferred to the lam, so it became "yalūna." The Book in this place is the Torah. The pronoun of the subject in His saying "li-tahsabūhu" refers to the Muslims.

His saying, "wa mā huwa min 'indi Allāh" (but it is not from Allah), is a negation that it was revealed as they claimed. As for being "from Allah" in the sense of creation, invention and bringing into existence, all things are from Allah in that sense, and some by acquisition. The verse concerns only the meaning of revelation, so the Qadariyya's attachment to the apparent meaning of His saying "wa mā huwa min 'indi Allāh" is invalid. A parallel to His saying Exalted is He, "wa yaqūlūna 'alā Allāh al-kadhib wa hum ya'lamūn" (and they speak a lie against Allah while they know), has already been mentioned.

His saying Exalted is He, "mā kāna li-basharin" (it is not for a human being), means: for anyone among people. Basharun is a collective noun that applies to the one and the many, and it has no singular form from its own letters. This statement's wording is a complete negation, like the saying of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is not for the son of Abū Quḥāfa to lead prayer in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Its full extent is known from the negation through the context in which it occurs, like His saying: ﴿It is not for a soul to die except by Allah's permission﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 145] and His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾ [al-Naml: 60]. That is rationally impossible. As for our verse, the negation is absolute, because we are certain that Allah does not give prophethood to liars and pretenders. "Al-kitāb" in this verse is a collective noun, and "al-ḥukm" means al-ḥikma (wisdom). From it is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Indeed, some poetry is wisdom." And "thumma" in His saying Exalted is He, "thumma yaqūl" (then he should say), indicates the magnification of the sin in the statement, after an interval from this blessing.

His saying "ʿibādan" is the plural of ʿabd. Among its plurals are ʿabīd and ʿibidda. Some linguists said: these plurals have one meaning. Others said: ʿibād is used for Allah's servants, while ʿabīd and ʿibidda are used for human beings. Others said: ʿibidda is only said of slaves who are the children of slaves, and it seems to be an intensive form implying immersion in servitude. What I have deduced regarding the word ʿibād is that it is the plural of ʿabd whenever the word is used in a context of elevation and indication of obedience, without any meaning of belittlement or diminishing of status. Consider His saying Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 30], "ʿibādun mukramūn" (honored servants), ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah's mercy﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and the saying of Jesus, in the sense of intercession and appeal to Allah's mercy: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 118], thereby honoring them. Some linguists said: the Christians of al-Ḥīra, who were Arabs, when they obeyed Kisrā and came under his command, the Arabs called them al-ʿibād, and they were not called ʿabīd. Others said: rather, they were a group of Arabs from various tribes who gathered, became Christians, and named themselves al-ʿibād, as if it were an affiliation to the worship of Allah. As for ʿabīd, it is used for belittlement, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Say to Dūdān, slaves of the stick, what deceived you about the brave lion?"

From it is the saying of Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib: "Are you anything but slaves of my father?" And from it is the saying of Allah Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46], because it is a place of compassion and information about the paucity of their victory and power, and that He Exalted is not unjust to them despite that. Since the word ʿibād requires obedience, it was not used here; for this reason it is appropriate in His saying Exalted: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. This kind of reflection is pursued to reveal the marvels in distinguishing the eloquence of the Glorious Qur'an according to the sound Arabic manner.

The meaning of His saying, "kūnū ʿibādan lī min dūni Allāh" (Be servants to me rather than to Allah), is: worship me and make me a god.

The exegetes differed regarding whom the reference in His saying Exalted, "mā kāna li-basharin," points to. Al-Naqqāsh and others said: the reference is to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and the verse refutes the Christians who said ʿĪsā is God, and claimed that his worship is a law and is grounded in his commands. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, Ibn Jurayj and a group of exegetes said: rather, the reference is to Muḥammad, peace be upon him. The occasion of revelation of the verse: "Abū Rāfiʿ al-Quraẓī said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when the rabbis of the Jews and the delegation of the Christians of Najrān gathered: 'O Muḥammad, do you only want us to worship you and take you as a god, as the Christians worshipped ʿĪsā?' The leader of the Christians of Najrān said: 'Is that what you want, O Muḥammad, and to that you call us?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I seek Allah's refuge, I was not commanded with that, nor did I call to it,' and the verse was revealed concerning that." Some scholars said: the rabbis wanted to impose this statement on Muḥammad (ﷺ) when he recited to them: ﴿Say, if you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 31], and the meaning of the verse is: follow me in what I call you to of obedience to Allah, but they distorted it by their interpretation, and this is of the kind of their twisting the Book with their tongues.

The majority of reciters read "thumma yaqūla" with the naṣb (fatḥah). Shibl related from Ibn Kathīr, and Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr, "thumma yaqūlu" with the lam raised, and this is on the basis of resumption (qaṭʿ) and an implied subject. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited "ʿibādan liya" with the yā' vocalised with a fatḥah.

﴿And indeed, among them is a party who distort their tongues with the Book, so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah. And they speak a lie against Allah while they know.﴾ ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment, and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants to me rather than to Allah."﴾

The pronoun in "minhum" refers to the People of the Book. And the firq (party) is a group of people, derived from faraqa, meaning to separate and make one thing distinct from another. And "yalwūna" means: they distort and devise by altering meanings, through the resemblance of words, their shared usage, and the diversity of interpretations they admit. An example of this is their saying: ﴿We have heard and disobeyed, and hear without being made to hear﴾ [al-Nisa: 46] and the like. Mere substitution is not called layy (twisting), while the real meaning of layy in garments, ropes and the like is twisting and bending them. From it comes laywu al-'unuq (twisting of the neck). Then this was used for proofs, disputes and arguments, by analogy with that bending found in bodies. From it comes their saying: khasm alwā (a disputant who twists his argument). From it is the saying of the poet:

"If there were in Layla any fragrance of dispute, I would twist the necks of the disputants, the stubborn ones."

And another said:

"You found me twisting far from the path."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 80–81 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿But rather, be rabbaniyyin (lordly ones) by what you have taught of the Book and by what you have studied.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79] ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelief after you have submitted?﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall support him."﴾

The meaning: "But rather, say: 'Be rabbaniyyin'," which is the plural of rabbani (lordly).

The grammarians (al-nuhat) differed over this relative form (nisba). One group said it is attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb), in that he is a scholar of His knowledge, one who acts in obedience to Him, and one who teaches people what He has commanded. The alif and nun were added for emphasis, as they say lihyani (bearded) and sha'rani (hairy) in attribution to lihya (beard) and sha'r (hair). Another group said that rabbani is attributed to al-rubban, which means the teacher and scholar of people who manages their affairs. It is derived from rabba, yarubbu, meaning to set right and to nurture, and this nun was added to it as it was added in ghadban and 'atshan, and then rabbani was formed as its attribution.

The scholars differed over the description of the one who deserves to be called rabbani. Abu Razin said: the rabbani is the wise scholar. Mujahid said: the rabbani is the jurist (faqih). Qatada and others said: the rabbani is the knowledgeable and forbearing scholar. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is the wise jurist. al-Dahhak said: he is the jurist and scholar. Ibn Zayd said: the rabbani is the ruler of affairs, who nurtures (yarubbu) the people, that is, sets them right. So the rabbaniyyun are the rulers, the rabbis (ahbar) and the scholars. Mujahid also said: the rabbani is above the habr (rabbi), because the habr is the scholar, whereas the rabbani is the one who combines knowledge and jurisprudence with insight into governance and management, and with taking charge of the affairs of the subjects and what sets them right in their religion and their worldly life. In al-Bukhari: the rabbani is the one who nurtures people with the minor aspects of knowledge before its major aspects. So the sum of what is said about the rabbani is that he is the one who knows the Lord and the Law, who is correct in judgement regarding the words and deeds he undertakes among people.

His saying "bima kuntum" means: because of your being scholars and students. Here ma is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and it cannot be a relative pronoun (mawsula), because the returning pronoun that would have been required could not be contained in "kuntum tu'allimuna," and none of this is valid, since kana has already fulfilled its predicate explicitly, which is "tu'allimuna," and likewise "tu'allimuna" has already fulfilled its object, which is "al-Kitab," explicitly. Nothing remains except that ma is a verbal-source particle, since no returning pronoun is possible. And "tu'allimuna" here means "tu'arrifuna" (you make known), so it is transitive to one object.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ta'lamuna" with a sukun on the 'ain and a light lam. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tu'allimuna" with the letter heavy, with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the lam. This is on the basis of transitivising the verb by doubling, and the second object in this reading is omitted, its estimate being: "tu'allimuna al-nas al-Kitab" (you teach people the Book). The two readings are close in meaning. I have preferred the light reading because of their lightening of "tadrusun," and because knowledge is the cause which obliges a person who is granted success to be rabbani, whereas teaching is not a condition for this. I have preferred the other reading on the basis that teaching includes knowledge, whereas knowledge does not include teaching, so the heavy reading comes out as more emphatic in praise. And from the point of view that the one who knows the state of one who knows, teaching is, as it were, contained within knowledge. In my view the light reading is more preferable.

Mujahid and al-Hasan read "ta'allamuna" with a fatha on the ta' and the 'ain and a shadda on the open lam. The majority of people read "tadrusun" with a damma on the ra', from darasa, meaning to persist in reading the Book and to repeat it. Abu Haywa read "tadrisun" with a kasra on the ra', and this is on the basis that it is said of the imperfect of darasa: yadrusu and yadrisu. It was also transmitted from Abu Haywa that he read "tudarrisun," with a damma on the ta' and a kasra and shadda on the ra', meaning: you teach others.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read "wa la ya'murukum" with a raf' (damma) on the ra'. Abu 'Amr used to elide the vowel of the ra' for lightness. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read "wa la ya'murakum" with a nasb (fatha). There is no disagreement about the ra' in His saying "a-ya'murukum" except the elision by Abu 'Amr. Whoever reads "la ya'murukum" with raf' has it as a fresh sentence (qat'). Sibawayh said: the meaning is "wa la ya'murukumu Allah" (nor would God command you). Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is "wa la ya'murukum hadha al-bashar alladhi utiya hadhihi al-ni'am," that is, this human who was given these blessings, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa lan ya'murakum," and this reading indicates a fresh sentence. As for the reading of the one who put the ra' in the nasb, it is coordinated with His saying "an yu'tiyahu" (that He should give him), and the meaning is: "nor is it for him to command you," as Abu 'Ali and others said. Al-Tabari said: His saying "wa la ya'murakum" with nasb is coordinated with His saying "thumma yaqula" (then he should say). This is a mistake, and the meaning does not fit with it. And al-arbab (the lords) in this verse means al-alihah (the deities).

His saying, may He be exalted, "a-ya'murukum bil-kufr" (would He command you to disbelief) is a confirmation based on this apparent meaning, whose corruption is evident.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets...﴾ the verse. The meaning: "Remember, O Muhammad, when..." It is possible that the taking of this covenant was when He brought the children of Adam out of the loins of Adam as particles (nasama), and it is possible that this taking was from every prophet in his time and at the moment of his sending. Then the wording is collected in the narration of the state in this verse. The meaning is that God, may He be exalted, took the covenant of every prophet that he and whoever believed in him would commit to belief in whoever came after him of the messengers whose proofs are manifest, and to supporting him.

The exegetes differed over the expression of what is required by the words of this verse. Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: He only took the covenant of the People of the Book, not the covenant of the prophets. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud: "wa idh akhadha Allah mithaq alladhina utu al-Kitab" (when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book). Mujahid said: "This is how the Qur'an is, and the affirmation of 'the prophets' is an error by the scribes." This wording is rejected by the consensus (ijma') of the Companions upon the codex of 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: God only took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples, so it is a taking of the covenant of all of them. Tawus said: God took the covenant of the prophets that some of them would confirm others. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: God did not send any prophet, from Adam and whoever came after him, except that the covenant was taken from him concerning Muhammad: if he is sent while he is alive, he shall surely believe in him and surely support him; and He commanded him to take it from his people. Then he recited this verse. al-Suddi also said this. And it is transmitted from Tawus that he said: the beginning of the verse is the taking of the covenant from the prophets, and His saying "thumma ja'akum" (then there comes to you) is an address to the People of the Book about the taking of the covenant from them. This was related by al-Tabari, but it is an opinion whose grammatical structure of the verse refutes it. All these sayings return to what 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas said, because the taking of the covenant from the prophets is a taking from their nations.

Hamza and others apart from the seven read "lima" with a kasra on the lam, and it is the lam of the genitive (lam al-jarr). The estimate is: "li-ajli ma ataynakum" (because of what We have given you), since you are the leaders and chiefs, and whoever is in this state is the one from whom the covenant is taken. In this reading, "ma" has the meaning of the relative pronoun alladhi, and the returning pronoun from its clause is estimated as "ataynakumuhu" (We have given you it). "Min" is for specifying the kind. His saying "thumma ja'akum" ... the verse, is a sentence coordinated upon the clause, and in this sentence a pronoun must return to the relative. Its estimate according to Sibawayh is: "rasul bihi musaddiq lima ma'akum" (a messenger, with it confirming what is with you). It was elided for lightness, just as alladhi was elided in the same clause because of the length of the speech, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. Elision from clauses is common and beautiful. As for Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, he said that His saying, may He be exalted, "lima ma'akum" is the returning pronoun to the relative in his view, since it is in meaning in the position of the pronoun which Sibawayh estimated. Al-Akhfash similarly said in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient, then God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Yusuf: 90], because the meaning is: "He does not waste their reward," since the good-doers are those who fear and are patient. Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, We surely do not waste the reward of whoever does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and likewise whatever resembles these verses. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, did not hold that the apparent noun should be placed in the position of the pronoun, as al-Akhfash held.

The lam in "la-tu'minunna" is the lam attached to the oath contained in the taking of the covenant, and the oath is separated from what is sworn upon by a prepositional phrase, which is permissible.

(Page 272) The rest of the seven read "lamma" with a fatha on the lam, and this can be construed in two ways. The first is that ma is a relative pronoun in the position of the nominative, as the subject, and the lam is the lam of the subject, and it receives what has been treated as an oath from His saying, may He be exalted, "wa idh akhadha Allah mithaq" (and when God took the covenant), and the predicate of the subject is His saying "la-tu'minunna" (you shall surely believe). "La-tu'minunna" is attached to an estimated oath, and the meaning is: "By God, you shall surely believe." This is what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said. There is an objection from the point of view of meaning when you consider what the swearing fell upon, but it is valid on the ground that the oath occurs twice for emphasis, so consider it. The returning pronoun in the clause and the returning pronoun in the sentence coordinated upon the clause, in this reading, are as we mentioned them in the reading of Hamza. As for the fact that this interpretation requires a returning pronoun from the predicate, which is "la-tu'minunna," it is His saying "bihi" (with it). The ha' in "bihi" returns to "ma," and it cannot return to "rasul," because then the relative would have no mention in its predicate returning to it.

The second way in which the reading of the readers "lamma" with a fatha on the lam can be construed is that "ma" is a conditional particle (shart), and so it is in the position of the accusative by the verb following it, which is jussive (majzum). "Ja'akum" is coordinated in the position of the jussive. The lam attached to "ma" is not the one that receives the oath, but rather the preparatory lam (al-muwatti'a), which announces the coming of the lam of the oath. It is in the position of the lam in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease do not cease, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], because it announces the coming of the one that receives the oath in His saying "la-nughriyannaka bihim" (We will surely incite you against them) [al-Ahzab: 60]. Likewise this lam announces the coming of the one that receives the oath in His saying "la-tu'minunna bihi." This lam entering upon "inna" is not one upon which the oath relies, so it is permissible for it to be elided at times and affirmed at other times, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will surely befall those among them who disbelieved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. Al-Zajjaj said: because your saying, "By God, if you come to me, I will surely honour you," is only an oath upon your action, not that the condition is attached to it, and therefore the lam entered upon the condition. In this interpretation, the fact that it is a conditional response does not require a returning pronoun, because it is an object, and an object does not require mention of a returning pronoun. The pronoun in His saying, may He be exalted, "la-tu'minunna bihi" returns to "rasul," and so it is in the reading of the one who put a kasra on the lam. As for the pronoun in His saying "wa la-tansurunnahu" (and you shall surely support him), it admits of no interpretation except that it returns to "rasul." Abu 'Ali said in al-Idghal: the response of the condition (page 273) is elided, its evidence being His saying "la-tu'minunna" upon it. Sibawayh said: I asked him (meaning al-Khalil) about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets, "Whatever I have given you..."﴾ and he said: "ma" here is in the position of "alladhi," and the lam entered upon it as it entered upon "inna" when you say, "la-in fa'alta la-af'alanna" (if you do it, I will surely do it). Then he went on explaining the aspect of the response. Abu 'Ali said: al-Khalil meant by his saying "it is in the position of alladhi" that it is a noun just as alladhi is a noun, and he did not mean that it is a relative like alladhi. He only fled from its being a particle, as it came as a particle in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed all of them, your Lord will surely pay them in full their deeds﴾ [Hud: 111], and in His saying: ﴿And indeed all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 35].

And God is the one sought for help.

Al-Mahdawi and Makki reported from Sibawayh and al-Khalil that the predicate (khabar) of the inceptive (mubtada') in the case of those who made "ma" the inceptive, according to the reading of those who pronounce the lam with a fatha, is in His words: ﴿from a Book and wisdom﴾. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 80–81 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿But rather, be rabbaniyyin (lordly ones) by what you have taught of the Book and by what you have studied.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79] ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelief after you have submitted?﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall support him."﴾

The meaning: "But rather, say: 'Be rabbaniyyin'," which is the plural of rabbani (lordly).

The grammarians (al-nuhat) differed over this relative form (nisba). One group said it is attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb), in that he is a scholar of His knowledge, one who acts in obedience to Him, and one who teaches people what He has commanded. The alif and nun were added for emphasis, as they say lihyani (bearded) and sha'rani (hairy) in attribution to lihya (beard) and sha'r (hair). Another group said that rabbani is attributed to al-rubban, which means the teacher and scholar of people who manages their affairs. It is derived from rabba, yarubbu, meaning to set right and to nurture, and this nun was added to it as it was added in ghadban and 'atshan, and then rabbani was formed as its attribution.

The scholars differed over the description of the one who deserves to be called rabbani. Abu Razin said: the rabbani is the wise scholar. Mujahid said: the rabbani is the jurist (faqih). Qatada and others said: the rabbani is the knowledgeable and forbearing scholar. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is the wise jurist. al-Dahhak said: he is the jurist and scholar. Ibn Zayd said: the rabbani is the ruler of affairs, who nurtures (yarubbu) the people, that is, sets them right. So the rabbaniyyun are the rulers, the rabbis (ahbar) and the scholars. Mujahid also said: the rabbani is above the habr (rabbi), because the habr is the scholar, whereas the rabbani is the one who combines knowledge and jurisprudence with insight into governance and management, and with taking charge of the affairs of the subjects and what sets them right in their religion and their worldly life. In al-Bukhari: the rabbani is the one who nurtures people with the minor aspects of knowledge before its major aspects. So the sum of what is said about the rabbani is that he is the one who knows the Lord and the Law, who is correct in judgement regarding the words and deeds he undertakes among people.

His saying "bima kuntum" means: because of your being scholars and students. Here ma is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and it cannot be a relative pronoun (mawsula), because the returning pronoun that would have been required could not be contained in "kuntum tu'allimuna," and none of this is valid, since kana has already fulfilled its predicate explicitly, which is "tu'allimuna," and likewise "tu'allimuna" has already fulfilled its object, which is "al-Kitab," explicitly. Nothing remains except that ma is a verbal-source particle, since no returning pronoun is possible. And "tu'allimuna" here means "tu'arrifuna" (you make known), so it is transitive to one object.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ta'lamuna" with a sukun on the 'ain and a light lam. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tu'allimuna" with the letter heavy, with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the lam. This is on the basis of transitivising the verb by doubling, and the second object in this reading is omitted, its estimate being: "tu'allimuna al-nas al-Kitab" (you teach people the Book). The two readings are close in meaning. I have preferred the light reading because of their lightening of "tadrusun," and because knowledge is the cause which obliges a person who is granted success to be rabbani, whereas teaching is not a condition for this. I have preferred the other reading on the basis that teaching includes knowledge, whereas knowledge does not include teaching, so the heavy reading comes out as more emphatic in praise. And from the point of view that the one who knows the state of one who knows, teaching is, as it were, contained within knowledge. In my view the light reading is more preferable.

Mujahid and al-Hasan read "ta'allamuna" with a fatha on the ta' and the 'ain and a shadda on the open lam. The majority of people read "tadrusun" with a damma on the ra', from darasa, meaning to persist in reading the Book and to repeat it. Abu Haywa read "tadrisun" with a kasra on the ra', and this is on the basis that it is said of the imperfect of darasa: yadrusu and yadrisu. It was also transmitted from Abu Haywa that he read "tudarrisun," with a damma on the ta' and a kasra and shadda on the ra', meaning: you teach others.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read "wa la ya'murukum" with a raf' (damma) on the ra'. Abu 'Amr used to elide the vowel of the ra' for lightness. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read "wa la ya'murakum" with a nasb (fatha). There is no disagreement about the ra' in His saying "a-ya'murukum" except the elision by Abu 'Amr. Whoever reads "la ya'murukum" with raf' has it as a fresh sentence (qat'). Sibawayh said: the meaning is "wa la ya'murukumu Allah" (nor would God command you). Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is "wa la ya'murukum hadha al-bashar alladhi utiya hadhihi al-ni'am," that is, this human who was given these blessings, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa lan ya'murakum," and this reading indicates a fresh sentence. As for the reading of the one who put the ra' in the nasb, it is coordinated with His saying "an yu'tiyahu" (that He should give him), and the meaning is: "nor is it for him to command you," as Abu 'Ali and others said. Al-Tabari said: His saying "wa la ya'murakum" with nasb is coordinated with His saying "thumma yaqula" (then he should say). This is a mistake, and the meaning does not fit with it. And al-arbab (the lords) in this verse means al-alihah (the deities).

His saying, may He be exalted, "a-ya'murukum bil-kufr" (would He command you to disbelief) is a confirmation based on this apparent meaning, whose corruption is evident.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets...﴾ the verse. The meaning: "Remember, O Muhammad, when..." It is possible that the taking of this covenant was when He brought the children of Adam out of the loins of Adam as particles (nasama), and it is possible that this taking was from every prophet in his time and at the moment of his sending. Then the wording is collected in the narration of the state in this verse. The meaning is that God, may He be exalted, took the covenant of every prophet that he and whoever believed in him would commit to belief in whoever came after him of the messengers whose proofs are manifest, and to supporting him.

The exegetes differed over the expression of what is required by the words of this verse. Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: He only took the covenant of the People of the Book, not the covenant of the prophets. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud: "wa idh akhadha Allah mithaq alladhina utu al-Kitab" (when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book). Mujahid said: "This is how the Qur'an is, and the affirmation of 'the prophets' is an error by the scribes." This wording is rejected by the consensus (ijma') of the Companions upon the codex of 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: God only took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples, so it is a taking of the covenant of all of them. Tawus said: God took the covenant of the prophets that some of them would confirm others. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: God did not send any prophet, from Adam and whoever came after him, except that the covenant was taken from him concerning Muhammad: if he is sent while he is alive, he shall surely believe in him and surely support him; and He commanded him to take it from his people. Then he recited this verse. al-Suddi also said this. And it is transmitted from Tawus that he said: the beginning of the verse is the taking of the covenant from the prophets, and His saying "thumma ja'akum" (then there comes to you) is an address to the People of the Book about the taking of the covenant from them. This was related by al-Tabari, but it is an opinion whose grammatical structure of the verse refutes it. All these sayings return to what 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas said, because the taking of the covenant from the prophets is a taking from their nations.

Hamza and others apart from the seven read "lima" with a kasra on the lam, and it is the lam of the genitive (lam al-jarr). The estimate is: "li-ajli ma ataynakum" (because of what We have given you), since you are the leaders and chiefs, and whoever is in this state is the one from whom the covenant is taken. In this reading, "ma" has the meaning of the relative pronoun alladhi, and the returning pronoun from its clause is estimated as "ataynakumuhu" (We have given you it). "Min" is for specifying the kind. His saying "thumma ja'akum" ... the verse, is a sentence coordinated upon the clause, and in this sentence a pronoun must return to the relative. Its estimate according to Sibawayh is: "rasul bihi musaddiq lima ma'akum" (a messenger, with it confirming what is with you). It was elided for lightness, just as alladhi was elided in the same clause because of the length of the speech, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. Elision from clauses is common and beautiful. As for Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, he said that His saying, may He be exalted, "lima ma'akum" is the returning pronoun to the relative in his view, since it is in meaning in the position of the pronoun which Sibawayh estimated. Al-Akhfash similarly said in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient, then God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Yusuf: 90], because the meaning is: "He does not waste their reward," since the good-doers are those who fear and are patient. Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, We surely do not waste the reward of whoever does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and likewise whatever resembles these verses. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, did not hold that the apparent noun should be placed in the position of the pronoun, as al-Akhfash held.

The lam in "la-tu'minunna" is the lam attached to the oath contained in the taking of the covenant, and the oath is separated from what is sworn upon by a prepositional phrase, which is permissible.

(Page 272) The rest of the seven read "lamma" with a fatha on the lam, and this can be construed in two ways. The first is that ma is a relative pronoun in the position of the nominative, as the subject, and the lam is the lam of the subject, and it receives what has been treated as an oath from His saying, may He be exalted, "wa idh akhadha Allah mithaq" (and when God took the covenant), and the predicate of the subject is His saying "la-tu'minunna" (you shall surely believe). "La-tu'minunna" is attached to an estimated oath, and the meaning is: "By God, you shall surely believe." This is what Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said. There is an objection from the point of view of meaning when you consider what the swearing fell upon, but it is valid on the ground that the oath occurs twice for emphasis, so consider it. The returning pronoun in the clause and the returning pronoun in the sentence coordinated upon the clause, in this reading, are as we mentioned them in the reading of Hamza. As for the fact that this interpretation requires a returning pronoun from the predicate, which is "la-tu'minunna," it is His saying "bihi" (with it). The ha' in "bihi" returns to "ma," and it cannot return to "rasul," because then the relative would have no mention in its predicate returning to it.

The second way in which the reading of the readers "lamma" with a fatha on the lam can be construed is that "ma" is a conditional particle (shart), and so it is in the position of the accusative by the verb following it, which is jussive (majzum). "Ja'akum" is coordinated in the position of the jussive. The lam attached to "ma" is not the one that receives the oath, but rather the preparatory lam (al-muwatti'a), which announces the coming of the lam of the oath. It is in the position of the lam in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease do not cease, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], because it announces the coming of the one that receives the oath in His saying "la-nughriyannaka bihim" (We will surely incite you against them) [al-Ahzab: 60]. Likewise this lam announces the coming of the one that receives the oath in His saying "la-tu'minunna bihi." This lam entering upon "inna" is not one upon which the oath relies, so it is permissible for it to be elided at times and affirmed at other times, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will surely befall those among them who disbelieved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. Al-Zajjaj said: because your saying, "By God, if you come to me, I will surely honour you," is only an oath upon your action, not that the condition is attached to it, and therefore the lam entered upon the condition. In this interpretation, the fact that it is a conditional response does not require a returning pronoun, because it is an object, and an object does not require mention of a returning pronoun. The pronoun in His saying, may He be exalted, "la-tu'minunna bihi" returns to "rasul," and so it is in the reading of the one who put a kasra on the lam. As for the pronoun in His saying "wa la-tansurunnahu" (and you shall surely support him), it admits of no interpretation except that it returns to "rasul." Abu 'Ali said in al-Idghal: the response of the condition (page 273) is elided, its evidence being His saying "la-tu'minunna" upon it. Sibawayh said: I asked him (meaning al-Khalil) about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets, "Whatever I have given you..."﴾ and he said: "ma" here is in the position of "alladhi," and the lam entered upon it as it entered upon "inna" when you say, "la-in fa'alta la-af'alanna" (if you do it, I will surely do it). Then he went on explaining the aspect of the response. Abu 'Ali said: al-Khalil meant by his saying "it is in the position of alladhi" that it is a noun just as alladhi is a noun, and he did not mean that it is a relative like alladhi. He only fled from its being a particle, as it came as a particle in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed all of them, your Lord will surely pay them in full their deeds﴾ [Hud: 111], and in His saying: ﴿And indeed all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 35].

And God is the one sought for help.
