The verse concerns the Prophets being questioned about their affirmation of this covenant, their commitment to it, and the taking of Allah's pledge concerning it. This may refer to the occasion of the oath, and the expression may be intended as a comprehensive description of what was done with every prophet in his time. "And you took" in this verse refers to what they obtained of the Book and wisdom; from the point that it was taken from them, they also took. Al-Tabari said: "Take" in this verse means "accept," and "al-isr" means the covenant, and there is no explanation of it in this place other than that.

Allah's words "Then bear witness" (fashhadu) may have two meanings. The first: bear witness against your believing nations, and against yourselves by committing to this covenant. This is the view of al-Tabari and a group of scholars. The second meaning: make the matter clear to your nations and bear witness to it. On this interpretation, Allah's witnessing, which is in His words "and I am with you among the witnesses" [Aal 'Imran: 81], is the granting of miracles and the affirmation of their prophethoods. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and others, so reflect on it. The first view is the deposit of testimony and entrusting it to be preserved; the second view is the command to deliver it.

Allah judged as defiantly disobedient (fasiq) those among the nations who turned away after this covenant. This was stated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. It is also possible that the intended meaning is turning away after the testimony given among the nations to this covenant, on the basis that His words "then bear witness" are a command to deliver it.

Abu 'Amr recited "yabghuna" with a yā' vowelled with a fatḥa and "turji'un" with a tā' vowelled with a ḍamma. 'Asim recited "yabghuna" and "yarji'un" with a yā' dotted from below in both. The rest recited both with a tā'. The bases of these recitations are not hidden from anyone who reflects even slightly.

"Tabghun" means "you seek." "Aslama" in this verse means "submitted" (istaslama) according to the majority of the exegetes, and "man" in this verse includes the angels and both jinn and humankind.

They differed concerning the meaning of His words "willingly and unwillingly." Mujahid said: this verse is like His words "And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, Allah" [Luqman: 25]. So the meaning is that every disbeliever's acknowledgment of the Creator is a submission under compulsion. This is a general statement in the wording of the verse, because on this interpretation no one remains who does not submit, and "aslama" here means "istaslama." Abu al-'Aliyah Rafi' said something similar, and his words, may Allah have mercy on him, are: every human has acknowledged against himself that Allah is living and that he worships Him; so whoever associates others in His worship, this is the one who submitted unwillingly, and whoever is sincere, this is the one who submitted willingly. Ibn 'Abbas said: rather, the submission of the unwilling among them was at the time the covenant was taken. It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: the unwillingness in this verse is the prostration of the disbeliever's shadow, so the believer prostrates willingly and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates while he is unwilling. Al-Sha'bi said: the verse is an expression of the submission of all of mankind to Allah and their yielding to His power, even if some of them attribute divinity to another; and that is what prostrates unwillingly. This is the view of Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah mentioned earlier, though the expressions differ. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that some people submitted willingly, and some submitted out of fear of the sword. Mattar al-Warraq said: the angels submitted willingly, and likewise the Ansar, Banu Salim, and 'Abd al-Qays, while the rest of people submitted unwillingly, fearing fighting and the sword. This is a view in which "submission" is that which includes faith within it. The apparent wording of the verse is general, but its meaning is particular, since among the people of the earth there are those who did not submit either willingly or unwillingly in this sense. Qatadah said: submission under compulsion is the submission of the disbeliever at death and at the moment of witnessing, when it no longer benefits him. It follows from this view that every disbeliever does this, and this is not found except in individual cases. The meaning of this verse is understood by every observer to be that this division, which is the unwillingness, is specifically among the people of the earth, and the rebuke in His words "Do they seek other than" is directed only at the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the rabbis and disbelievers.

This is the view of Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah mentioned earlier, though the expressions differ. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that some people submitted willingly, and some submitted out of fear of the sword. Mattar al-Warraq said: the angels submitted willingly, and likewise the Ansar, Banu Salim, and 'Abd al-Qays, while the rest of people submitted unwillingly, fearing fighting and the sword. This is a view in which "submission" is that which includes faith within it. The apparent wording of the verse is general, but its meaning is particular, since among the people of the earth there are those who did not submit either willingly or unwillingly in this sense. Qatadah said: submission under compulsion is the submission of the disbeliever at death and at the moment of witnessing, when it no longer benefits him. It follows from this view that every disbeliever does this, and this is not found except in individual cases. The meaning of this verse is understood by every observer to be that this division, which is the unwillingness, is specifically among the people of the earth, and the rebuke in His words "Do they seek other than" is directed only at the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the rabbis and disbelievers.

Abu Bakr, narrating from 'Asim, recited "uṣrī" with a ḍamma on the alif, and this is a dialectal form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 84–85:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus and the Prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.﴾

(p-276) The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, you and your community: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us," which is the Qur'an and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). The sending down upon the prophet of a community is a sending down upon that community. He mentioned Ishmael first because of his age. The rest of the verse is clear.

Then, in His saying, "And whoever seeks..." to the end of the verse, God judged that He does not accept from any human a religion other than the religion of Islam, which is the one that agrees in its beliefs with the religion of every prophet He named, and it is the tolerant ḥanīfiyya (ḥanīfiyya: the pure monotheistic disposition).

ʿIkrima said: When this verse was revealed, the people of the (other) religions said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We submitted before you, and we are the Muslims." So God said to him: "Then argue with them, O Muhammad," and He revealed to him: ﴿And for God, pilgrimage to the House is a duty upon mankind﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 97]. So the Muslims performed the pilgrimage and the disbelievers stayed back.

Al-Ṭabarī narrated with a chain of transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: The verse ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians—whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqara: 62] down to His saying ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqara: 62] was revealed, and then God revealed after it: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him...﴾ to the end of the verse. This is an indication of abrogation (naskh: the annulment of a ruling by a later revelation).

His saying "in the Hereafter" is connected to an implied element, its estimate being: "he is a loser in the Hereafter," because the alif and lām in "the losers" carry the sense of a relative pronoun. Some of the exegetes said: the verse "And whoever seeks..." was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith ibn Suwayd, but al-Ṭabarī did not mention this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 86–89:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief and had testified that the Messenger is true and clear proofs had come to them? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿Those – their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of the people, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and make amends; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: "These verses, from His statement ﴿How will Allah guide﴾, were revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari," who had been a Muslim, then apostatised and joined the polytheists. Then he regretted it and sent to his people asking them to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is there any repentance for me?" He said: then ﴿How will Allah guide﴾… the verses were revealed, up to His statement ﴿except those who repent﴾, so his people sent to him and he embraced Islam.

Mujahid said: a man from his people carried the verses to him and recited them to him. Al-Harith said to him: "By Allah, as far as I know, you are truthful, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is more truthful than you, and Allah is more truthful than the three." So al-Harith returned and embraced Islam, and his Islam became good.

As-Suddi said: Allah, exalted is He, abrogated by His statement ﴿except those who repent﴾ His statement ﴿Those – their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah﴾. In this expression there is much figurative usage (tajawwuz), and this is not the place for abrogation (naskh).

'Ikrimah said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu 'Amir the monk, al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit, and Wahwah ibn al-Aslat, along with twelve men who turned back from Islam and joined Quraysh; then they wrote to their families: "Is there any repentance for us?" Then these verses were revealed.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan: these verses were revealed concerning the Jews and Christians, who testified to the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) and believed in him, but when one came from the Arabs they envied him and disbelieved in him. Al-Tabari preferred this view. Al-Naqqash said: these verses were revealed concerning Tu'aymah ibn Ubayriq. Whoever has been mentioned, the wording of the verse encompasses them all.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿How will Allah guide﴾ is a question about a state, but it is a question of censure (tawqif) in the sense of deeming the matter improbable, as he, peace be upon him, said: "How will a people prosper who have bloodied the face of their prophet?" The meaning, then, is that because of the severity of these crimes, it is unlikely that Allah, exalted is He, would guide them.

His statement, exalted is He: "and they testified" is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "disbelieved" by the rule of wording, and the meaning is understood that the testimony was before the disbelief; the waw does not indicate order. Some people said: the meaning of His statement "after their belief" is "after they had believed," so "and they testified" is coordinated upon this estimation.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a general statement whose meaning is particular, concerning those whose disbelief and dying upon it has been decreed. It is possible that it intends to inform that the wrongdoer, in his wrongdoing, is not upon guidance from Allah, in which case the verse is general in its full generality. "Curse" (la'nah) is distancing and the absence of mercy and compassion; and this, together with the indication of disbelief, is a guarantee of their being made to abide in the Fire. The cursing of the angels is a statement (qawl). "And the people" means the children of Adam. And it appears from the words of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in some of his notes that the jinn enter into the term "people" (al-nas), and he recited as evidence:

"I said, 'To the food!' and some of them said, 'A people who envy mankind the food.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears is that the word "al-nas", when it comes unrestricted, in the speech of the Arabs means only the children of Adam and no others. When it comes restricted with the jinn, that is by way of metaphor (isti'arah), since it is a group like a group. Likewise: ﴿men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6] and likewise: ﴿a company of the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]; and the word "nafar" (company) is closer to being shared than "rijal" (men) and "nas" (people). And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿from the jinn and the people﴾ [al-Nas: 6] requires that the two categories are distinct.

His statement, exalted is He: "and the people, all together" either means particularity in regard to the believers, He calling them "the people" because they are the reference; or it intends that in the Hereafter the believers curse them, and some of them curse others, so there results for each one of them that all the people have cursed him; or it intends that this curse occurs in this world from all the people upon whoever has this description. And everyone who has this description – and Satan has misled him – curses the possessor of these attributes without perceiving within himself that he is characterised by them; so there results from this that all the people curse them in this world, to the point that they curse themselves too, but without specification.

The pronoun in His statement "abiding therein" – al-Tabari said it returns to the punishment of Allah which is implied by the meaning of curse. Some of the exegetes said the pronoun returns to the curse. The indications of the verse require that this curse makes them abide in Hell, so the pronoun returns to the Fire, even though no mention of it has preceded, because the meaning conveys it in this place, just as His statement ﴿everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26] conveys that it is the earth. Some of the Khurasanis said regarding His statement ﴿you are only a warner to whoever fears it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]: the pronoun returns to the Hour.

"Yunzarun" in this verse means "they will be reprieved," and there is no relief except in the lightening or the postponement, and both are lifted from them. It is not permissible for "yunzarun" here to be from seeing with the eye, except on an interpretation that is not eloquent and does not befit the Book of Allah, exalted is He.

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Except those who repent﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), clarified by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿after that﴾. Repentance (tawbah) is return, and amendment (islah) is general, encompassing speech and action.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a promise. And al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited: "and the people, all together" (wa-l-nasi ajma'una).

'Ikrimah said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu 'Amir the monk, al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit, and Wahwah ibn al-Aslat, along with twelve men who turned back from Islam and joined Quraysh; then they wrote to their families: "Is there any repentance for us?" Then these verses were revealed.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan: these verses were revealed concerning the Jews and Christians, who testified to the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) and believed in him, but when one came from the Arabs they envied him and disbelieved in him. Al-Tabari preferred this view. Al-Naqqash said: these verses were revealed concerning Tu'aymah ibn Ubayriq. Whoever has been mentioned, the wording of the verse encompasses them all.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿How will Allah guide﴾ is a question about a state, but it is a question of censure (tawqif) in the sense of deeming the matter improbable, as he, peace be upon him, said: "How will a people prosper who have bloodied the face of their prophet?" The meaning, then, is that because of the severity of these crimes, it is unlikely that Allah, exalted is He, would guide them.

His statement, exalted is He: "and they testified" is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "disbelieved" by the rule of wording, and the meaning is understood that the testimony was before the disbelief; the waw does not indicate order. Some people said: the meaning of His statement "after their belief" is "after they had believed," so "and they testified" is coordinated upon this estimation.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a general statement whose meaning is particular, concerning those whose disbelief and dying upon it has been decreed. It is possible that it intends to inform that the wrongdoer, in his wrongdoing, is not upon guidance from Allah, in which case the verse is general in its full generality. "Curse" (la'nah) is distancing and the absence of mercy and compassion; and this, together with the indication of disbelief, is a guarantee of their being made to abide in the Fire. The cursing of the angels is a statement (qawl). "And the people" means the children of Adam. And it appears from the words of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in some of his notes that the jinn enter into the term "people" (al-nas), and he recited as evidence:

"I said, 'To the food!' and some of them said, 'A people who envy mankind the food.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears is that the word "al-nas", when it comes unrestricted, in the speech of the Arabs means only the children of Adam and no others. When it comes restricted with the jinn, that is by way of metaphor (isti'arah), since it is a group like a group. Likewise: ﴿men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6] and likewise: ﴿a company of the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]; and the word "nafar" (company) is closer to being shared than "rijal" (men) and "nas" (people). And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿from the jinn and the people﴾ [al-Nas: 6] requires that the two categories are distinct.

His statement, exalted is He: "and the people, all together" either means particularity in regard to the believers, He calling them "the people" because they are the reference; or it intends that in the Hereafter the believers curse them, and some of them curse others, so there results for each one of them that all the people have cursed him; or it intends that this curse occurs in this world from all the people upon whoever has this description. And everyone who has this description – and Satan has misled him – curses the possessor of these attributes without perceiving within himself that he is characterised by them; so there results from this that all the people curse them in this world, to the point that they curse themselves too, but without specification.

The pronoun in His statement "abiding therein" – al-Tabari said it returns to the punishment of Allah which is implied by the meaning of curse. Some of the exegetes said the pronoun returns to the curse. The indications of the verse require that this curse makes them abide in Hell, so the pronoun returns to the Fire, even though no mention of it has preceded, because the meaning conveys it in this place, just as His statement ﴿everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26] conveys that it is the earth. Some of the Khurasanis said regarding His statement ﴿you are only a warner to whoever fears it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]: the pronoun returns to the Hour.

"Yunzarun" in this verse means "they will be reprieved," and there is no relief except in the lightening or the postponement, and both are lifted from them. It is not permissible for "yunzarun" here to be from seeing with the eye, except on an interpretation that is not eloquent and does not befit the Book of Allah, exalted is He.

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Except those who repent﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), clarified by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿after that﴾. Repentance (tawbah) is return, and amendment (islah) is general, encompassing speech and action.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a promise. And al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited: "and the people, all together" (wa-l-nasi ajma'una).

(p-280) The Exalted's saying:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted, and they are the astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—never will be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold, even if he should ransom himself with it. For those is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.﴾

The interpreters (al-mutaʾawwilun) differed over how there can be disbelief after belief, and then an increase in disbelief. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said: the verse concerns the Jews, who disbelieved in ʿIsa after believing in Musa, then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ). But in this view there is confusion, because the one who disbelieved in ʿIsa after believing in Musa is not the one who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ); so on this interpretation the verse mixes the predecessors with the addressees.

Abu al-ʿAliyah Rafiʿ said: the verse concerns the Jews, who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) after believing in his attributes and acknowledging that they are in the Torah, and then increased in disbelief through the sins they committed in opposing the Prophet (ﷺ): slander, deceit, striving against Islam, and other things. According to this order, the apostates who joined Quraysh and others also enter the verse.

Mujahid said: the meaning of His saying ﴿then increase in disbelief﴾ is that they persisted in their disbelief and reached death in it. So the Jews and the apostates enter into this view. As-Suddi said something similar.

Then the Exalted informed that the repentance of these will never be accepted. Yet the Sharia has established that the repentance of every disbeliever is accepted, whether he disbelieved after belief and increased in disbelief, or was a disbeliever from the outset. So this verse necessarily requires a restriction by which the negation of accepting repentance is made valid. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and as-Suddi said: the negation of the acceptance of their repentance is specific to the time of the death-rattle (al-hashrajah), the gasping (al-ghargharah) and direct witnessing (al-muʿayanah). So the meaning is: their repentance will not be accepted at the time of witnessing. Abu al-ʿAliyah said:

The meaning of the verse: their repentance will not be accepted from those sins they committed while persisting in disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ), for they used to say at times: "We repent of these deeds," while they remained upon their disbelief. So the Exalted informed that He does not accept that repentance.

In my view, the verse may also be a reference to specific people among the apostates whom God sealed with disbelief, making that the requital for their crime and their harm to the religion. They are those to whom He alluded with His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people...﴾ [Al ʿImran: 86]. So He informed about them that they will have no repentance such that its acceptance could be conceived. The verse then comes in the manner of the poet's saying:(p-281)

"On a path whose landmarks cannot guide one..."

That is: Allah has placed them, by His wrath, in the category of those for whom no repentance is accepted, since they have none. So they will inevitably die in disbelief. Therefore He explained the ruling on those who die as disbelievers right after the verse, and thus the status of these people became clear; it is as if He informed about these specific people that they will die as disbelievers, and then informed people about the ruling on whoever dies as a disbeliever. "Al-ḍāllūn" means those who miss the straight path in statements and deeds.

ʿIkrimah recited: "lan naqbala" with the nun of majesty, "tawbatahum" with the taʾ in the accusative.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾... the verse is a definitive ruling on every person who meets death in disbelief until the Day of Resurrection.

ʿIkrimah recited: "fa-lan naqbala" with the nun of majesty, "mala'a al-ardi" in the accusative. "Al-milʾ" is what a vessel is filled with; with a kasrah on the mim it is the noun, and with a fathah it is the verbal noun. You say: "malaʾtu al-shayʾa amlauhu malʾan," and "al-milʾ" is the name of what you filled it with. Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ and Abu al-Sammal recited "milla" without a hamzah, and it is related from Nafiʿ; and "dhahaban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited "dhahaban law iftada" with it, without the waw.

People differed over this verse in His saying "wa-law iftadā." Al-Tabari said: it is connected to an elided element at the end of the speech, indicated by the entry of the waw, just as it entered in His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-Anʿam: 75], for an omitted part of the speech, its estimate being: "And that he might be among the certain, We showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth." In this illustration there is room for scrutiny, so consider it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: his spending and his acts of devotion in this world will not be accepted from any one of them, even if he spends the earth full of gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it in the Hereafter, it will not be accepted from him. He said: So Allah made known that He will not reward them for their good deeds, nor accept from them a ransom from punishment. This is a fine view. Some said the waw is superfluous, but this view is rejected. It is possible that the meaning is the negation of acceptance in general across all aspects, and then He singled out from those aspects the most fitting and most deserving of acceptance, as you say: "I will not do such-and-such for you in any way, even if you should beseech me." The remainder of the verse is a clear warning.

[p-283] Ibn 'Atiyya said, concerning the words of the Exalted:

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love. And whatever you spend, indeed Allah knows it.﴾ ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.﴾

Some people went to link the meanings of these verses with one another, on the basis that He, may He be exalted, informed that He does not accept from one who dies in disbelief the weight of the earth in gold. It is clear that He accepts from a believer both little and much. So He urged spending from what is beloved and desired. Then He mentioned Israel's (peace be upon him) drawing near to Allah by making unlawful for himself what he loved, so that the Exalted might show that all acts of drawing near to Him enter, in meaning, into the category of spending from what is beloved. Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) explained these verses as meanings that are interconnected, arranged by miraculous eloquence in the most beautiful arrangement.

As for His saying, "You will never attain..." through the end of the verse, it is an address to all the believers. Al-Suddi and 'Amr ibn Maymun said: al-birr (righteousness) is Paradise. This is an interpretation by meaning. The specific sense of the word is what the righteous person does of good deeds. So the verse may mean: you will never attain the righteousness of Allah toward you, that is, His mercy and kindness. It may also mean: you will never attain the degree of perfection in the act of righteousness until you become righteous (abrar), except through spending added to your other deeds.

[p-283 continued] Because of the revelation of this verse, Abu Talha gave in charity his orchard called Bayruha, and Zayd ibn Haritha gave in charity a mare that he loved. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave her to his son Usama. It seemed that this grieved Zayd, so the Prophet said to him: "Indeed Allah has accepted your charity." Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari asking him to buy for him a slave girl from the captives of Jalula at the time of the conquest of the cities of Kisra at the hands of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. She was brought to him, and he loved her. One day he called her and said: "Indeed Allah says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾," and he freed her. All of this is an interpretation of the verse, taking His saying "from what you love" to mean: from the desirable wealth that one is reluctant to part with. It is explained by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best charity is that you give while you are healthy and stingy, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth..." the hadith.

Some scholars held that what is loved among foods, according to one's appetite, enters into the verse. 'Abd Allah ibn Umar desired to eat sweets with almonds, so he would buy them, give them in charity, and recite the verse.

If you reflect on all acts of obedience, you will find that they are spending from what a person loves: either from his wealth, or from his health, or from his ease and comfort. All of these are beloved things. A man asked Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him): "Which deeds are best?" He said: "Prayer is the pillar of Islam, jihad is the peak of action, and charity is a remarkable thing." The man said to him: "I see you have left out something that is most trustworthy to me: fasting." Abu Dharr said: "It is an act of drawing near, but it is not there." Then he recited: ﴿You will never attain righteousness...﴾ the verse.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever you spend, indeed Allah knows it﴾ is a conditional clause with a response containing a promise, meaning: He knows it and will reward for it, even if it is small.

His saying, "All food..." through the verse, is a report of an unseen matter concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and all the unlettered (ummiyyun), which none knows except Allah and the scholars of the People of the Book.

Many exegetes held that the meaning of the verse is a refutation of the Jews in their claim, concerning everything they had made unlawful for themselves, that it was forbidden to them by the command of Allah in the Torah. So Allah refuted them with this verse, and informed that all food had been lawful to them, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself specifically, and he did not intend it for his descendants. When they followed his example, the Torah came with the prohibition of that upon them. Nothing in the Torah contains the additional prohibitions they claim Allah made unlawful. To this the words of al-Suddi incline. He said: Allah, the Exalted, made that unlawful for them in the Torah as a punishment for their imitation in prohibiting something that Jacob had done only for himself. He said: this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 160].

Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The apparent meaning of the word "wrongdoing" (zulm) is that it is specific to prohibition and the like. The evidence for this is that the punishment fell in that category. Some scholars held that the meaning of the verse is a refutation of a group of Jews who said: What we now make unlawful for ourselves of things not mentioned in the Torah was forbidden to us in the religion of our father Abraham. So Allah refuted them and informed that all food had been lawful to them before the Torah, except what Israel prohibited for his own person. Then the Torah came with the prohibition of what it stated explicitly, and these additions remained within the sphere of their fabrication and lying. To this the words of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) incline. [p-285] al-Tabari arranged chapters for the interpretation of this verse and placed under them sayings that agreed with his chapters. He read into the words of al-Dahhak that the exception (istithna') is disconnected (munqati'), as if the meaning were: all food was lawful to them before the revelation of the Torah and after its revelation. This is something al-Dahhak did not say, and his wording does not allow it. Yet in itself it is a statement that can be derived by taking "kana" (was) not as restricted to past time, but as functioning like the "kana" in His saying: ﴿And Allah was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa: 96]. Then the meaning returns to the first view we have related. al-Tabari read into al-Dahhak's statement that its meaning is: but Israel made unlawful for himself alone, and Allah did not make unlawful for the Children of Israel anything in the Torah or other than it. This is an imposition that is refuted by His saying, the Exalted: ("We made unlawful for them") and by His saying (ﷺ): "The fats were made unlawful for them," among other evidences.

His saying, the Exalted: "Lawful" (hillan) means: permitted (halal). "Israel" is Jacob.

From this verse it is derived that prophets may, through their own reasoning, make unlawful for themselves what consideration requires for the sake of benefit, drawing near to Allah, or asceticism. Of this kind, for the sake of benefit, is the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of his slave girl upon himself, for which Allah rebuked him, whereas He did not rebuke Jacob. It is said that this was for the right of a human being that arose in the incident of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said that this was a prohibition for drawing near and asceticism, while the prohibition of the slave girl was a prohibition of anger and of the benefit of the soul.

The people differed about the thing that Jacob made unlawful for himself. Yusuf ibn Mahak said: A Bedouin came to Ibn 'Abbas and said to him: "Indeed he made his wife unlawful upon himself." Ibn 'Abbas said: "She is not unlawful to you." The Bedouin said: "Why? For Allah the Exalted says in His Book: ﴿except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾?" [p-286] Ibn 'Abbas laughed and said: "And what do you know of what Israel made unlawful?" Then he turned to the people, speaking to them, and said: "Israel was afflicted with sciatica (al-anasa'), which wasted him, so he vowed to Allah that if He cured him of it, he would not eat a vein (irq)." He said: "That is why the Jews remove the veins from meat." Qatada, Abu Mijlaz, and others said the same.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir, and Mujahid also said: What Israel made unlawful was the flesh and milk of camels. As far as I know, there is no disagreement that the cause of the prohibition was an illness that afflicted him, so he made the prohibition of that a thanksgiving to Allah the Exalted if he were healed. It is also said: it was the pain of sciatica (irq al-nasa). In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A group of the Children of Israel said to him: 'O Muhammad, what did Israel make unlawful for himself?' He said to them: 'I ask you by Allah, do you know that Jacob fell very ill, and his sickness lasted long, so he vowed to Allah that if Allah cured him of his sickness, he would forbid the food and drink most beloved to him, and the most beloved food to him was camel meat and camel milk?' They said: 'O Allah, yes.'"

The apparent meaning of the hadiths and exegeses on this matter is that Jacob (peace be upon him) made unlawful the flesh and milk of camels, though he loved them, drawing near to Allah by that, for abandoning ease and luxury is an act of nearness. This is asceticism in this world. To this Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) inclined when he said: "Beware of these slaughterhouses, for they have a craving like the craving for wine." Of the same kind is the saying of Abu Hazim the ascetic, when he passed by the fruit market and saw its fine produce, and said: "Your appointment is Paradise, if Allah wills." Jacob (peace be upon him) also made unlawful the veins, but out of dislike for them, because he had been tested with them. This is something that comes over human souls for no particular reason. There is no nearness to Allah in prohibiting veins, as far as is apparent, and Allah knows best. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that Jacob made unlawful the veins and the flesh of camels.

[p-287] Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to order them to bring the Torah, so that its content would show how the matter truly stands. The meaning: O Jews, as Allah revealed it to me, not as you claim. Al-Zajjaj said: In this there is a challenge to them and the establishment of proof against them. It is like the story of the mubahala (mutual invocation of curse) with the Christians of Najran.

All of these are beloved things. A man asked Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him): "Which deeds are best?" He said: "Prayer is the pillar of Islam, jihad is the peak of action, and charity is a remarkable thing." The man said to him: "I see you have left out something that is most trustworthy to me: fasting." Abu Dharr said: "It is an act of drawing near, but it is not there." Then he recited: ﴿You will never attain righteousness...﴾ the verse.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever you spend, indeed Allah knows it﴾ is a conditional clause with a response containing a promise, meaning: He knows it and will reward for it, even if it is small.

His saying, "All food..." through the verse, is a report of an unseen matter concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and all the unlettered (ummiyyun), which none knows except Allah and the scholars of the People of the Book.

Many exegetes held that the meaning of the verse is a refutation of the Jews in their claim, concerning everything they had made unlawful for themselves, that it was forbidden to them by the command of Allah in the Torah. So Allah refuted them with this verse, and informed that all food had been lawful to them, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself specifically, and he did not intend it for his descendants. When they followed his example, the Torah came with the prohibition of that upon them. Nothing in the Torah contains the additional prohibitions they claim Allah made unlawful. To this the words of al-Suddi incline. He said: Allah, the Exalted, made that unlawful for them in the Torah as a punishment for their imitation in prohibiting something that Jacob had done only for himself. He said: this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 160].

Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The apparent meaning of the word "wrongdoing" (zulm) is that it is specific to prohibition and the like. The evidence for this is that the punishment fell in that category. Some scholars held that the meaning of the verse is a refutation of a group of Jews who said: What we now make unlawful for ourselves of things not mentioned in the Torah was forbidden to us in the religion of our father Abraham. So Allah refuted them and informed that all food had been lawful to them before the Torah, except what Israel prohibited for his own person. Then the Torah came with the prohibition of what it stated explicitly, and these additions remained within the sphere of their fabrication and lying. To this the words of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) incline. [p-285] al-Tabari arranged chapters for the interpretation of this verse and placed under them sayings that agreed with his chapters. He read into the words of al-Dahhak that the exception (istithna') is disconnected (munqati'), as if the meaning were: all food was lawful to them before the revelation of the Torah and after its revelation. This is something al-Dahhak did not say, and his wording does not allow it. Yet in itself it is a statement that can be derived by taking "kana" (was) not as restricted to past time, but as functioning like the "kana" in His saying: ﴿And Allah was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa: 96]. Then the meaning returns to the first view we have related. al-Tabari read into al-Dahhak's statement that its meaning is: but Israel made unlawful for himself alone, and Allah did not make unlawful for the Children of Israel anything in the Torah or other than it. This is an imposition that is refuted by His saying, the Exalted: ("We made unlawful for them") and by His saying (ﷺ): "The fats were made unlawful for them," among other evidences.

His saying, the Exalted: "Lawful" (hillan) means: permitted (halal). "Israel" is Jacob.

From this verse it is derived that prophets may, through their own reasoning, make unlawful for themselves what consideration requires for the sake of benefit, drawing near to Allah, or asceticism. Of this kind, for the sake of benefit, is the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of his slave girl upon himself, for which Allah rebuked him, whereas He did not rebuke Jacob. It is said that this was for the right of a human being that arose in the incident of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said that this was a prohibition for drawing near and asceticism, while the prohibition of the slave girl was a prohibition of anger and of the benefit of the soul.

The people differed about the thing that Jacob made unlawful for himself. Yusuf ibn Mahak said: A Bedouin came to Ibn 'Abbas and said to him: "Indeed he made his wife unlawful upon himself." Ibn 'Abbas said: "She is not unlawful to you." The Bedouin said: "Why? For Allah the Exalted says in His Book: ﴿except what Israel made unlawful for himself﴾?" [p-286] Ibn 'Abbas laughed and said: "And what do you know of what Israel made unlawful?" Then he turned to the people, speaking to them, and said: "Israel was afflicted with sciatica (al-anasa'), which wasted him, so he vowed to Allah that if He cured him of it, he would not eat a vein (irq)." He said: "That is why the Jews remove the veins from meat." Qatada, Abu Mijlaz, and others said the same.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir, and Mujahid also said: What Israel made unlawful was the flesh and milk of camels. As far as I know, there is no disagreement that the cause of the prohibition was an illness that afflicted him, so he made the prohibition of that a thanksgiving to Allah the Exalted if he were healed. It is also said: it was the pain of sciatica (irq al-nasa). In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A group of the Children of Israel said to him: 'O Muhammad, what did Israel make unlawful for himself?' He said to them: 'I ask you by Allah, do you know that Jacob fell very ill, and his sickness lasted long, so he vowed to Allah that if Allah cured him of his sickness, he would forbid the food and drink most beloved to him, and the most beloved food to him was camel meat and camel milk?' They said: 'O Allah, yes.'"

The apparent meaning of the hadiths and exegeses on this matter is that Jacob (peace be upon him) made unlawful the flesh and milk of camels, though he loved them, drawing near to Allah by that, for abandoning ease and luxury is an act of nearness. This is asceticism in this world. To this Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) inclined when he said: "Beware of these slaughterhouses, for they have a craving like the craving for wine." Of the same kind is the saying of Abu Hazim the ascetic, when he passed by the fruit market and saw its fine produce, and said: "Your appointment is Paradise, if Allah wills." Jacob (peace be upon him) also made unlawful the veins, but out of dislike for them, because he had been tested with them. This is something that comes over human souls for no particular reason. There is no nearness to Allah in prohibiting veins, as far as is apparent, and Allah knows best. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that Jacob made unlawful the veins and the flesh of camels.

[p-287] Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to order them to bring the Torah, so that its content would show how the matter truly stands. The meaning: O Jews, as Allah revealed it to me, not as you claim. Al-Zajjaj said: In this there is a challenge to them and the establishment of proof against them. It is like the story of the mubahala (mutual invocation of curse) with the Christians of Najran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 94–96:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after that, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah has spoken the truth. So follow the religion of Ibrahim, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾ ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾

His saying: ﴿Then whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after that﴾. The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) may refer to three things. The first: that it refers to the recitation, since its content is the clarification of the doctrine and the establishment of the proof. That is: whoever among us lies against Allah, the Exalted, or attributes to the books of Allah what is not in them, is a wrongdoer, one who puts a thing in other than its place. The second: that the reference is to the establishment of the prohibition in the Torah, because the meaning of the verse is: all food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel (Ya'qub) prohibited for himself; then the Torah prohibited it for them as a punishment. So whoever fabricates a lie against Allah and adds to the prohibited things, he is the wrongdoer. The third: that the reference is to the situation after Israel prohibited it for himself and before the Torah was revealed; that is, whoever establishes a custom in the manner of Ya'qub and legislates that without permission from Allah, and prohibits something and attributes it to the religion of Ibrahim, he is the wrongdoer. This last possibility is supported by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]. He stated explicitly that there was wrongdoing on their part in the matter of making lawful and unlawful, and they were making things strict, so Allah made things strict upon them, as they had done in the matter of the cow. In contrast to this course, Islam came with His saying ﷺ: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult," and His saying: "The religion of Allah is ease," and His saying: "I have been sent with the upright, tolerant monotheism."

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet to declare openly the disagreement and the debate with the rabbis, by His saying: ﴿Say, "Allah has spoken the truth"﴾, meaning: the matter is as He described it, not as you lie, you people. So if you take pride in Ibrahim, then follow his religion as Allah has mentioned.

Aban ibn Taghlib recited: "qul ṣaddaqa" with the assimilation of the lam into the ṣad (idgham), and likewise "qul sīrū", which he recited with the assimilation of the lam into the sin. Abu al-Fath said: the reason for the permissibility of that is the prominence of these two letters in the mouth and the spread of the resonance emanating from them, so they approach the point of articulation of the lam, and thus their assimilation into it is permissible. The majority of people recited "wuḍiʿa" in the passive form, in the sense that Allah established it. So the verse on this reading begins a new meaning separate from the first statement. ʿIkrima recited "waḍaʿa" with a fatha on the waw and the ḍad, which may mean "Allah established," so the meaning is separate as in the majority's reading. It may also mean "Ibrahim, peace be upon him, established," so the meaning is connected to what precedes, and this verse becomes a call to them to his religion, in the pilgrimage and otherwise, according to what ʿIkrima narrated: when the verse ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]... was revealed, the Jews said: "We are upon Islam." Then the verse ﴿And for Allah is a duty upon mankind toward the House, pilgrimage to it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97] was recited. It was said to him: "Call them to pilgrimage, O Muhammad, if they are upon the religion of Ibrahim, which is Islam."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is supported by what Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, which mosque was established first? He said: The Sacred Mosque. I said: Then which? He said: The Farthest Mosque. I said: How much time was between them? He said: Forty years." From this it appears that both are from the establishment of Ibrahim together, and this weakens what al-Zajjaj said, that Bayt al-Maqdis is from the building of Sulayman ibn Dawud, except that he renewed it. But where is the period of Sulayman from the period of Ibrahim? There is no doubt that Ibrahim established the House of Makkah; the disagreement is only whether it was an initial establishment or a renewal.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of this "firstness" in the phrase "Indeed, the first (awwal)". ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning of His saying "Indeed, the first House established ... blessed and a guidance" is this House which is in Makkah, and there were houses before it which were not established in the manner of its blessing and guidance. Others said: rather, it is the first House Allah created, and beneath it the earth was spread out.

(p-289) Stories have been related on this point concerning Adam's descent to it from Paradise and a specification of the period between his creation and the spreading of the earth, and what al-Zajjaj said, that it is the frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur). Their chains are weak, so I have left them. On this view, Ibrahim's raising of the foundations is a renewal. Qatada said: it was mentioned to us that the House was sent down with Adam and was raised at the time of the Flood.

The people differed concerning "Bakkah." al-Dahhak and a group of scholars said: Bakkah is Makkah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this is the substitution of the ba' for the mim, according to the dialect of Mazin and others. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Shihab and a large group of scholars said: Makkah is the entire Sacred Precinct (haram), and Bakkah is the crowded place where people jostle one another (yatabakkawna), which is the mosque and what surrounds the House. Malik, in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from al-'Utbiyya, said: Bakkah is the site of the House, and Makkah is other places. Ibn al-Qasim said: he means the town. al-Tabari said: whatever lies outside the place of circumambulation is Makkah, not Bakkah. Others said: Bakkah is what lies between the two mountains, and Makkah is the entire Sacred Precinct.

"Mubarakan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Its governing element, according to the view of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that it is the first House established in this state, is the verb "wuḍiʿa"; and its governing element according to the other view is the verb to which the preposition "bi-" in "bi-Bakkah" is attached, its estimated form being: it is situated at Bakkah, blessed. In describing the House as "a guidance" there is an eloquent metaphor, because it is something that sets right and reforms, so it is a guide, and there is guidance in it. The phrase "wa-hudan" is thus understood as "and it is a guidance." It may also be that "hudan" in this verse means a call, that is, from the point at which the worlds are called to it.
