**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 97 (part 1 of 2)**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿In it are clear signs: the standing-place of Abraham. Whoever enters it is safe. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people, for whoever is able to make his way there. Whoever disbelieves, [let him know that] Allah is free from need of the worlds.﴾

The pronoun in His words "فِيهِ" (in it) refers to the House (al-Bayt). This is acceptable even though the signs lie outside it (p. 290), because the House was established with its sanctuary (ḥaram) and all its virtues, so they are "in it" even if they are not inside its walls.

The majority of readers recited "آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ" (clear signs) in the plural. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas recited "آيَةٌ بَيِّنَةٌ" (a clear sign) in the singular. Al-Tabari said: he means one sign, namely the standing-place alone. This is also reported from Mujahid.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It is possible that "āyah" is meant as a collective noun (ism al-jins), which comes close to the meaning of the first reading.

The exegetes (mufassirun) differed in their explanation of "the clear signs." Ibn 'Abbas said: among the signs is the standing-place, meaning the well-known stone, and the Mash'ar, and other things. This indicates that his reading "āyah" in the singular is meant as a collective noun.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the clear signs are the standing-place of Abraham, and that whoever enters it is safe. Mujahid said: the standing-place is the sign. His words "وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كانَ آمِنًا" (whoever enters it is safe) are a separate statement.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The raising of "maqām" according to the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid is either as an apposition (badal) to "āyāt," or as the predicate of an implied subject, its sense being: "they are the standing-place of Abraham." According to the view of Ibn 'Abbas and those who follow his approach, it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate omitted and placed first, its sense being: "among them is the standing-place of Abraham."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
What I find more likely is that the standing-place and the safety of whoever enters were given as examples of the signs within the sanctuary of Allah, and were singled out for mention because of their greatness. By them the proof is established against the disbelievers, since they perceive these two signs with their senses. Among the signs of the sanctuary and the House by which the proof is established against the disbelievers is the affair of the Elephant, and the casting down upon its people of stones of baked clay by the birds of Allah. This is a matter about which all the Arabs did not differ in its transmission and its authenticity, until Allah revealed it in His Book. Among its signs is the restraint of tyrants from it throughout the ages. Among its signs is the Black Stone, and what is reported concerning it, that it is from Paradise, and the hearts of all the world were steeped in venerating it before Islam. Among its signs is the Stone of the Standing-Place (ḥajar al-maqām), and that is that Abraham, peace be upon him, stood upon it at the time he was raising the foundations of the House, when the building had grown tall. Whenever the wall rose, the stone would rise with him into the air, (p. 291) and he continued to build while standing upon it, and Isma'il was handing him the stones and the clay until he completed the wall. Then, when Allah the Exalted willed to preserve that as a sign for all the worlds, He softened the stone, so that Abraham's feet sank into it as if into mud. That great imprint remains in the stone to this day. All the Arabs transmitted this in the Jahiliyyah across the ages. Abu Talib said:

"And the footprint of Abraham in the rock was soft, as I stood barefoot, without sandal."

No one is known to have disputed this report. Among his clear signs is Zamzam in its spring, for Hagar, when Gabriel, peace be upon him, struck the earth with his heel. And [there is the sign in] 'Abd al-Muttalib's digging of it again after it had been buried, through that well-known vision; and [the sign in] the water that gushed forth beneath the hoof of his camel during his journey; and [the account of] the dispute of the Quraysh and their contention over the matter of Zamzam. Ibn Ishaq related this at length. Among the signs of the House is the benefit of the water of Zamzam for whatever it is drunk for, and that its water increases greatly during the season and multiplies in the wells in a manner that breaks the customary course. Among its signs is the security that has remained within it from ancient times. The Arabs would raid one another and people would be snatched away by killing, the seizing of property, and all kinds of injustice, except within the sanctuary. On this basis, the safety of animals within it and the safety of its trees were established. All of this is due to the blessing with which Allah specially favoured it, and to the supplication of the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, in His words: ﴿Make this a secure land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. And the submission of the souls of the Arabs and others altogether to honouring this sacred place, without any prohibiter or restrainer, is a great sign by which the proof is established. This is what was explained by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe.﴾ Among its signs is that it lies in a valley without cultivation, while provision comes to it from every region, from near and from far. Among its signs is what Ibn al-Qasim al-'Utaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned. He said in al-Nawadir and elsewhere: I heard that the sanctuary is known by the fact that no torrent comes from outside it (al-Hill) and enters the sanctuary.

(p. 292) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
—And Allah knows best— because Allah the Exalted made it an elevated place or one in the status of an elevated place, so as to be better protected for it. The boundary of the sanctuary, as Ibn Abi Zayd related in the second Hajj section of al-Nawadir, is on the side of Madinah about four miles, up to the end of al-Tan'im; on the side of Iraq about eight miles, up to a place called al-Maqta'; on the side of 'Arafah nine miles; on the side of the Yemen road seven miles, up to a place called Adāh; and on the side of Jeddah ten miles, up to the end of al-Hudaybiyyah. Malik said in al-'Utbiyyah: al-Hudaybiyyah is within the sanctuary.

Among its signs, as mentioned by Makki and others, is that birds do not fly over it, and if a bird does fly over it, that is only because of an illness in it, so it seeks healing through the House.

The qadi Abu Muhammad said:
All of this, in my view, is weak, for birds are observed flying over it. An eagle flew over it when it seized the snake that was poised over its wall, and that was among its signs.

Among its signs, as people have mentioned in ancient and recent times, is that when rain falls upon it from its four sides in a single year, the horizons of the earth become fertile, and if rain does not fall on one side of it, that horizon adjacent to it does not become fertile that year.

The people differed regarding the standing-place of Abraham. The majority said it is the well-known stone. Some said the whole House is the standing-place of Abraham, because he built it and stood in all its regions. Some of the scholars said all of Makkah is the standing-place of Abraham. Others said the whole sanctuary is the standing-place of Abraham. The pronoun in His words "وَمَن دَخَلَهُ" (whoever enters it) refers to the sanctuary according to the view of those who said the standing-place of Abraham is the sanctuary, and it refers to the House according to the view of the majority, since no other thing has been mentioned before it. Nevertheless, the meaning implies that whoever enters the sanctuary is in security, since the sanctuary is a part of the House, as it exists by its cause and by its sanctity.

The people differed about the meaning of His words "كانَ آمِنًا" (was safe). Al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Ata' and Mujahid, and others, said: this is a description of a state that existed in the Jahiliyyah, that whoever committed a crime and then entered the sanctuary would not be seized or pursued. As for in Islam, and the safety of all regions, the sanctuary does not prevent any of the prescribed punishments (hudud) of Allah: whoever steals within it has his hand cut off, whoever commits adultery is stoned, and whoever kills is killed. Many of those who held this view found it good (istaḥsana) that whoever deserves execution should be taken out to the lawful area (al-ḥill) and executed there. (p. 293) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: whoever commits an offence and then seeks refuge in the House is safe, and the matter in Islam is as it was in the Jahiliyyah, though Islam has increased the House in honour and reverence. So no one may attack the killer of his guardian (walī) in Makkah, but it is obligatory upon the Muslims not to trade with that offender, nor speak to him, nor shelter him, until he is forced to leave the sanctuary, whereupon the prescribed punishment is carried out upon him. Similar to this was said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Suddi and others. However, most of them said this about one who kills outside the sanctuary and then flees to the sanctuary. As for one who kills within the sanctuary, the prescribed punishment is carried out upon him within the sanctuary.

The qadi Abu Muhammad said:
When the matter of this one who is not spoken to and not traded with is considered carefully, he is not in fact safe.

Yahya ibn Ja'dah said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever enters the House is safe from the Fire. Al-Naqqash related from one of the worshippers, who said: I was circumambulating the Ka'bah at night, and I said: O Lord, You said: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾; from what, O Lord, is he safe? Then I heard one speaking to me, saying: "From the Fire." I looked and reflected, but there was no one in the place.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people﴾ … the verse. This is the obligation of Hajj in the Book of Allah by scholarly consensus (ijma'). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: all of Hajj is in the Book of Allah. As for prayer and zakat, they are among its general principles (mujmal), which the Prophet, peace be upon him, explained. Hajj is one of the pillars of Islam upon which it is built, according to the hadith. Its conditions of obligation are five: puberty, sanity, freedom, Islam, and the ability to find a way (istiṭā'at al-sabīl). Hajj in the language means intention (al-qaṣd), but in the House of Allah it is specified with particular acts and utterances.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs, from 'Asim, recited "ḥijj al-bayt" with a kasrah on the ḥā', and the others recited "ḥajj al-bayt" with a fatḥah on it. Sibawayh said: ḥajja ḥijjan, like dhakara dhikran. Abu 'Ali said: (p. 294) so ḥijj in this sense is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Sibawayh also said: they say ghazāh (a raid), intending the act of one occurrence, just as it is said ḥijjah (one pilgrimage).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
His saying ḥijj with a kasrah on the ḥā' means the act of one year, and they did not use it in the original form, but it became a noun for it. Abu 'Ali said: his saying "they did not use it in the original form" means in the fatḥah form, which is the single occurrence of the verb, but they gave it a kasrah and made it a noun for this meaning, just as ghazāh is so, and the form ghazwah did not occur, though it would have been the analogical form.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The kasrah on the ḥā' is most consistently kept in their phrase dhū al-ḥijjah. As for their phrases ḥijjat al-wadā' and the like, they are in the original form. Al-Zajjaj and others said: ḥajj with a fatḥah on the ḥā' is the verbal noun, and with a kasrah it is the name of the act. Al-Tabari said: they are two dialects: the kasrah is the dialect of Najd, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the people of al-'Aliyah.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿for whoever is able to make his way there﴾: "man" (whoever) is in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) to "al-nās" (the people), and it is an apposition of part to whole (badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull). Al-Kisa'i and others said: it is a conditional (sharṭ) in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'). Its response (jawāb) is omitted, its implied sense being: then upon him is the Hajj, and what indicates this is the conjunction of the second condition after it in His words: "وَمَن كَفَرَ" (whoever disbelieves). Some of the Basran grammarians said: "man" is in the nominative as the agent of the verbal noun "ḥijj al-bayt," and the verbal noun is then annexed to its object.

The people differed about the condition of one who is able to find a way: what is it? 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the state of one who finds provision and a mount. Al-Tabari related from al-Hasan, through the chain of Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, and a man said to him: O Messenger of Allah, what is the way (al-sabīl)? He said: 'Provision and a mount.'" Al-Tabari also traced to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever possesses provision and a mount but does not perform Hajj, it makes no difference whether he dies a Jew or a Christian." 'Abd al-Razzaq and Sufyan related from Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi, from Muhammad ibn 'Abbad ibn Ja'far, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "A man stood up before the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: What is the way? He said: 'Provision and a mount.'"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Some people declared this hadith weak, because Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Khuzi was criticized by Ibn Ma'in and others. The hadith does not depend on the chain of Ibrahim. Some of the Baghdadis said: this hadith indicates that Hajj is not obligatory on foot.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

[p-296] What I say is that this hadith was spoken with reference to the common circumstances of people, namely distance from Makkah and the great difficulty of walking on foot. As for one who lives near, he is not included in the hadith, because proximity makes him independent of provisions and a mount. As for one who is able to walk from distant regions, a mount is available to him through the meaning and the strength that he has been given. Allah the Exalted has mentioned this in His saying ﴿they will come to you on foot﴾. Likewise, the meaning of the hadith is: provisions and a mount are for the one who has no excuse in his body, such as sickness, or fear for his dependants, or one who is obliged to pay a wage or a debt and is striving to discharge it and hopes to do so by managing the wealth before him. As for the one who has no means, he may perform Hajj if he exerts himself and is able. So the purpose of the hadith is to define the point at which obligation falls upon the one who lives far away. As for those who walk and those with excuses, many of them undertake the journey even though Hajj is not obligatory for them, and then this exertion [p-296 continues] leads them to a point at which Hajj becomes obligatory for them. This is an emphasis on seeking and attaining reward, if Allah the Exalted wills.

A group of scholars held that the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿whoever is able to make his way to it﴾, is a general statement which is not explained by provisions and a mount or anything else. Rather, when a person is able without it being burdensome to himself, Hajj has become obligatory upon him. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Dahhak. Al-Hasan said: whoever finds something that will convey him has become able to make his way to it. ʿIkrimah said: the ability to make the way is health. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever possesses three hundred dirhams, that is the way to it. Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, in the report of Ashhab from al-ʿUtbiyya and in the Kitab of Muhammad, when it was said to him, "Do you say that the way is provisions and a mount?", "No, by Allah. A man may have provisions and a mount and yet be unable to travel, and another may be able to walk on foot, and a small person may be sturdier than a large one. So there is no description in this clearer than what Allah the Exalted has said."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is the most excellent of statements. All that has been related from the scholars does not contradict one another. Provisions and a mount are, in the majority of people's circumstances, what is needed for distance, and for those who are healthy but unable to walk on foot. Ability, whenever it is attained, is general in this and in other than this. So if we suppose a man able to travel on foot, accustomed to doing so, who asks people for support in his residence and lives on their service and their charity, and he finds companions, then Hajj is obligatory upon him without provisions or a mount. This is among the matters in which fiqh of the situation (fiqh al-hal, understanding of the actual circumstances) plays a role. Al-Shafiʿi used to say: ability is of two kinds; ability by oneself first. So whoever is prevented by sickness or an excuse, while having wealth, must appoint someone to perform Hajj on his behalf, while he is able to do so.

People differed as to whether the obligation of Hajj is immediate (ʿala al-fawr) or may be delayed (ʿala al-taraakhi). There are two opinions. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, has issues which imply both opinions. He said in al-Majmuʿa concerning one who wished to perform Hajj and his parents prevented him: he should not hasten against them in the obligatory Hajj, but should seek their permission for a year or two. This is delay. He said in the Kitab of Ibn al-Mawwaz: no one may perform Hajj except with the permission of his parents, except for the obligatory Hajj; so let him set out and leave them. This is immediacy. Malik said concerning a woman whose husband dies and who wishes to go out for Hajj: she should not go out during the days of her waiting period (ʿidda). Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: so he made it a matter of delay.

[p-297] The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is an inference that is open to question.

Malik's opinion differed concerning one who goes out to Hajj on condition that he asks people as he travels and returns, one whose habit is not to do so in his home. Ibn Wahb related from him that he said: there is no harm in that. It was said to him: "What if he dies on the road?" He said: "His reckoning is with Allah." Ibn al-Qasim related from him that he said: I do not see that those who do not find what to spend should go out to Hajj or to raid and ask (for support), and I dislike that, because of the saying of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿There is no blame upon those who cannot find what to spend﴾ [al-Tawba: 91]. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik disliked that women perform Hajj by sea, because it involves exposure; and he disliked that anyone perform Hajj by sea except people like the people of al-Andalus, who have no alternative. He said in the Kitab of Muhammad and others:
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj: 27]; and I do not hear any mention of the sea.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is a reassurance from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, for the absence of the word "sea." The verse does not require the exclusion of the sea. The explanation of that will come in its place, if Allah wills. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Some people from my community were shown to me as kings upon thrones, or like kings upon thrones, riding the crest of this green sea, as raiders in the way of Allah."

There is no difference between raiding and Hajj.

People differed concerning the Hajj of women on foot when they are able to do so. Malik said in al-Mudawwana concerning a woman who vows to walk and then becomes unable partway along the road: she must return a second time. He said: men and women are equal in this. On this basis, Hajj becomes obligatory if she is able to walk, because the obligatory Hajj is more binding than a vow.

He said in the Kitab of Muhammad: I do not see Hajj on foot as obligatory for a woman, even if she is strong enough for it, because a woman walking is a matter of nakedness (ʿawra), except if the place is near Makkah.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This looks, through fiqh of the situation, at a woman who is attractive or one who is past the age of attracting.

There is no Hajj for a woman except when a mahram (a close male relative whom she may not marry) is with her. People differed if she lacks one, whether Hajj becomes obligatory through someone who is in the same position as a mahram, from among trustworthy women who travel with her in the caravan, or trustworthy men. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Abu Hanifa and his companions said: the mahram is part of the (meaning of) "way," and there is no Hajj for her except with a mahram.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is standing by the wording of the hadith.

Malik said: she goes out with a group of women. Al-Shafiʿi said: she goes out with a free, trustworthy, Muslim woman. Ibn Sirin said: she goes out with a trustworthy man from among the Muslims. Al-Awzaʿi said: she goes out with a company of upright men, and she takes a ladder which she climbs up and comes down by, and no man approaches her.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
These opinions have taken account of the meaning of the hadith. The majority of the Community hold that a woman may perform the obligatory Hajj even if her husband dislikes it, and he has no right to prevent her. The opinion of al-Shafiʿi on this matter is inconsistent.

People differed concerning the obligation of Hajj in the presence of unjust tolls (mukus, illegal levies) and fines. Sufyan al-Thawri said: if there is a toll, even of one dirham, the obligation falls. The apparent meaning of this is that if it is large and not crushing given the breadth of one's means, the obligation does not fall. On this view is a group of the people of knowledge, and the ages have proceeded upon it.

[p-299] The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is a brief extract of the fiqh of ability. This compilation is not the place for an exhaustive account of it. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Al-sabil (the way) is treated as both masculine and feminine, and the more common and more eloquent usage is feminine. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿you seek to make it crooked﴾ [Al ʿImran: 99] and He said: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. From the masculine usage is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Malik:

"He decreed on the day of Badr that you should meet a people who transgressed, and the way of transgression among people is permitted."

The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the House, and it may also refer to Hajj.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: whoever claims that Hajj is not obligatory upon him. Al-Dahhak, ʿAta', ʿImran al-Qattan, al-Hasan and Mujahid said the same. It is related from the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, that he recited the verse, and a man from Hudhayl said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, whoever abandons it has disbelieved?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Whoever abandons it does not fear its punishment, and whoever performs it does not hope for its reward, so that is it." Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid also said something of this meaning. This and what precedes it refer to disbelief of denial and departure from the religion. Ibn ʿUmar and a group of scholars said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day. This is close to the first. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever disbelieves in these signs which are in the House. Al-Suddi and a group of the people of knowledge said: the meaning of the verse is: and whoever disbelieves by finding what he needs for Hajj and then not performing it. Al-Suddi said: whoever is in this state is a disbeliever.

[p-300] The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is disbelief of disobedience, like His (ʿalayhi al-salam) saying: "Whoever abandons the prayer has disbelieved," and his saying: "Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking the necks of one another," according to the most apparent of the possible meanings of this hadith. It is clear that whoever Allah has blessed with wealth and health and does not perform Hajj has ungratefully disbelieved the blessing.

The meaning of His saying, ﴿Free of need from the worlds﴾, is a warning to the one who disbelieves. The intent of the statement is: indeed Allah is free of need from them, but He has generalised the wording so that the meaning may be comprehensive, and to alert the mind to the power and sovereignty of Allah and His self-sufficiency in every respect, so that there is no need in Him for anything, there is no lord but Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 98–99:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is Witness over what you do?"﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert [people] from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾

These verses are a rebuke to the Jews contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ). "The Scripture" (al-Kitab) is the Torah, and they are called its people according to their own claim and lineage; otherwise, its people in truth are the believers. "The signs of Allah" may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to the manifest signs that appeared at the hands of Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah is Witness over what you do﴾ is a pure threat: that is, He will requite you for it and punish you.

Al-Tabari said: These two verses, His saying ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve..."﴾ and what follows them, up to His saying ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 105], were revealed because of a Jewish man who tried to incite discord between the Aws and the Khazraj. Ibn Ishaq said: The trustworthy one related to me from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Shas ibn Qays, a Jew – who was an old man who had grown decrepit in the Jahiliyya, of great disbelief, of intense rancor and envy toward the Muslims – passed by a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Aws and the Khazraj, who were in an assembly conversing. He was angered by what he saw of their unity and the good harmony between them after the enmity that had existed among them. He said: 'The leaders of the Banu Qaylah have gathered in this land; by Allah, we have no place among them when their leaders gather here.' So he ordered a young Jewish man, saying: 'Go to them, sit with them, remind them of the Day of Bu'ath and what came before it of their days of war, and recite to them what they said of poetry about that.' The young man did so. The people then spoke, boasting and disputing, until two men from the two clans leapt up on their knees: Aws ibn Qayzi, of the Banu Harithah ibn al-Harith from the Aws, and Jabbar ibn Sakhr from the Khazraj. They quarreled, then one of them said to his companion: 'If you wish, by Allah, we can take it up again as it was!' The two groups became angry and said: 'We have done so! Arms, arms! Our appointment is al-Zahira,' meaning al-Harra. They went out to it, and the people argued over their claims which they held in the Jahiliyya. The news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the Emigrants who were with him, and said: 'O assembly of Muslims, Allah, Allah! Are you invoking the claims of the Jahiliyya while I am among you?' He admonished them, and the people recognized that it was a stirring of Satan. They threw down their weapons and wept, and some of the Aws and Khazraj embraced one another, and they departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), listening and obeying. So Allah revealed concerning Shas ibn Qays and what he did these verses." Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: These verses were revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews who used to turn the Muslims away from Islam by telling them: "Muhammad is not described in our Book."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that these two causes and what resembles them of the actions and statements of the Jews did occur, so the verses were revealed concerning all of that.

Sadda (صَدَّ) means: he turned away from a thing and departed from it. It is an intransitive verb which is also transitive with the same form. You say: "Sadadtu 'an kadha" (I turned away from such-and-such), and "Sadadtu ghayri 'anhu" (I turned another away from it). What is in this verse is the transitive form. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "tuṣiddūna" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the sad, and this is the intransitive form, made transitive by the hamzah. "The way of Allah" (sabil Allah) in this verse is Islam, which is the path to the pleasure of Allah and His Paradise. "Man" (مَن) is the object of "tasuddun", and the pronoun in "tabghunaha" refers back to the way. The meaning of "tabghun", according to what al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari and others explained, is "you seek": so the meaning is "you seek for it crookedness," that is, deviation and corruption. The Arabs say: "ibghini kadha" (with a connected alif), meaning "seek it for me"; and when they want "help me in seeking it and seek it with me," they cut the alif and open it. It has also been said that "tabghun" here derives from baghy, which is transgression, meaning "you seek to transgress against it," and in this interpretation "'iwajan" (crookedness) is in the accusative as a circumstantial object of the pronoun in "tabghun," meaning: crookedness from you and lack of uprightness.

"'Iwaj" with a kasrah on the ayn is what occurs in matters, arguments and non-solid things, whereas "'awaj" with a fathah on the ayn is what occurs in solid bodies such as a wall, a staff and the like. Ibn Qutaybah said: The earth in particular, among solid bodies, is described as "'iwaj" with a kasrah on the ayn, and from this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿You will not see in it crookedness or elevation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 107]. Some linguists said: they are two dialects with one meaning. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"And you are witnesses"﴾ means the plural of shahid, referring to what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his truthfulness; and the rest of the verse is a threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 98–99:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is Witness over what you do?"﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert [people] from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾

These verses are a rebuke to the Jews contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ). "The Scripture" (al-Kitab) is the Torah, and they are called its people according to their own claim and lineage; otherwise, its people in truth are the believers. "The signs of Allah" may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to the manifest signs that appeared at the hands of Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah is Witness over what you do﴾ is a pure threat: that is, He will requite you for it and punish you.

Al-Tabari said: These two verses, His saying ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve..."﴾ and what follows them, up to His saying ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 105], were revealed because of a Jewish man who tried to incite discord between the Aws and the Khazraj. Ibn Ishaq said: The trustworthy one related to me from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Shas ibn Qays, a Jew – who was an old man who had grown decrepit in the Jahiliyya, of great disbelief, of intense rancor and envy toward the Muslims – passed by a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Aws and the Khazraj, who were in an assembly conversing. He was angered by what he saw of their unity and the good harmony between them after the enmity that had existed among them. He said: 'The leaders of the Banu Qaylah have gathered in this land; by Allah, we have no place among them when their leaders gather here.' So he ordered a young Jewish man, saying: 'Go to them, sit with them, remind them of the Day of Bu'ath and what came before it of their days of war, and recite to them what they said of poetry about that.' The young man did so. The people then spoke, boasting and disputing, until two men from the two clans leapt up on their knees: Aws ibn Qayzi, of the Banu Harithah ibn al-Harith from the Aws, and Jabbar ibn Sakhr from the Khazraj. They quarreled, then one of them said to his companion: 'If you wish, by Allah, we can take it up again as it was!' The two groups became angry and said: 'We have done so! Arms, arms! Our appointment is al-Zahira,' meaning al-Harra. They went out to it, and the people argued over their claims which they held in the Jahiliyya. The news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the Emigrants who were with him, and said: 'O assembly of Muslims, Allah, Allah! Are you invoking the claims of the Jahiliyya while I am among you?' He admonished them, and the people recognized that it was a stirring of Satan. They threw down their weapons and wept, and some of the Aws and Khazraj embraced one another, and they departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), listening and obeying. So Allah revealed concerning Shas ibn Qays and what he did these verses." Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: These verses were revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews who used to turn the Muslims away from Islam by telling them: "Muhammad is not described in our Book."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that these two causes and what resembles them of the actions and statements of the Jews did occur, so the verses were revealed concerning all of that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 100–101:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ ﴿And how could you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and among you is His Messenger? And whoever holds firmly to Allah has already been guided to a straight path.﴾

The address in His saying, "O you who have believed," is general to the believers, and the reference in this, at the time of its revelation, was to the Aws and the Khazraj because of the flare-up caused by Shas ibn Qays. "Faction" (firqah) means a group of people, and what is meant by it here is the rabbis and the leaders. "Return you" (yaruddukum) means: by misguidance, sowing doubt, deception, and displaying deceit under the guise of counsel.

Then He made the believers stand before this matter, which is far-fetched and abhorrent, which the Jews intend for them, so He said: ﴿And how could you disbelieve while you are﴾ in these described states? "How" (kayfa) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), as it is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. The meaning is: "Do you disbelieve while denying? Do you disbelieve out of ignorance, or out of contempt, or as apostates?" and similar estimations of this kind. The "wa" (and) in His saying "wa kayfa takfurūn" is a conjunction joining one sentence to another sentence, and it is not permissible for "kayfa" in this verse to be as it is in your saying, "kayfa tafʿalu kadhā?" (how do you do such-and-such?) while you are asking about something whose occurrence is established and realized, because that would necessitate that the disbelief of the believers be affirmed and established as having occurred. Consider the meaning of "kayfa" when a verb follows it, and its meaning when a noun follows it.

Al-Jumhur recited "tutlā" with a *tā'* on top, while al-Ḥasan recited "yutlā" with a *yā'*, since the verses (āyāt) are the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He, "wa fīkum" (and among you) indicates the adverbial sense of presence and direct witnessing of his person, peace be upon him, and he is among his community until the Day of Resurrection through his sayings and his traces. "Yaʿtaṣim" means: holds fast and seeks protection; and "ʿuṣima al-shayʾ" means that a thing was prevented and protected. From it is His saying: ﴿He will shelter me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43]. The ʿuṣum are the means by which one is attached and by which one is protected from failure in the sought objective. Al-A'sha said:

"To the man Qays I lengthen the journeys, and I take from every tribe their ʿuṣum."

(p-304) The derivations of this word are very numerous, and the rest of the verse is clear, and Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 102–103:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except while you are Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together, and do not become divided.﴾

The address in this verse encompasses all the believers, but what was intended at the time of its revelation were the Aws and the Khazraj, among whom there had arisen that dispute caused by the incitement of Shas ibn Qays.

Tuqat is a verbal noun of the form fu'lah, its original form being tuqyah. His saying ﴿except when you fear a danger from them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28] has already been discussed. It is also permissible that tuqat in this verse be the plural of fa'il, though no verb is conjugated from it, so it would be like rumat and rami (archers and an archer). Or it may be the plural of taqiyy, since fa'il and fa'il are equivalent. The meaning according to this is: fear Allah as is due to those who truly fear Him exclusively, and for this reason they are attributed to the pronoun of Allah, exalted is He.

The scholars differed concerning His saying "as He should be feared." One group said: the verse was revealed in the generality of its wording, and it obliged the community to fear Allah to the utmost degree of God-consciousness, so that no lapse occurs in anything. Then Allah abrogated this for the community by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun: 16], and by His saying ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]. This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Ibn Zayd and others.

Another group of the people of knowledge said: there is no abrogation in any of this, and these verses are in agreement. The meaning of this one is: fear Allah as He should be feared, to the extent you are able. This is because "as He should be feared" is in accordance with His commands and prohibitions, and Allah, exalted is He, has made the religion easy. This is the correct view. For a son of Adam not to disobey entirely, neither in minor nor in major matters, and not to slacken in worship, is an objective that is impossible given human nature. Had Allah imposed this, it would have been imposing what cannot be borne, and no one has upheld that in the interpretation of this verse (p-305). Rather, they expressed the meaning of this verse by saying, as Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "As He should be feared" means: that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, that He be thanked and not denied, and that He be remembered and not forgotten. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, Qatadah and al-Hasan expressed it similarly. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ is: strive for Allah with the striving that is due to Him, and there is no abrogation in the verse. Tawus said concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾: He, exalted is He, says: if you do not fear Him and are not able to do so, then do not die except while you are Muslims.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ means: remain upon Islam until death reaches you while you are upon it. This is the real sense of the matter, and the expression came in this concise and elegant form. Its parallel is what Sibawayh related of their saying: "I shall not see you here," whereas what is meant is: "Do not be here, so that I do not see you." "Muslims" in this verse is the comprehensive meaning encompassing belief and deeds, and it is the religion with Allah, and it is that which is built upon five (pillars).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together﴾ means: take refuge and be protected by it. Holding fast may be by grasping with the hand, by climbing mountain ledges, or by other means that provide protection; from it comes al-a'sam (the one with a protected place) in the mountain, and from it comes 'ismat al-nikah (the bond of marriage). The "rope" in this verse is a metaphor: since the means by which one holds fast is an extended connection between the one who protects and the one protected, and a relation between the two, it was likened to the rope whose function is to join one thing to another. Covenants and pacts are also called ropes (hibal). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"When the tribe's ropes pass beyond her, the ropes of the nearest ones take hold of you."

And from it is another's saying:

"Indeed, I join my rope to your rope..."

And from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112].

The expressions of the exegetes differed regarding what is meant by "the rope of Allah" in this verse. Ibn Mas'ud said: the rope of Allah is the community (al-jama'ah). Anas ibn Malik related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Children of Israel divided into seventy-one sects, and my community will divide into seventy-two sects, all of which are in the Fire except one." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is this one?" He said: he clasped his hand and said: "The community," and he recited: ﴿and hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said in a sermon: "Upon you all, adherence to obedience and the community, for it is the rope of Allah which He commanded." Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the rope of Allah which He commanded to hold fast to is the Qur'an. Al-Suddi said: the rope of Allah is the Book of Allah, and Ibn Mas'ud and al-Dahhak also said this. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Book of Allah is the rope of Allah extended from the heaven to the earth." Abu al-'Aliyah said: the rope of Allah in this verse is sincerity in monotheism. Ibn Zayd said: the rope of Allah is Islam.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Other things have been said besides this, all of which are close to one another.

His saying, exalted is He: "all together" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hold fast" (i'tasimu), so the meaning is: be gathered together in your holding fast. "And do not become divided" intends the division that does not allow concord in striving and in protecting the religion and the word of Allah, exalted is He. This is division through strife and division in creed. As for division in the matters of subsidiary rulings and jurisprudence, it does not enter into this verse. Rather, that is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ referred to when he said: "The difference of opinion within my community is a mercy." The Companions differed greatly in the subsidiary matters (p-307), yet they were one hand against every disbeliever.

As for the strife concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, it is among the forbidden division. Indeed, interpretation (ta'wil) is what drew into it more than those among the Companions who entered it, may Allah be pleased with all of them.

**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs that you may be guided.﴾

This verse indicates that the address in it is specifically to the Aws and the Khazraj. For although this term could apply to all the Arabs, they had not, at the time of the revelation of this verse, united upon Islam nor had their hearts been brought together. Rather, it was in the story of Shas ibn Qays at the beginning of the Hijrah, and at that time this verse was revealed. So it refers to the Aws and the Khazraj, who had enmity and wars between them, among them the Day of Bu'ath and others. Those wars and enmity had lasted between the two tribes for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah lifted them through Islam. Then the six men of the Ansar came to Makkah as pilgrims, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented himself to them and recited the Qur'an to them, as he used to do with the tribes of the Arabs. They believed in him, and he wished to go out with them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you come to our land with the enmity and war that is between us, we fear that what you desire from you will not be accomplished. Rather, we will go ourselves, spread your affair, and mingle with the people, and our appointment with you will be the coming year." So they departed and did so. The Ansar came in the following year, and that was the second 'Aqabah, and they were twelve men, among them five of the first six. Then they came in the third year, and that was the Pledge of 'Aqabah the Great, attended by seventy, among them twelve chiefs (naqib). The description of this story is fully given in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.

Allah, exalted is He, facilitated Islam for the Ansar in two ways. One of them: the Children of Israel were neighbors to them, and they used to say to those Arabs whom they threatened: "A prophet will be sent to us now, and we will kill you with him as the slaying of 'Ad and Iram." When the group of Ansar saw Muhammad ﷺ, some of them said to others: "By Allah, this is the Prophet of whom the Children of Israel spoke, so do not let them get ahead of you to him." The other way: the war which had mauled them and destroyed their nobles, so they hoped that Allah would unite their word through him as had been the case. Thus Allah, exalted is He, enumerated to them His favor in uniting them after enmity, and reminded them of it.

His saying, exalted is He: "fa-asbahtum" is an expression for continuity, even though the word is specific to a certain time. This word was specifically given this meaning because it is the beginning of the day, and in it is the beginning of actions. So the state that a person perceives within himself at that time is his state which he generally continues upon through the day. From this is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Dab':

"I have become one who does not bear arms, nor own the head of a camel if they flee."

"Ikhwan" is the plural of akh, and it is pluralized as ikhwah; these two are the most well-known plurals of it. However, Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that ikhwah is a collective noun and not a plural pattern, because fa'al is not pluralized as fi'lah. Some people said: "akh" in religion is pluralized as ikhwan, and "akh" in lineage is pluralized as ikhwah; this is how their usage has become common.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In the Book of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 10], and in it: ﴿or their brothers' sons﴾ [An-Nur: 31]. So the correct view is that both are used of lineage and both are used of religion.

Ash-shafa: the edge of every body that has a drop, such as a pit, a well, a precipice, a roof, a wall, and the like. In usage it is attributed to the upper part, as in "the edge of a precipice" (shafa jurf), and to the lower part, as in "the edge of a pit" (shafa hufrah). Its dual is shafawan. Allah, exalted is He, likened their disbelief in which they were, and their war that brought them close to death, to the edge, because they were falling into Jahannam continually, so Allah saved them through Islam. The pronoun in "minha" refers to the Fire or to the pit, and returning it to the nearer is better. Some people, related by al-Tabari, said that the pronoun refers to the edge (shafa), and the pronoun was made feminine since shafa is made genitive to a feminine noun. So the verse is like the saying of Jarir:

"She saw the passing of years take from me as the crescent is diminished by the thinning..."

and other examples of that kind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The matter is not as he mentioned, and the verse does not require this technicality, except if there were no antecedent for the pronoun other than "shafa." But since there is a feminine noun in the sentence to which the pronoun refers, supported by the meaning being discussed, there is no need for that technicality.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs﴾ refers to what He made clear in these verses, meaning: thus does He make clear to you other than them. His saying: "la'allakum" (that you may) expresses hope with respect to human beings, meaning: whoever among you reflects upon the situation hopes for guidance.

Tawus said concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾: He, exalted is He, says: if you do not fear Him and are not able to do so, then do not die except while you are Muslims.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ means: remain upon Islam until death reaches you while you are upon it. This is the real sense of the matter, and the expression came in this concise and elegant form. Its parallel is what Sibawayh related of their saying: "I shall not see you here," whereas what is meant is: "Do not be here, so that I do not see you." "Muslims" in this verse is the comprehensive meaning encompassing belief and deeds, and it is the religion with Allah, and it is that which is built upon five (pillars).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together﴾ means: take refuge and be protected by it. Holding fast may be by grasping with the hand, by climbing mountain ledges, or by other means that provide protection; from it comes al-a'sam (the one with a protected place) in the mountain, and from it comes 'ismat al-nikah (the bond of marriage). The "rope" in this verse is a metaphor: since the means by which one holds fast is an extended connection between the one who protects and the one protected, and a relation between the two, it was likened to the rope whose function is to join one thing to another. Covenants and pacts are also called ropes (hibal). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"When the tribe's ropes pass beyond her, the ropes of the nearest ones take hold of you."

And from it is another's saying:

"Indeed, I join my rope to your rope..."

And from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112].

The expressions of the exegetes differed regarding what is meant by "the rope of Allah" in this verse. Ibn Mas'ud said: the rope of Allah is the community (al-jama'ah). Anas ibn Malik related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Children of Israel divided into seventy-one sects, and my community will divide into seventy-two sects, all of which are in the Fire except one." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is this one?" He said: he clasped his hand and said: "The community," and he recited: ﴿and hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said in a sermon: "Upon you all, adherence to obedience and the community, for it is the rope of Allah which He commanded." Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the rope of Allah which He commanded to hold fast to is the Qur'an. Al-Suddi said: the rope of Allah is the Book of Allah, and Ibn Mas'ud and al-Dahhak also said this. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Book of Allah is the rope of Allah extended from the heaven to the earth." Abu al-'Aliyah said: the rope of Allah in this verse is sincerity in monotheism. Ibn Zayd said: the rope of Allah is Islam.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Other things have been said besides this, all of which are close to one another.

His saying, exalted is He: "all together" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hold fast" (i'tasimu), so the meaning is: be gathered together in your holding fast. "And do not become divided" intends the division that does not allow concord in striving and in protecting the religion and the word of Allah, exalted is He. This is division through strife and division in creed. As for division in the matters of subsidiary rulings and jurisprudence, it does not enter into this verse. Rather, that is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ referred to when he said: "The difference of opinion within my community is a mercy." The Companions differed greatly in the subsidiary matters (p-307), yet they were one hand against every disbeliever.

As for the strife concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, it is among the forbidden division. Indeed, interpretation (ta'wil) is what drew into it more than those among the Companions who entered it, may Allah be pleased with all of them.

**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs that you may be guided.﴾

This verse indicates that the address in it is specifically to the Aws and the Khazraj. For although this term could apply to all the Arabs, they had not, at the time of the revelation of this verse, united upon Islam nor had their hearts been brought together. Rather, it was in the story of Shas ibn Qays at the beginning of the Hijrah, and at that time this verse was revealed. So it refers to the Aws and the Khazraj, who had enmity and wars between them, among them the Day of Bu'ath and others. Those wars and enmity had lasted between the two tribes for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah lifted them through Islam. Then the six men of the Ansar came to Makkah as pilgrims, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented himself to them and recited the Qur'an to them, as he used to do with the tribes of the Arabs. They believed in him, and he wished to go out with them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you come to our land with the enmity and war that is between us, we fear that what you desire from you will not be accomplished. Rather, we will go ourselves, spread your affair, and mingle with the people, and our appointment with you will be the coming year." So they departed and did so. The Ansar came in the following year, and that was the second 'Aqabah, and they were twelve men, among them five of the first six. Then they came in the third year, and that was the Pledge of 'Aqabah the Great, attended by seventy, among them twelve chiefs (naqib). The description of this story is fully given in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.

Allah, exalted is He, facilitated Islam for the Ansar in two ways. One of them: the Children of Israel were neighbors to them, and they used to say to those Arabs whom they threatened: "A prophet will be sent to us now, and we will kill you with him as the slaying of 'Ad and Iram." When the group of Ansar saw Muhammad ﷺ, some of them said to others: "By Allah, this is the Prophet of whom the Children of Israel spoke, so do not let them get ahead of you to him." The other way: the war which had mauled them and destroyed their nobles, so they hoped that Allah would unite their word through him as had been the case. Thus Allah, exalted is He, enumerated to them His favor in uniting them after enmity, and reminded them of it.

His saying, exalted is He: "fa-asbahtum" is an expression for continuity, even though the word is specific to a certain time. This word was specifically given this meaning because it is the beginning of the day, and in it is the beginning of actions. So the state that a person perceives within himself at that time is his state which he generally continues upon through the day. From this is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Dab':

"I have become one who does not bear arms, nor own the head of a camel if they flee."

"Ikhwan" is the plural of akh, and it is pluralized as ikhwah; these two are the most well-known plurals of it. However, Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that ikhwah is a collective noun and not a plural pattern, because fa'al is not pluralized as fi'lah. Some people said: "akh" in religion is pluralized as ikhwan, and "akh" in lineage is pluralized as ikhwah; this is how their usage has become common.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In the Book of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 10], and in it: ﴿or their brothers' sons﴾ [An-Nur: 31]. So the correct view is that both are used of lineage and both are used of religion.

Ash-shafa: the edge of every body that has a drop, such as a pit, a well, a precipice, a roof, a wall, and the like. In usage it is attributed to the upper part, as in "the edge of a precipice" (shafa jurf), and to the lower part, as in "the edge of a pit" (shafa hufrah). Its dual is shafawan. Allah, exalted is He, likened their disbelief in which they were, and their war that brought them close to death, to the edge, because they were falling into Jahannam continually, so Allah saved them through Islam. The pronoun in "minha" refers to the Fire or to the pit, and returning it to the nearer is better. Some people, related by al-Tabari, said that the pronoun refers to the edge (shafa), and the pronoun was made feminine since shafa is made genitive to a feminine noun. So the verse is like the saying of Jarir:

"She saw the passing of years take from me as the crescent is diminished by the thinning..."

and other examples of that kind.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The matter is not as he mentioned, and the verse does not require this technicality, except if there were no antecedent for the pronoun other than "shafa." But since there is a feminine noun in the sentence to which the pronoun refers, supported by the meaning being discussed, there is no need for that technicality.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs﴾ refers to what He made clear in these verses, meaning: thus does He make clear to you other than them. His saying: "la'allakum" (that you may) expresses hope with respect to human beings, meaning: whoever among you reflects upon the situation hopes for guidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 104–105:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And let there be among you a community (ummah) who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a tremendous punishment.﴾

Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu Haywa read "Wa-litakun" with a kasra on the lam, according to the original form, since its origin is the kasra. Likewise they read the lam of the imperative throughout the Qur'an.

(p-310) al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and others said: the believers were commanded that a group from among them should have this characteristic, and they are specifically the Companions of the Messenger, and they are specifically the narrators.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, "min" (from) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Allah commanded the community that there should be among them scholars who perform these actions in their proper forms and preserve their rules perfectly, and that the rest of the community should follow them, since these acts cannot be done except with broad knowledge; and Allah, exalted is He, knew that not all of them would be scholars. Al-Zajjaj and more than one of the exegetes held that the meaning is: "And let all of you be a community that invites," and "min" is for explaining the genus (li-bayan al-jins). He said: a similar usage in the Book of Allah is ﴿So shun the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. A similar usage in poetry is the saying of the poet:

"A man of desires who gives them and asks for them; the Nawfal al-Zufar refuses injustice from him."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, this verse on this interpretation is equivalent to your saying: "Let there be from you a righteous man" (li-yakun minka rajulun salih), so in it is the meaning which the grammarians call "al-tajrid" (abstraction). Note that the meaning of ibtida' al-ghayah (the starting point of the limit) enters it, and likewise it enters Allah's saying "min al-awthan," and you do not find it entering the poet's line "minhu al-nawfal al-zufar," nor do you find it entering the "min" which is a clear explanation of the genus, as in your saying: "a garment of silk (min khazz), and a ring of silver (min fiddah)." Rather, the meaning of partitiveness opposes this. The meaning of the verse on this interpretation is: the command to the community that they should invite all the world to good, the disbelievers to Islam and the disobedient to obedience, and that each one of these matters should be according to its rank in knowledge and capability. The people of knowledge said: Allah made obligatory through this verse the enjoining of good and forbidding of wrong, and it is a communal obligation (fard al-kifayah): when someone performs it, it is lifted from others. For the obligation of enjoining good there are conditions, among them that it be done with what is good and not with harshness, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever commands good, let his command be with good." Among them is that the one who commands should not fear harm that will befall him; if he does this despite that, he has greater reward (p-311), and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he is not able, then with his tongue; if he is not able, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

People differ in changing wrong and enjoining good in levels. The obligation of scholars in this is to alert the rulers and governors and to guide them to the path of knowledge; the obligation of governors is to change it by their strength and authority, and for them is "the hand"; and the obligation of the rest of the people is to raise it to the rulers and governors after forbidding it verbally. This applies to wrong that persists. As for one who sees a sudden calamity of wrong such as robbery or fornication and the like, he changes it himself according to the situation and his ability. It is fitting for every believer to bear, in changing wrong, even if some harm reaches him. This approach is supported by the fact that in the recitation of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Zubayr: "They enjoin good and forbid wrong, and they seek help from Allah for what afflicts them." Although this was not recorded in the Mushaf, it contains an indication to face what befalls one after enjoining and forbidding, just as in His saying:

﴿And enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what afflicts you﴾ [Luqman: 17], and His saying: ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves; he who strays cannot harm you when you are guided﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 105], meaning: when it is not accepted from you and you are not able to change the wrong.

Some scholars said: "the good" (al-ma'ruf) is monotheism (tawhid), and "the wrong" (al-munkar) is disbelief (kufr), and the verse was revealed concerning jihad.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Undoubtedly, monotheism and disbelief are the head of the two matters, but whatever falls below the level of monotheism and disbelief necessarily enters the verse.

"Al-muflihun" are those who attain their desire, and this is a generous promise.

(p-312) Then Allah, exalted is He, forbade this community from being like the divided peoples.

The exegetes differed in their expressions regarding those referred to. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a reference to every people who split up in religion, so that division destroyed them. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the Jews and the Christians. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that the reference is also to the sects of the Jews and the sects of the Christians. The "coming of the clear proofs" is through the sending of messengers and the sending down of books. He attributed the verb without a feminine marker to "al-bayyinat" because they were in the position of clarification (bayan), and because there is no true feminine in them. The rest of the verse is a warning.

His saying: ﴿a tremendous punishment﴾ means that it is greater than what is other than it. These two aspects differ in that one of them has interruptions of slackness, whereas the single unit of this and that is equal. This is the clarification of the doctrine of our Usuli scholars, may Allah have mercy on them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 106–107:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turned black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." But as for those whose faces turned white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide eternally.﴾

The governing word (al-'āmil) of "Day" (yawm) in His saying is the verb to which the lām in His saying "and for them there is a great punishment" is attached. Al-Zajjaj said: its implied sense is "and a great punishment will be established for them." The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak in terms of meaning, because it would require that the punishment be magnified on that Day. Nor may the governing word be "punishment" ('adhāb), because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has already been qualified by an adjective.

The whitening of faces is an expression for their brightening, radiance and joy through the mercy of Allah, as al-Zajjaj and others said. In my opinion, it is also possible that this is from the traces of wuḍū' (ablution), as the Prophet ﷺ said: "You are the bright ones with white marks (al-ghurr al-muḥajjalūn) from the traces of ablution." As for the blackening of faces, the exegetes said that it is an expression for their becoming dusty and darkened by the distress of punishment. It is also possible that this is a blackening that Allah will bring upon them in the manner of disfigurement and depiction of them, similar to their being gathered blue-eyed (zurqan), and this is the most ugly appearance. Among examples of this is the verse of Bashshar:

*For the miser, regarding his wealth, there are excuses,*
*blue-eyed, and upon them are black faces.*

Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "tibyaḍḍu wa tiswaddu" with a kasra on the tā' (taʾ), and al-Zuhri recited "tabyāḍḍu wujūhun, wa tiswādḍu wujūhun" with an alif, and this is a dialectal form (lugha).

Since the opening of this verse is information about a state that does not single out any specific person, mention of whiteness was begun with, for its honour, and because it is the best state. When the meaning was understood and it became specific to the disbelievers and the believers, mention of "those whose faces turned black" was begun with, for the purpose of warning against their condition.

His saying, exalted is He, "Did you disbelieve?" is a confirmation and rebuke, connected to an omitted element whose implied sense is: "then it will be said to them: Did you disbelieve?" In this omitted element is the response (jawāb) of "as for" (ammā), and this is what is called the implied sense of the discourse (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), namely that there is something implied in the speech on which the meaning does not depend, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then [the same number of] days later﴾ [al-Baqara: 184], the meaning being: "then he breaks his fast, and [he must make up] the same number of days later."

His saying, exalted is He, "after your belief" (ba'da īmānikum) requires that those being questioned had a prior belief. The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wīl) differed about identifying them. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: those being questioned are all the disbelievers, and the belief by which they are addressed, "after your belief," is the belief they affirmed on the Day when it was said to them: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes." Most of those who interpreted said: the questioning in this verse refers only to the people of the qibla (ahl al-qibla) of this Community. Then they differed. Al-Hasan said: the verse concerns the hypocrites, who believe with their tongues and disbelieve in their hearts, so it is said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" That is, that belief which was only with their tongues. Al-Suddi said: it concerns those among the people of the qibla who disbelieved when they fought one another. Abu Umama said: the verse concerns the Kharijites. Qatada said: the verse concerns the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda), and from this is the ḥadīth: "Men from among my companions will come to the Basin, and when they are brought up to me they will be pulled away, so I will say: 'My companions! My companions!' Then it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' So I will say: 'Away with them, away with them!'" And in one of its chains: "So I will call to them: 'Come! Come!'"

Al-Nahhas mentioned an opinion that the verse concerns the Jews, because they believed in the description of Muhammad and sought victory through him, but when he came to them from other than them, they disbelieved. Thus this is disbelief after belief. It is also reported from Malik that he said: the verse concerns the people of desires (ahl al-ahwā').

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If this is so, then among those who are pulled away from the Basin are those who say what is disbelief. A ḥadīth is also reported that the verse concerns the Qadariyya. Abu Umama said: "We heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that it concerns the Ḥarūriyya (Kharijites of Ḥarūrā')," and it was previously reported from him that it concerns the Kharijites, and this is one statement. The "mā" in His saying "bi-mā kuntum" is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. His saying, exalted is He, "then in the mercy of Allah" means: in the bliss which is the requirement of the mercy of Allah. His saying after that, "they will abide therein," is an emphasis by two clauses, since the speech would stand without them.
