Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "tibyaḍḍu wa tiswaddu" with a kasra on the tā' (taʾ), and al-Zuhri recited "tabyāḍḍu wujūhun, wa tiswādḍu wujūhun" with an alif, and this is a dialectal form (lugha).

Since the opening of this verse is information about a state that does not single out any specific person, mention of whiteness was begun with, for its honour, and because it is the best state. When the meaning was understood and it became specific to the disbelievers and the believers, mention of "those whose faces turned black" was begun with, for the purpose of warning against their condition.

His saying, exalted is He, "Did you disbelieve?" is a confirmation and rebuke, connected to an omitted element whose implied sense is: "then it will be said to them: Did you disbelieve?" In this omitted element is the response (jawāb) of "as for" (ammā), and this is what is called the implied sense of the discourse (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), namely that there is something implied in the speech on which the meaning does not depend, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then [the same number of] days later﴾ [al-Baqara: 184], the meaning being: "then he breaks his fast, and [he must make up] the same number of days later."

His saying, exalted is He, "after your belief" (ba'da īmānikum) requires that those being questioned had a prior belief. The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wīl) differed about identifying them. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: those being questioned are all the disbelievers, and the belief by which they are addressed, "after your belief," is the belief they affirmed on the Day when it was said to them: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes." Most of those who interpreted said: the questioning in this verse refers only to the people of the qibla (ahl al-qibla) of this Community. Then they differed. Al-Hasan said: the verse concerns the hypocrites, who believe with their tongues and disbelieve in their hearts, so it is said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" That is, that belief which was only with their tongues. Al-Suddi said: it concerns those among the people of the qibla who disbelieved when they fought one another. Abu Umama said: the verse concerns the Kharijites. Qatada said: the verse concerns the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda), and from this is the ḥadīth: "Men from among my companions will come to the Basin, and when they are brought up to me they will be pulled away, so I will say: 'My companions! My companions!' Then it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' So I will say: 'Away with them, away with them!'" And in one of its chains: "So I will call to them: 'Come! Come!'"

Al-Nahhas mentioned an opinion that the verse concerns the Jews, because they believed in the description of Muhammad and sought victory through him, but when he came to them from other than them, they disbelieved. Thus this is disbelief after belief. It is also reported from Malik that he said: the verse concerns the people of desires (ahl al-ahwā').

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If this is so, then among those who are pulled away from the Basin are those who say what is disbelief. A ḥadīth is also reported that the verse concerns the Qadariyya. Abu Umama said: "We heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that it concerns the Ḥarūriyya (Kharijites of Ḥarūrā')," and it was previously reported from him that it concerns the Kharijites, and this is one statement. The "mā" in His saying "bi-mā kuntum" is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. His saying, exalted is He, "then in the mercy of Allah" means: in the bliss which is the requirement of the mercy of Allah. His saying after that, "they will abide therein," is an emphasis by two clauses, since the speech would stand without them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 108–110:

(p-315) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth; and Allah does not desire injustice toward the worlds.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah. And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

The reference of "these" (tilka) is to the preceding verses, which include the punishment of the disbelievers and the bliss of the believers. Since there is mention of punishment in them, Exalted is He informs that He does not desire that any injustice should befall any of the servants. And if He does not desire that, it does not exist at all, because nothing occurs except what Exalted Allah wills. His saying, Exalted is He, "in truth" (bil-haqq), means: "with true information." It is also possible that the meaning is: "We recite them to you, containing actions which are true in themselves, of honouring one people and punishing others."

Abu Nuhayk recited "yatluhā" with the letter ya (yatluhu), and the announcement came that He, Exalted is He, does not desire injustice in His judgment, so it does not exist.

Since the mind might pause here regarding the aspect by which Allah singled out a people with an action for which He shows them mercy, and others with an action for which He punishes them, Exalted is He mentioned the decisive proof of His dominion over all creatures, and that the Truth cannot be opposed. This is in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, the verse, and He said "mā" and did not say "man," in terms of their being classes and kinds.

Al-Tabari mentioned that some of the Basrans considered His saying, "wa-ilā Allāh," and so he made the noun explicit and did not say "ilayhi," following the words of the poet:

؎ I see that death does not precede death; something has troubled death, the wealthy man and the poor man alike.

(p-316) And what follows its path. This was said by al-Zajjaj, and it is related that the Arabs do this intending to magnify the speech and to draw attention to the greatness of the meaning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse resembles the line of poetry in the intent of grandeur of composition, and differs from it in that the verse consists of two sentences that are separate in meaning. So if many sentences were repeated in this manner, it would be fine to make the noun explicit in all of them, and using a pronoun in that case is not customary. As for the line of poetry and what resembles it, the pronoun there is the norm, since the speech concerns a single meaning. It is not permissible to make the noun explicit except in matters that are grand in souls and in which confusion for the hearer is not feared. Some of the Seven Readers recited "tarji'u al-umūr" with a fatha on the ta, on the basis of the verb being active, and mention of that has already preceded.

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: this is for our first generation, and it does not apply to our last generation. ʿIkrima said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Masʿud, Salim the client of Abu Hudhayfa, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and Muʿadh ibn Jabal.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means: and those who resemble them. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it was revealed concerning those who emigrated with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to Madina.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is one opinion, whose implication is that the verse was revealed concerning the Companions. It was said to them: "You are the best nation," so the reference in His saying "nation" is to the nation of Muhammad specifically, for these are its best.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and a group of the people of knowledge said: the meaning of the verse is an address to the community, that they are the best nation brought forth for mankind. So the word "nation" on this interpretation is a generic noun, as if it was said to them: "You are the best of nations." (p-317) This interpretation is supported by their being witnesses over mankind, and by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the last, yet the foremost..." the hadith. Bahz ibn Hakim related from his father, from his grandfather: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said one day, while leaning his back against the Kaʿba: "We will complete seventy nations on the Day of Resurrection; we are the last of them and the best of them." Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: "You are the best of mankind." Al-Hasan said: "We are the last of them and the most honoured of them before Allah, Exalted is He." Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning of the verse is: "You are the best of mankind for mankind."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So "nation" on this interpretation is a generic noun. Abu Hurayra said: "They will bring the disbelievers in chains and admit them into Islam."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

No prophet was sent to the whole nation except Muhammad ﷺ. So he and his community call to faith and fight the world over it, and thus they are the best of mankind for mankind. It does not follow on this interpretation that they are the most excellent of nations from the wording of the verse itself, but this is known from another wording, like his ﷺ saying: "The most compassionate of my community toward my community is Abu Bakr." This wording does not imply that Abu Bakr is the most compassionate of people absolutely, toward believer and disbeliever.

(p-318) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Compassion in the absolute sense does not operate in harmony with the Sharia as it should. As for His saying "kuntum" in the past form, it is the form that carries the meaning of permanence, as He said: ﴿And Allah has always been Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 96], and other such examples. Some said: the meaning is "you were" in the knowledge of Allah; and it was said: in the Preserved Tablet; and it was said: in what He informed the nations of concerning you in ancient times. "Khayra" according to all these opinions is the predicate of "kāna," and it is possible that "kāna" is complete, with "khayra ummatin" in the accusative as a circumstantial state. This is plausible on some of the interpretations we have mentioned but not others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This excellence which Allah has imposed on this nation is only attained in its share by one who fulfils these conditions: enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah.

His saying: ﴿enjoining what is right﴾ and what follows it are states in a position of accusative.

Then Exalted is He informed concerning the People of the Book, in the manner of reproach coupled with counsel, that if they had believed they would have saved their own souls from the punishment of Allah. The word "khayr" in this verse is in the form of a comparative, and there is no sharing between their disbelief and their belief in goodness; rather it is permissible because of what the word "khayr" contains of generality and the branching of aspects. Likewise is the word "afḍal" (more excellent), "aḥabb" (more beloved), and what goes in their path. This meaning has been explained in other than this place more thoroughly than this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Among them are believers﴾ is an alert to the condition of ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his brother, Tha'laba ibn Sa'ya, and others among those who believed. Then Allah judged most of them to be defiantly disobedient in their disbelief, because (p-319) they distorted, altered, and obstinately opposed after their knowledge of the reality of the affair of Muhammad ﷺ. So they are disbelievers and transgressors in disbelief, having combined the two blameworthy qualities.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 111–112:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They will not harm you, except for a little annoyance. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿Humiliation is imposed upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have returned with anger from Allah, and poverty is imposed upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They will not harm you, except for a little annoyance﴾ means: they will not inflict upon you any harm to the body or to wealth; rather, it is only annoyance by the tongue. So the exception (istithna', "exception") is connected (muttasil). Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said: "The annoyance" is their distorting the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and their denying him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Their disparaging the believers and their attacking them, collectively and individually, all of this is grave and disturbing, and because of it they deserved killing, expulsion, and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). But Allah the Exalted intended by this verse that the believers should view them with the eye of contempt, so that they would not turn anyone away from his religion or distract him from the worship of his Lord. This is also the eloquence of the Arabs, and of this meaning in belittling is the saying of Thumamah ibn Uthal: "O Muhammad, if you kill me, you will kill one who has blood (dhu dam). If you show favor, you will show favor to one who is grateful. And if you desire wealth, ask of it whatever you wish." So his saying "dhu dam" has been narrated with the dhal dotted (dhamm) and with the dal undotted (dam). "Dhamm," with a fatha or kasra on the dhal, means protection (dhimam). As for the undotted dal, it may be that he meant to magnify his own matter, in one of two ways: either he meant a threat, that is, "you will kill one whose blood is sought for vengeance, whose protectors will avenge him, so beware the consequence of that," or he meant "you will kill a king by whose blood one seeks healing," as the Arabs used to believe concerning the blood of kings. In that case it is an appeal for mercy, not a threat, meaning: it is not fitting for you to destroy one like me. This is found among people when one reflects. Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, said when explaining this verse: "Avoid disobedience and transgression, for by them were destroyed those who were before you among the people."

This interpretation is open to objection: all the Jews have been crooked since the time of Jesus. The pronoun in "they are not" refers to those mentioned earlier in God's words: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾ (Q. 3:110). This is like the words of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"I disobeyed my heart in her matter, though I hearken to her command; I do not know whether her pursuit is rightness or error?"

The meaning is: "or is it error?" He omitted the second part because what was mentioned indicates it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The correct reading is that the pronoun in "they are not" refers to those mentioned earlier, "alike" is the predicate of "is not" (laysa), ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate, and "community" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada').

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: When 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tha'laba ibn Sa'ya, Usayd ibn Sa'ya, Asad ibn 'Ubayd, and those Jews who embraced Islam with them became Muslims, the disbelieving rabbis (ahbar, the learned men of the Jews) said: "Only our wicked ones have believed in Muhammad. If they were good, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers." So God, exalted is He, revealed concerning this: "They are not alike..." to the end of the verse. Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said the same.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is the most correct of the interpretations. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: the meaning of the verse is: the Jews and the community of Muhammad are not alike. This was also said by al-Suddi.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Since this community was mentioned earlier in God's words ﴿You are the best community﴾ (Q. 3:110), and the Jews are also mentioned, God said to His Prophet: "They are not alike." The Book here is according to this the genus of God's books, and is not restricted to the known Torah and Gospel alone. The meaning is: from among the People of the Book, who are the people of the Qur'an, there is an upright community.

The exegetes differed in their wording on "upright" (qa'ima). Mujahid said: it means just (adila). Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn 'Abbas said: it means standing upon the Book of God and its limits, guided. Al-Suddi said: "the obedient, devoted" (al-qanita al-mut'a).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this returns to one meaning: moderation in obeying God's command. From this comes the saying that weighty dinars or dirhams are "standing" (qa'ima). This verse allows this meaning, and the word need not be understood as referring to the physical posture of persons at the time of reciting God's signs. It is also possible that "standing" describes the state of those who recite during the watches of the night, and whoever has this state is undoubtedly moderate in obeying God's command. In these two possibilities, this verse is like what preceded in God's words: ﴿except as long as you stand over him﴾ (Q. 3:75).

"Yatlūna" (they recite) means they recite in sequence (yasrudun). "The signs of God" in this verse are His books. "Al-anaʾ" means the hours, its singular being inᵘ (pronounced with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the nun). It is also said anyⁱ with a fatha on the hamza, inā with a kasra on the hamza, a fatha on the nun and a short vowel, anā with a fatha on the hamza, or inw with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the nun, and a damma-marked waw. From this is the verse of al-Hudhali:

"Sweet and bitter like the twist of the arrow-shaft is its bitterness, in every watch of the night that it spends in sandal-wearing."

The ruling of this verse does not apply to one person in such a way that each individual prays through all the hours of the night. Rather this ruling is realised through the community as a whole, for some people stand in prayer at the beginning of the night, some at its end, and some after a short sleep before returning to sleep. Thus from the totality of this, in the cities and the communities, the phrase "the watches of the night" in standing prayer is fulfilled. This was the state of the early part of this community. People knew the night vigil as being at the first third of the last part of the night or somewhat before it, and at that time most people used to stand in prayer. Standing the entire night is rare, though there were some among the righteous who maintained it. God, exalted is He, mentioned the moderate course in this respect in Surat al-Muzzammil. Standing the night to study knowledge sought for the sake of God's face falls within this verse, and it is better than voluntary worship for one whose knowledge is expected to benefit the Muslims.

As for the exegetes' explanation of "the watches of the night": al-Rabi', Qatada and others said: "the watches of the night" are the hours of the night. 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said: "We heard the Arabs say: 'the watches of the night' are the hours of the night." Al-Suddi said: "the watches of the night" are the middle of the night.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is unsound, since the middle of the night is certainly part of the watches.

Ibn Mas'ud said: this verse was revealed because "the Prophet ﷺ was delayed from us one night from the prayer of 'atama (the night prayer after dusk), and he was with some of his wives. He did not come until part of the night had passed. He came, and among us were those praying and among us were those lying down. He said: 'Rejoice, for none of the People of the Book prays this prayer.'" [p. 326] Then God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿They are not alike...﴾ to the end of the verse. Therefore the meaning of His words ﴿they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night﴾ is the prayer of 'Isha' (night prayer). Sufyan al-Thawri related from Mansur that he said: "It has reached me that this verse was revealed concerning those who pray between the two night prayers."

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they prostrate themselves﴾: some people held that prostration here is a figurative expression for prayer, naming it by a noble part of it, just as it is called bowing (ruku') in many places. On this reading the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), as if He said: "they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night while praying." Al-Tabari and others held that it is a separate clause detached from the first sentence, informing that they are also people of prostration.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This second reading is good, because one may think that recitation in the watches of the night is outside prayer. Furthermore, standing in the recitation of knowledge falls outside the verse on the first interpretation, but is included on this second interpretation. So ﴿and they prostrate themselves﴾, on this reading, is a descriptive qualification of a group, joined by the conjunction waw, as you say: "Zayd the generous and the wise came to me."

"Yu'minūna" (they believe) means they affirm (yusaddiqun). Faith in the Last Day includes faith in the prophets, because it is among the matters the intellect may accept and which revelation established through the prophets.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾: this describes them as those who, whenever they are called to good, such as aiding the oppressed, relieving the distressed, mending the broken, or worshipping God, respond. From this is the action of Malik, may God be pleased with him, concerning the two rak'as of the mosque; he said: "You called me to good, so I responded to it." Among what falls within God's words ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that a person seizes the five before the five, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Seize five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your free time before your preoccupation, your life before your death, and your wealth before your poverty." So whenever one wishes to do good he hastens to it and does not postpone himself with hope; this too is hastening to good deeds. Some people related: "I entered a boat with some of the righteous, and I said to him: 'What do you say, may God set you right, about fasting while travelling?' He said to me: 'It is haste, my nephew.'" The narrator said: "By God, he gave me an answer that is not one of the answers of the jurists."

He said: 'Rejoice, for none of the People of the Book prays this prayer.'" [p. 326] Then God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿They are not alike...﴾ to the end of the verse. Therefore the meaning of His words ﴿they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night﴾ is the prayer of 'Isha' (night prayer). Sufyan al-Thawri related from Mansur that he said: "It has reached me that this verse was revealed concerning those who pray between the two night prayers."

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they prostrate themselves﴾: some people held that prostration here is a figurative expression for prayer, naming it by a noble part of it, just as it is called bowing (ruku') in many places. On this reading the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), as if He said: "they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night while praying." Al-Tabari and others held that it is a separate clause detached from the first sentence, informing that they are also people of prostration.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This second reading is good, because one may think that recitation in the watches of the night is outside prayer. Furthermore, standing in the recitation of knowledge falls outside the verse on the first interpretation, but is included on this second interpretation. So ﴿and they prostrate themselves﴾, on this reading, is a descriptive qualification of a group, joined by the conjunction waw, as you say: "Zayd the generous and the wise came to me."

"Yu'minūna" (they believe) means they affirm (yusaddiqun). Faith in the Last Day includes faith in the prophets, because it is among the matters the intellect may accept and which revelation established through the prophets.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾: this describes them as those who, whenever they are called to good, such as aiding the oppressed, relieving the distressed, mending the broken, or worshipping God, respond. From this is the action of Malik, may God be pleased with him, concerning the two rak'as of the mosque; he said: "You called me to good, so I responded to it." Among what falls within God's words ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that a person seizes the five before the five, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Seize five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your free time before your preoccupation, your life before your death, and your wealth before your poverty." So whenever one wishes to do good he hastens to it and does not postpone himself with hope; this too is hastening to good deeds. Some people related: "I entered a boat with some of the righteous, and I said to him: 'What do you say, may God set you right, about fasting while travelling?' He said to me: 'It is haste, my nephew.'" The narrator said: "By God, he gave me an answer that is not one of the answers of the jurists."

Then God, exalted is He, described those in whom these qualities are gathered as being among the righteous. The word "min" (from among) may be partitive, and it may also be explanatory of kind.

[p. 328] Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 115–117:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And whatever good they do, it will never be denied them, and Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. They are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever.﴾ ﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind containing frost, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir read "taf'alu" and "tukfarūhu" with the *ta'* (the second person, addressing this community). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read both with the *ya'* (third person), in conformity with what precedes them: "yatlūna" and "yu'minūna," and what follows them. Abu 'Amr used to read with both forms.

"Tukfarūhu" means: it will be covered over from you, so you will not be rewarded for it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever I have bestowed a favour upon, let him mention it; for if he mentions it, he has thanked it, and if he does not do so, he has denied it." From this is also the words of the poet:

"...and disbelief is a corrupting thing for the soul of the benefactor."

As for His saying, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious﴾, it contains both promise and warning. Then the Exalted followed the mention of this righteous category with the mention of the condition of the disbelievers, to show the difference. Allah singled out wealth and children for mention for several reasons. Among them: they are the adornment of the worldly life and the greatest of what hopes aim at. Among them: they are the closest and easiest forms of support for a human being. Among them: the disbelievers who deny the Hereafter have no aspiration except in these, and in their view these are the ultimate goal of a person, and by them they boasted over the believers. So Allah stated that these two, which have these attributes, will not avail anything against the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter. If these do not avail, then other, more distant matters are all the more unable to avail.

His saying, ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, is an idafa (genitive construction) of specification, which requires that this status be established for them and be permanent.

His saying, ﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ ... the verse. Its meaning: the image that stands in the minds regarding their spending, which they regard as a means of drawing near (to God), as a reckoning, and as an act of devotion; and regarding its being nullified on the Day of Resurrection and becoming "scattered dust"; and its going away is like the image that stands in the minds of the crop of a people which grew, turned green, and whose hope in it was strong, but then a wind containing burning frost blew upon it and destroyed it. Thus the comparison occurs between two things and two things. Allah, Exalted and Majestic, mentioned one of the two compared things and left out the other. Then He mentioned one of the two things compared with, which is not the one that corresponds to the first mentioned, and left out the other. The two mentioned ones point to the two omitted ones. This is the utmost in eloquence and concision. A similar example is His saying: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171].

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz al-A'raj read "tunfiqūna" with the *ta'*, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad. "Mathal" is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in an omitted element, to which the *kaf* in "ka-mathali" is attached. The "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which).

Most of the exegetes hold that "yunfiqūna" refers to the wealth they used to spend in devotional practices and in hostility to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that this was, in their view, a means of drawing near (to God). Al-Suddi said: "yunfiqūna" means: from their words, which conceal the opposite of what they express.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because it implies that the verse is about the hypocrites, whereas the verse is about disbelievers who openly display what they conceal. Some exegetes held that "yunfiqūna" refers to their deeds, such as disbelief and the like; that is, these deeds are like the wind containing frost, which nullifies everything they have of kinship ties and devotional acts such as freeing slaves and the like, just as the wind destroys the crop. This is a good opinion, were it not for the remoteness of the metaphor in applying "spending" (to these deeds).

Al-sirr (ṣirr, "frost"): intense cold that burns everything upon which it blows; it is well known. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of exegetes said: al-ṣirr is cold. The Arabs call it al-ḍarīb. Al-Zajjaj and others held that the word derives from vocalization, from the expression "ṣarra al-shay'" (the thing made a sound), and from it is "al-riḥ al-ṣarṣar" (the howling wind). Al-Zajjaj said: so al-ṣirr is the sound of the fire that is in the wind.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-ṣirr is the breath of Hell that is in the zamharir (the extreme cold), which burns in a manner similar to what fire burns.

Al-ḥarth (tilth) encompasses both crops and fruits, because all of them come from the cultivation of the land, which is the literal meaning of al-ḥarth. From this is the hadith: "There is no zakat except on gold, or tilth, or livestock."

And the Exalted said: ﴿who wronged themselves﴾. What then is the reason for this specification, since the example is valid even if the tilth belongs to someone who did not wrong himself? The answer: the majority of exegetes interpreted the wronging of oneself in this verse as wronging by means of disobedience to Allah. On this basis, the comparison is made with the tilth of one who has this attribute, because his punishment is more hoped for (to be a warning), Allah's seizing of him is more severe, and the vengeance upon him comes more swiftly and is more powerful. This is as was narrated: "in the belly of the wild ass," and other (reports). Also, among the people of knowledge are those who hold that all the calamities of the world are only due to the disobedience of servants, and they derive this from more than one verse of the Qur'an. Thus, it is consistent with his saying that every tilth burned by a wind belongs to one who has wronged himself. Some people, and al-Mahdawi inclined toward this, held that His saying, ﴿the tilth of a people who wronged themselves﴾, means: they sowed outside the proper time for sowing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It should be said regarding this: they wronged themselves by placing the acts of farming outside their proper place, either in time or in the manner of the work. Allah singled these people out for mention because the burning in such a case is more comprehensive and more firmly established. This line of thought resembles, in some respect, the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And a tall palm-tree like the dried stalks of palm fronds, which the wicked one set aflame with kindling."

He singled out the "wicked one" (al-ghawī) because he kindles fire in a green, fine palm tree that should not be burned; the fire then draws out its moisture after it has been stripped of its branches and has turned black; so the image comes out well. The rational man does not kindle fire except in what has dried out and deserves it, so it goes away and nothing remains of it that could be compared to.

The pronoun in "ẓalamahum" refers to the disbelievers whose pronoun was mentioned earlier in "yunfiqūna," and it does not refer to the people who own the tilth, because they have not been mentioned, so that it could refer back to them or so that it could clarify their wrongdoing. Also, His saying, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾, indicates the present act among those who are present.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 118:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimate friends (bitana) those outside your own [ranks]. They will spare no effort in ruining you; they love what distresses you. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their chests conceal is greater. We have already made the signs clear for you, if you use your reason.﴾

(p-331) God, exalted is He, forbade the believers in this verse from taking as companions, from among the disbelievers and the Jews, close friends with whom they would feel at ease regarding their inner affairs, consult them on opinions, and rely upon them.

His saying "min dunikum" means: from outside the believers. The word "dun" (outside, beneath) implies, regarding what it is attached to, that it is absent from the matter under discussion. So close friends are likened to what lies against a person's belly (batn) beneath his garment. In this sense is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no caliph nor any holder of authority except that he has two inner circles (bitanatan): an inner circle that commands him to good and urges him toward it, and an inner circle that commands him to evil and urges him toward it. The one protected is he whom God protects."

His saying "la ya'lunakum khabalan" means: they will not fall short for you in what contains corruption for you. You say: "ma alawtu fi kadha," meaning: I did not fall short, rather I exerted myself. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"A people came after them, so that they might reach them, but they did not reach them, nor did they blame, nor did they fall short."

That is, they did not fall short. "Khabal" and "khabal" mean corruption.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Some men among the believers used to associate with some Jewish men because of the neighborly ties and alliance that existed between them in the pre-Islamic era, so the verse was revealed concerning that. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi also said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and God forbade the believers from them. Anas ibn Malik narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not seek illumination from the fire of the polytheists, and do not engrave 'Arabi' on your rings." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan explained it, saying: He (peace be upon him) meant: Do not consult the polytheists in any of your affairs, and do not engrave "Muhammad" on your rings.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This verse also includes employing the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah) as scribes, and entrusting them with buying and selling, and relying upon them. It is narrated that Abu Musa al-Ash'ari employed a dhimmi as a scribe, so 'Umar wrote to him rebuking him, and recited this verse to him. It was said to 'Umar: "There is a man here from the Christians of al-Hira, and no one is a better scribe or more skilled with the pen than him; would he not write for you?" He said: "Then I would be taking intimate friends from outside the believers."

The "ma" in His saying "ma 'anittum" is verbal-masdariyyah (the infinitive particle). The meaning is: they love your distress. "Anat" means hardship and harm that a person encounters; "'aqabatun 'anut" means a difficult ascent. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿That is for whoever fears 'anat﴾ [al-Nisa': 25] means hardship, either in fornication or in lacking the means of marriage. Al-Suddi said: its meaning is: they love that you go astray. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is: they love that you be led into error regarding your religion. It is said: "'Anita al-rajul ya'natu" with the vowel of the "n" in the past tense being kasra.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ means through their words; they are above the concealed, in whose eyes hatred appears. God specified the mouths for mention rather than the tongues, as an indication of their boasting and their chattering in these statements. Similar to what we have said is what is in the hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade a man to tashahha in the honor of his brother," meaning: to open his mouth with it. It is said: "shaha al-himar fahu bil-nahiq" (the donkey opened its mouth with braying), and "shaha al-liajam fi al-faras" (the bit opened in the horse's mouth). The prohibition against someone taking his brother's honor in a whisper is established; so the mention of tashahhi is only an indication of boasting and expansiveness.

His saying: ﴿and what their chests conceal is greater﴾ is an announcement that they conceal more hatred than what they show with their mouths. In the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "qad bada al-baghda'" with the verb in the masculine form, since al-baghda' carries the meaning of al-bughd.

Then God, the Exalted, said to the believers: ﴿We have already made the signs clear for you, if you use your reason﴾, as a warning and an alert. God, the Exalted, knew that they were reasonable, but this is a stirring of souls, just as you say: "If you are a man, then do such and such."

(p-333) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Here you are, you love them, but they do not love you, and you believe in the Book, all of it. When they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say: Die in your rage. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) and the qira'a (recitation) of the like of this verse have already been discussed in His saying, may He be exalted, just before: ﴿Here you are, you argued about what you have knowledge of﴾ [Al 'Imran: 66]. The pronoun in "they love them" refers to the hypocrites among the Jews, whose mention preceded in His saying: ﴿intimates from other than you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. The pronoun in this verse is a noun of genus, meaning: you believe in all the books, while they do not believe in your recitation. Allah, exalted is He, only set the believers before this verse with these states that necessitate the believers' hatred of the hypocritical Jews and their rejection of them. Among those states: they do not love the believers, they disbelieve in their Book, they feign faith toward them, they belittle them, they are enraged, and they await misfortunes to befall them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they bite their fingertips at you﴾ is an expression for intense rage together with the inability to carry it out. From it is the saying of Abu Talib:

"... they bite their fingertips behind us out of rage"

And from it is the saying of another:

"Qays has witnessed, and their help was nothing but Qutayba's biting of the thumbs."

This biting is with the teeth, and it is a bodily posture that follows the posture of the enraged soul, just as biting the hand upon the hand follows the posture of the regretful soul longing for a loss that is near at hand, and just as striking the tooth is the posture of the regretful soul alone, and so on, including counting pebbles and drawing lines in the earth for the distressed person and the like. This biting is written with the letter ḍād, and the "grinding of the time" (ʿaẓẓ al-zamān) is written with the emphatic ẓāʾ. The singular of al-anāmil is unmula, with a ḍamma on the mīm, and it is said with a fatḥa on it, but the ḍamma is more well-known. There is no parallel to this noun in its pattern except ashudd, and it has parallels in the plurals.

His saying: ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ requires that the verse concerns the hypocritical Jews and not the hypocritical Arabs. What objects to this is that it is not transmitted of the hypocritical Jews that they used to display an absolute faith outwardly while disbelieving inwardly, as the hypocrites among the Arabs used to do, except what is narrated about the matter of Zayd ibn al-Sayt al-Qaynuqaʿi. So there remains only that their saying "We believe" means: we confirm that he is a prophet sent to you. That is, remain upon your religion, and we are your allies and your brothers, and we harbour toward you nothing but affection. For this reason some of the believers used to take them as intimates. This is a line of thought that has been transmitted, that many of the Jews used to adopt it. This interpretation is indicated by the fact that what stands in opposition to their saying "We believe" is the biting of the fingertips out of rage, and this does not imply apostasy, as it does in His saying: ﴿And when they go alone to their devils, they say: Indeed we are with you﴾ [Al-Baqara: 14]. Rather, it implies hatred and the absence of affection. Abu al-Jawza, when he recited this verse, used to say: "They are the Ibadiyya."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This attribute may apply to the people of innovation until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ — al-Tabari and many of the exegetes said about it: it is a supplication against them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Upon this, it is appropriate that they be cursed with this, directly and indirectly. Others said: rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community were commanded to confront them with this. Upon this, the meaning of supplication disappears and the meaning of reproach and provocation remains. The meaning runs along with the saying of Musafir ibn Abi Amr:

"We grow in our stock, and we gouge the eye of whoever envies."

In looking at this meaning in His saying, "Die in your rage," is His saying: ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut it﴾ [Al-Hajj: 15].

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ is a warning with which they are confronted according to this last interpretation of "Die in your rage." It is a plain informing addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ) in the interpretation of the supplication in ﴿Die in your rage﴾. "What is in the breasts" means what they conceal within themselves, and the reference here is to beliefs. From this is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is only the one with the belly of the daughter of Kharija." And from it is their saying: "The wolf is envied for the one in its belly." The word dhāt is a homonym with many meanings, of which only what we have mentioned enters into this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 120:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed, Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾

The "good" (al-hasanah) and the "evil" (al-sayyi'ah) in this verse are general terms for everything that is good and everything that is bad. What the commentators have mentioned, such as fertility and drought, the gathering of the believers, the entry of division among them, and other sayings, are only examples, and there is no disagreement over that. Allah, the Exalted, mentioned "touching" (mass) with regard to good to show that with the slightest touch of good, distress falls upon the souls of these haters. Then He paired this with evil using the word "striking" (al-isabah), which is an expression for gaining power over something, since the thing that strikes another thing has power over it or within it. This eloquent expression indicates the intensity of enmity, for it is a grudge that does not depart in times of hardship; rather, they rejoice at the descent of hardships upon the believers. This is how the enmity of envy generally is, especially in a matter as great as this, which is the foundation of this world and the Hereafter. The poet said:

"Every enmity may hope to be removed, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy."

When the Exalted had established this state for those mentioned, and the verse required that the believers should regard them with this attribute, His saying came: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheming will not harm you at all﴾ as consolation for the believers and strengthening of their souls, and He made that conditional upon patience and God-consciousness.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Nafi' recited "lā yiḍirkum" (لا يَضِرْكُمْ) with a kasra on the dad and a jazm on the ra', and it is from ḍāra yaḍīru, meaning ḍarra yaḍurru, and it is an eloquent dialect. Al-Kisa'i related ḍāra yaḍūru, but he did not recite in this dialect. From ḍāra yaḍīru in the Book of Allah comes "lā ḍayra" (no harm), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

"It was said: 'Bear beyond your capacity, for it is...' ... one who comes to it, it does not harm it."

He describes a city, and the meaning is: so it does not harm it. In this negation implied by the fa' is the answer of the conditional. From the usage is the saying of Tawba ibn al-Humayyir:

"Some people said: 'Its distance does not harm you,' but whatever wears down souls does harm them."

Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "lā yuḍurrukum" (لا يَضُرُّكُمْ) with a damma on the dad and the ra' and a shaddah on the ra', and this is from ḍarra yaḍurru. It is related from Hamza the same as the recitation of Abu 'Amr. As for the grammatical analysis of this recitation, it is jazm; the ra' was given a damma for the sake of juncture, and this is the preference of Sibawayh in such cases, following the damma of the dad. It is permissible to pronounce the ra' with a fatha or a kasra while intending jazm. As for the kasra, I do not know it as a recitation, and al-Zajjaj's expression in this is loose, since it appears from the flow of his speech that it is a recitation. As for the fatha of the ra' in "lā yaḍurrakum," Asim recited it, as related by Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal from him. It is also permissible that the grammatical status of "lā yuḍurrukum" be raf', either by estimating: "so it does not harm you," in the manner mentioned in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb, or by intending that it precedes "wa in tasbirū," as the poet said:

"O Aqra' ibn Habis, O Aqra'! Indeed, if your brother is struck down, you will be struck down."

The meaning is: you will be struck down. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "lā yaḍrurkum" with two ra's, and this is on the unmerging of the idgham, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and upon it is the verse's saying "in tamassukum." The dialect of the rest of the Arabs is idgham in all such cases. Al-kayd is the scheming through falsehoods. His saying, "wa akīdu kaydan," is only naming a punishment by the name of the sin.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is encompassing of what they do﴾ is a warning, and the meaning is: its recompense and punishment encompass them, and by power and authority. Al-Hasan recited "bi-mā ta'malūn" with a ta', and this is either a warning to the believers regarding their taking these people as intimates, or a warning to these hypocrites, with the implied sense: say to them, O Muhammad.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 121–122:

(p-338) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And when you set out from your family in the morning to assign the believers their positions for battle—and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ ﴿when two groups among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their Protector. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

Al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) held that this verse is connected in meaning to the verses preceding it, but the apparent sense is that it introduces a different matter, since those verses dealt with the hypocrite Jews, whereas this is the beginning of rebuke of the believers concerning the affair of Uhud. Accordingly, the governing element of "idh" (when) is an implied verb whose estimate is: "and remember." Al-Hasan said: this morning departure mentioned in this verse, for assigning the believers, was at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

People disagreed with him. The majority hold that this was at the Battle of Uhud, and that all these verses were revealed concerning it. The matter of the Battle of Uhud was that the polytheists gathered, three thousand men, and headed for Madina to avenge themselves for the Day of Badr. They camped at Uhud on Wednesday, the twelfth of Shawwal in the third year after the Hijra, at the end of thirty-one months after the Hijra, and they remained there on Thursday, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madina managing affairs and awaiting the command of Allah the Exalted. When it was the morning of Friday, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the people and consulted them, and he informed them that he had seen in his dream a cow being slaughtered, and a notch in the edge of his sword, and that he put his hand into a strong coat of mail, and that he interpreted it as Madina. He said to them: "I think we should not go out to these disbelievers." 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said to him: "Stay, Messenger of Allah, and do not go out to them with the people. If they stay, they will stay in the worst of prisons; if they withdraw, they will go away defeated; and if they come to us in Madina, we will fight them in the open spaces, and the women and children will pelt them with stones from the fortresses. By Allah, we never fought an enemy in this city without defeating him, and we never went out from it against an enemy without being defeated." This opinion agreed with the opinion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the opinion of a group of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. But some of the righteous believers, among those who had missed Badr, said: "Messenger of Allah, take us out against our enemy." They encouraged the people and called them to war. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood and led the people in the Friday prayer, and those who called to war had burdened him. After the prayer he entered his house and put on his armour. Those people then regretted and said: "We have compelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." When the Prophet (ﷺ) came out to them in his armour, (p-339) they said: "Messenger of Allah, stay if you wish, for we do not want to compel you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until he fights."

Then he went out with the people and marched until he came near the camp of the polytheists there, and he spent that night there. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul became angry and said: "He obeyed them and disobeyed me." When it was the morning of Saturday, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to march to engage the polytheists, and he set out with a thousand men. At that point 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul withdrew from him with three hundred men, from hypocrites and their followers, and they said: "We think you will not meet fighting." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proceeded with seven hundred. At that moment the clan of Banu Haritha from the Aws and the clan of Banu Salama from the Khazraj resolved to turn back, seeing the great number of the polytheists and the small number of the Muslims, and they nearly lost courage and lost heart, but Allah the Exalted protected them, and they urged one another on, and rose up with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then proceeded until he came in sight of the polytheists, and the people drew up their lines. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had appointed 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr over the archers, and they were fifty men, and he placed them to guard the mountain behind the Muslims, and he himself leaned against the mountain. When the fighting blazed, the polytheists were routed and fled, and the women of the polytheists began to show their anklets as they hitched up their skirts on the slope of a mountain. When the archers saw that, they said: "The spoils, the spoils, O Muslims!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them: "Do not leave this place, even if you see us being snatched by the birds." 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr and a group of them said to them: "Fear Allah and stand firm as your Prophet commanded you." But they disobeyed and opposed, and they moved away in pursuit. Khalid ibn al-Walid had come out with a troop of cavalry and came from behind the Muslims where the archers had been, and he charged at the people, and disarray occurred, and a cry rose against the Muslims from their vanguard and their rear, and a shouter cried: "Muhammad has been killed!" So the people fell into disarray, and more than seventy of the Muslims were martyred. Makki said: Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Four of the Muhajirun were killed on the Day of Uhud, and seventy of the Ansar, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) withdrew to the top of the mountain and passed beyond the people.

(p-340) This is an abridged account of the story on which the interpretation of the verse is built. The affair of "Uhud" in full, with what came between its actions and words, is comprehensively recorded in the books of biography (sira), and this commentary does not require mentioning it.

Makki related from al-Suddi what indicates that the fighting was on Friday, and al-Tabari related from him that Abu Sufyan's descent at Uhud was on the third of Shawwal. All of this is weak. Al-Naqqash said: the event of Uhud was on the eleventh of Shawwal, and that is an error. Al-Tabari and others said: the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) going out on Friday to arrange matters with the people and consult them is what is expressed by His saying: ﴿assign the believers their positions for battle﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Especially since the Prophet's (ﷺ) going out was only with the intention that the people should not go out, so he had no doubt in himself that he would divide the quarters of Madina among the Ansar clans.

Others than al-Tabari said: rather, the Prophet's (ﷺ) rising on Friday after the prayer is his "going out" (ghuduw), and the assigning of the believers at the time of the presence of battle; and it was said that this was on the night before. He called it "going out" since he had resolved to arrange matters, and the beginning of the affair was from the time of going out.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Especially since the Friday prayer was perhaps before midday, as traditions have reported, so the word "ghuduw" fits well. It was also said that the aforementioned going out was the morning of Saturday toward the fighting, and since that night did not correspond to a morning departure, it is as if he was in his family; and he assigned the Muslims, by his command, the archers and other arrangements of his in arranging the lines of the people. "Tubawwi'" means: you assign them positions in which they settle and remain firm. You say: "I took up (tabawwa'tu) the place of such-and-such," when you alighted there firmly and remained in it. From this is His saying: ﴿We dwell in the Garden wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): ("Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.") From this is the saying of the poet:

(p-341)

Many a righteous companion of mine—with my own hands I laid him in his grave.

From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

And the Merciful did not settle your House in a place, in the east of the hills of al-Safa and al-Muharram.

His saying "maqa'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a place of sitting. This is equivalent to your saying "mawaqif" (positions), but the word "qu'ud" (sitting) is more indicative of firmness, especially since the archers were seated, and likewise the lines of the Muslims were at first, while the duelists and the eager ones would charge about. His saying "Allah is All-Hearing" means: He hears what you say and what is said to you at the time of consultation and otherwise.

The second "idh" is a substitute (badal) for the first. "Hammat" means: they intended but did not act. "Fashal" in this place is the cowardice which nearly befell the clans of Banu Salama and Banu Haritha. "Fashal" in the body is exhaustion and weariness; "fashal" in opinion is incapacity, confusion, and corruption of resolve. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "We did not wish that this had not been revealed, because of His saying: 'and Allah is their Protector.'"

His saying: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ is a command which implicitly encourages the believers to emulate what Banu Haritha and Banu Salama did in marching with the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud recited: "tubawwi'u lil-mu'minin" with the preposition lam, and he recited "wallahu waliyyuhum" according to the meaning of the two groups, not according to the wording.

From this is His saying: ﴿We dwell in the Garden wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): ("Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.") From this is the saying of the poet:

(p-341)

Many a righteous companion of mine—with my own hands I laid him in his grave.

From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

And the Merciful did not settle your House in a place, in the east of the hills of al-Safa and al-Muharram.

His saying "maqa'id" is the plural of "maq'ad," which is a place of sitting. This is equivalent to your saying "mawaqif" (positions), but the word "qu'ud" (sitting) is more indicative of firmness, especially since the archers were seated, and likewise the lines of the Muslims were at first, while the duelists and the eager ones would charge about. His saying "Allah is All-Hearing" means: He hears what you say and what is said to you at the time of consultation and otherwise.

The second "idh" is a substitute (badal) for the first. "Hammat" means: they intended but did not act. "Fashal" in this place is the cowardice which nearly befell the clans of Banu Salama and Banu Haritha. "Fashal" in the body is exhaustion and weariness; "fashal" in opinion is incapacity, confusion, and corruption of resolve. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "We did not wish that this had not been revealed, because of His saying: 'and Allah is their Protector.'"

His saying: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ is a command which implicitly encourages the believers to emulate what Banu Haritha and Banu Salama did in marching with the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud recited: "tubawwi'u lil-mu'minin" with the preposition lam, and he recited "wallahu waliyyuhum" according to the meaning of the two groups, not according to the wording.

(p-342) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr, when you were humiliated. So fear Allah that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked.﴾

When Allah the Exalted commanded reliance upon Him, He reminded them of the matter of Badr, which was the fruit of reliance upon Allah and trust in Him. Whoever among the exegetes says that the Prophet's ﷺ saying to the believers, "Is it not sufficient for you...", was at the battle of Badr, then the reminder of the matter of Badr and of the angels and their fighting alongside the believers in it comes as an incitement to earnestness and reliance upon Allah. And whoever says that the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "Is it not sufficient for you...", the verse, was only at the battle of Uhud, then His saying, "And Allah had already helped you at Badr," up to "that you may be grateful," is a beautiful interjection within the speech. The victory at Badr is the famous one in which the chieftains of Quraysh were killed, and upon that day Islam was founded. Badr was on the seventeenth of Ramadan, a Friday, in the eighteenth month after the Hijrah. Badr is a water there, and the place was named after it. Al-Sha'bi said: that water belonged to a man of Juhaynah called Badr, and it was named after him. Al-Waqidi said: I mentioned this to 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far and Muhammad ibn Salih, and they denied it and said: "For what reason were al-Safra' and al-Jar and other places named?" He said: I mentioned that to Yahya ibn al-Nu'man al-Ghifari, and he said: I heard elders of Banu Ghifar say: "It is our water and our dwelling place, and no one ever owned it who was called Badr, and it is not from the lands of Juhaynah; it is only the lands of Ghifar." Al-Waqidi said: this is what is known to us.

(p-343) His saying, "when you were humiliated" (adhillah), its meaning is: few in number. That is because they were three hundred and thirteen or fourteen men, while their enemy was between nine hundred and a thousand. "Adhillah" is the plural of "dhalil," and the term "humiliation" in this place is used metaphorically. They were not in themselves anything but mighty, but their relation to their enemy and to all the disbelievers in the regions of the earth implies, upon reflection, their lowliness, and that they were overcome. The Prophet ﷺ said on that day: "O Allah, if this band is destroyed, You will not be worshipped." This metaphor is like the metaphor of "lying" in his saying in the Muwatta': "Ka'b lied," and like his saying: "Abu Muhammad lied," and like the metaphor of "poverty" (maskanah) for the people of the ship according to some opinions, since their poverty was relative to the king who is powerful and usurping.

Then Allah the Exalted commanded the believers to be mindful of Him, and gave them hope in the bounty that necessitates gratitude. It may be that the meaning is: fear Allah, perhaps your piety will be gratitude for the blessing of His victory at Badr.

His saying, "When you said" (idh taqul): the governing element of "idh" is a hidden verb. The governing element may be "nasarakum" (He helped you). This is according to the view of the majority: that this saying of the Prophet ﷺ was at Badr. Al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said that this was at Badr. Al-Sha'bi said: It reached the believers that Kurz ibn Jabir ibn Hisl al-Muharibi, a warrior of Fihr, had come with reinforcements for the polytheists, and this distressed the believers. So the Prophet ﷺ said this saying to the believers, from Allah's command, and the believers were patient and feared Allah, and the polytheists were defeated. The defeat reached Kurz and those with him, so they withdrew and did not come upon them suddenly. The believers were not reinforced by the angels, and the angels after that used to attend the wars of the Prophet ﷺ as reinforcement, and they attend the wars of the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

People disagreed with al-Sha'bi in this statement, and the reports are abundant that the angels attended Badr and fought. Among that is the saying of Abu Usayd Malik ibn Rabi'ah: "If I were with you now at Badr, and my sight with me, I would show you the ravine from which the angels came out, without doubt or dispute." And among it is the hadith of the Ghifari and his cousin, who heard from the Companions: "Advance, Haizum!" and the veil over the heart of one of them was lifted, and he died in his place, and the other held firm.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The angels did not fight on any day except the day of Badr; on the other days they were a number and reinforcement, not striking. Among that is the saying of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith to Abu Lahab: "It was only that we met the people and they gave us their backs, killing and capturing. Yet by Allah, I did not blame the people; we met men, white, on piebald horses, between heaven and earth, nothing stood in their way and nothing could withstand them." And among it: "that Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, of Banu Salamah, captured al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib on the day of Badr, and Abu al-Yusr was a small, compact man, while al-'Abbas was a tall, large man. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'..." the hadith in its entirety. Some Companions said: "On the day of Badr I was pursuing a man of the polytheists to strike him with my sword, but when I approached him his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that an angel had killed him."

(p-345) Qatadah ibn Di'amah said: Allah reinforced the believers on the day of Badr with five thousand angels. Al-Tabari said: Others said: Allah promised the believers on the day of Badr that He would reinforce them in all their wars if they were patient and feared Allah, but they did not do that except on the day of the Confederates, so He reinforced them when they besieged Qurayzah. Then he included under this discussion a report from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa who said: "We besieged Qurayzah for a period, and it was not opened to us, so we returned. While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had called for water to wash his head, Jibril, upon him be peace, came to him and said: 'You have laid down your weapons, but the angels have not laid down their burdens.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrapped his head in a cloth and did not wash it, and called out among us, and we rose weary and exhausted, until we came to Qurayzah and al-Nadir. On that day Allah reinforced us with three thousand angels, and opened for us an easy conquest, and we returned with a blessing from Allah and grace."

'Ikrimah said: The promise was on the day of Badr, but they were not patient on the day of Uhud, nor did they fear Allah, so they were not reinforced, and had they been reinforced they would not have been defeated.

Al-Dahhak said: This promise and this saying were to the believers on the day of Uhud, when the people fled and turned their backs, so Allah did not reinforce them; they were reinforced only on the day of Badr with a thousand angels riding behind.

Ibn Zayd said: "The Muslims said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Uhud while they were awaiting the polytheists: 'O Messenger of Allah, will Allah not reinforce us as He reinforced us on the day of Badr?' The Prophet ﷺ said to them: 'Is it not sufficient for you...' the verse." He reinforced them on the day of Badr with a thousand only. Ibn Zayd said: So they were not patient.

His saying, "Is it not sufficient for you" is a confirmation of their belief in sufficiency in this number of angels. Since the matter was clear in itself, that the angels are sufficient, the speaker hastened to the answer in order to build upon it what he would continue saying, so he said: "Yes," and it is the answer of those who confirm. This is fitting in matters that are clear, from which there is no escape in answering. Similar to it is His saying: "Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah." [al-An'am: 19]. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: "Alla yakfikum" (Is it not sufficient for you). The discussion of reinforcement has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: "And He extends them in their transgression" [al-Baqarah: 15].

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read: "bi-thalathah alaf" with a pause on the ha', and likewise "bi-khamsah alaf". The basis of this reading is weak, because the mudaf and mudaf ilayhi require continuity, as they are like one noun, and the second is a completion of the first, while the ha' is merely a sign of pause, so pausing in a place that is meant for continuity is awkward. However, similar things have come from the Arabs in places. Among that is what al-Farra' related, that they say: "akaltu lahman shah," meaning lahm shah, so they prolonged the fatha until an alif arose from it, as they said in pausing: "qala" meaning "qala" (he said) ... Then they prolonged the fatha in rhymed verse and similar places of pause and deliberation. Among that in poetry is the saying of the poet:

"Yunba'u min dhifri ghadubin jasratin..."

meaning yanbu'u, so it was prolonged. And among it is the saying of another:

"Aqulu idh kharrat 'ala al-kalkali — ya naqata ma jultu min majal"

meaning 'ala al-kalkal, so it was prolonged. And among it is the saying of another:

"Fa anta min al-ghawa'ili hina turma — wa min dhammi al-rijali bi-muntazah"

(p-347) meaning bi-muntazih. Abu al-Fath said: If this extension may intervene within the middle of a single word, then extension and deliberation may also occur between the mudaf and mudaf ilayh, since in reality they are two.

Ibn 'Amir alone read: "munazzalin" with fatha on the nun and shadda on the zay. The rest read: "munzalin" with sukun on the nun and fatha on the zay, lightened. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "munazzilin" with fatha on the nun and kasra on the zay, shaddah, meaning: they bring down victory. Al-Nahhas related a reading without attribution: "munzilin" with sukun on the nun and kasra on the zay, lightened, and he explained it as: they bring down victory.

"Bala" is the answer to the negation in "alan," whose meaning has already been stated. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the condition under which reinforcement occurs, which is patience and piety. Al-Fawr: the swift rising toward a thing, derived from the boiling of a cooking pot or water and the like, and from it His saying: "and the oven boiled over" [Hud: 40]. So the meaning is: they will come upon you in this their rising. Ibn 'Abbas said: "min fawrihim hadha" means: from this their journey. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: its meaning is: from this their direction. Qatadah said likewise. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Abu Salih, freedman of Umm Hani', said: from this their anger.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an explanation that does not restrict the word. "Al-fawr" may be due to anger, to greed, or to desire for reward, and from it is "al-fawr" in the Hajj and the ablution.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read: "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw. The rest read:

(p-348) "musawwamin" with fatha on the waw. As for the one who reads with fatha on the waw, its meaning is: marked with signs. Abu Zayd al-Ansari said: al-sawmah is the mark placed on a sheep or other animal, a color contrary to its color so that it may be recognized. It is related that the angels were identified that day by white turbans, related by al-Mahdawi from al-Zajjaj, except Jibril, upon him be peace, who had a yellow turban in the style of al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam's turban; Ibn Ishaq also said this. Mujahid said: their horses had cropped tails and manes, marked at the forelocks and tails with wool and red-dyed wool. Al-Rabi' said: their sign was that they were on piebald horses. 'Abbad ibn Hamzah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: the angels descended in the sign of al-Zubayr, wearing yellow turbans, and this was said by 'Urwah and 'Abd Allah, the sons of al-Zubayr. 'Abd Allah said: it was a yellow cloth, and al-Zubayr wrapped his turban with it. As for the one who reads "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw, the meaning may be as already mentioned: they marked themselves with a sign and marked their horses. Al-Tabari and others preferred this reading because the Prophet ﷺ said to the Muslims on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves," so they are then "musawwimun." Many of the people of exegesis said: the meaning of "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw is that they have made their horses "sawwamu": that is, they gave them their pasture of running, fighting, and readiness, so they are grazing animals, as in "sa'imat al-mashiyah" (grazing livestock), because they were left to their grazing. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this meaning for "musawwamin" with fatha on the waw, that they sent forth their "wusum" (marks).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is unsettled, and Ibn Furak also said it.
