﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr, when you were humiliated. So fear Allah that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked.﴾

When Allah the Exalted commanded reliance upon Him, He reminded them of the matter of Badr, which was the fruit of reliance upon Allah and trust in Him. Whoever among the exegetes says that the Prophet's ﷺ saying to the believers, "Is it not sufficient for you...", was at the battle of Badr, then the reminder of the matter of Badr and of the angels and their fighting alongside the believers in it comes as an incitement to earnestness and reliance upon Allah. And whoever says that the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "Is it not sufficient for you...", the verse, was only at the battle of Uhud, then His saying, "And Allah had already helped you at Badr," up to "that you may be grateful," is a beautiful interjection within the speech. The victory at Badr is the famous one in which the chieftains of Quraysh were killed, and upon that day Islam was founded. Badr was on the seventeenth of Ramadan, a Friday, in the eighteenth month after the Hijrah. Badr is a water there, and the place was named after it. Al-Sha'bi said: that water belonged to a man of Juhaynah called Badr, and it was named after him. Al-Waqidi said: I mentioned this to 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far and Muhammad ibn Salih, and they denied it and said: "For what reason were al-Safra' and al-Jar and other places named?" He said: I mentioned that to Yahya ibn al-Nu'man al-Ghifari, and he said: I heard elders of Banu Ghifar say: "It is our water and our dwelling place, and no one ever owned it who was called Badr, and it is not from the lands of Juhaynah; it is only the lands of Ghifar." Al-Waqidi said: this is what is known to us.

(p-343) His saying, "when you were humiliated" (adhillah), its meaning is: few in number. That is because they were three hundred and thirteen or fourteen men, while their enemy was between nine hundred and a thousand. "Adhillah" is the plural of "dhalil," and the term "humiliation" in this place is used metaphorically. They were not in themselves anything but mighty, but their relation to their enemy and to all the disbelievers in the regions of the earth implies, upon reflection, their lowliness, and that they were overcome. The Prophet ﷺ said on that day: "O Allah, if this band is destroyed, You will not be worshipped." This metaphor is like the metaphor of "lying" in his saying in the Muwatta': "Ka'b lied," and like his saying: "Abu Muhammad lied," and like the metaphor of "poverty" (maskanah) for the people of the ship according to some opinions, since their poverty was relative to the king who is powerful and usurping.

Then Allah the Exalted commanded the believers to be mindful of Him, and gave them hope in the bounty that necessitates gratitude. It may be that the meaning is: fear Allah, perhaps your piety will be gratitude for the blessing of His victory at Badr.

His saying, "When you said" (idh taqul): the governing element of "idh" is a hidden verb. The governing element may be "nasarakum" (He helped you). This is according to the view of the majority: that this saying of the Prophet ﷺ was at Badr. Al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said that this was at Badr. Al-Sha'bi said: It reached the believers that Kurz ibn Jabir ibn Hisl al-Muharibi, a warrior of Fihr, had come with reinforcements for the polytheists, and this distressed the believers. So the Prophet ﷺ said this saying to the believers, from Allah's command, and the believers were patient and feared Allah, and the polytheists were defeated. The defeat reached Kurz and those with him, so they withdrew and did not come upon them suddenly. The believers were not reinforced by the angels, and the angels after that used to attend the wars of the Prophet ﷺ as reinforcement, and they attend the wars of the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

People disagreed with al-Sha'bi in this statement, and the reports are abundant that the angels attended Badr and fought. Among that is the saying of Abu Usayd Malik ibn Rabi'ah: "If I were with you now at Badr, and my sight with me, I would show you the ravine from which the angels came out, without doubt or dispute." And among it is the hadith of the Ghifari and his cousin, who heard from the Companions: "Advance, Haizum!" and the veil over the heart of one of them was lifted, and he died in his place, and the other held firm.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The angels did not fight on any day except the day of Badr; on the other days they were a number and reinforcement, not striking. Among that is the saying of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith to Abu Lahab: "It was only that we met the people and they gave us their backs, killing and capturing. Yet by Allah, I did not blame the people; we met men, white, on piebald horses, between heaven and earth, nothing stood in their way and nothing could withstand them." And among it: "that Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, of Banu Salamah, captured al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib on the day of Badr, and Abu al-Yusr was a small, compact man, while al-'Abbas was a tall, large man. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A noble angel helped you against him'..." the hadith in its entirety. Some Companions said: "On the day of Badr I was pursuing a man of the polytheists to strike him with my sword, but when I approached him his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that an angel had killed him."

(p-345) Qatadah ibn Di'amah said: Allah reinforced the believers on the day of Badr with five thousand angels. Al-Tabari said: Others said: Allah promised the believers on the day of Badr that He would reinforce them in all their wars if they were patient and feared Allah, but they did not do that except on the day of the Confederates, so He reinforced them when they besieged Qurayzah. Then he included under this discussion a report from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa who said: "We besieged Qurayzah for a period, and it was not opened to us, so we returned. While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had called for water to wash his head, Jibril, upon him be peace, came to him and said: 'You have laid down your weapons, but the angels have not laid down their burdens.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrapped his head in a cloth and did not wash it, and called out among us, and we rose weary and exhausted, until we came to Qurayzah and al-Nadir. On that day Allah reinforced us with three thousand angels, and opened for us an easy conquest, and we returned with a blessing from Allah and grace."

'Ikrimah said: The promise was on the day of Badr, but they were not patient on the day of Uhud, nor did they fear Allah, so they were not reinforced, and had they been reinforced they would not have been defeated.

Al-Dahhak said: This promise and this saying were to the believers on the day of Uhud, when the people fled and turned their backs, so Allah did not reinforce them; they were reinforced only on the day of Badr with a thousand angels riding behind.

Ibn Zayd said: "The Muslims said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Uhud while they were awaiting the polytheists: 'O Messenger of Allah, will Allah not reinforce us as He reinforced us on the day of Badr?' The Prophet ﷺ said to them: 'Is it not sufficient for you...' the verse." He reinforced them on the day of Badr with a thousand only. Ibn Zayd said: So they were not patient.

His saying, "Is it not sufficient for you" is a confirmation of their belief in sufficiency in this number of angels. Since the matter was clear in itself, that the angels are sufficient, the speaker hastened to the answer in order to build upon it what he would continue saying, so he said: "Yes," and it is the answer of those who confirm. This is fitting in matters that are clear, from which there is no escape in answering. Similar to it is His saying: "Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah." [al-An'am: 19]. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: "Alla yakfikum" (Is it not sufficient for you). The discussion of reinforcement has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: "And He extends them in their transgression" [al-Baqarah: 15].

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read: "bi-thalathah alaf" with a pause on the ha', and likewise "bi-khamsah alaf". The basis of this reading is weak, because the mudaf and mudaf ilayhi require continuity, as they are like one noun, and the second is a completion of the first, while the ha' is merely a sign of pause, so pausing in a place that is meant for continuity is awkward. However, similar things have come from the Arabs in places. Among that is what al-Farra' related, that they say: "akaltu lahman shah," meaning lahm shah, so they prolonged the fatha until an alif arose from it, as they said in pausing: "qala" meaning "qala" (he said) ... Then they prolonged the fatha in rhymed verse and similar places of pause and deliberation. Among that in poetry is the saying of the poet:

"Yunba'u min dhifri ghadubin jasratin..."

meaning yanbu'u, so it was prolonged. And among it is the saying of another:

"Aqulu idh kharrat 'ala al-kalkali — ya naqata ma jultu min majal"

meaning 'ala al-kalkal, so it was prolonged. And among it is the saying of another:

"Fa anta min al-ghawa'ili hina turma — wa min dhammi al-rijali bi-muntazah"

(p-347) meaning bi-muntazih. Abu al-Fath said: If this extension may intervene within the middle of a single word, then extension and deliberation may also occur between the mudaf and mudaf ilayh, since in reality they are two.

Ibn 'Amir alone read: "munazzalin" with fatha on the nun and shadda on the zay. The rest read: "munzalin" with sukun on the nun and fatha on the zay, lightened. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "munazzilin" with fatha on the nun and kasra on the zay, shaddah, meaning: they bring down victory. Al-Nahhas related a reading without attribution: "munzilin" with sukun on the nun and kasra on the zay, lightened, and he explained it as: they bring down victory.

"Bala" is the answer to the negation in "alan," whose meaning has already been stated. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the condition under which reinforcement occurs, which is patience and piety. Al-Fawr: the swift rising toward a thing, derived from the boiling of a cooking pot or water and the like, and from it His saying: "and the oven boiled over" [Hud: 40]. So the meaning is: they will come upon you in this their rising. Ibn 'Abbas said: "min fawrihim hadha" means: from this their journey. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: its meaning is: from this their direction. Qatadah said likewise. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Abu Salih, freedman of Umm Hani', said: from this their anger.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an explanation that does not restrict the word. "Al-fawr" may be due to anger, to greed, or to desire for reward, and from it is "al-fawr" in the Hajj and the ablution.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read: "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw. The rest read:

(p-348) "musawwamin" with fatha on the waw. As for the one who reads with fatha on the waw, its meaning is: marked with signs. Abu Zayd al-Ansari said: al-sawmah is the mark placed on a sheep or other animal, a color contrary to its color so that it may be recognized. It is related that the angels were identified that day by white turbans, related by al-Mahdawi from al-Zajjaj, except Jibril, upon him be peace, who had a yellow turban in the style of al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam's turban; Ibn Ishaq also said this. Mujahid said: their horses had cropped tails and manes, marked at the forelocks and tails with wool and red-dyed wool. Al-Rabi' said: their sign was that they were on piebald horses. 'Abbad ibn Hamzah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: the angels descended in the sign of al-Zubayr, wearing yellow turbans, and this was said by 'Urwah and 'Abd Allah, the sons of al-Zubayr. 'Abd Allah said: it was a yellow cloth, and al-Zubayr wrapped his turban with it. As for the one who reads "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw, the meaning may be as already mentioned: they marked themselves with a sign and marked their horses. Al-Tabari and others preferred this reading because the Prophet ﷺ said to the Muslims on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves," so they are then "musawwimun." Many of the people of exegesis said: the meaning of "musawwimin" with kasra on the waw is that they have made their horses "sawwamu": that is, they gave them their pasture of running, fighting, and readiness, so they are grazing animals, as in "sa'imat al-mashiyah" (grazing livestock), because they were left to their grazing. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this meaning for "musawwamin" with fatha on the waw, that they sent forth their "wusum" (marks).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is unsettled, and Ibn Furak also said it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 126–129:

(p-349) His, the Mighty and Wise, Exalted One's, saying:

﴿And Allah did not make it except as good news for you and so that your hearts would be reassured by it. And victory is not except from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may cut off a part of those who disbelieved or subdue them, so they turn back defeated.﴾ ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter, whether He relents toward them or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The pronoun in "jaʿalahu Allahu" (Allah made it) refers to the sending down and the reinforcement. Al-bushrā (good news) is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The lām in "wa-li-taṭmaʾinna" (and so that they would be reassured) is connected to a hidden verb indicated by "jaʿalahu". The meaning of the verse: this reinforcement was not except so that you would rejoice by it and your hearts would be reassured by it, and so that you would see Allah's care for you; otherwise, multitude avails nothing except that Allah grants victory.

His saying "wa-mā al-naṣr" (and victory is not) means for the believers, and likewise the overturning (al-idālah) against the disbelievers is also from Allah. The lām in His saying "li-yaqṭaʿa" (that He may cut off) is connected to His saying: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾. On this reading, the cutting off of a part is not restricted to one day, unless the alif and lām in "al-naṣr" (victory) are for a previously known reference. It was said that the governing element is "wa-laqad naṣarakum" (and Allah had already given you victory), related by Ibn Fūrak, but it is unsound, because His saying "aw yakbitahum" (or subdue them) is not consequent upon it. It is also possible that the lām in His saying "li-yaqṭaʿa" is connected to "jaʿalahu", so that the cutting off of a part refers to those who were killed at Badr, according to what al-Ḥasan, Ibn Isḥāq and others said, or to those who were killed at Uhud, according to what al-Suddī said. Seventy of the polytheists were killed at Badr, and twenty-two men of them were killed on the day of Uhud. Al-Suddī said: eighteen of them were killed. The first is more sound.

Al-ṭaraf (part) means the group. Whenever Muslims kill disbelievers in battle, they have cut off a part, because it is the part that is adjacent to them of the disbelievers; so it is as if all the disbelievers are a patch, and these slain are a part of it, that is, an edge. It is possible that His exalted saying "li-yaqṭaʿa ṭarafan" (that He may cut off a part) is equivalent to "li-yaqṭaʿa dābiran" (that He may cut off the last remnant).

His saying "aw yakbitahum" means: or disgrace them. Al-kabt is throwing down onto the hands. Al-Naqqāsh and others said: the tāʾ is a substitute for the dāl in kabatahu, whose origin is kabadahu, meaning he did to him what harms his liver (kabid). When Allah grants victory over a disbelieving community, one of these two aspects must occur: either some of them are killed, or they are disappointed, and that is a kind of defeat.

(p-350) His exalted saying: ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ is a restriction establishing that the whole matter belongs to Allah. This restriction implies that it had a cause concerning the side of the Prophet ﷺ. It has been related concerning this that when his companions were routed, he was wounded in the face until some of the links of the armour entered his cheek, his lower front tooth was broken, and he was struck by stones until he fell on his side; he withdrew from the battle line and began wiping the blood from his face, saying: "A people will never prosper who do this to their prophet." This is the wording of the hadith through the route of Anas ibn Mālik. In some routes: "And how would they prosper?" In some of them: that Sālim, the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah, was washing the blood from the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: he regained consciousness while saying: "How (could) a people who did this to their prophet, while he calls them to Allah, (prosper)?" Then the verse was revealed, because of this statement.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that the Prophet ﷺ felt despair at that time about the success of the disbelievers of Quraysh, so his soul inclined to Allah uprooting them and granting him rest from them. It is related that he supplicated against them, or asked permission to supplicate against them. Ibn ʿUmar and others related that he invoked curses upon Abū Sufyān, al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām and Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah, and other things of this meaning. So it was said to him on account of that: ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾, meaning: the outcomes of affairs are in the hand of Allah; so proceed with your affair and persist in calling to your Lord. Al-Ṭabarī and other exegetes said: His saying ﴿or He relents toward them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "yakbitahum" (subdue them).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So His saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ is an interjection in the midst of the speech. His saying "aw yatūba" (or He relents) (p-351) means: so that they become Muslims. His saying "aw yuʿadhdhibahum" (or punishes them) means: in the Hereafter, by their dying upon disbelief. Al-Ṭabarī and others said: it is possible that His saying "aw yatūba" means "ḥattā yatūba" (until He relents), or "ilā an yatūba" (until He relents), and it comes in the sense of your saying: "I will not leave you until you pay me my right," and as you say: "This matter will not be completed until so-and-so comes." On this interpretation, His exalted saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ is not an interjection; rather, the meaning is to inform Muhammad, peace be upon him, that nothing from the affair of these disbelievers will be obtained by him that he hopes for, except that Allah relents toward them so that they become Muslims, and Muhammad, peace be upon him, sees one of his two hopes concerning them, or Allah punishes them with killing in this world, or with the Fire in the Hereafter, or both, and Muhammad ﷺ sees the other hope. On this interpretation, there is no rebuke in His saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ as there is in the first interpretation; and the first interpretation is stronger.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read "aw yatūbu" and "aw yuʿadhdhibu" with a ḍammah on the letter bāʾ in both, meaning: "or He Himself relents," and then Allah affirmed the wrongdoing of these disbelievers. Then He emphasised the meaning of His saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ with a general statement, and mentioned the manifest proof in that, which is His ownership of things, since that requires that He do what He wills with His property, with no objection to Him and no one to repel His judgment. He mentioned that forgiveness or punishment is only by His will and according to what preceded in His knowledge. Then at the end He gave hope, to comfort souls and draw them to His obedience. All of that is in His exalted saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The "mā" in His saying ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ refers to the totality of the world, and therefore "mā" is appropriate. What is mentioned in this verse, that this verse abrogates the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against the polytheists, is entirely weak speech, and this is not one of the places of abrogation (naskh).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 126–129:

(p-349) His, the Mighty and Wise, Exalted One's, saying:

﴿And Allah did not make it except as good news for you and so that your hearts would be reassured by it. And victory is not except from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may cut off a part of those who disbelieved or subdue them, so they turn back defeated.﴾ ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter, whether He relents toward them or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. The pronoun in "jaʿalahu Allahu" (Allah made it) refers to the sending down and the reinforcement. Al-bushrā (good news) is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The lām in "wa-li-taṭmaʾinna" (and so that they would be reassured) is connected to a hidden verb indicated by "jaʿalahu". The meaning of the verse: this reinforcement was not except so that you would rejoice by it and your hearts would be reassured by it, and so that you would see Allah's care for you; otherwise, multitude avails nothing except that Allah grants victory.

His saying "wa-mā al-naṣr" (and victory is not) means for the believers, and likewise the overturning (al-idālah) against the disbelievers is also from Allah. The lām in His saying "li-yaqṭaʿa" (that He may cut off) is connected to His saying: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾. On this reading, the cutting off of a part is not restricted to one day, unless the alif and lām in "al-naṣr" (victory) are for a previously known reference. It was said that the governing element is "wa-laqad naṣarakum" (and Allah had already given you victory), related by Ibn Fūrak, but it is unsound, because His saying "aw yakbitahum" (or subdue them) is not consequent upon it. It is also possible that the lām in His saying "li-yaqṭaʿa" is connected to "jaʿalahu", so that the cutting off of a part refers to those who were killed at Badr, according to what al-Ḥasan, Ibn Isḥāq and others said, or to those who were killed at Uhud, according to what al-Suddī said. Seventy of the polytheists were killed at Badr, and twenty-two men of them were killed on the day of Uhud. Al-Suddī said: eighteen of them were killed. The first is more sound.

Al-ṭaraf (part) means the group. Whenever Muslims kill disbelievers in battle, they have cut off a part, because it is the part that is adjacent to them of the disbelievers; so it is as if all the disbelievers are a patch, and these slain are a part of it, that is, an edge. It is possible that His exalted saying "li-yaqṭaʿa ṭarafan" (that He may cut off a part) is equivalent to "li-yaqṭaʿa dābiran" (that He may cut off the last remnant).

His saying "aw yakbitahum" means: or disgrace them. Al-kabt is throwing down onto the hands. Al-Naqqāsh and others said: the tāʾ is a substitute for the dāl in kabatahu, whose origin is kabadahu, meaning he did to him what harms his liver (kabid). When Allah grants victory over a disbelieving community, one of these two aspects must occur: either some of them are killed, or they are disappointed, and that is a kind of defeat.

This restriction implies that it had a cause concerning the side of the Prophet ﷺ. It has been related concerning this that when his companions were routed, he was wounded in the face until some of the links of the armour entered his cheek, his lower front tooth was broken, and he was struck by stones until he fell on his side; he withdrew from the battle line and began wiping the blood from his face, saying: "A people will never prosper who do this to their prophet." It is related that he supplicated against them, or asked permission to supplicate against them. Al-Ṭabarī and other exegetes said: His saying ﴿or He relents toward them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "yakbitahum" (subdue them).

So His saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ is an interjection in the midst of the speech. His saying "aw yatūba" (or He relents) (p-351) means: so that they become Muslims. His saying "aw yuʿadhdhibahum" (or punishes them) means: in the Hereafter, by their dying upon disbelief. Al-Ṭabarī and others said: it is possible that His saying "aw yatūba" means "ḥattā yatūba" (until He relents), or "ilā an yatūba" (until He relents), and it comes in the sense of your saying: "I will not leave you until you pay me my right," and as you say: "This matter will not be completed until so-and-so comes." On this interpretation, His exalted saying ﴿Not for you is any part of the matter﴾ is not an interjection; rather, the meaning is to inform Muhammad, peace be upon him, that nothing from the affair of these disbelievers will be obtained by him that he hopes for, except that Allah relents toward them so that they become Muslims, and Muhammad, peace be upon him, sees one of his two hopes concerning them, or Allah punishes them with killing in this world, or with the Fire in the Hereafter, or both, and Muhammad ﷺ sees the other hope. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 130–132:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury (riba), doubled and redoubled, and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾ ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may be shown mercy.﴾

(p-352) This prohibition of consuming riba comes as an interjection within the narrative of Uhud, and I do not know of any reported cause for it. Riba means increase (al-ziyada), and the mention of this verse and the rulings on riba has already preceded in Surat al-Baqara. His saying "doubled" (adafan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its meaning is: the riba in which the Arabs would double the debt, so that the creditor would say, "Will you pay or will you increase it?" His saying "redoubled" (mudaafa) indicates the repetition of doubling year after year, as they used to do. This emphatic expression indicates the abominable and ugly nature of their act, and for this reason it mentioned specifically the state of doubling. Allah has prohibited all kinds of riba. This is the understanding (mafhum) of the address, since what is silent regarding riba is in the ruling of what is mentioned. Also, riba encompasses all its kinds: doubling and increase in various forms, whether in the commodity, or in the deferral, or the like.

The Fire in His saying "and fear the Fire" is the generic noun (ism al-jins), and it is possible that it is for a specific reference (al-'ahd). Then He mentioned that it has been prepared for the disbelievers, meaning that they are the intended and primary target, though others of the disobedient may also enter it. Thus He magnified the matter of the Fire by mentioning disbelief, and He made it appealing for the believer to beware of it and to keep far from it through obedience to Allah. This is like His saying regarding Paradise: "prepared for the God-fearing," meaning that they are the intended ones, even though others may also enter it, such as a child, a madman, and the like, who are not charged with obligation and are not described as possessing piety. This is the position of the scholars regarding this verse.

Al-Mawardi and others related from a group of people that they held that the consumers of riba are only threatened by Allah with the Fire of the disbelievers, since the Fire has seven levels: the highest of them is Jahannam for the disobedient, the five for the disbelievers, and the lowest level for the hypocrites. They said: the consumers of riba are punished on the Day of Resurrection only with the Fire of the disbelievers, not the Fire of the disobedient, and it is with this that they were threatened. Thus the alif and lam in His saying "and fear the Fire" according to this view is only for specific reference.

Then He commanded obedience to Himself and obedience to His Messenger. Obedience is the conformity of the act commanded, as it stands with the one commanded, to the intent of the command. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah, and whoever obeys the commander has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys the commander has disobeyed me."

(p-353) Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: this verse, from His saying "and obey Allah," is the beginning of the rebuke concerning the matter of Uhud, the rout of those who fled, and the departure of the archers from their positions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 133–134:

His Majestic and Exalted saying:

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾ ﴿Who spend in ease and in hardship, and who restrain their anger and pardon people. And God loves the good-doers (al-muhsinin)﴾

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "sari'u" (hasten) without a waw, and so it is in the codices of the people of Medina and the people of Syria. The rest of the Seven read it with a waw. Abu 'Ali said: Both readings are common and sound. Whoever reads with the waw does so because he has conjoined one sentence to another; whoever omits the waw does so because the second sentence is closely linked to the first and so dispenses with conjunction by waw. Al-Kisa'i inclined the alif in his saying "sari'u" and in his saying "yusari'una fi al-khayrat" and "nusari'u lahum fi al-khayrat", in all of these. Abu 'Ali said: The inclination (imala) here is good because of the occurrence of a kasra-ed ra' after it.

Al-musara'a (hastening) means al-mubadara (hurrying ahead), and it is a form of mufa'ala, since people are as if each one hastens so as to arrive before the others; so there is a mutual element (mufa'ala) among them in this. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148].

His saying "ila maghfiratin" means: hasten through piety, obedience and drawing near to your Lord, to a state in which God will forgive you, that is, cover your sins by His pardon of them and the removal of their judgment, and admit you into a garden. Anas ibn Malik and Makhul said, in explanation of ﴿And hasten to forgiveness﴾, that it means: to the takbir al-ihram (opening takbir) with the imam.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a good statement, to be followed in every act of obedience.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ — its estimate is: like the width of the heavens and the earth. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28], i.e., like the creation of a single soul and its resurrection. Thus this elliptical construction came, understood and eloquent. From it is the saying of the poet:

"You thought the cry of my riding-camel was the call of a she-goat, and it is not — woe to you, other than the she-goat!"

And from it is the saying of another:

"As if their pool at the edge of Sella
were an ostrich's cry (qaq) in a barren land."

The estimate is: the sound of a she-goat and the pool of an ostrich.

As for the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, the scholars differed on it according to three positions. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the heavens and the earths are joined one to another as a cloth is spread out; that is the width of the Garden, and none knows its length but God. All of this strengthens the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority: that Paradise is greater than these mentioned creations, and it extends from the heaven wherever God the Exalted wills, and that is not denied. Indeed, in the hadith of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The seven heavens and the seven earths in relation to the Kursi are but like dirhams thrown into a desert of the earth, and the Kursi in relation to the Throne is but like a ring in a desert of the earth."

These are creations far greater, by very much, than the heavens and the earth, and the power of God, exalted is He, is greater than all of that.

He handed the scroll to a man on his left. I said: Who is your companion who reads? They said: Mu'awiyah. Ibn Furak said: The Garden is in the heaven, and it will be increased on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is a point of attachment for Mundhir ibn Sa'id and others who said: the Garden and the Fire have not yet been created. That is a weak view. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 135–136:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who, when they commit an immoral act or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins except Allah? — and do not persist in what they have done while they know.﴾ ﴿Those — their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally. And excellent is the reward of the doers.﴾

Allah Most High mentions in this verse a category other than the first category, and He joins them to those (the first) by His mercy and bounty. These are the repentant (tawwabun). It has been narrated concerning the cause of these two verses that the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, the Children of Israel were more honoured by Allah than us, when the wrongdoer among them would wake up to find his punishment written on the door of his house." So Allah revealed this verse as an expansion and mercy, and as a substitute for that practice given to the Children of Israel. It is also narrated that Iblis wept when this verse was revealed. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no servant who commits a sin, then stands up, purifies himself, prays two rak'ahs, and seeks forgiveness, except that he is forgiven."

His saying "and those who" is a conjunction of one clause of people upon another clause, and "alladhina" is not a qualifier (na't) with which the conjunction particle waw is repeated, because that first class is free from falling into immoral acts. Here "fahisha" (immoral act) is an adjective of an omitted noun which the adjective has taken the place of; the implied sense is: "they committed an immoral deed (fa'lah fahisha)." It is a term that encompasses all acts of disobedience, though its specific application to illicit sexual intercourse (zina) has become common, to the extent that al-Suddi interpreted this verse as referring to zina, and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said when he recited it: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, the people have committed zina." Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "The immoral act is from wrongdoing, and wrongdoing is from the immoral act." Others said: "The immoral act in this verse refers to the major sins (kaba'ir), and wronging oneself refers to the minor sins (saghair)."

"Remembered Allah" means: out of fear of His punishment and shame before Him, since He is the Bestower of favours and the Benefactor. From this is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): "May Allah have mercy on Suhayb; if he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him."

"Istaghfaru" means: they sought forgiveness. The lam (in "li-dhunubihim") means: for the sake of their sins. Then there intervenes in the midst of the speech His saying, Most High: ﴿and who forgives sins except Allah﴾, as a parenthetical remark that softens the soul, calling to Allah, and giving hope in His pardon when one returns to Him. The name of Allah came in the nominative after the exception while the sentence is affirmative, by reasoning according to meaning, since it carries the sense: "and none forgives sins except Allah."

His saying, Most High: "and did not persist" (wa lam yusirru). Al-Ischrar (persistence) means: resolving to continue upon a matter and not ceasing from it. From it comes "sarr al-dananir" (tying up dinars), i.e., binding them; and from it the saying of Abu al-Sammal Qa'nab al-'Adawi: "Allah knows that they are from me a sirr," meaning: a firm resolve. So istirar is the resolve to remain upon a sin. From it is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no repentance with persistence," and he also said: "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist."

The expressions of the exegetes differed concerning persistence. Qatadah said: it is one who goes forward in sin, whom the fear of Allah does not restrain. Al-Hasan said: the servant's committing of sin is persistence until he dies. Mujahid said: "lam yusirru" means "they did not proceed." Al-Suddi said: persistence is leaving off seeking forgiveness and remaining silent about it along with the sin.

His saying, Most High: "while they know." Al-Suddi said: its meaning is "while they know that they have sinned." Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is "while they know what has been made unlawful for them." Others said: its meaning is "while they know that the door of repentance is open for them." It was also said: the meaning is "while they know that I punish for persistence."

Then Allah, Most High, associated the two mentioned groups in His saying: "Those — their reward..." to the end of the verse. This indicates that Allah, by this true report, has obligated Himself to accept the repentance of the penitent; yet nothing is obligatory upon Him, Most High, by way of reason, but rather He acts by the authority of ownership, with none to question His command.

His saying: ﴿and excellent is the reward of the doers﴾ is equivalent to His saying: "and excellent is the reward," because "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" require definite genera or what is added to them. This verse is not equivalent to His saying, Most High: ﴿Evil is the example of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 177], because the "mathal" here is added to a known referent, not to a genus. Therefore Abu 'Ali estimated it as: "Evil is the example, the example of the people." It is possible that "mathal al-qawm" is raised by "sa'a" without anything being implied.

Then Allah, Most High, associated the two mentioned groups in His saying: "Those — their reward..." to the end of the verse. This indicates that Allah, by this true report, has obligated Himself to accept the repentance of the penitent; yet nothing is obligatory upon Him, Most High, by way of reason, but rather He acts by the authority of ownership, with none to question His command.

His saying: ﴿and excellent is the reward of the doers﴾ is equivalent to His saying: "and excellent is the reward," because "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" require definite genera or what is added to them. This verse is not equivalent to His saying, Most High: ﴿Evil is the example of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 177], because the "mathal" here is added to a known referent, not to a genus. Therefore Abu 'Ali estimated it as: "Evil is the example, the example of the people." It is possible that "mathal al-qawm" is raised by "sa'a" without anything being implied.

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Indeed there have passed away before you examples (sunan). So travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied.﴾ ﴿This is an explanation for mankind, a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will have the upper hand if you are believers.﴾ ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people.﴾

The meaning: let it not lead you to despair if the disbelieving deniers prevail over you at Uhud, for the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing. Indeed, God has long granted the deniers victory over the believers in turn; but look how the deniers were destroyed after that, and so will be the end of these people. Al-Naqqash said: the address after "there have passed away" is to the disbelievers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That is weak, and the meaning of khalat is: passed away and gone before.

Al-Zajjaj said: the implied phrase is "people of examples" (ahl sunan). The sunan (ways, examples): the paths of conduct, the laws, dominion, trials and the like. The sunnah of a person is the thing he does and persists in. From this is the saying of Khalid al-Hudhali to Abu Dhu'ayb:

"So do not be distressed by a practice you yourself have followed; the first to be content with a practice is the one who follows it."

"Indeed those of the Ta'f from the family of Hashim who set an example, followed it, and established for the noble the custom of emulation."

Labid said:

"From a people whose fathers set a practice for them, and every people has a practice and its leader."

Ibn Zayd said: "There have passed away before you examples (sunan)" means: parables (amthal).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation that does not restrict the word.

He said, "So travel" (fa-siru). This command indicates reporting rather than journeying, because reporting only comes from one who has travelled and witnessed, since it is something perceived by sight, and from that its report is transmitted; so God referred them to the most complete manner. His saying "so see" (fa-nzuru) is, according to the majority, seeing with the eye; others said it means seeing with reflection.

His Exalted saying "This is an explanation for mankind": al-Hasan said the reference is to the Qur'an. Qatada, in interpreting the verse, said: it is this Qur'an, which God made an explanation for mankind in general, and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing in particular. Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi' said the same.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That it is an explanation for mankind is evident, and in itself it is also guidance and admonition; but one who is blinded by disbelief, goes astray, and whose heart has hardened, it is not fitting to attribute the Qur'an to him, whereas it is fitting to attribute it to the God-fearing, in whom there is benefit and for whom it is guidance. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and a group said: the reference of "this" (hadha) is to His saying "there have passed away before you examples" ... the verse. Ibn Ishaq said: the meaning is: this is an interpretation for mankind if they accept it. Al-Sha'bi said: the meaning is: this is an explanation for mankind from blindness.

Weakness (wahn) and wahan: feebleness, softness and decay. From it is: "my bone has weakened" (Maryam 4), and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"... so the rope from it became weak and worn."

Among the noble character is that a person not weaken in his war and his contention, nor soften when he is in the right, and that he exhaust all his capacity and not abase himself even if he dies. Softness is only fitting in peace and contentment. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The believer is gentle and soft" and "The believers are gentle and soft." From it is the saying of the poet:

"By your life, Abu Malik is neither feeble nor weak in strength; when you lead him he leads obedient followers, and whatever you entrust to him, he suffices."

In this manner that I have mentioned goes the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that restrains the oppressor, and do not sit upon the grudge,

except for one like you, or one whom you outrun, as a racehorse outruns when it takes the lead over the course."

In this also goes the saying of the Arabs: "If you cannot prevail, then scratch" (ikhlub), according to the one who interprets it from "claw" (mikhlab), meaning: fight even with the fingernails. This was the deed of 'Abd Allah ibn Tariq, one of the companions of 'Asim ibn 'Adi, when he withdrew his hand from the captors and fought until he was killed; and the deed of al-Mundhir ibn (p-365) Muhammad ibn 'Uqba ibn Uhayha ibn al-Julah on the day of Bi'r Ma'una. Whoever understands it in the sense of deception and trickery (khilaba), which is cunning and guile, that is the opinion of the clever Arabs, not of the majority of them. From it is the deed of 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq with 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan when he killed him. Examples of this are many. Moreover, guile and deception are not pure humiliation, and for that reason some regarded it so.

As for their saying, "If your brother becomes mighty, then be soft" (fa-hin), the correct narration has the meaning with a kasra on the ha', meaning: be soft and weaken like the submissive. As for the narration with a damma on the ha', it is a command to humiliation, and I know of nothing like that in any of the Arabs' expressions. As for the Shari'a, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for a believer to abase himself." I have seen for 'Asim that the proverb with a damma on the ha' is only from al-hawn, which is gentleness, not from al-hawan (humiliation).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: by this verse it is required that the enemy not be granted a truce as long as the Muslims have strength; if they are in a land otherwise, the Imam shall consider for them what is most suitable.

His Exalted saying "while you are the ones on high" (wa-antumu al-a'lawn) is a report of the elevation of the word of Islam; this is the saying of the majority and the apparent sense of the expression, and Ibn Ishaq said it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj: God only said this to them because of their elevation on the mountain. That is because the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he withdrew with a small group of his companions to the mountain, while he was thus, Khalid ibn al-Walid rose above them on the mountain; the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "O God, let them not overcome us." Then he stood, and those with him stood, and his companions fought; 'Umar ibn al-Khattab fought at that time until they removed the polytheists from the summit of the mountain. The Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions ascended it, and God the Exalted revealed to him: "Do not weaken, nor grieve, for you are the ones on high."

His Exalted saying "if you are believers" may be connected to the condition in His saying "do not weaken, nor grieve," so that the purpose is to stir and strengthen souls; or it may be connected to His saying "while you are the ones on high," so that the condition retains its literal sense without figurative extension. From this follows a reproach to those whose hypocrisy appeared on that day, and to those whose faith was weakened and whose certainty wavered: the promise is not attained except through faith, so hold fast to it.

"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.

They do not weep over a brother like mine, but I console myself for him with consolation."

Solace through consolation (al-tasa-ssi) is the benefit that the bearer of a prescribed punishment brings to himself; therefore his testimony is rejected in matters for which he was punished, even if he repents and his condition becomes good. Qarh (wound): killing and injuries, as said by Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qatada and others.

The meaning: if you were touched at Uhud, then the disbelievers of Quraysh were touched at Badr by your hands.

Abu 'Ali said: they are two dialects, like al-da'f and al-du'f, and al-karh and al-kurh. The fatha is preferable, because it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and adopting it is more binding, since the Qur'an was revealed in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

These readings are not thought to be anything but narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, and Jibril, peace be upon him, reviewed all of them with him over the long years as a widening for this community and a completion of the seven ahruf, according to what we have explained at the beginning of this commentary. Ibn Jinni said: I have no kinship with the Basrans, but my kinship is with the truth, and praise be to God.

I have seen for 'Asim that the proverb with a damma on the ha' is only from al-hawn, which is gentleness, not from al-hawan (humiliation).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: by this verse it is required that the enemy not be granted a truce as long as the Muslims have strength; if they are in a land otherwise, the Imam shall consider for them what is most suitable.

His Exalted saying "while you are the ones on high" (wa-antumu al-a'lawn) is a report of the elevation of the word of Islam; this is the saying of the majority and the apparent sense of the expression, and Ibn Ishaq said it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj: God only said this to them because of their elevation on the mountain. That is because the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he withdrew with a small group of his companions to the mountain, while he was thus, Khalid ibn al-Walid rose above them on the mountain; the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "O God, let them not overcome us." Then he stood, and those with him stood, and his companions fought; 'Umar ibn al-Khattab fought at that time until they removed the polytheists from the summit of the mountain. The Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions ascended it, and God the Exalted revealed to him: "Do not weaken, nor grieve, for you are the ones on high."

His Exalted saying "if you are believers" may be connected to the condition in His saying "do not weaken, nor grieve," so that the purpose is to stir and strengthen souls; or it may be connected to His saying "while you are the ones on high," so that the condition retains its literal sense without figurative extension. From this follows a reproach to those whose hypocrisy appeared on that day, and to those whose faith was weakened and whose certainty wavered: the promise is not attained except through faith, so hold fast to it.

Then the Exalted One said, consoling the believers: "If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people." Consolation (uswa) is a solace for mankind, and from it is the saying of al-Khansa':

"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.

They do not weep over a brother like mine, but I console myself for him with consolation."

Solace through consolation (al-tasa-ssi) is the benefit that the bearer of a prescribed punishment brings to himself; therefore his testimony is rejected in matters for which he was punished, even if he repents and his condition becomes good. Qarh (wound): killing and injuries, as said by Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qatada and others.

The meaning: if you were touched at Uhud, then the disbelievers of Quraysh were touched at Badr by your hands.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim in the narration of Hafs read "qarh" with a fatha on the qaf; Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "qurh" with a damma on the qaf; all of them pronounced the ra' with sukun. Abu 'Ali said: they are two dialects, like al-da'f and al-du'f, and al-karh and al-kurh. The fatha is preferable, because it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and adopting it is more binding, since the Qur'an was revealed in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

These readings are not thought to be anything but narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, and Jibril, peace be upon him, reviewed all of them with him over the long years as a widening for this community and a completion of the seven ahruf, according to what we have explained at the beginning of this commentary. On this basis it is not said that one of them is preferred on account of the revelation of the Qur'an in it; if one reading is preferred, it is on a ground other than the ground of revelation. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: qarh and qurh (p-367) are two verbal nouns with one meaning; and whoever says: qarh with a fatha is the wounds themselves, and qurh with a damma on the qaf is the pain of the wounds, is accepted from him if he brings a transmission, since this is not known by analogy. Al-Tabari also said this interpretation.

al-A'mash read "in tamsaskum" with the taa' from above, "quruh" in the plural, "faqad massa al-qawm qarh mithluh." Muhammad ibn al-Sameyfa' al-Yamani read "qarah" with a fatha on the qaf and the ra'. Abu al-Fath said: it is a dialect of qarh, like shall and shalal, and tard and tarad. This is the view of the Basrans, and they do not consider it the effect of a guttural letter. I incline in this to the view of our Baghdadi companions, that a guttural letter has a well-founded effect in such cases; I have heard some of the Banu 'Uqayl say "nahwahu" with a fatha on the ha', meaning "nahwahu" (toward it); had the word been built on a fatha of the ha', the waw would have been changed as in 'usah and qanah; and I heard another say: "ana mahmum" with a fatha on the ha'. Ibn Jinni said: I have no kinship with the Basrans, but my kinship is with the truth, and praise be to God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 137–140:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Indeed there have passed away before you examples (sunan). So travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied.﴾ ﴿This is an explanation for mankind, a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will have the upper hand if you are believers.﴾ ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people.﴾

The address in His saying, Exalted is He, "there have passed away" (qad khalat), is to the believers. The meaning: let it not lead you to despair if the disbelieving deniers prevail over you at Uhud, for the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing. Indeed, God has long granted the deniers victory over the believers in turn; but look how the deniers were destroyed after that, and so will be the end of these people. Al-Naqqash said: the address after "there have passed away" is to the disbelievers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That is weak, and the meaning of khalat is: passed away and gone before.

Al-Zajjaj said: the implied phrase is "people of examples" (ahl sunan). The sunan (ways, examples): the paths of conduct, the laws, dominion, trials and the like. The sunnah of a person is the thing he does and persists in. From this is the saying of Khalid al-Hudhali to Abu Dhu'ayb:

"So do not be distressed by a practice you yourself have followed; the first to be content with a practice is the one who follows it."

(p-362) Sulayman ibn Qatta said:

"Indeed those of the Ta'f from the family of Hashim who set an example, followed it, and established for the noble the custom of emulation."

Labid said:

"From a people whose fathers set a practice for them, and every people has a practice and its leader."

Ibn Zayd said: "There have passed away before you examples (sunan)" means: parables (amthal).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation that does not restrict the word.

He said, "So travel" (fa-siru). This command indicates reporting rather than journeying, because reporting only comes from one who has travelled and witnessed, since it is something perceived by sight, and from that its report is transmitted; so God referred them to the most complete manner. His saying "so see" (fa-nzuru) is, according to the majority, seeing with the eye; others said it means seeing with reflection.

His Exalted saying "This is an explanation for mankind": al-Hasan said the reference is to the Qur'an. Qatada, in interpreting the verse, said: it is this Qur'an, which God made an explanation for mankind in general, and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing in particular. Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi' said the same.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That it is an explanation for mankind is evident, and in itself it is also guidance and admonition; but one who is blinded by disbelief, goes astray, and whose heart has hardened, it is not fitting to attribute the Qur'an to him, whereas it is fitting to attribute it to the God-fearing, in whom there is benefit and for whom it is guidance. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and a group said: the reference of "this" (hadha) is to His saying "there have passed away before you examples" ... the verse. Ibn Ishaq said: the meaning is: this is an interpretation for mankind if they accept it. Al-Sha'bi said: the meaning is: this is an explanation for mankind from blindness.

(p-363) Then the Exalted and Majestic One forbade the believers from weakness over what had befallen them at Uhud, and from grief over those who were lost and over the disgrace of defeat, and He comforted them by saying that they are the ones on high, the people of the final outcome. Weakness (wahn) and wahan: feebleness, softness and decay. From it is: "my bone has weakened" (Maryam 4), and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"... so the rope from it became weak and worn."

Among the noble character is that a person not weaken in his war and his contention, nor soften when he is in the right, and that he exhaust all his capacity and not abase himself even if he dies. Softness is only fitting in peace and contentment. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The believer is gentle and soft" and "The believers are gentle and soft." From it is the saying of the poet:

"By your life, Abu Malik is neither feeble nor weak in strength; when you lead him he leads obedient followers, and whatever you entrust to him, he suffices."

In this manner that I have mentioned goes the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that restrains the oppressor, and do not sit upon the grudge,

except for one like you, or one whom you outrun, as a racehorse outruns when it takes the lead over the course."

In this also goes the saying of the Arabs: "If you cannot prevail, then scratch" (ikhlub), according to the one who interprets it from "claw" (mikhlab), meaning: fight even with the fingernails. This was the deed of 'Abd Allah ibn Tariq, one of the companions of 'Asim ibn 'Adi, when he withdrew his hand from the captors and fought until he was killed; and the deed of al-Mundhir ibn (p-365) Muhammad ibn 'Uqba ibn Uhayha ibn al-Julah on the day of Bi'r Ma'una. Whoever understands it in the sense of deception and trickery (khilaba), which is cunning and guile, that is the opinion of the clever Arabs, not of the majority of them. From it is the deed of 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq with 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan when he killed him. Examples of this are many. Moreover, guile and deception are not pure humiliation, and for that reason some regarded it so.

As for their saying, "If your brother becomes mighty, then be soft" (fa-hin), the correct narration has the meaning with a kasra on the ha', meaning: be soft and weaken like the submissive. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 141:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And these days We alternate among the people, so that Allah may know those who believe and take martyrs from among you. And Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 140] ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers.﴾

He informs, by way of consolation, that the days, in the earliest and latest of time, He has only made as turns (duwal) among mankind; that is, do not deny that the disbelievers may gain the upper hand over you. He, Exalted, said "nudawiluha" (We alternate them), which is a form of mufa'ala (reciprocity) from one side only. This was permissible because the alternation from Him, Exalted, is between two things; since those two groups alternate, the usage is apt. The word duwla with a damma on the dal is the verbal noun, while daulah with a fatha on the dal is a single instance of that; hence one says "in the daulah of so-and-so," because it is one occurrence in time. Some of the pure Arabs heard a reciter recite this verse and said: "It is only 'And these days We alternate among the Arabs'." It was said to him: "It is only 'among the people'." He said: "Surely we belong to Allah; the kingship of the Arabs has gone, by the Lord of the Ka'ba."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so that Allah may know those who believe﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 140], the waw has entered to indicate that the lam is connected to an implied element at the end of the sentence; its estimate is: "and so that Allah may know those who believe, He did that." His saying, Exalted is He, "wa liya'lama" (so that He may know), means: that the faith of those whom He has known from eternity to believe may become manifest in existence, and that His knowledge may coincide with their faith and their existence. Otherwise He knew them from the beginning, and His knowledge is not subject to change. Something similar to this is when a ruler strikes someone and then explains the reason for the striking, saying: "I did this explaining so that I might strike one who deserves it"; its meaning is: so that it may become evident that my action accorded with his deserving it.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and take martyrs from among you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 140], means: people of success in His path, as is reported in the virtues of the martyr.

Then He, Exalted, informed that His alternating of the disbelievers over the believers is only for purifying the believers, and that the alternating of the believers over the disbelievers is only for destroying the disbelievers; this is what the wording of the verse requires. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Allah gave the upper hand to His Messenger on the day of Badr, and against him on the day of Uhud. Many scholars went to interpreting the alternation of the believers as victory, and the alternation of the disbelievers as their gaining the upper hand, and there is a hadith reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this regard: "They gain the upper hand just as you are granted victory."

Al-tamhis (purification) is cleansing. Al-Khalil said: tamhis is removal from a defect; it is said: "mahhasa al-habl" when its fuzz has gone from it through much rubbing on the hand and it becomes smooth. Al-Zajjaj cited the word as "al-habl" (the rope), while al-Naqqash related it as "mahhasa al-jamal" (the camel became bare) when its hair has gone and it became smooth. Hanif al-Hanatim said, when he came to a water called Tuwayli': "You are indeed smooth of rope, far from the watering place, overlooking the enemies"; the meaning is that, because of its distance, its rope becomes smooth through long drawing and the passing of hands.

So the meaning of the verse is: that Allah purifies the believers when He gives the disbelievers the upper hand over them, by cleansing those who are martyred from their sins, and cleansing the living from their hypocrites, as He distinguishes them; and that He destroys the disbelievers when He grants victory over them, that is, He diminishes them. Al-mahq is going away little by little, and from it comes "mihaq al-qamar" (the waning of the moon).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 142–143:

(p-369) His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying:

﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove, nor known the patient?﴾ ﴿And you had certainly wished for death before you encountered it. Then you have seen it, while you were looking on.﴾

"Am" (أمْ) carries the meaning of turning away from the first speech and abandoning it, and it implies the sense of interrogation (al-istifham). For this reason Sibawayh (Sibawayh) estimated it as "bal" (بَلْ, "rather") together with the interrogative alif.

"Hasibtum" (حَسِبْتُمْ) means "you thought" (ظَنَنْتُمْ). This verse and what follows are a rebuke and reproach directed at groups of the believers who committed the well-known lapses on the day of Uhud.

His saying "wa-lamma ya'lam" (﴿وَلَمّا يَعْلَمِ﴾) is an emphatic negation, and it corresponds to the speaker's saying "qad kana kadha" (قَدْ كانَ كَذا, "such a thing has indeed happened"). When this affirmative statement is emphasised with "qad," its corresponding negation is emphasised with "lamma." If the speaker says "kana hadha" (كانَ هَذا, "this happened"), its counterpart is "lam yakun" (لَمْ يَكُنْ) without emphasis in both cases, as Sibawayh said.

The majority of readers (Jumhur al-Nas) read "yalami" (يَعْلَمِ) with a kasra on the mim, because of the meeting of two consonants in His saying "wa-lamma ya'lami." Yahya ibn Waththab and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "wa-lamma ya'lama" (وَلَمّا يَعْلَمَ) with a fatha on the mim, assimilating it to the fatha of the lam. The majority read "wa-ya'lama" (وَيَعْلَمَ) in the accusative, with "an" (أنْ) understood, according to the Basrans, and with the waw of accompaniment (waw al-sarf) according to the Kufans. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that he read "wa-ya'lamu" (وَيَعْلَمُ) in the nominative, as a resumption of the verb. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Abu Haywa and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa-ya'lami" (وَيَعْلَمِ) with a kasra on the mim in the jussive, coordinated with His saying "wa-lamma ya'lami."

Then He addressed the believers with His saying: ﴿And you had certainly wished for death﴾. The reason for this is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out on the expedition of Badr, intending the caravan of Quraysh, moving swiftly, so the people did not gather fully with him, since they thought he would not encounter battle. When Allah decreed at Badr what He decreed, and those who were present were granted a lofty station, those of the believers who had stayed behind from it began to wish to be present at fighting the disbelievers with the Prophet (ﷺ), so that they might have some share of this effort, which would join them, in the sight of their Lord and their Prophet, to the rank of the people of Badr. Concerning this there is a well-known statement of Anas ibn al-Nadr. When the matter of Uhud came and the fighting took place, not all (p-370) of the believers were truthful. So Allah reproached them with this verse, and He obliged them to the wish for death, from the angle that they had wished to meet men with iron and to strike them with it, and in that situation death is for the most part present. Only one whose soul is content with death wishes for it, so death became as though it were the object of the wish. Otherwise, the very killing of a Muslim by a polytheist cannot be wished for as killing; rather, its consequences are wished for, such as martyrdom and bliss.

Qur'an readers: The majority read "min qabli an talqawhu" (مِن قَبْلِ أنْ تَلْقَوْهُ). Al-Zuhri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "min qabli an tulaquhu" (مِن قَبْلِ أنْ تُلاقُوهُ). These two readings are the same in meaning as the first, since "laqiya" (لَقِيَ) implies that it is between two parties, even though it is not on the pattern of "faa'ala." Mujahid read "min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) with a damma on the lam and without the idafa, making "an talqawhu" a substitute (badal) for "al-mawt."

His, Exalted is He, saying "fa-qad ra'aytumuhu" (فَقَدْ رَأيْتُمُوهُ) means: you saw its causes, namely the blazing war and men with swords in their hands. This is like what 'Umayr ibn Wahb said on the day of Badr: "I saw calamities carrying deaths." Al-Harith ibn Hisham said:

"And I found the scent of death from their direction, in a narrow pass, while the horses had not yet scattered."

He means the matter was near. Similar to this is the saying of 'Amir ibn Fuhayra:

"Indeed I saw death before tasting it."

(p-371) He means when his illness intensified. Talha ibn Musarrif read "fa-laqad ra'aytumuhu" (فَلَقَدْ رَأيْتُمُوهُ). His, Exalted is He, saying "wa-antum tanzurun" (وَأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ) may carry three meanings. The first: it is an emphasis of the seeing, removing it from the ambiguity that exists in the wording between seeing with the heart and seeing with the eye. The second: the meaning is "while you were looking into the means of salvation and flight, and into the matter of Muhammad (peace be upon him), whether he had been killed or not." All of this is a violation of what you had covenanted with Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Makki and others related from some people that they said: the meaning is "while you were looking at Muhammad." This is a weak opinion, unless it is redirected to the view I have mentioned, that it is the looking into his affair, whether he had been killed, and the agitation according to that.

The third meaning: it may be that He made them stand upon their wish and their covenant, and upon the fact that they saw what they had wished for. Then He said, by way of rebuke and reproach: "﴿and you are looking﴾" at your present conduct after the end of the war, whether you have fulfilled or broken [your word]. As though He said: "and you are the reckoners of your own selves, so consider the ugliness of your action." In this rebuke, in this manner, there is a fine kind of sparing, protection and invitation. Ibn Fawrak said: the meaning is "and you are contemplating the situation in this matter and reflecting upon it, how it is," and this is similar to what has preceded.
