Yahya ibn Waththab and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "wa-lamma ya'lama" (وَلَمّا يَعْلَمَ) with a fatha on the mim, assimilating it to the fatha of the lam. The majority read "wa-ya'lama" (وَيَعْلَمَ) in the accusative, with "an" (أنْ) understood, according to the Basrans, and with the waw of accompaniment (waw al-sarf) according to the Kufans. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that he read "wa-ya'lamu" (وَيَعْلَمُ) in the nominative, as a resumption of the verb. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Abu Haywa and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa-ya'lami" (وَيَعْلَمِ) with a kasra on the mim in the jussive, coordinated with His saying "wa-lamma ya'lami."

Then He addressed the believers with His saying: ﴿And you had certainly wished for death﴾. The reason for this is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out on the expedition of Badr, intending the caravan of Quraysh, moving swiftly, so the people did not gather fully with him, since they thought he would not encounter battle. When Allah decreed at Badr what He decreed, and those who were present were granted a lofty station, those of the believers who had stayed behind from it began to wish to be present at fighting the disbelievers with the Prophet (ﷺ), so that they might have some share of this effort, which would join them, in the sight of their Lord and their Prophet, to the rank of the people of Badr. Concerning this there is a well-known statement of Anas ibn al-Nadr. When the matter of Uhud came and the fighting took place, not all (p-370) of the believers were truthful. So Allah reproached them with this verse, and He obliged them to the wish for death, from the angle that they had wished to meet men with iron and to strike them with it, and in that situation death is for the most part present. Only one whose soul is content with death wishes for it, so death became as though it were the object of the wish. Otherwise, the very killing of a Muslim by a polytheist cannot be wished for as killing; rather, its consequences are wished for, such as martyrdom and bliss.

Qur'an readers: The majority read "min qabli an talqawhu" (مِن قَبْلِ أنْ تَلْقَوْهُ). Al-Zuhri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "min qabli an tulaquhu" (مِن قَبْلِ أنْ تُلاقُوهُ). These two readings are the same in meaning as the first, since "laqiya" (لَقِيَ) implies that it is between two parties, even though it is not on the pattern of "faa'ala." Mujahid read "min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) with a damma on the lam and without the idafa, making "an talqawhu" a substitute (badal) for "al-mawt."

His, Exalted is He, saying "fa-qad ra'aytumuhu" (فَقَدْ رَأيْتُمُوهُ) means: you saw its causes, namely the blazing war and men with swords in their hands. This is like what 'Umayr ibn Wahb said on the day of Badr: "I saw calamities carrying deaths." Al-Harith ibn Hisham said:

"And I found the scent of death from their direction, in a narrow pass, while the horses had not yet scattered."

He means the matter was near. Similar to this is the saying of 'Amir ibn Fuhayra:

"Indeed I saw death before tasting it."

(p-371) He means when his illness intensified. Talha ibn Musarrif read "fa-laqad ra'aytumuhu" (فَلَقَدْ رَأيْتُمُوهُ). His, Exalted is He, saying "wa-antum tanzurun" (وَأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ) may carry three meanings. The first: it is an emphasis of the seeing, removing it from the ambiguity that exists in the wording between seeing with the heart and seeing with the eye. The second: the meaning is "while you were looking into the means of salvation and flight, and into the matter of Muhammad (peace be upon him), whether he had been killed or not." All of this is a violation of what you had covenanted with Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Makki and others related from some people that they said: the meaning is "while you were looking at Muhammad." This is a weak opinion, unless it is redirected to the view I have mentioned, that it is the looking into his affair, whether he had been killed, and the agitation according to that.

The third meaning: it may be that He made them stand upon their wish and their covenant, and upon the fact that they saw what they had wished for. Then He said, by way of rebuke and reproach: "﴿and you are looking﴾" at your present conduct after the end of the war, whether you have fulfilled or broken [your word]. As though He said: "and you are the reckoners of your own selves, so consider the ugliness of your action." In this rebuke, in this manner, there is a fine kind of sparing, protection and invitation. Ibn Fawrak said: the meaning is "and you are contemplating the situation in this matter and reflecting upon it, how it is," and this is similar to what has preceded.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 144–145:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all, and Allah will reward the grateful.﴾ ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah, at a decreed term.﴾

This is a continuation of their reproach and the establishment of Allah's proof against them. The meaning: Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger (p-372) like the other messengers. He has conveyed as they conveyed, and it is incumbent upon you, O believers, to act upon the content of the message. The life and continued existence of the Messenger among you is not a condition for that, because the Messenger dies just as the messengers before him died. "Khalat" means: passed on and elapsed, and went into the emptiness of the earth.

The majority of readers recited "al-Rusul" with the definite article. In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is "Rusul" without the article, and this is the reading of Hittan ibn 'Abd Allah. The rationale of the first reading is the magnification of the mention of the messengers and honouring them in accordance with their status with Allah, the Exalted. The rationale of the second reading is that it is the place of explaining the Prophet's ﷺ matter concerning the meaning of life, and a place of equating him with mankind in that regard; so the indefinite "Rusul" comes within the course of this restriction (iqtisad) concerning him ﷺ. This is how one proceeds in places where something is being restricted, such as His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13], and His saying: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ [Hud: 40], and other examples besides these. Abu al-Fath mentioned this, and the reading with the definite "al-Rusul" is more eloquent in speech.

As for His saying, "So if he dies..." up to the end of the verse: the interrogative alif has entered upon the whole statement in the manner in which it informs about the one who is committed to it, because the most reprehensible of their states would be for them to say: "If Muhammad dies or is killed, we turn back." Since their action was tending toward this course, they were held to the limit by which the report is made. Many of the exegetes said: the interrogative alif has entered where it does not belong, because the purpose is only: "You will turn back on your heels if Muhammad dies"; so the question is only about the answer to the conditional.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

By the consideration I have already presented, the eloquence of the alif upon the conditional becomes clear, and this is similar to the entry of the alif of approximation (taqrib) in His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170] and similar speech, as if you have introduced affirmation (taqrir) upon what you have obliged the addressee to say. Turning back on the heels entails turning away from what one has turned back from (p-373). Then Allah, may He be exalted, threatened the one who turns back on his heels with His saying: ﴿He will not harm Allah at all﴾, because the meaning is: he only harms himself and destroys himself by it. Then He promised the grateful, who are those who were truthful and patient and none of them turned back on his heels, but rather continued on his religion steadfastly until he died. Among them is Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', and his testament to the Ansar attests to this; among them is Anas ibn al-Nadr; and among them is the Ansari whom al-Tabari mentioned, with a chain, that a man from the Muhajirun passed by him while he was writhing in his blood, and said: "O so-and-so, did you know that Muhammad has been killed?" The Ansari said: "If Muhammad has been killed, he has indeed conveyed the message, so fight for your religion."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These were the people of that event, whose action matched their words. Then the grateful of every age until the Day of Resurrection enter into the verse. Ibn Ishaq said: the meaning of ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ is: those who obey Him and act upon His command. Al-Tabari mentioned, with a chain from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and others, that he said in explanation of this verse: "The grateful are those who remain steadfast upon their religion: Abu Bakr and his companions," and he used to say: "Abu Bakr is the commander of the grateful."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, refers to Abu Bakr's, may Allah be pleased with him, declaration of this verse on the day of the Prophet's ﷺ death and his steadfastness in that position and in the matter of apostasy. This is because when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken, and his death spread, the hypocrites were agitated, spoke out, and resolved to gather and reveal themselves. Allah the Exalted placed in the heart of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet had not died, so he delivered his famous sermon warning the hypocrites that the Prophet ﷺ would return. This weakened the hypocrites' resolve and their word was scattered. Then Abu Bakr came after he had looked at the Prophet ﷺ, heard 'Umar's words, and said to him: "Be silent." 'Umar continued his speech, so Abu Bakr recited the testimony (tashahhud), and the people turned their attention to him. He said: "As for what follows: whoever worshipped Allah, then Allah is Living and does not die; and whoever worshipped Muhammad, then Muhammad has died." ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾, and he recited the whole verse. The people wept, and there was no one who did not recite the verse, as if the people had not heard it before that day. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said in al-Bukhari: "So Allah benefited by the sermon of 'Umar and then by the sermon of Abu Bakr."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is one of the occasions in which the gratitude of Abu Bakr and the gratitude of the people because of him became manifest.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed about souls that they die only at a written, fixed, single term with Allah, the Exalted; that is, cowardice does not increase it, and boldness and advancing do not decrease it. In this verse is a strengthening of souls for jihad. Ibn Fawrak said: in it is also a consolation for what occurred in the death of the Prophet ﷺ. The expression "wa ma kana" may come concerning what is possible and near, such as the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It was not for the son of Abu Quhafa to lead prayer in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

It may also occur concerning what is rationally impossible, as in His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾ [al-Naml: 60]. It is an expression that has no fixed form and does not contain a prohibition as some exegetes say; rather, the extent of its meaning is understood from the contextual indicators of the speech in which the expression occurs. "Nafs" in this verse is a generic noun (ism al-jins). Idhn (permission) is enabling someone to have a thing with knowledge of the thing permitted; if speech is added to that, it is a command. His saying "kitaban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and "mu'ajjalan" is an adjective. This verse refutes the Mu'tazila in their claim of two terms (al-ajalayn). As for the resolution of their reliance on His saying: ﴿And He defers you to a named term﴾ [Nuh: 4] and similar verses, it will come in its proper places, Allah willing, may He be exalted.

(p-375) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it; and We will reward the grateful.﴾ [Al-Imran: 145]

﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him were many devoted (rabbiyyun), and they did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they grow weak, nor did they submit. And Allah loves the patient.﴾ [Al-Imran: 146]

His saying, "We will give him from it," is conditioned by the will (of Allah): that is, We will give whomever We wish from it what has been decreed for him. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the hastened (world), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish﴾ [Al-Isra: 18]. The context of the speech requires that he is not given any portion of the Hereafter, because whoever's intention in his deed is restricted to seeking this world has no share in the Hereafter, and deeds are by intentions. The context of His saying, ﴿whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it﴾ [Al-Imran: 145], does not prevent that he be given a portion of this world.

The majority of people read "nu'tihi" (both occurrences) and "sanajzi" all with the nun of majesty (we). Al-A'mash read them all with the ya' (he), which is by omitting the agent, since the context indicates it. Ibn Furak said concerning the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾ [Al-Imran: 145]: it is an indication that He bestows upon them the bounties of this world, not that they are confined to the Hereafter.

Then the Exalted set forth an example for the believers from among the righteous nations that preceded them, whom the killing of the disbelievers of their prophets did not turn away from their religion. So He said: ﴿And how many a prophet…﴾ to the end of the verse.

In "ka'ayyin" there are four dialects: "ka'ayyin" on the pattern of ka'ayyin (with fatha on the ayn); "wa-ka'in," on the pattern of ka'in; "ka'yan," on the pattern of ka'yan with sukun on the ayn; and "ka'in," on the pattern of ka'in with kasra on the ayn. The Arabs used most in their poetry the form on the pattern of ka'in. From that is the saying of the poet:

"And how many a mailed warrior we have repelled from you,
coming before the people, lowering his face, veiled."

Jarir said:

"And how many in the valleys (of Mecca) is a friend who sees me
—if I were struck, he would be the one struck."

(p-376) Another said:

"And how many a silent one you see, admiring you,
whose increase or decrease lies in his speech."

And there has come in the dialect I mentioned first the saying of the poet:

"Ka'ayyin among the people are folk whose brother is above them,
and they are noble."

This dialect is the origin of this word, for the kaf is the particle of comparison that entered upon "ayy," just as it entered upon "dha" in your saying: "li-fulan kadha wa-kadha," and as it entered upon "anna" in your saying: "ka-anna Zaydan asad." But the meaning of comparison remained for it in "ka-anna," and it ceased to have that in "kadha wa-kadha" and in "ka'ayyin." The Arabs used "ka'ayyin" with the meaning of "kam," which is for multiplicity. Their usage of the word became frequent, until the tongue of the Arabs played with it in the four dialects I mentioned. This is like the way it played in their saying:

"La-'amri," until they said "ra'amli," and like their saying "atyab" and "aytab," and like their saying "tibbikh" in place of "bittikh." So the kaf and "ayy" were treated as if they were one thing.

As for the derivation of the dialect of the one who said "ka'in" on the pattern of fa'il: they took the original form, which is "ka'ayyin," and transposed the ya' before the hamza, and the vowel of each of them was transferred to its counterpart, so "kayya'" came on the pattern of "kayya'," and they deleted the second ya', which was fatha, for lightness, just as they deleted the ya' from "mayyit," "hayyin," and "layyin," so they said "mayt," "hayn," (p-377) and "layn." And just as they deleted the second ya' from "ayy" for lightness. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib al-Tamimi:

"I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, which of them
(the rain) from the cloud whose downpours have poured forth shall be upon me?"

So "kay'" came on the pattern of "kay'," and this quiescent ya' was changed into an alif out of regard for the fatha that preceded it, just as they said "yawjal" becomes "yajal," and just as they changed the ya' into an alif in "tay'," and as it was changed in "ayah" according to Sibawayh, since its original form in his view is "ayyah" on the pattern of "fa'lah" with sukun on the ayn, so it came as "ka'," and then this tanwin was written as a nun in the Mushaf. As for the analogy of the language, it is its deletion in pause. Just as they say "marartu bi-Zayd," so they say "ka'ayy," and Abu 'Amr paused on it as "ka'ay" with a ya' without a nun, and likewise Sawra ibn al-Mubarak transmitted from al-Kisa'i. The rest of the readers paused with the nun, out of regard for the script of the Mushaf. Abu 'Ali said: If it were said that when the word was inflected by transposition, it came to be in the position of the nun that is from the word itself, and came to be in the position of the lam of the agent, so it was retained in pause, that would be a valid view. What supports this is that when they deleted the speech in their saying "imal" (for "ima la"), they made it by deletion like one word, so they permitted imala in the alif of "la," just as it is permitted in the one that is from the word itself in nouns and verbs. So one pauses on "ka'ayyin" with the nun, and does not pause on the nun if it is not transposed, just as the alif of "la" is not inclined if its verb is not deleted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

With this dialect in which there is this transposition, Ibn Kathir alone read. The rest of the Seven read with the dialect which is the original: "ka'ayyin." Yunus ibn Habib went to the view that "ka'ayyin" is a noun of agency from "kawn" (being), but his saying is rejected, since it would entail that the word be declined, and none of the Arabs declined it. As for the dialect which is "ka'ayn" on the pattern of "ka'ayn," it is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli. The reasoning for this dialect is that they gave the cause for the original form, which is "ka'ayn," by the reasoning previously mentioned. When it came to "kay'" on the pattern of "kay'," these (readers) left the changing of the quiescent ya' into an alif as previously explained in the first reasoning, and they transposed the word and made it "ka'ayn" on the pattern of "ka'ayn." This was good for two reasons: one is that playing with and altering this word is a well-trodden path, and the second is that they returned to the original, which is putting the hamza before the ya'. As for the dialect which is "ka'in" on the pattern of "ka'in," it is also the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, reported from him by Abu 'Amr al-Dani, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it, except that he eased the hamza into a ya', so he read "kay" in all of the Qur'an. The reasoning for this dialect is that they deleted the alif from "ka'in" (with the long vowel) on the pattern of "ka'in," after all that alteration, for lightness. This is like their saying "am wallahi" meaning "amma," and like their saying on the tongue of the lizard:

"I do not desire to come to water
except for cold, sour-tasting water,
and lukewarm, lustrous ... "

They meant "'aridan" and "baridan," so they deleted for lightness, and this is frequent in their speech. And "ka'ayyin" in this verse is in the position of nominative by being the subject (of the sentence), and it is in the position of "kam" and in its meaning, and it generally gives the meaning of multiplicity.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Nafi' read "qutila" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the ta', lightened. The rest read "qatala ma'ahu," with an alif between the qaf and the ta'. Qatada read "quttila" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the ta', doubled, for multiplicity.

As for His saying, the Exalted, "qutila," a group of the exegetes, among them al-Tabari, said: it is attributed to the pronoun of "nabi" (prophet), and the meaning according to them is that the prophet was killed. Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying: ﴿And it is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾ [Al-Imran: 161]: the prophet is killed, so how could he not be betrayed? And if this is so, then "rabbiyyun" is in the nominative by the adverbial (preposition) without any disagreement.

His saying, "ma'ahu rabbiyyun," on this interpretation, may be an attributive adjective of "nabi," and it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun to which "qutila" is attributed. If you make it an adjective, you must supply for the subject, which is "ka'ayyin," a predicate, its estimated form at the end of the speech being: "passed away," or "went," or "perished," then "fa-ma wahanu" (they did not weaken). If you make "ma'ahu rabbiyyun" a circumstantial clause from the pronoun, then the predicate of the subject is in His saying "qutila." When you make it an adjective, the pronoun in "ma'ahu" refers back to "nabi," and when you make it a circumstantial clause, the pronoun in "ma'ahu" refers back to the pronoun that is the one in the circumstance. On both views, whether adjective or circumstance, "ma'ahu rabbiyyun" is originally connected to an omitted element, and is not connected to "qutila." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and a group with him said: "qutila" is attributed only to His saying "rabbiyyun," and they are the ones who were killed. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: no prophet was ever killed in battle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, His saying "ma'ahu" is connected to "qutila," and this clause, "qutila ma'ahu rabbiyyun," is the predicate of the subject. In the reading of the one who read "qatala," all the estimations I have mentioned in the reading of "qutila" are conceivable. As for the reading of Qatada, "qutilla," Abu al-Fath said: it is not good for the verb to be attributed except to the rabbiyyin, because of what it contains of the meaning of multiplicity, which may not be used for the killing of one person. If it is said: it is attributed to "nabi," out of regard for the meaning of "kam," the answer is that the wording has proceeded in the manner of the singular in His saying "min nabi," and the singular pronoun in "ma'ahu" indicates that what is intended is only the illustration with one individual after another, so the speech came out in the meaning of "kam." Abu al-Fath said: This reading strengthens the view of those among the Seven who said that "qutila" with the lightened ta', or "qatala," is attributed only to the rabbiyyin. Al-Tabari preferred the attribution of "qutila" to the prophet, by the indication of the incident of Muhammad ﷺ, since the believers only became weak when it was said: "Muhammad has been killed." So He set forth as an example a prophet who was killed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If the verb is not attributed to "nabi," the meaning of the verse becomes only: the strengthening of the believers after those among them who were killed. Al-Tabari's preference is good, and what supports it is the previous saying of the Exalted: ﴿So if he dies or is killed﴾ [Al-Imran: 144]. The argument of the one who read "qatala" is that it is more general in praise, because it includes both the one who was killed and the one who remained.

(p-380) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, on this reading, it is good to attribute the verb to the rabbiyyin, and on the reading "qutila," to attribute it to "nabi."

The Seven and a group of people agreed on the kasra of the ra' in "rabbiyyun." Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, and 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib read "rubbiyyun" with a damma on the ra'. Qatada reported from Ibn 'Abbas "rabbiyyun" with a fatha on the ra'. Ibn Jinni said: the fatha on the ra' is the dialect of Tamim, and all of them are dialects. People differed concerning the meaning of "rabbiyyun." Ibn Mas'ud said: the rabbiyyun are thousands of people and a large number. Ibn 'Abbas said: rabbiyyun are large crowds, and this was said by al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ikrima. And according to the saying of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, "they are thousands," some exegetes said: they are ten thousand or more; this was taken from the pattern of the plural of multiplicity in their saying, "they are thousands." As for the rabbiyyin being large groups, that is from "ribbah" with a kasra on the ra', which is a large group. Yunus ibn Habib said this, and he said: the saying of the Exalted, ( qatal ma'ahu rabbiyyun ), means they are attributed to it. Qutrub said: the majority of scholars follow the view of Yunus. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said that a "ribbah" is ten thousand. And it was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others that they said: "rabbiyyun" means "scholars." Al-Hasan said: jurists, scholars. He also said: patient scholars. This saying is on the basis of attribution to the Lord (Rabb), either because they are obedient to Him, or because, as scholars, they know what He has legislated. This view is strengthened in the reading of the one who read "rabbiyyun" with a fatha on the ra'. As for the damma and kasra on the ra', it comes by altering the attribution, as they said in attributing to al-Haram: "Hirami" with a kasra on the ha', and to al-Basra: "Basri" with a kasra on the ba'. In this there is room for consideration. Ibn Zayd said: the rabbaniyyun are the rulers, and the rabbiyyun are the subjects, the followers of the rulers.

(p-381) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is as if this is from the viewpoint that they are those who are nurtured (marbubun).

Al-Naqqash said: the derivation of "rabbiyy" is from "raba al-shay'" (the thing grew), "yarbu," when it increased, so the one with much knowledge was named by that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad said:

This is weak.

Makki said: "Ribbiyyun" with a kasra on the rā' is a nisba to "al-Rabb" (the Lord), but its rā' was given a kasra to match the kasra and the yā' that follow the rā'. It is also reported with a ḍamma on the rā' in the same way, but they put the ḍamma as is said in "dahriyy" with a ḍamma on the dāl in the nisba to "al-dahr" (time).

The majority of readers recited "fa-mā wahanū" with a fatḥa on the hā'. Al-A'mash, al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Sammāl recited "wahinū" with a kasra on the hā'. Both are dialectal forms with the same meaning: it is said wahina (with a kasra on the hā') yahinu (wahina, with a fatḥa on the hā', yahinu). 'Ikrima and Abū al-Sammāl also recited "wahnū" with the hā' sukūn, and this is for the sake of lightness, as they said in "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" and other such patterns. The meaning of wahn (weakness) has already been explained in His words earlier, "wa lā tahinū" (do not be weak).

The pronoun in His words "fa-mā wahanū" refers to all of the Ribbiyyūn according to the one who attributes "qutila" (was killed) to "nabiyy" (a prophet). According to the one who attributes it to "al-Ribbiyyīn", this pronoun refers to those among them who remained, since the meaning understands itself.

As for His words, exalted is He, "wa mā ḍa'ufū": its meaning is that they did not acquire, through weakness and submission by the hand, anything that would indicate their feebleness.

As for His words, exalted is He, "wa mā istakānū": a group of grammarians held that it is from sukūn (stillness), so its pattern is ifta'alū, istakanū, and the fatḥa of the kāf was prolonged, so an alif arose from its prolongation. Another group held that it is derived from kāna yakūnu (to be), so its pattern according to this derivation is istaf'alū, whose origin is istakwanū; the movement of the wāw was moved to the kāf and the wāw was changed into an alif, as they did in your saying "ista'ānū" and "istaqāmū". The meaning is that they did not become weak, nor were they close to that, just as you say: "I did not do such-and-such, nor did I come close (kidtu)", and the verb is elided because the speech indicates that the intended meaning is: "I was not about to do it." And Allah's love for the patient is what becomes apparent upon them of His help and His bestowal of blessings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 147–148:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And their saying was only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet and give us victory over the disbelieving people." So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

This verse is about the Rabbiyyun (the devoted worshippers of the Lord), meaning: this was their saying, not what some of you, O companions of Muhammad, said, such as the saying of one who said, "Let us take safe-conduct from Abu Sufyan," and the saying of one who said, "Let us return to our former religion," and the saying of one who fled. There is no doubt that his saying is suitable to his action, even if only to a slight degree, and to other sayings that that situation required.

The Seven Readers and the majority of people read "qawlahum" (their saying) with the accusative (naṣb), so that the noun is what follows "illa" (except). A group of readers read "qawluhum" with the nominative (raf'), and they made the predicate what follows "illa." Ḥammād ibn Salama transmitted this from Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The seeking of forgiveness by these praised people in this situation inclines towards the view that they saw the calamities of this world that befell them as caused only by sins of the human beings, just as the story of Uhud befell them because of the disobedience of those who disobeyed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿our sins and our excesses in our affair﴾ are two expressions for a meaning close to one another. This was done for emphasis and to make known the various paths of sins, and Ibn 'Abbas and others explained it in this way. Al-Dahhak said: "The sins" is general, while "excess in the affair" is intended specifically as the major sins.

His saying: ﴿and make firm our feet﴾ may be understood along with what precedes it in the sense of seeking forgiveness, so the meaning would be: make us persistent in Your obedience and in belief in You; and the firmness of the foot in this sense is a metaphor. It may also be understood in the sense of what follows it, His saying: ﴿and give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾, so that the firmness of the feet is intended literally in the positions of battle. Ibn Furak said: In this supplication there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, for their saying that Allah does not create the actions of the servant; and if that were so, it would not be proper to ask for something that He does not do.

The phrase "thawab al-dunya" (the reward of this world) in this verse means: victory over their enemy; this was said by Ibn Ishaq, Qatada and others. Ibn Jurayj said: victory and booty. A group of compilers of tafsir explained it this way. Al-Naqqash said: it is nothing but victory and dominance only, because booty was not made lawful except for this nation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This objection is sound.

As for ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, it is Paradise without any disagreement; and He expressed it with the word "husn" (good) as an addition in encouragement. The rest of the verse is clear.

[p-384]

The Almighty's words:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will turn about as losers.﴾ ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.﴾ ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved because they associated with Allah that for which He had sent down no authority. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers.﴾

By His words "those who disbelieved" is meant the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) who made the Muslims fearful and said, concerning the affair of Uhud: "If Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been defeated," and those who said: "Muhammad has been killed, so let us return to our former religion," and similar statements. Then the wording applies to every disbeliever who existed at that time and will exist until the Day of Resurrection. Allah forbade the believers from obeying them. "Rather" (bal) marks a departure from the first statement and a move to another.

Most of the people read "Bal Allahu mawlakum" (Rather, Allah is your Protector) as an inchoative (mubtada', subject) and predicate (khabar), and this is an affirmation. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "bal Allaha" with a fatha, meaning: "Rather, obey Allah."

His statement, "sanulqi" (We will cast), is a metaphor (isti'ara), since the true sense of casting belongs to physical bodies. This is like His statement: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. Similar to it is the statement of al-Farazdaq:

They both spat into my mouth from their two mouths,
upon the barking, howling dog, with the severest of stones.

Most of the people read "sanulqi" with the first-person plural "nun" of majesty. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "sayulqi" with a ya', meaning "He." Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-ru'ub" with a damma on the 'ayn wherever it occurs, while the rest read "al-ru'b" with a sukun on the 'ayn. This is like their saying "unuq" and "unq," both of which are good and eloquent.

The cause of this verse: when Abu Sufyan withdrew with the disbelievers, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and said: "Look at the people. If they have left the horses and mounted the camels, then they are hastening toward Makkah; but if they are on horses, then they are intending to go to Madinah." 'Ali went and saw that they had left the horses, so he informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was pleased, and the Muslims were pleased. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to Madinah, prepared himself, and followed the polytheists, showing them his strength. He reached Hamra' al-Asad. Abu Sufyan said to him, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "When we have killed them and defeated them, and nothing remains but the remnant and the fugitives, shall we turn away from them? Return with us to them, so that we may wipe them out." They resolved upon this. Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i had come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while still upon his disbelief, except that the whole of Khuza'a was inclined toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to him: "By Allah, O Muhammad, what has befallen you has grieved us; we would have liked you not to have been afflicted in your companions." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people heard what Quraysh had resolved upon of returning, it weighed heavily upon them. So Allah subjected that man, Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad, to this, and by means of him cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. When he heard the news he rode out until he caught up with Abu Sufyan at al-Rawha', while Quraysh had resolved upon returning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. When Abu Sufyan saw Ma'bad, he said: "What is behind you, O Ma'bad?" He said: "Muhammad has gone out with his companions seeking you, in a host the like of which I have never seen before, burning with rage against you. Those who had stayed behind from him have joined him, and they regret what they did." He said: "Woe to you, what are you saying?" He said: "By Allah, I do not think you should depart until you see the forelocks of the horses." He said: "By Allah, we had resolved to return against them to wipe out what remains of them." He said: "Then I forbid you from that. By Allah, what I saw has moved me to compose a poem about it." He said: "And what did you say?" He said, "I said":

My mount nearly broke from the clamor,
when the earth was flowing with the dark-coloured, cloud-like horses.

Riding with noble lions, not weak-footed ones,
nor cowardly, weak-hearted men, at the meeting.

So I went on, thinking the earth was tilting,
when they rose up with a leader who is not forsaken.

…to the end of the poem. Then terror fell into the hearts of the disbelievers. Safwan ibn Umayya said: "Do not return, for I see that there will be a battle for the people other than the one that was." So this verse was revealed concerning this casting of terror. It still encompasses every disbeliever, and along with it goes the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "I have been supported with terror over a distance of a month's march." It appears that this excellence was made known to him (peace be upon him) after all these circumstances, when the shade of Islam had extended.

Some scholars of knowledge have said: When Allah commanded the believer to be patient, and promised him victory, and informed him that terror is cast into the hearts of the disbelievers, the terror was diminished in each disbeliever by a portion, together with an increase in the courage of the believer, since he had been promised victory. For this reason the believer was charged with standing firm against the disbelievers.

His statement, "bima ashraku" (because they associated), here the "ba'" is the ba' of cause. The meaning is that the one who associates partners with Allah has a divided self in this world, and has no trust in Allah, the Exalted. So he hates death and feels terror of it. "Sultan" means proof and evidence. Then the Exalted informed of the end of the disbelievers in the Hereafter. "Ma'wa" (refuge) is a noun of place from awaytu ila al-makan, when you enter it and dwell in it. "Mathwa" is from thawaytu. The implied reading is: "and wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers, it."
