His statement, "sanulqi" (We will cast), is a metaphor (isti'ara), since the true sense of casting belongs to physical bodies. This is like His statement: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. Similar to it is the statement of al-Farazdaq:

They both spat into my mouth from their two mouths,
upon the barking, howling dog, with the severest of stones.

Most of the people read "sanulqi" with the first-person plural "nun" of majesty. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "sayulqi" with a ya', meaning "He." Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-ru'ub" with a damma on the 'ayn wherever it occurs, while the rest read "al-ru'b" with a sukun on the 'ayn. This is like their saying "unuq" and "unq," both of which are good and eloquent.

The cause of this verse: when Abu Sufyan withdrew with the disbelievers, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and said: "Look at the people. If they have left the horses and mounted the camels, then they are hastening toward Makkah; but if they are on horses, then they are intending to go to Madinah." 'Ali went and saw that they had left the horses, so he informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was pleased, and the Muslims were pleased. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to Madinah, prepared himself, and followed the polytheists, showing them his strength. He reached Hamra' al-Asad. Abu Sufyan said to him, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "When we have killed them and defeated them, and nothing remains but the remnant and the fugitives, shall we turn away from them? Return with us to them, so that we may wipe them out." They resolved upon this. Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i had come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while still upon his disbelief, except that the whole of Khuza'a was inclined toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to him: "By Allah, O Muhammad, what has befallen you has grieved us; we would have liked you not to have been afflicted in your companions." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people heard what Quraysh had resolved upon of returning, it weighed heavily upon them. So Allah subjected that man, Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad, to this, and by means of him cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. When he heard the news he rode out until he caught up with Abu Sufyan at al-Rawha', while Quraysh had resolved upon returning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions. When Abu Sufyan saw Ma'bad, he said: "What is behind you, O Ma'bad?" He said: "Muhammad has gone out with his companions seeking you, in a host the like of which I have never seen before, burning with rage against you. Those who had stayed behind from him have joined him, and they regret what they did." He said: "Woe to you, what are you saying?" He said: "By Allah, I do not think you should depart until you see the forelocks of the horses." He said: "By Allah, we had resolved to return against them to wipe out what remains of them." He said: "Then I forbid you from that. By Allah, what I saw has moved me to compose a poem about it." He said: "And what did you say?" He said, "I said":

My mount nearly broke from the clamor,
when the earth was flowing with the dark-coloured, cloud-like horses.

Riding with noble lions, not weak-footed ones,
nor cowardly, weak-hearted men, at the meeting.

So I went on, thinking the earth was tilting,
when they rose up with a leader who is not forsaken.

…to the end of the poem. Then terror fell into the hearts of the disbelievers. Safwan ibn Umayya said: "Do not return, for I see that there will be a battle for the people other than the one that was." So this verse was revealed concerning this casting of terror. It still encompasses every disbeliever, and along with it goes the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "I have been supported with terror over a distance of a month's march." It appears that this excellence was made known to him (peace be upon him) after all these circumstances, when the shade of Islam had extended.

Some scholars of knowledge have said: When Allah commanded the believer to be patient, and promised him victory, and informed him that terror is cast into the hearts of the disbelievers, the terror was diminished in each disbeliever by a portion, together with an increase in the courage of the believer, since he had been promised victory. For this reason the believer was charged with standing firm against the disbelievers.

His statement, "bima ashraku" (because they associated), here the "ba'" is the ba' of cause. The meaning is that the one who associates partners with Allah has a divided self in this world, and has no trust in Allah, the Exalted. So he hates death and feels terror of it. "Sultan" means proof and evidence. Then the Exalted informed of the end of the disbelievers in the Hereafter. "Ma'wa" (refuge) is a noun of place from awaytu ila al-makan, when you enter it and dwell in it. "Mathwa" is from thawaytu. The implied reading is: "and wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers, it."

[p. 386] The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were slaying them by His permission, until when you lost heart, disputed about the matter, and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you were those who desired the world, and among you were those who desired the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them in order to test you. Yet He has pardoned you, and Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾.

In these verses the address is made with the plural pronoun for the believers, although the matters for which Allah the Exalted reproached them were not committed by all of them. There are aspects of eloquence (fasaha) in this. Among them is admonishing and rebuking everyone, for whoever did not do it is liable to do it if he is not rebuked. Among them is concealing and sparing the one who did it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had promised the believers victory on that day, based on the report of Allah the Exalted that they would prevail if they were patient and striving. So Allah fulfilled the promise first. This was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lined up the Muslims that day and arranged the archers, as we have mentioned at the beginning of the commentary on these verses in the account of Uhud. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib then fought Abu Sa'd ibn Abi Talha, who was the standard-bearer of the polytheists. Al-Zubayr and Abu Dujana charged and routed the army of the polytheists. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) advanced with the people, Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and 'Asim ibn Abi al-Aqlah distinguished themselves, the polytheists were defeated, and twenty-two men of them were killed. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿when you were slaying them by His permission﴾. Al-hass (الحَسّ) is a devastating killing. It is said: ḥassahum (حَسَّهم) when he wiped them out by killing, and ḥassa al-bard al-nabat (حَسَّ البَرْدُ النَباتَ) when the cold destroyed the vegetation. Ru'ba said:

"When we complain of a year of blight that consumes the green after it has become dry stalk."

Some people said: it is derived from al-hasa (الحاسَّة, the senses), and the meaning of ḥassa is that it corrupted the senses.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. And al-idhn (الإذْن) is enabling together with knowledge of the one enabled.

His words: ﴿until when you lost heart﴾. It is possible that "until" (ḥattā, حتّى) is a plain limit, as if he said: "up to the point that you lost heart." [p. 387] This is strengthened by the fact that "when" (idhā, إذا) has the sense of "when" (idh, إذْ), because the matter had already passed and this is only a narration of a state. On this reading, "idhā" needs no response. However, the more apparent and stronger view is that "idhā" retains its own function and requires a response, and "ḥattā" is then like a particle of inception, in the manner of its entering upon sentences.

The grammarians differed concerning the response of "idhā". One group held that the response is His words "disputed," with the waw being superfluous. Al-Mahdawi reported from Abu 'Ali that he said: the response is His words "turned you away," and "thumma" (ثُمَّ) is superfluous.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view does not resemble the reasoning of Abu 'Ali. The position of Sibawayh, al-Khalil and the masters of the craft (furs an-sina'a, فُرْسانِ الصِناعَةِ, i.e. the leading grammarians) is that the response is omitted and implied, which the meaning indicates. Its estimate is: "you were routed" or something similar. Al-fashal (الفَشَلُ) is feeling incapable and abandoning earnestness, and this is something a group did that day. Al-tanazu' (التَنازُعُ) is what occurred among the archers: some of them said, "The spoils, the spoils! Join us with the Muslims!" and others said, "Rather, we will hold firm as we were commanded." And "you disobeyed" (عَصَيْتُمْ) is an expression for the departure of those archers who left, until Khalid ibn al-Walid was able to take advantage of the heedlessness of the Muslims.

His words: ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾ mean the defeat of the enemy people. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: "By Allah, I saw myself looking at the servants of Hind bint 'Utba and her companions, girded up and fleeing, with nothing to stop them from taking anything, little or much, when the archers turned toward the army once we had cleared the enemy from it, wanting the plunder, and left our backs exposed to the cavalry. We were attacked from behind. A crier shouted, 'Behold, Muhammad has been killed!' So we turned back, and the enemy turned back upon us."

His words: ﴿Among you were those who desired the world﴾ are a report about those who were eager for booty and whose concern was wealth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the exegetes. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "I did not think that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) desired the world until this was revealed about us on the day of Uhud: ﴿Among you were those who desired the world﴾."

[p. 388] His words: ﴿and among you were those who desired the Hereafter﴾ are a report about the steadfastness of those archers who remained firm with 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, obeying the command, until they were killed. This includes Anas ibn al-Nadr and everyone among the believers who strove earnestly and did not waver.

His words: "in order to test you" mean: to bring upon you that trial of killing and purification (tamhis, التَمْحِيصِ).

His words: ﴿Yet He has pardoned you﴾ inform that the sin deserved more than what befell them. This is a warning. The meaning is: He pardoned you by not wiping you out. It is therefore like saying: "He spared you." It is also possible that it is a report that He pardoned their sins in the account of Uhud, so that it would be the pardon mentioned afterward. The first interpretation was held by Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Ishaq and a group of exegetes. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Seventy of them were killed, the uncle of the Prophet, peace be upon him, was killed, his face was wounded, and his front tooth was broken. The pardon was only that He did not wipe them out. These were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the way of Allah, angry for the sake of Allah, fighting the enemies of Allah. They were forbidden from something and they neglected it. By Allah, they were not abandoned until they were grieved with this grief. So the most profligate of sinners today commits every major sin, plunges into every calamity, drags his garments over it, and claims that there is no harm upon him. He will surely come to know."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 153–154 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted and Majestic said:
﴿When you were climbing [the slope] and not turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you, so He rewarded you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you nor over what had befallen you. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after the grief, security in the form of drowsiness overcoming a group of you, while another group was concerned only with themselves.﴾

The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" is His saying: "'afa" (He pardoned).

The majority of reciters read: "tus'idun" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the 'ayn, from aş'ada, and its meaning is: he went into the low ground (al-ard). In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "idh tus'idun fi al-wadi" (when you were going up into the valley).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, and Su'da is one of the names of the earth. So aş'ada means: he entered al-sa'id, just as aş­baha means he entered the morning (al-sabah), and so on. The Arabs say: "We ascended (aş'adna) from Makkah and elsewhere," when they set out on a long journey. Abu 'Ubayda cited for a camel-driver:
﴿...﴾ You used to weep over the departure; now you have made it clear, and the driver has cried out.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Yazidi, Mujahid and Qatada read: "idh ta'sadun" with a fathah on the ta' and the 'ayn, from sa'ida, meaning: to ascend, to climb. The meaning here is the ascent of one who climbs a mountain. The first reading is more common.

His saying, exalted is He: "wa la talwuna" is an exaggeration in describing the rout. It is as Duraid said: "Does anything turn back one who has been routed?" This is stronger than the words of Imru' al-Qays:
﴿...﴾ The one exhausted by effort does not turn back for one who has been left behind.

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, read: "idh yas'adun wa la yalwuna" with the ya' in both, referring to the third person. Some reciters read: "wa la talu'una" with a hamza on the damma'd waw, and this is a dialect. Some read: "wa la talunna" with a damma on the lam and one waw, which is a reading formed on the dialect of hamzating the damma'd waw; then the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lam and one of the two quiescent waws was deleted. Al-A'mash and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read: "tulwuna" with a damma on the ta', from alwa, and this is a dialect. Humayd ibn Qays read: "'ala uhudin" with a damma on the alif and the ha', meaning the mountain. The well-known reading is stronger, because the Prophet ﷺ was not on the mountain except after the people had fled from him, and this state of their ascent was while he was calling them. It is narrated that he was calling out: "Come to me, servants of Allah," while the people were fleeing.

In His saying, exalted is He: "fi ukhrakum" there is praise for the Prophet, peace be upon him, for that is the position of heroes at the rear of the people. From it is the saying of al-Zubayr ibn Batta: "What became of our vanguard when we charged, and our rearguard when we fled?" Likewise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most courageous of people. From it is the saying of Salama ibn al-Akwa': "When the battle grew fierce, we would shelter ourselves behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

His saying, exalted is He: "fa-athabakum" means: He recompensed you for your conduct. Grief was called a reward in the sense that it stood in this event in the place of reward, like His saying:
﴿...﴾ Their greeting among them is a painful blow.
And like the saying of another:
I fear that Ziyad's gift will be shackles, black ones, or thick-spun cords of the smooth-dark kind.
So he made the fetters and whips a gift; and "muhdarajah" means "mudahrajah" (rolled).

The people differed concerning the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "ghaman bi-ghamm." Some said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief because of the grief that you caused the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and all the believers, through your cowardice, your disputing and your disobedience.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
So the ba' here is the ba' of causation.

Others said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief for the grief that befell you at the hands of the disbelievers on the Day of Badr.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
So the ba' here is the ba' of equivalence, as Abu Sufyan said: "A day for a day of Badr, and war is in turns."

A large group of the commentators said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief upon grief, or grief along with grief, and this is the bare ba' of the genitive.

They differed concerning the order of these two griefs. Qatada and Mujahid said: the first grief was when they heard: "Verily Muhammad has been killed," and the second was the killing and wounding that fell upon them. Al-Rabi' and Qatada also said the reverse of this order. Al-Suddi, Mujahid and others said: rather, the first grief was their killing, their wounding and all that happened in that narrow place, and the second grief was Abu Sufyan's looking down upon the Prophet and those with him. That is because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began that day calling the people, until he reached a group of his companions who had climbed a rock on the face of the mountain. He walked toward them, and a man aimed an arrow at him to shoot it, so he said: "I am the Messenger of Allah." They rejoiced at that, and he, peace be upon him, rejoiced when he saw his companions refraining. Then they began to grieve over what they had missed of victory and over those of their companions who had died. While they were in that state, Abu Sufyan looked down upon them from a height with many horses, so they forgot what had befallen them earlier, and the matter of Abu Sufyan concerned them. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "They shall not get the upper hand over us. O Allah, if this band is killed, You will not be worshipped." Then he urged his companions, and they pelted them with stones, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was of great help until they brought them down.

The reports concerning this episode of the defeat at Uhud differ greatly, because the matter was terrifying, and everyone described what he saw and heard. Ka'b ibn Malik said: "The first to recognise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was I; I saw his eyes shining beneath the helmet." It is also reported that the horsemen who were higher up were only the charge of Khalid ibn al-Walid, and that Abu Sufyan only approached while the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was at the summit of the mountain. Abu Sufyan has many statements regarding that position, and 'Umar had a well-preserved exchange with him, which I have abridged since it does not pertain to the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: "li-kay la tahzanu 'ala ma fatakum" means: of the spoils; "wa ma asabakum" means: of the killing, the wounding, the humiliation of the rout, and what was inflicted upon your Prophet.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The lam in "li-kayla" is connected to "athabakum." The meaning: so that you would know that what befell you was only because of your own transgression; you harmed yourselves. It is the habit of humans that the one who commits a sin endures the punishment, and the greatest anguish and grief of the one being punished is with his thinking himself innocent. In His saying, exalted is He: "wa Allahu khabirun bi-ma ta'malun" there is a warning.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the drowsiness by which He granted security to the believers, covering the people of sincerity. It is reported that when Abu Sufyan departed from the place of battle, the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali in the presence of his companions who had withdrawn to him at that hour: "Go and look at the people. If they have led the horses away, they are heading for Makkah; but if they are on their horses, they intend Madinah. Be mindful of Allah and be patient." He settled them for fighting. 'Ali went and then returned and reported that they had led the horses aside and sat upon their baggage in haste. Then the certain believers, who affirmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, were given security, and Allah cast drowsiness upon them, while the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease remained, not believing. Rather, their assumption was that Abu Sufyan would surely head for Madinah, so none of them slept; their concern was only with their worldly affairs. Abu Talha said: "I slept on that day until my sword fell from my hand several times." Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: "On the day of Uhud I raised my head from sleep and began looking at the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and there was not one of them but was swaying beneath his shield." Ibn Mas'ud said: "We dozed on the day of Uhud, and drowsiness in battle is security from Allah, while drowsiness in prayer is from Satan."

The majority of reciters read "amanatan" with a fathah on the mim; Ibn Muhaysin and al-Nakha'i read "amnatan" with a sukun on the mim. Both have the meaning of security (al-amn), and the fathah on the mim is more eloquent. His saying "nu'asan" is a substitution (badal). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "yaghsha" with the ya', taking account of the wording of "nu'as" with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the substituted term. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "taghsha" with the ta', taking account of the wording of "amanah" with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the term substituted for.

The waw in His saying, exalted is He: "wa ta'ifatun qad ahammatbum" is the waw of circumstance (wa al-hal), as you say: "I came while Zayd was standing." So said Sibawayh and others. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that the predicate of "wa ta'ifatun" be His saying "yazunnuna," and "qad ahammathum" be a qualifying clause for the group.

His saying, exalted is He: "qad ahammathum anfusuhum" — most of the exegetes, Qatada, al-Rabi', Ibn Ishaq and others, held that the term is from al-hamm, meaning grief and sorrow. The meaning: their sick souls and evil assumptions had brought them concern, fear of being killed and the loss of their wealth. The Arabs say: "The matter worried me (ahammani)" when it brought concern. Some exegetes mentioned that the term is from your saying: "hamma bi-al-shay'," meaning he intended to do it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The meaning: their own souls made them intend to disclose their disbelief and to cast off the religion. This is the view of the one who said: "Muhammad has been killed, so let us return to our former religion," and the like of these sayings.

**

His saying, exalted is He: "yazunnuna bi-Allahi ghayra al-haqq zanna al-jahiliyyah, yaqulina hal lana min al-amri min shay'? Qul inna al-amra kullahu lillah. Yukhfuna fi anfusihim ma la yubduna laka. Yaqulina law kana lana min al-amri shay' ma qutilna ha huna. Qul law kuntum fi buyutikum labaraza alladhina kutiba 'alayhim al-qatlu ila madaji'ihim, wa liyabtaliya Allahu ma fi sudurikum wa liyumahhisa ma fi qulubikum, wa Allahu 'alimun bi-dhat al-sudur."

His saying, exalted is He: "ghayra al-haqq" means: they assumed that Islam is not true, and that the affair of Muhammad, peace be upon him, would vanish and perish. As for His saying: "zanna al-jahiliyyah": the majority of people held that it refers to the ancient period of ignorance before Islam, as in "hamiyyat al-jahiliyyah" and "tabarruj al-jahiliyyah," and as you say "poetry of the jahiliyyah," and as Ibn 'Abbas said: "I heard my father in the jahiliyyah saying: give us a brimming cup." Some exegetes held that what is meant in this verse is the assumption of the ignorant faction, referring to Abu Sufyan and those with him. The matter is open to this, and Qatada and al-Tabari took this path.

His saying, exalted is He: "yaqulina hal lana min al-amri min shay'" is a quotation of words they said. Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: it was said to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "The Banu al-Khazraj have been killed." He said: "Is there any say for us in the matter?" meaning that the decision is not ours; had we any say in it, we would have been consulted and would not have gone out, and none of us would have been killed. This statement of theirs bears two meanings, and their words may imply disbelief and hypocrisy, in the sense: we have no share in the command of Allah, and we are not upon the truth in following Muhammad. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and Ibn Furak. However, what weakens this is that the reply to them came on the basis that their words meant bad opinion about going out, and that had he not gone out, no one would have been killed.

His saying, exalted is He: "qul inna al-amra kullahu lillah" is an eloquent interjection within the speech.

The majority of reciters read "kullahu" with a fathah, for emphasis of the matter, since "kullahu" means "ajma'" (entirely). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read "kullu-hu lillah" with a damma on "kull," as a subject and predicate. The people preferred the reading of the majority because the emphatic is more deserving of the word "kull."

His saying, exalted is He: "yukhfuna fi anfusihim ma la yubduna laka" may be understood as information about their concealment of such statements, which are not pure disbelief but ignorance; and it may be understood as information about what they conceal of disbelief, which they cannot show beyond these outbursts. Allah, exalted is He, spoke of them in general without specification, and this was His practice regarding the hypocrites. There is no god but He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 153–154 (part 2 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿They say, "If we had any part in the affair, we would not have been killed here."﴾ This is a statement that was heard from Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, who was marked with hypocrisy (nifaq).

Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said, as al-Tabari transmitted from him: "By Allah, it is as if I hear the words of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, brother of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, while drowsiness was overtaking me. I only heard it as in a dream, when he said: 'If we had any part in the affair, we would not have been killed here.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The words of Mu'attib may carry the same meanings that the words of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy carried. This Mu'attib was among those who witnessed Badr; Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned this. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said that he witnessed 'Aqaba, but that is a mistake, and the correct view is that he did not witness 'Aqaba.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: "Even if you had been in your houses, those destined to be killed would have gone forth to their places of death."﴾ ... The verse is a refutation of these statements and an announcement that the term (ajal) of every person is singular, so whoever is not killed will die at that term in the manner Allah the Exalted has decreed, and when someone is killed, that is what was in the eternal foreknowledge.

Most of the reciters read "فِي بُيُوتِكُمْ" with a damma on the ba' (bi-buyutikum). Some reciters, and it is among the paths of the Seven Readings, read "فِي بِيُوتِكُمْ" with a kasra on the ba' (bi-buyutikum). Most of the reciters read "لَبَرَزَ" with a fatha on the ra' and the ba' (labaraza), meaning: they would have gone out into the open country (al-baraz) of the earth. Abu Haywa read "بُرِّزَ" with a damma on the ba', a kasra on the ra' and a shadda on it (burriza). Most of the reciters read "عَلَيْهِمُ القَتْلُ" (ʿalayhimu l-qatl), meaning: it was written upon them in Allah's decree and His measuring. Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "عَلَيْهِمُ القِتالُ" (ʿalayhimu l-qital), "the fighting." This reading may carry the sense of being independent of the hypocrites, i.e., even if you had stayed behind, the believers who are certain and obedient would have gone forth to the fighting that was written for them.

Allah's words: ﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts.﴾ ... The verse: the lam in Allah's words "wa-liyabtaliya" (and that He might test) is connected to a later verb, whose implied sense is: and so that He might test and purify, He did these events that occurred. Here "ibtila'" (testing) means examination (ikhtibar), and "tamhis" (purification) means separating a thing from other things. The meaning is: that He might examine it, thereby making Him know it with a knowledge coexistent with its existence, though it had been firmly established before the existence of the test, from eternity. And "dhat al-sudur" (what is in the breasts) is what the breasts contain of beliefs. This is what is meant in this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 153–154 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted and Majestic said:
﴿When you were climbing [the slope] and not turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you, so He rewarded you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you nor over what had befallen you. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after the grief, security in the form of drowsiness overcoming a group of you, while another group was concerned only with themselves.﴾

The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" is His saying: "'afa" (He pardoned).

The majority of reciters read: "tus'idun" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the 'ayn, from aş'ada, and its meaning is: he went into the low ground (al-ard). In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "idh tus'idun fi al-wadi" (when you were going up into the valley).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, and Su'da is one of the names of the earth. So aş'ada means: he entered al-sa'id, just as aş­baha means he entered the morning (al-sabah), and so on. The Arabs say: "We ascended (aş'adna) from Makkah and elsewhere," when they set out on a long journey. Abu 'Ubayda cited for a camel-driver:
﴿...﴾ You used to weep over the departure; now you have made it clear, and the driver has cried out.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Yazidi, Mujahid and Qatada read: "idh ta'sadun" with a fathah on the ta' and the 'ayn, from sa'ida, meaning: to ascend, to climb. The meaning here is the ascent of one who climbs a mountain. The first reading is more common.

His saying, exalted is He: "wa la talwuna" is an exaggeration in describing the rout. It is as Duraid said: "Does anything turn back one who has been routed?" This is stronger than the words of Imru' al-Qays:
﴿...﴾ The one exhausted by effort does not turn back for one who has been left behind.

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, read: "idh yas'adun wa la yalwuna" with the ya' in both, referring to the third person. Some reciters read: "wa la talu'una" with a hamza on the damma'd waw, and this is a dialect. Some read: "wa la talunna" with a damma on the lam and one waw, which is a reading formed on the dialect of hamzating the damma'd waw; then the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lam and one of the two quiescent waws was deleted. Al-A'mash and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read: "tulwuna" with a damma on the ta', from alwa, and this is a dialect. Humayd ibn Qays read: "'ala uhudin" with a damma on the alif and the ha', meaning the mountain. The well-known reading is stronger, because the Prophet ﷺ was not on the mountain except after the people had fled from him, and this state of their ascent was while he was calling them. It is narrated that he was calling out: "Come to me, servants of Allah," while the people were fleeing.

In His saying, exalted is He: "fi ukhrakum" there is praise for the Prophet, peace be upon him, for that is the position of heroes at the rear of the people. From it is the saying of al-Zubayr ibn Batta: "What became of our vanguard when we charged, and our rearguard when we fled?" Likewise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most courageous of people. From it is the saying of Salama ibn al-Akwa': "When the battle grew fierce, we would shelter ourselves behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

His saying, exalted is He: "fa-athabakum" means: He recompensed you for your conduct. Grief was called a reward in the sense that it stood in this event in the place of reward, like His saying:
﴿...﴾ Their greeting among them is a painful blow.
And like the saying of another:
I fear that Ziyad's gift will be shackles, black ones, or thick-spun cords of the smooth-dark kind.
So he made the fetters and whips a gift; and "muhdarajah" means "mudahrajah" (rolled).

The people differed concerning the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "ghaman bi-ghamm." Some said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief because of the grief that you caused the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and all the believers, through your cowardice, your disputing and your disobedience.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
So the ba' here is the ba' of causation.

Others said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief for the grief that befell you at the hands of the disbelievers on the Day of Badr.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
So the ba' here is the ba' of equivalence, as Abu Sufyan said: "A day for a day of Badr, and war is in turns."

A large group of the commentators said: the meaning is: He rewarded you with grief upon grief, or grief along with grief, and this is the bare ba' of the genitive.

They differed concerning the order of these two griefs. Qatada and Mujahid said: the first grief was when they heard: "Verily Muhammad has been killed," and the second was the killing and wounding that fell upon them. Al-Rabi' and Qatada also said the reverse of this order. Al-Suddi, Mujahid and others said: rather, the first grief was their killing, their wounding and all that happened in that narrow place, and the second grief was Abu Sufyan's looking down upon the Prophet and those with him. That is because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began that day calling the people, until he reached a group of his companions who had climbed a rock on the face of the mountain. He walked toward them, and a man aimed an arrow at him to shoot it, so he said: "I am the Messenger of Allah." They rejoiced at that, and he, peace be upon him, rejoiced when he saw his companions refraining. Then they began to grieve over what they had missed of victory and over those of their companions who had died. While they were in that state, Abu Sufyan looked down upon them from a height with many horses, so they forgot what had befallen them earlier, and the matter of Abu Sufyan concerned them. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "They shall not get the upper hand over us. O Allah, if this band is killed, You will not be worshipped." Then he urged his companions, and they pelted them with stones, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was of great help until they brought them down.

The reports concerning this episode of the defeat at Uhud differ greatly, because the matter was terrifying, and everyone described what he saw and heard. Ka'b ibn Malik said: "The first to recognise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was I; I saw his eyes shining beneath the helmet." It is also reported that the horsemen who were higher up were only the charge of Khalid ibn al-Walid, and that Abu Sufyan only approached while the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was at the summit of the mountain. Abu Sufyan has many statements regarding that position, and 'Umar had a well-preserved exchange with him, which I have abridged since it does not pertain to the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: "li-kay la tahzanu 'ala ma fatakum" means: of the spoils; "wa ma asabakum" means: of the killing, the wounding, the humiliation of the rout, and what was inflicted upon your Prophet.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The lam in "li-kayla" is connected to "athabakum." The meaning: so that you would know that what befell you was only because of your own transgression; you harmed yourselves. It is the habit of humans that the one who commits a sin endures the punishment, and the greatest anguish and grief of the one being punished is with his thinking himself innocent. In His saying, exalted is He: "wa Allahu khabirun bi-ma ta'malun" there is a warning.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the drowsiness by which He granted security to the believers, covering the people of sincerity. It is reported that when Abu Sufyan departed from the place of battle, the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali in the presence of his companions who had withdrawn to him at that hour: "Go and look at the people. If they have led the horses away, they are heading for Makkah; but if they are on their horses, they intend Madinah. Be mindful of Allah and be patient." He settled them for fighting. 'Ali went and then returned and reported that they had led the horses aside and sat upon their baggage in haste. Then the certain believers, who affirmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, were given security, and Allah cast drowsiness upon them, while the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease remained, not believing. Rather, their assumption was that Abu Sufyan would surely head for Madinah, so none of them slept; their concern was only with their worldly affairs. Abu Talha said: "I slept on that day until my sword fell from my hand several times." Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: "On the day of Uhud I raised my head from sleep and began looking at the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and there was not one of them but was swaying beneath his shield." Ibn Mas'ud said: "We dozed on the day of Uhud, and drowsiness in battle is security from Allah, while drowsiness in prayer is from Satan."

The majority of reciters read "amanatan" with a fathah on the mim; Ibn Muhaysin and al-Nakha'i read "amnatan" with a sukun on the mim. Both have the meaning of security (al-amn), and the fathah on the mim is more eloquent. His saying "nu'asan" is a substitution (badal). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "yaghsha" with the ya', taking account of the wording of "nu'as" with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the substituted term. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "taghsha" with the ta', taking account of the wording of "amanah" with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the term substituted for.

The waw in His saying, exalted is He: "wa ta'ifatun qad ahammatbum" is the waw of circumstance (wa al-hal), as you say: "I came while Zayd was standing." So said Sibawayh and others. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that the predicate of "wa ta'ifatun" be His saying "yazunnuna," and "qad ahammathum" be a qualifying clause for the group.

His saying, exalted is He: "qad ahammathum anfusuhum" — most of the exegetes, Qatada, al-Rabi', Ibn Ishaq and others, held that the term is from al-hamm, meaning grief and sorrow. The meaning: their sick souls and evil assumptions had brought them concern, fear of being killed and the loss of their wealth. The Arabs say: "The matter worried me (ahammani)" when it brought concern. Some exegetes mentioned that the term is from your saying: "hamma bi-al-shay'," meaning he intended to do it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The meaning: their own souls made them intend to disclose their disbelief and to cast off the religion. This is the view of the one who said: "Muhammad has been killed, so let us return to our former religion," and the like of these sayings.

**

His saying, exalted is He: "yazunnuna bi-Allahi ghayra al-haqq zanna al-jahiliyyah, yaqulina hal lana min al-amri min shay'? Qul inna al-amra kullahu lillah. Yukhfuna fi anfusihim ma la yubduna laka. Yaqulina law kana lana min al-amri shay' ma qutilna ha huna. Qul law kuntum fi buyutikum labaraza alladhina kutiba 'alayhim al-qatlu ila madaji'ihim, wa liyabtaliya Allahu ma fi sudurikum wa liyumahhisa ma fi qulubikum, wa Allahu 'alimun bi-dhat al-sudur."

His saying, exalted is He: "ghayra al-haqq" means: they assumed that Islam is not true, and that the affair of Muhammad, peace be upon him, would vanish and perish. As for His saying: "zanna al-jahiliyyah": the majority of people held that it refers to the ancient period of ignorance before Islam, as in "hamiyyat al-jahiliyyah" and "tabarruj al-jahiliyyah," and as you say "poetry of the jahiliyyah," and as Ibn 'Abbas said: "I heard my father in the jahiliyyah saying: give us a brimming cup." Some exegetes held that what is meant in this verse is the assumption of the ignorant faction, referring to Abu Sufyan and those with him. The matter is open to this, and Qatada and al-Tabari took this path.

His saying, exalted is He: "yaqulina hal lana min al-amri min shay'" is a quotation of words they said. Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: it was said to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "The Banu al-Khazraj have been killed." He said: "Is there any say for us in the matter?" meaning that the decision is not ours; had we any say in it, we would have been consulted and would not have gone out, and none of us would have been killed. This statement of theirs bears two meanings, and their words may imply disbelief and hypocrisy, in the sense: we have no share in the command of Allah, and we are not upon the truth in following Muhammad. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and Ibn Furak. However, what weakens this is that the reply to them came on the basis that their words meant bad opinion about going out, and that had he not gone out, no one would have been killed.

His saying, exalted is He: "qul inna al-amra kullahu lillah" is an eloquent interjection within the speech.

The majority of reciters read "kullahu" with a fathah, for emphasis of the matter, since "kullahu" means "ajma'" (entirely). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read "kullu-hu lillah" with a damma on "kull," as a subject and predicate. The people preferred the reading of the majority because the emphatic is more deserving of the word "kull."

His saying, exalted is He: "yukhfuna fi anfusihim ma la yubduna laka" may be understood as information about their concealment of such statements, which are not pure disbelief but ignorance; and it may be understood as information about what they conceal of disbelief, which they cannot show beyond these outbursts. Allah, exalted is He, spoke of them in general without specification, and this was His practice regarding the hypocrites. There is no god but He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 153–154 (part 2 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿They say, "If we had any part in the affair, we would not have been killed here."﴾ This is a statement that was heard from Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, who was marked with hypocrisy (nifaq).

Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said, as al-Tabari transmitted from him: "By Allah, it is as if I hear the words of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, brother of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, while drowsiness was overtaking me. I only heard it as in a dream, when he said: 'If we had any part in the affair, we would not have been killed here.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The words of Mu'attib may carry the same meanings that the words of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy carried. This Mu'attib was among those who witnessed Badr; Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned this. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said that he witnessed 'Aqaba, but that is a mistake, and the correct view is that he did not witness 'Aqaba.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: "Even if you had been in your houses, those destined to be killed would have gone forth to their places of death."﴾ ... The verse is a refutation of these statements and an announcement that the term (ajal) of every person is singular, so whoever is not killed will die at that term in the manner Allah the Exalted has decreed, and when someone is killed, that is what was in the eternal foreknowledge.

Most of the reciters read "فِي بُيُوتِكُمْ" with a damma on the ba' (bi-buyutikum). Some reciters, and it is among the paths of the Seven Readings, read "فِي بِيُوتِكُمْ" with a kasra on the ba' (bi-buyutikum). Most of the reciters read "لَبَرَزَ" with a fatha on the ra' and the ba' (labaraza), meaning: they would have gone out into the open country (al-baraz) of the earth. Abu Haywa read "بُرِّزَ" with a damma on the ba', a kasra on the ra' and a shadda on it (burriza). Most of the reciters read "عَلَيْهِمُ القَتْلُ" (ʿalayhimu l-qatl), meaning: it was written upon them in Allah's decree and His measuring. Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "عَلَيْهِمُ القِتالُ" (ʿalayhimu l-qital), "the fighting." This reading may carry the sense of being independent of the hypocrites, i.e., even if you had stayed behind, the believers who are certain and obedient would have gone forth to the fighting that was written for them.

Allah's words: ﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts.﴾ ... The verse: the lam in Allah's words "wa-liyabtaliya" (and that He might test) is connected to a later verb, whose implied sense is: and so that He might test and purify, He did these events that occurred. Here "ibtila'" (testing) means examination (ikhtibar), and "tamhis" (purification) means separating a thing from other things. The meaning is: that He might examine it, thereby making Him know it with a knowledge coexistent with its existence, though it had been firmly established before the existence of the test, from eternity. And "dhat al-sudur" (what is in the breasts) is what the breasts contain of beliefs. This is what is meant in this verse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 155:**

The Almighty's saying:

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

The exegetes (al-mutawwilun) differed concerning who is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met﴾? 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It refers to all who turned away from the enemy on that day.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means all forms of turning away that were not a maneuver (taharruf) for the sake of fighting.

Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related with a chain of narration: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered a sermon on Friday and recited [Al 'Imran]. He used to like to recite it when he delivered a sermon. When he reached His saying, ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met﴾, he said: When the day of Uhud came, we were defeated, and I fled until I climbed the mountain. I saw myself leaping like a fox, and the people were saying, "Muhammad has been killed." I said: I will not find anyone saying "Muhammad has been killed" except that I will kill him. Then we gathered on the mountain, and this whole verse was revealed. Qatada said: This verse concerns everyone who fled, through the frightening and deception of Satan, and Allah pardoned this slip for them.

Ibn Furak said: No one remained with the Prophet that day except thirteen men: Abu Bakr, 'Ali, Talha, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and the rest were from the Ansar, including Abu Talha and others. Al-Suddi and others said: When the Muslims withdrew from the charge of the polytheists against them, some people climbed the mountain, and others fled until they reached Medina. Allah, in this verse, mentioned specifically those who fled to Medina.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He regarded fleeing to the mountain as a tahayyuz (withdrawal to a company of one's own side, a regrouping).

'Ikrima said: This verse was revealed concerning those among the believers who fled in great flight, among them Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla, Abu Hudhayfa ibn 'Utba, and another man. Ibn Ishaq said: "'Uthman ibn 'Affan fled, and 'Uqba ibn 'Uthman and his brother Sa'd, and two men from the Ansar of the Zuraiq clan, until they reached al-Ja'lab, a mountain on the side of Medina toward al-A'was, and they remained there three days. Then they returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said to them: 'You have gone off in a wide flight.'" Ibn Zayd said: I do not know whether He pardoned this group specifically or the believers all together.

(p-398) Its meaning of istazalla: he sought from them that they slip, because that is what his whispering and intimidation require. The Almighty's saying, "because of some of what they had earned," in the view of the majority of the mufassirun, apparently means that they had sins for which Allah punished them by empowering Satan to make them slip, and also by creating in them the flight they had earned. Al-Zajjaj and others held that the meaning is: Satan reminded them of earlier sins they had committed, so they disliked dying before repenting of them and giving them up. Al-Mahdawi said: "because of what they had earned" refers to their love of booty and their greed for life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording of the verse may allow that the reference in "because of some of what they had earned" is to this consideration, meaning: Satan had a role in this act which they had earned, so he is a partner in some of it.

Then the Almighty informed of His pardon for them. The majority of scholars interpreted this as the removal of consequence (hatt al-tabi'a) in this world and the Hereafter. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan interpreted it in the same way in his report with 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Adi ibn al-Khiyar, and Ibn 'Umar interpreted it in the same way in his report with the Iraqi man. Ibn Jurayj said: The meaning of the verse is: Allah pardoned them, in that He did not punish them. Fleeing from the battle line (al-zahf) is one of the major sins by consensus (ijma') as far as I know, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) counted it among the destructive sins (al-mu'biqat), together with polytheism, killing a soul, and others.

(p-399)His words, may He be exalted:

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers, when they journeyed in the land or were campaigning, "Had they stayed with us, they would not have died or been killed," so that God may make that a regret in their hearts. God gives life and causes death, and God is Seeing of what you do.﴾

God, exalted is He, forbade the believers from being like the disbelievers and hypocrites in this corrupt belief, which is that whoever travels for trade or the like, or whoever fights and is killed, would have lived and not died at that time, had he stayed at home instead of exposing himself to travel or fighting. This is the belief of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) in their saying that there are two terms (al-ajalayn, the two appointed times), and it is similar to it.

His words, "to their brothers," refer to kinship brotherhood, because the slain of Uhud were from the Ansar, most of them from the Khazraj, and there were none among them of the Muhajirun except four. This saying was voiced, as reported by al-Suddi, Mujahid and others, by Abdullah ibn Ubayy the hypocrite and his companions. It has also been said that all the hypocrites said it.

The particle "idha" (when) is used in this verse, and it is a particle of the future, because "alladhina" (those who) is a noun with generality that covers those who said it in the past and those who say it in the future. Also, this event can be imagined in future time, and the prohibition applies to the believers in it on a continuing basis. So "idha" was used to indicate the continuing character of the matter in future time. This is the purpose of putting the future in the place of the past, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], and similar verses, and as the poet said:

"And among us is a prophet who knows what tomorrow holds."

Likewise, the purpose of their putting the past in the place of the future is to indicate the affirmation of the matter, because the form of the past is certain in its occurrence. Among that is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I come to you, thanking what has passed of the matter and anticipating what will be tomorrow."

And from it is the saying of al-Rabi':

"I have become one who no longer bears a weapon, nor controls the camel's head if it bolts."

"Darb fi al-ard" means going far in travel. From it comes: "The age struck its blow" (daraba al-dahr darbanah), meaning the period became long. "Darb al-ard" is going in it for a person's need, specifically with the dropping of "fi." Al-Suddi and others said regarding this verse that "darb fi al-ard" means travelling for trade. Ibn Ishaq and others said rather that it means travelling in all acts of obedience to God and His Messenger. "Darb fi al-ard" encompasses both views.

"Ghuzza" is the plural of "ghazin" (one who campaigns). Its form is "fu“‘‘al," with a dammah on the first letter and a shaddah on the middle letter, which is fatha-ed, like "shahid" and "shuhhad," and "qa'il" and "qawwal." The verse of Ru'ba is recited:

"Now, indeed, my restraining has restrained me, and the first forbearance is not one of foolishness.
And the saying 'except the ill-tempered, then no ill-temper,'"

He means: if you do not repent now, you will never repent. This is similar in meaning to: "If you are not such, then such will not be." It has also been transmitted: "And their saying, 'except the ill-tempered, then no ill-temper.'" Sibawayh and others said: "Ghuzza" takes neither the genitive nor the nominative case.

The majority of reciters read it with a shaddah on the letter zay. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "ghuzan," with the zay unstressed. Its basis is either that they intended "ghuzat" (campaigners), and deleted the ta' marbuta, following the dialect of those who say "ghuzzan" with a shaddah. This deletion is common in their speech, and from it is the saying of a poet praising al-Kisa'i:

"The noble character of al-Kisa'i refused blame, and was affiliated with it the glory of the ancestral noble qualities."

He means "al-ubuwwa" (fatherhood), the plural of "ab" (father), just as "al-umumah" is the plural of "amm" (paternal uncle), and "al-bunuwwa" is the plural of "ibn" (son). They have also said "ibn" and "binw." Both readings may be a lightening of the zay of "ghuzzan," and a parallel to it is the reading of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "And they denied Our signs as a lie (kidhaban)," according to the view of one who said it is a lightening. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) that follows a pattern other than the regular verbal noun. Al-Hasan read "wa ma qutτilu" with a shaddah on the ta'.

His words, "so that God may make that a regret," Mujahid said: its meaning is that His saying grieves them and does not benefit them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The reference of "that" is to this belief they hold: God made that a regret, because the one who is certain that every death and every killing is by a prior appointed term finds the coolness of despair and submission to God in his heart. But the one who believes that his close one, had he stayed at home, would not have died, grieves and laments. This interpretation is the one taken by the commentators, and it is the most apparent meaning of the verse.

Some people said: the reference of "that" is to the believers' differing from the disbelievers in this belief, so their opposition to them becomes a regret in their hearts. Others said: the reference of "that" is to God's very prohibition against being like the disbelievers in this belief, because when they see that God has marked them with a belief and commanded opposition to them, that becomes a regret in their hearts. In my opinion it is possible that the reference is to both the prohibition and the refraining together, so consider this carefully. "Hasra" means regret over a thing and grief over it.

Then God, exalted is He, related a definite fact that He is the One who gives life and causes death, by a decisive decree, not as these people believe. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wallahu bima ya'malun" with the ya', which is a warning to the hypocrites. The rest read "ta'malun" with the ta', addressing the believers, which is an emphasis on the prohibition in His saying "do not be" and a warning to whoever opposes it, and a promise to whoever complies with it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 157–159:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah, or you die, forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾ ﴿And if you die or are killed, indeed to Allah you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient toward them; and if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you.﴾

The lām in His saying, exalted is He, "And if you are killed" is the lām that announces the coming of an oath, and the lām in His saying "forgiveness" is the lām that receives the oath. The estimate is: "By Allah, indeed forgiveness..."

Death is placed before killing in His saying, ﴿Whether they died or were killed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 156], in observance of the order of striking the earth and of military campaigning (ghazw). So He placed death, which corresponds to what was mentioned earlier, namely striking (ḍarb). He placed killing in His saying, exalted is He, "And if you are killed," because it is the beginning of the report, so He placed the more noble and more important first. The meaning is: "or you die in the way of Allah," so your reward falls upon Allah. Then He placed death first in His saying, exalted is He, "And if you die or are killed," because this is a verse of admonition regarding the Hereafter and the gathering, and a verse of renunciation of this world and its life. The death mentioned in it is death in general, whether in the way (of Allah) or at home and however it occurs, so it is placed first for its generality, and because it is the more common among people compared with killing.

Nāfiʿ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "mitum" with a kasra on the mīm, and "mitnā" and "mitta" with a kasra throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read with a ḍamma on the mīm throughout the Qur'an. Abū Bakr narrated from ʿĀṣim a ḍamma on the mīm throughout the Qur'an, while Ḥafṣ narrated from him a ḍamma on the mīm only in these two places: "awi mutum" and "wa la'in mutum," and a kasra on the mīm wherever it occurs in the whole Qur'an. Abū ʿAlī said: the ḍamma on the mīm is the more well-known and the more regular (analogical), "mutta tamūtu," like "qulta taqūlu" and "ṭufta taṭūfu." The kasra is anomalous in analogy, though it has been used a great deal, and it is not anomalous in analogy and usage in the way that such forms as al-yajadda' and the like are anomalous. The parallel of "mitta tamūtu" with a kasra on the mīm is "faḍila" with a kasra on the ḍād, "yafḍulu," in the sound (usage), and they recited in verse:

I remembered Ibn ʿAbbās at the gate of Ibn ʿĀmir, and what passed of my life I remembered, and what remained (faḍil).

His saying, exalted is He, "la-maghfiratun" is in the nominative by the inchoative (mubtadaʾ). "Wa raḥmatun" is conjoined to "al-maghfirah," and "khayrun" is the predicate of the inchoative. The meaning: forgiveness and the mercy that follows from being killed or dying in the way of Allah are better. The word "maghfirah" came indefinite as an eloquent indication that the least part of it is better than the world, and that it suffices for the success of the believing servant. The verse may also admit that His saying "la-maghfiratun" refers to being killed or dying in the way of Allah; He named that forgiveness and mercy since both are linked to it. The estimate then becomes: "for that is forgiveness and mercy," the forgiveness being raised as the predicate of the presumed inchoative, and His saying "khayrun" is an attribute of the predicate of the inchoative.

The majority of people read "tajmaʿūn" with a tāʾ, as address (muKhāṭabah), and this is more suited to the context. A group among them, ʿĀṣim as narrated from Ḥafṣ, read "yajmaʿūn" with a yāʾ, and the meaning is: what the hypocrites and others amass.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the gathering to Him, and that it is the final end for everyone who is killed or dies. In the verse there is a belittling of the affairs of this world and an urging to seek martyrdom; that is, if the gathering occurs in both circumstances, then going to it in the state of martyrdom is more fitting.

His saying, exalted is He, "So by mercy from Allah," its meaning is "so by a mercy from Allah," and "mā" has been stripped of the sense of negation and is included for emphasis; it is not superfluous absolutely, having no meaning. Sībawayh applied to it the name of superfluity because its governing effect has ceased. This is like His saying, exalted is He, "so by their breaking their covenant" [al-Nisāʾ: 155]. Al-Zajjāj said: the bāʾ is, by the consensus of the grammarians, a connecting particle (ṣilah) and carries the sense of emphasis. The meaning of the verse: a reproach to all those who on the Day of Uḥud failed to hold their position, meaning that they deserved blame from you, and that you should not be gentle with them. But Allah had mercy upon all of you: you, O Muḥammad, by making Allah place you upon a great character, and sending you to perfect the noble qualities of character; and them, by making you gentle toward them. You were made with these attributes because of what Allah, exalted is He, knew of their righteousness in that, and that if you had been harsh and hard-hearted they would have scattered and dispersed from around you.

Al-faẓẓ (harshness) is the one coarse in his speech and his manner of address. In the description of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the revealed Books: he was not harsh (faẓẓ), nor hard (ghalīẓ), nor clamorous in the markets. The slave-girls said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: "You are harsher and more severe than the Messenger of Allah..." the hadith. The harshness of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was only used by him as an instrument for supporting the truth and firmness in religion. Al-faẓāẓah is coarseness in dealing with people, in speech and in action, and from it is the saying of the poet:

I fear the harshness of an uncle or the rudeness of a brother, and I used to fear for them from the harm of words.

Ghilaẓ al-qalb (hardness of heart) is an expression for a scowling face, little responsiveness to desires, and little compassion and mercy. From this is the saying of the poet:

They weep over us, and we do not weep over anyone; we are harder of livers than camels.

Al-infiḍāḍ is the scattering of gatherings, and from it comes the breaking of a seal (faḍḍ al-khātam).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 160:

God the Exalted said: ﴿So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. And when you have resolved, then rely upon God. Indeed, God loves those who rely upon Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159] ﴿If God helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon God let the believers rely﴾.

God the Exalted commanded His Messenger with these commands, which are in eloquent gradation. That is, He commanded him to pardon them (upon him be peace) for whatever right and claim he personally had against them. When they reached this level, He commanded him to ask forgiveness for them regarding what they owed to God. When they reached this level, they became fit for consultation in matters.

Consultation (shura) is among the foundations of the Sharia and the firm rulings. Whoever does not consult the people of knowledge and religion, his dismissal is obligatory; this is something on which there is no disagreement. God praised the believers by His saying: ﴿And their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 38]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "He who seeks guidance (istikhara) is not disappointed, and he who consults is not regretful." He (upon him be peace) also said: "The one consulted is trustworthy." The qualification of a consultant in rulings is that he be a knowledgeable, religious person, and this is rarely found except in a person of intellect. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "The religion of a man is not complete unless his intellect is complete." The qualification of a consultant in worldly affairs is that he be intelligent, experienced, and sincerely well-wishing to the one who consults him. Consultation is a blessing. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab made the caliphate, which is the greatest of calamities, a matter of consultation. Al-Hasan said: "By God, no people consult among themselves except that God guides them to the best of what is before them." The Messenger of God ﷺ used to consult his companions, and he said on the day of Badr: "Advise me, O people," on the day when al-Miqdad spoke, then Sa'd ibn 'Ubada. His (upon him be peace) consultation was only in matters of war, expeditions, and the like of specific emerging events. As for what is lawful or unlawful, or a hadd punishment, these are the laws of the Sharia: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. It seems the verse was revealed to comfort the believers, since their overpowering of opinion in the story of Uhud would have required that they be punished by not being consulted about what follows.

Ibn 'Abbas recited "and consult them in some of the affair" (wa-shawirhum fi ba'd al-amr). The recitation of the majority is with the generic noun, which applies to part and to whole. There is no doubt that the wording is specific to what is not of lawful or unlawful. Consultation is based on the difference of opinions; the one consulting considers that difference and chooses. When God the Exalted guides him to what He wills of it, he resolves upon it and executes it, relying upon God, for this is the ultimate effort required of him. It is with this that God commanded His Prophet in this verse.

Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Nuhayk, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Ikrima recited "'azamtu" with a dammah on the ta', God named His guidance and firming of him a resolve from Him. This in meaning is similar to His saying: ﴿So that you may judge between people by what God has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa: 105], and His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17]. So God made the defeat of the polytheists at Hunayn and the disfiguring of their faces a throwing, since it was connected to Muhammad's ﷺ throwing of pebbles. Umm Salama said: "Then God resolved for me."

Reliance upon God the Exalted is among the obligations and distinguishing features of faith, but it is joined with earnest diligence in obedience, exertion, and caution to the utmost effort. Casting oneself down and similar acts are not reliance. Rather, it is, as he (upon him be peace) said: "Tie it and rely (on God)."

Then God the Exalted strengthened the believers by His saying: ﴿If God helps you, none can overcome you﴾, meaning: hold fast to the matters which He commanded you and promised you victory with them.

Khadhl (forsaking) is leaving someone in situations where that person needs help. Its root is from the forsaking of gazelles, and for this reason she was called "khadhil" when her mother left her. This is by way of attribution, meaning "one having forsaking," because the one left behind is the khadhil in the sense of makhdhula (forsaken).

His saying: ﴿who is there that can help you﴾: the estimated answer to it is "no one." The pronoun in "ba'dihi" (after Him) may refer to the written decree, and it may refer to the forsaking contained in His saying: "and if He forsakes you."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 161–163**

(p. 407) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle. Whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs wrath from Allah, whose refuge is Hell? What an evil destination!﴾ ﴿They are of varying degrees with Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾

The discussion of the construction "wa-ma kana li-kadha an yakuna kadha" (it is not for such-and-such to be such-and-such) has already passed, in His saying: ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 145].

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read *yaghulla* (يَغُلَّ) with a fatha on the *ya'* and a damma on the *ghayn*, and Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars also read it this way. The rest of the seven readers read *yughalla* (يُغَلَّ) with a damma on the *ya'* and a fatha on the *ghayn*, and Ibn Mas'ud and a group of scholars also read it this way. The word means betrayal in secrecy. Some lexicographers said it is derived from *al-ghalal*, which is the water flowing in the roots of trees and in thick-branched trees. Abu 'Amr said: The Arabs say *aghalla al-rajulu yughillu ighlalan* (the man embezzled) when he betrays and does not render the trust, and from this is the saying of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

*May Allah reward Jamrat, daughter of Nawfal, on my behalf, with the reward of one who embezzles trust and is a liar.*

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Shurayh said: There is no liability on the borrower except the one who embezzles. Abu 'Ali said: For *al-ghill*, which is rancour, one says *ghalla yaghillu* with a kasra on the *ghayn*. For embezzlement from the spoils, they say *ghalla yaghullu* with a damma on the *ghayn*. The argument for the one who reads *yaghulla* is that whatever comes in this form in the revelation has the verb attributed to the agent, as in: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 38], ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the law of the king﴾ [Yusuf: 76], ﴿It is not for a soul to die﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 145], ﴿Allah would not have led a people astray after He had guided them﴾ [al-Tawba: 115], and ﴿Allah would not have informed you of the unseen﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 179]. It does not occur, however, as in *ma kana Zayd li-yudraba* (it was not for Zayd to be beaten), where the verb is attributed to the object.

(p. 408) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is some scrutiny in this argument. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he read *yaghulla* with a damma on the *ghayn*. It was said to him: Ibn Mas'ud read *yughalla* with a fatha on the *ghayn*. Ibn 'Abbas said: Yes, by Allah, and he would be killed.

The exegetes differed about the reason that led Allah, exalted is He, to negate from the Prophet being an embezzler under this reading, which is with a fatha on the *ya'* and a damma on the *ghayn*. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others said: It was revealed concerning a red woollen cloak that was missing from the spoils on the day of Badr.
