Abu Hurayra narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and said: 'Beware! Perhaps one of you will come on the Day of Resurrection with a sheep on his neck that bleats, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I possess nothing for you from Allah; I have indeed conveyed it to you.'" Then he (ﷺ) mentioned the same about a cow that lows, a camel that groans, and a horse that neighs. Ibn 'Abbas narrated a similar hadith. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will not find any of you coming on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sheep that bleats..." and he related the hadith in full. Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Abd Allah ibn Unays narrated something similar, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give back the thread and the needle." A man stood up and brought a shoelace or two shoelaces, (p. 411) and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A shoelace or two shoelaces of fire." He (ﷺ) also said about Mid'am: "The cloak which he embezzled from the spoils on the day of Khaybar will indeed blaze with fire upon him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This disgrace which Allah brings upon the embezzler is comparable to the disgrace that befalls the treacherous, in that a banner is raised for him because of his treachery, according to his (ﷺ) saying. Allah made these punishments according to what humans are accustomed to and understand. Do you not see the saying of al-Hadira:

*O Asmayy, woe to you! Have you heard of a betrayal for which a banner was raised for us in the assembly?*

The Arabs used to raise a banner for the treacherous, and likewise the offender is paraded with his offence. The discussion of the parallel to: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ has already passed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs﴾... the verse is a statement of the difference between the two ranks and the divergence of the two states. *Al-ridwan* (pleasure) is a verbal noun. 'Asim, as narrated from him, read it with a damma on the *ra'*, and all the others read it with a kasra. Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates from al-A'mash that he read it with a kasra on the *ra'* and a damma on the *dad*. All of these have one meaning, being a verbal noun from *al-ridā* (contentment). The meaning is: they followed the obedience that secures the pleasure of Allah, so there is an elided *mudaf* (genitive) in the sentence.

*Bā'a bi-sakhat* (incurred wrath) means: he went along bearing it. *Al-sakhat* is an attribute of an action, and it may be understood as will when the sense of intention is considered. Al-Dahhak said: This verse indicates that whoever does not embezzle and fears Allah has the pleasure of Allah, and whoever embezzles and disobeys has the wrath. Others said: It indicates that whoever was martyred at Uhud has the pleasure of Allah, and the hypocrites who turned back from the Prophet (ﷺ) have the wrath. The rest of the verse is clear.

The exegetes differed about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are of varying degrees﴾. To whom does this refer? Ibn Ishaq and others said: It refers to the two groups mentioned, the people of pleasure and the people of wrath, meaning that each category among them differs in its own station: in the ranks of Paradise, and also in the levels of the Fire. Mujahid and al-Suddi said, in an apparent reading: the reference of "they" is only to those who follow the pleasure, meaning that they have noble degrees with their Lord. The elided *mudaf* in the sentence is estimated as: *hum darajat* (they are degrees), and *al-darajat* means stations, some higher than others in distance, or in honour, or in punishment. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read *hum darajatun* (هم دَرَجَةٌ) in the singular. The rest of the verse is both threat and promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 3, verses 164–165:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿Certainly Allah conferred a favour upon the believers when He raised among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, though before that they had been in clear error.﴾ ﴿When a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves. Indeed, Allah has power over all things."﴾

The lam in "لَقَدْ" (laqad) is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). The word "مَنَّ" (manna) in this verse means "to bestow kindness and favour." It is also said that "مَنَّ" can mean "to spoil one's kindness by reminding of it," so the word is homonymous (mushtarakah).

His saying, "مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ" (min anfusihim), means: of their own kind, in lineage, language, and proximity. Being of their kind creates familiarity with him and reduces their sense of estrangement from him. Being in their language creates good understanding and ease of comprehension. Being a neighbour and a close relative creates trust and tranquillity, since they knew him, recognised his truthfulness and trustworthiness. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent within the lineage of his people, and so were all the Messengers. Al-Naqqash said: "There is no Arab tribe except that it gave birth to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through its women, except the Banu Taghlib, because of their Christianity."

The "āyāt" (verses) in this verse may be understood as the Qur'an, or as signs. The first is more apparent.

"يُزَكِّيهِمْ" (yuzakkihim) means: he purifies them from the filth of disbelief and sins. Some exegetes said it means: he takes zakat from them. This view is weak.

"الكِتابَ" (al-Kitab) is the Qur'an, and "الحِكْمَةَ" (al-Hikmah) is the Sunnah learned from his tongue, peace be upon him. Then He mentioned their earlier state of error so that the difference might become evident through the juxtaposition of opposites. "قَبْلُ" (qabl) is a word built (mabniyy) because it contains the meaning of the genitive construction (idafah), so it resembles particles in carrying meanings, and therefore it is built.

Then the Almighty made the believers aware of their error in their anxiety over the calamity that had befallen them, and in their turning away from what had happened to the disbelievers. He informed them that this was because of their own selves.

The waw in His saying "أوَلَمّا" (awa-lamma) is a conjunction joining one sentence to another, and it is preceded by the interrogative alif of affirmation (alif al-taqrir), meaning to hold the believers to this statement in this situation. The calamity that struck the believers was the event of Uhud and the killing of seventy of them. Scholars differed about the two equal amounts that the believers had inflicted. Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority of interpreters, said: it refers to the day of Badr, when the believers killed seventy of the disbelievers of Quraysh and captured seventy. Al-Zajjaj said: one of the two equals is the killing of seventy on the day of Badr, and the second is the killing of twenty-two of the disbelievers on the day of Uhud, so it is a killing for a killing. Captives have no place in this verse, this being the meaning of his words, because the captives of Badr were taken and then ransomed, so there is no equivalence between their situation and the killing of seventy of the believers. "أنّى" (anna) means: how? and from where?

Then He commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to say to them: "It is from yourselves."

People differed about how it is from themselves and for what reason. The majority of exegetes said: because they opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in opinion when he preferred to remain in Madinah and leave the disbelievers of Quraysh in the worst confinement, but they insisted on going out until the event took place. Another group said: His saying "مِن عِنْدِ أنْفُسِكُمْ" (min 'indi anfusikum) is a reference to the disobedience of the archers and their causing the defeat of the believers. Al-Hasan and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: rather, it was when they accepted ransom on the day of Badr. That is because 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the defeat of the polytheists at Badr was completed, Jibril, peace be upon him, came and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed Allah dislikes what your people are doing regarding taking captives, and He has commanded you to offer them a choice between two matters: that they be brought forward and their necks struck, or that they accept ransom, on condition that a number of your companions equal to these captives be killed.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people and mentioned this to them. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are our clans and our brothers. Rather, we will take their ransom and strengthen ourselves thereby for fighting our enemy, and a number of us equal to them will be martyred. There is nothing in that which we dislike.' He said: So seventy men of them were killed on the day of Uhud."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 166–167:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met, it was by the permission of Allah, and that He might know the believers﴾ ﴿and that He might know those who played the hypocrite. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy]." They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.﴾

The address in His saying, "And whatever befell you," is to the believers. The two hosts are the army of the Prophet ﷺ and the army of Quraysh on the Day of Uhud. The particle fa' (fa, "then") entered His saying, "then by the permission of Allah," as a binding particle that is emphatic, because of the indefiniteness contained in "mā" (whatever), so the speech resembled a conditional clause. This is as Sibawayh said: "The one who stood up, then for him are two dirhams." The entry of the fa' is good when standing up is the cause of the giving. Likewise is the arrangement of this verse. The meaning is only: "Whatever Allah permitted in it, that is what befell," but He placed first what is more important in their souls and closer to their senses. Al-idhn (permission) is enabling someone to do a thing together with knowledge of it.

His saying, "and that He might know," its meaning is: so that knowledge would exist alongside the presence of the believers and the hypocrites, that is, in concomitance with the knowledge that has never ceased and does not cease. The lam in His saying, "that He might know," is connected to a verb understood (p-415) at the end of the speech. The reference in His saying, "those who played the hypocrite, and it was said to them," is to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions who turned away with him from the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Uhud. That is because "it was of the opinion of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy that he should not go out to the disbelievers of Quraysh. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out with the people in the manner that we have mentioned, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: 'He obeyed them and disobeyed me.' So about a third of the people withdrew. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari, the father of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, followed in their footsteps and said to them: 'Fear Allah and do not abandon your Prophet, and fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy],' or words similar to this. Ibn Ubayy said to him: 'I do not think there will be fighting. Had we known there would be fighting, we would have been with you.' When 'Abd Allah despaired of them, he said: 'Go away, enemies of Allah! Allah will suffice His Messenger without you.' And he went on with the Prophet ﷺ and was martyred.'"

The people differed about the meaning of His saying, "or repel [the enemy]." Al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and others said: its meaning is: increase the numbers even if you do not fight, so that the enemy is repelled by your multitude. Abu 'Awn al-Ansari said: its meaning is: stand guard (rabitu), and this is close to the first view. There is no doubt that one who stands guard is repelling, for were it not for the presence of those who guard the frontiers, the enemy would have come upon them, and one who increases the numbers is repelling. Anas ibn Malik said: "On the day of al-Qadisiyya I saw 'Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum, the blind, and upon him was a coat of mail whose skirts he dragged, and in his hand was a black banner. It was said to him: 'Has Allah not made your excuse [for not fighting] clear?' He said: 'Yes, but I increase the Muslims by my own person.' It is also narrated that he said: 'How then [would it be] with my numbers in the way of Allah?'"

Some exegetes held that the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, "or repel [the enemy]," was only a call to fight out of zeal, because he called them to fight in the way of Allah, which means that the word of Allah should be supreme. When he saw that they were not people of that, he presented to them the matter that would shame them and stir their pride, that is: "or fight in defence of the sanctuary." Do you not see that Quzman said: "By Allah, I fought only for the honour of my people"? And do you not see that some of the Ansar said on the day of Uhud, when he saw Quraysh had sent their beasts of burden into the crops of the canal: "Shall the crops of Banu Qaylah be grazed while we do not strike [the enemy]?" The Prophet ﷺ had ordered that no one should fight until he commanded them to fight. It seems that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram called them to this matter of Arab custom, which is outside of religion, rather than fighting in the way of Allah.

The majority of exegetes held that His saying, "closer" (aqrab), is derived from qurb, the opposite of distance, and the lam in His saying, "to disbelief" and "to faith," takes the place of "ila" (to). Al-Naqqash related that His saying "aqrab" is derived from qarab, with a fatha on the qaf and the ra', which means seeking, and the one who seeks water is qarib, and the night of qarab is the night of watering. So the word means "seeking," and the lam is retained according to this view.

His saying, "with their mouths," is an emphasis, like "flying with its two wings."

His saying, "what is not in their hearts," means what they show of the word that preserves their blood. Then Allah exposed them with His saying, "And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal," that is, of disbelief and enmity to the religion. And in the speech there is a warning to them.

(p-٤١٧) His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿Those who said of their brothers, while they themselves stayed behind: "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say: "Then ward off death from yourselves, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.﴾ ﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty.﴾

"Those who" (alladhina) is a *badal* (substitute or apposition, a grammatical term meaning a noun that restates and specifies the preceding noun) for the earlier "those who." "Their brothers" refers to those killed from the Khazraj, and it is a brotherhood of lineage and of neighbourhood. His statement "for their brothers" (li-ikhwanihim) means: for the sake of their brothers, and concerning the affair of their brothers. It is possible that his statement "for their brothers" refers to the living hypocrites, and that the pronoun in "obeyed us" (ata'una) refers to the dead. His statement "and stayed behind" (wa qa'adu) is a clause in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject), and it is an interposed *hal* within the speech. His statement "if they had obeyed us" means: in not going out toward Quraysh.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ma qutthilu" with a doubled *ta'* (qutthilu), and this is the position of those who hold the doctrine of the two terms (al-ajalayn, the view that a person has two appointed times of death, one of them being by killing). Allah answered them with His statement: "Say: Then ward off..." (fadra'u), and *al-dar'* means repelling. From it is the verse of Daghfal the genealogist:

"The repelling of the flood met a repelling that drives it back,
and the burden, you do not know it, or you lift it."

The implication of this argument is that you, who say that caution and the use of judgment ward off death, should then be cautious and consider what it is that overtakes you of death, "the death that comes upon your noses" (hatf anfikum), and repel it, if your statement is true. That is to say: these are only appointed terms (ajal, pl. ajal, fixed times) decreed with Allah.

The majority of the readers read "and do not think" (wa la tahsabanna) with a *ta'* as address to the Prophet, peace be upon him. Humayd ibn Qays read "wa la yahsabanna" with a *ya'* as referring to an absent third person; this is narrated from Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr mentioned it. It seems that the subject is implied: "and let no one think," or "let no thinker think." I consider this reading to be with a *damma* on the *ba'*, so the meaning is: "and let people not think." "Yahsabunna" means: he supposes.

Al-Hasan read "alladhina qutthilu" with a doubled *ta'*. Ibn 'Amir is among the seven readers. It is narrated from 'Asim that he read "alladhina qatalu" with an *alif* between the *qaf* and the *ta'*.

Allah, may He be exalted, informs in this verse about the martyrs that they are in Paradise, being provided for. This is the point of benefit. Without doubt they died, and their bodies are in the earth, while their spirits are alive like the spirits of all the believers. They are distinguished by being provided for in Paradise from the time of the killing, so that it is as if the life of this world were lasting for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 171–172:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170] ﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers.﴾ ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after injury had befallen them—for those among them who did good and were mindful (of God) is a great reward.﴾

"Yastabshirun" (they rejoice) means: they are gladdened and delighted. The form *istaf'ala* here does not mean "seeking good news." Rather, it means the same as *istaghna Allah* (Allah is self-sufficient) and *istamjada al-markh wal-'afar* (the marikh and the 'afar trees became glorious). Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj, and others, held that this rejoicing is that they say: "Our brothers whom we left behind us in the world are fighting in the way of Allah with their Prophet, and they will be martyred and will attain the same honour as what we are in, so they are gladdened for them by this," since they attain "no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve." A group of scholars, to which al-Zajjaj and Ibn Furak pointed, held that the reference in His words "those who have not yet joined them" [Al 'Imran: 170] is to all believers, meaning: they have not joined them in the excellence of martyrdom. But when the martyrs witnessed the reward of Allah, certainty settled that the religion of Islam is the truth by which Allah rewards, so they rejoice for themselves in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and they rejoice for the believers that "no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve." "Anna" (that) is in the accusative of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), the estimate being: "because there is no fear." It is also permissible that it be in the genitive position as a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*).

Then, the Exalted confirmed their rejoicing by His words "they rejoice in a blessing," then clarified with His words "and bounty." Thus His causing them to enter Paradise is a bounty from Him, not by the deed of anyone. As for the blessing in Paradise and the ranks, He has informed that they are according to the deeds.

Al-Kisa'i and a group of the people of knowledge read "wa inna Allah" with a kasra on the alif of "anna," while the rest of the Seven and the majority of scholars read "wa anna Allah" with a fatha on the alif. Whoever reads with the fatha, then that is included in what is rejoiced over; the meaning is: "in a blessing and that Allah..." Whoever reads with the kasra, then it is a new independent statement. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read "wa fadlin wa Allahu la yudi'u."

His words, may He be exalted, "alladhina istajabu" may be that "alladhina" is an attribute of the believers according to the reading of the one who read the alif of "anna" with a kasra. The more evident view is that "alladhina" is the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is in His words, exalted is He, "for those who did good..." (verse). This sentence is the predicate of the first subject.

Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger are those who went out with the Prophet ﷺ to Hamra' al-Asad, seeking Quraysh and showing strength against them. That was because when it was the day of Sunday, the second day after the day of Uhud, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to the people to follow the polytheists, and said: 'Let none go out with us except those who witnessed us yesterday.'" The people had injuries and great wounds, but they steeled themselves, and two hundred men of the believers rose with him until he reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madinah, and he stayed there (p. 422) three days. The story of Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad, which we have mentioned, took place, Quraysh passed by, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah. Then Allah revealed this verse concerning those who responded, and praised them for their patience.

It is related that two brothers went out among the people, and both had severe injuries, and one of them had become weak, so his brother would carry him one stretch and walk one stretch himself. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah asked the Prophet ﷺ to go out with him, and he permitted him. He, exalted is He, informed them that the great reward had been secured for them by this act. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed it is a ghazwa (military campaign)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 173–174:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith, and they said, "Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty, no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

"Those" (alladhina) is an attribute of the doers of good (al-muhsinin) mentioned. This saying is the one the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions when Abu Sufyan had charged them with it. I have mentioned it before. So the first "people" are the caravan of 'Abd al-Qays, and the second "people" are the army of Quraysh.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "But it increased them in faith", meaning: in steadfastness (thubutan) and readiness (isti'dadan). Thus the increase of faith in this context is in deeds.

The scholars have used the expression that faith increases and decreases. The creed on this matter is that the very faith, which is a single affirmation of something, is in fact a single meaning (ma'na fard) into which no increase enters when it is attained, and from which nothing remains when it departs. Therefore, only the increase and decrease remain in its objects (muta'allaqat) and not in its essence (dhat). (p-423) Some scholars held that it is said that it increases and decreases in respect of the actions issuing from it increasing and decreasing, especially since many scholars apply the name of faith to acts of obedience. Others held that the increase in faith is only through the descent of obligations and the reports during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and through knowledge of them after ignorance, for all time. This is only an increase of faith upon faith. So the statement that faith increases and decreases in this sense is figurative, and decrease cannot be conceived in it in this sense; decrease is conceivable only in relation to one who knows. Some scholars held that the increase and decrease of faith is only through the evidences (adilla), so that the evidences increase for one person and it is said that this is an increase in faith, just as it is said about clothing that it is an increase in the person. Abu al-Ma'ali, in al-Irshad, held that the increase and decrease of faith is only due to the persistence of belief and its recurring continually. He said: since faith is an accident ('arad) and does not persist for two times, it is for the Prophet (ﷺ) and the righteous a continuous succession, and for the wicked and the heedless not continuous; it accompanies them at times and leaves them at times in the interval (fatra). That other one has more faith. This is the increase and decrease.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this saying there is consideration.

His saying, Exalted is He, "But it increased them in faith", cannot be conceived as being through the evidences, and the other three aspects are conceivable in the verse. It is narrated that when the delegation from 'Abd al-Qays informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what Abu Sufyan had charged them with, and that he was turning toward them with the people to wipe them out, and a Bedouin also reported this, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Say: Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." They said it, and their resolve persisted in patience. Allah repelled from them every harm and cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers, so they passed by.

(p-424) His saying, Exalted is He, "So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty" means: in safety and in prominence in following the enemy and protecting the sanctuary, and with bounty in the reward they obtained and the honor they were clothed with. The rest of the verse is clear, and its parallels have already passed.

This is the interpretation of the majority (jumhur) concerning this verse, and that it was in the Battle of Uhud, in the expedition to Hamra' al-Asad. Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, departed from this and said:

Indeed this verse, from His saying "Those to whom the people said" to His saying "a great bounty", was revealed concerning the going out of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, to Badr al-Sughra. That was because he went out for the appointment of Abu Sufyan at Uhud, when he had said: "Our appointment is Badr in the coming year." The Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Say: yes." So the Messenger of Allah went out toward Badr, and there was a great market there. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave his companions dirhams, and when he drew near Badr, Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i came to him and informed him that Quraysh had gathered and were coming to fight him, they and whoever had joined them. The Muslims were anxious about this, but they said: "Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs," and they persisted until they reached Badr, and they found no enemy, and they found the market, so they bought with their dirhams food and merchandise, and returned having met no plot, and they profited in their trade. That is His saying, Exalted is He: "with favor from Allah and bounty", meaning: bounty in that trade.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is what the majority said: that this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of Hamra' al-Asad. As for what Ibn Qutayba and others said, that the word "people" in this verse refers to one man, it is a weak opinion.

"The saying of the Most High:

﴿Indeed, that is Satan, who frightens his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.﴾ ﴿And do not let those who race to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith will not harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

(p-425) The implication of "innama" (indeed, only; "innama" in the sense of restriction) in the language is restriction (ḥaṣr). This is the Arab speaker's intent when using it. Then, if it is considered rationally, which is the approach of the scholars of legal theory (uṣūliyyūn), it is suitable for restriction and for emphasis, for which the word of restriction is borrowed. And it is restrictive in this verse. The reference of "dhālikum" (that) is to everything that has preceded of the reports about the caravan of 'Abd (the Banū 'Abd), concerning the letter of Abū Sufyān, and Abū Sufyān's entrusting of that message, and the distress of whoever was distressed by that news, whether a believer or one wavering.

In terms of grammar, "dhālikum" is a subject (mubtada'), and "ash-shayṭān" is another subject, and "yukhawwifu awliyā'ahu" is the predicate concerning Satan. The clause is the predicate of the first subject. This parsing is better for the coherence of the meaning than that "ash-shayṭān" be the predicate of "dhālikum," because that would produce a distant metaphor in meaning. "Yukhawwifu" is a verb that transitively takes two objects, but it is permissible to limit it to one of them, since the other is understood from the structure of this verb. For when you say, "I frightened Zayd," it is necessarily understood that you frightened him with something that ought to be feared.

Most readers recite "yukhawwifu awliyā'ahu." Some said the meaning is: "He frightens you, O believers, with his allies, who are the unbelievers of Quraysh," so the first object is omitted. Others said the meaning is: "He frightens the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease, and they are his allies." Then his frightening does not affect you, O believers, since you are not his allies. The meaning is: "He frightens them, the unbelievers of Quraysh," so here the second object is omitted and only the first is mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by Abū 'Amr al-Dānī, recited "yukhawwifukum awliyā'uhu" (his allies frighten you), meaning: Quraysh and those with them frighten you, through Satan's misguidance of them, and all of that is vanishing. Al-Nakha'ī also recited thus. Abū al-Fatḥ Ibn Jinnī related from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited "yukhawwifukum awliyā'ahu," which is a reading in which both objects appear, and it explains the reading of the majority, "yukhawwifu awliyā'ahu." In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "yukhawwifukum bi-awliyā'ihi."

The pronoun in His saying, "fa-lā takhāfūhum" (so do not fear them), refers to the unbelievers of Quraysh and others among the allies of Satan. Allah belittled their status and strengthened the souls of the believers against them, and commanded them to fear Him, exalted is He, and to obey His command by patience and steadfastness. Then He affirmed with His saying, "in kuntum mu'minīn" (if you are believers), as you say: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such."

Nāfi' alone recited "yuḥzinka" with a dammah on the yā' from aḥzana, and he recited thus throughout the Qur'an, except in Sūrat al-Anbiyā': "lā yaḥzunuhumu al-faza' al-akbar," where he opened the yā'. The rest recited "yaḥzunka" with a fatḥah on the yā', from your saying: ḥazantu al-rajul. Sībawayh said: it is said ḥazina al-rajul and futina when the grief or the trial afflicts him, and ḥazantuhu and fatantuhu when you put grief or trial in him or with him, just as you say dahantu and kaḥḥaltu when you put oil or kohl on something, and aḥzantuhu and afatantuhu when you make him grieved and tried, just as you say adkhaltuhu and asma'tuhu. This is the meaning of Sībawayh's statement.

Al-musāra'a fi al-kufr (racing into disbelief) is hastening to its sayings and actions and being diligent in it. Al-Ḥurr al-Naḥwī recited "yusri'ūn" throughout the Qur'an, but the reading of the majority is more emphatic, because one who races others is more striving than one who hastens alone; for this reason they said: "Every runner in the empty field is made to hasten (yusarru)." Allah consoled His Prophet with this verse about the state of the hypocrites and the strivers, since all of them are racing.

His saying, the Most High, "innahum lan yaḍurrū Allāha shay'ā" (indeed they will not harm Allah at all), is a statement that implicitly contains a warning for them, meaning: they only harm themselves. The word ḥazz (share), when not qualified, is used only for good, do you not see His saying: "wa mā yulaqqāhā illā alladhīna ṣabarū wa mā yulaqqāhā illā dhū ḥazzin 'aẓīm" (Fuṣṣilat: 35).

His saying, "inna alladhīna ishtarawu" (indeed those who purchased), applied the term purchase to them from the perspective that they were empowered to accept this and that; so their taking of one and leaving of the other was like abandoning what had already been taken and obtained, since they were empowered to it. Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, has a connection to this verse in the issue of buying what its individual units differ in, of a kind in which excess exchange is not permitted: that prohibition of purchase applies so long as the buyer chooses. The remainder of the verse is a warning like the preceding.

Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr and Nāfi' read "yaḥsibanna" with a yā' at the beginning, a kasra on the sīn and a fatḥa on the bā'. Ibn 'Āmir read it likewise, except that he put a fatḥa on the sīn. Ḥamzah read "taḥsabanna" with a tā' at the beginning and a fatḥa on the sīn. 'Āṣim and al-Kisā'ī read every occurrence in this sūrah with a tā' at the beginning, except for two words: the statement "Wa lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna kafarū" in this verse, and after it, "Wa lā yaḥsabanna alladhīna yabkhalūn." As for the one who reads "wa lā yaḥsabanna" with a yā' at the beginning, "alladhīna" is the subject (fā'il). The phrase "annamā numlī lahum khayrun," with a fatḥa on the hamzah of "annamā," stands in place of the two objects of ḥasiba (to suppose). This is because ḥasiba and what follows its pattern take two objects, or one object that stands in place of two objects. This happens when, in the clause that follows, there is mention of the subject of the statement and the one spoken about.

Abū 'Alī (al-Fārisī) said: The kasra on "inna" in the reading of the one who reads "yaḥsabanna" with a yā' is not appropriate. It has been read this way, as reported by someone other than Aḥmad ibn Mūsā, and outside the seven canonical readings. The reasoning for this is that "inna" may be preceded by an oath, just as the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidā') may be, and both of them enter upon the initial subject and predicate, namely the lām and "inna." So the action of ḥusbān (supposing) is suspended from "annamā," just as it is suspended from the lām in your saying: "Ḥasibtu la-Zaydun qā'imun." The verb is suspended from its action verbally. As for the meaning, what follows "inna" or the lām is in the position of the two objects of ḥasiba. The "mā" may be taken to mean "alladhī," in which case "numlī" has a hidden returning pronoun. It may also be taken as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), in which case no returning pronoun needs to be supposed.

As for the one who reads "wa lā taḥsabanna" with a tā' at the beginning, "alladhīna" is the first object of ḥusbān. Abū 'Alī said: In this reading the hamzah of "annamā" should be kasra, and "inna" with what enters upon it is in the position of the second object of "taḥsabanna." It is not permissible to put a fatḥa on the hamzah of "annamā," because then it would be the second object, and in this construction the second object is in meaning the first object, while the granting of respite (al-imlā') is not directed at them.

Makkī said in his Mushkil: I do not know of anyone who read "taḥsabanna" with a tā' at the beginning and a kasra on the hamzah of "annamā." Al-Zajjāj permitted this reading, "taḥsabanna" with a tā' and "annamā" with a fatḥa on the hamzah. The apparent sense of his statement is that it governs "khayran" in the accusative. He said: A great number of people have read it this way, and he gave as an example the verse of the poet:

"So the death of Qays was not the death of one man..."

with the second "hulk" in the accusative, taking the first as an apposition (badal).

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise "annamā numlī" would be an apposition (badal) for "alladhīna kafarū," as in His saying, exalted is He: "Wa mā ansānīhu illā al-shayṭānu an adhkurahu" [al-Kahf: 63], and His saying: "Wa idh ya'iduкumu Allāhu iḥdā al-ṭā'ifatayni annahā lakum" [al-Anfāl: 7], and "khayran" would be the second object.

Abū 'Alī said: No one has read this reading. I asked Aḥmad ibn Mūsā about it, and he claimed that no one has read it this way. It appears from Abū 'Alī's statement that Abū Isḥāq (al-Zajjāj) permitted this question only together with the reading "khayrun" in the nominative. Abū 'Alī knows best, since he witnessed Abū Isḥāq. Some people mentioned that this reading is permissible by omitting a genitive-governing noun (muḍāf), its supposed form being: "Wa lā taḥsabanna sha'na alladhīna kafarū annamā numlī lahum," and this is like His saying, exalted is He: "Wa-s'ali al-qaryah" [Yūsuf: 82], and other such examples. The master Abū al-Ḥasan ibn al-Bādhish holds that it is permissible by making "anna" an apposition of "alladhīna," and omitting the second object of ḥasiba, since the statement indicates it.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The matter is permissible, since the meaning is: "Do not suppose that Our granting respite to those who disbelieved is good for them," or something similar to this.

The meaning of this verse is a refutation of the disbelievers in their saying: that our being dominant and wealthy in health is evidence of Allah's pleasure with our state and the soundness of our way before Him. So Allah informed them that this delay and respite is only a granting of respite and a drawing-on (istidrāj), so that they would acquire sins. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ūd said: No soul, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for it. As for the righteous, it is so that it may hasten to the mercy of Allah, and he recited: "Wa mā 'inda Allāhi khayrun lil-abrār" [Āl 'Imrān: 198]. As for the wicked, it is so that it may not increase in sin, and he recited this verse. The description of the punishment as "muhīn" (humiliating) means that it degrades them. A person may be punished without being humiliated, and that is when it is believed that his stumble will be pardoned at some point.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: "Mā kāna Allāhu liyadhara al-mu'minīn..." to the end of the verse. Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Isḥāq and others said: The address is to the believers, and the meaning is: Allah would not leave the believers mixed with the hypocrites, their affair unclear, with the hypocrite behaving like the believer. Rather He distinguished some of them from others by what appeared from these and those at Uḥud of deeds and words. Qatādah and al-Suddī said: The address is to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: until He distinguishes the believers from the disbelievers by faith and emigration (hijrah). Al-Suddī and others said: "The disbelievers said in some of their disputation: 'You, O Muhammad, claim about a man among us that he is of the people of the Fire, and that if he follows you he is of the people of Paradise. How can this be valid? But inform us of who among us will believe and who will remain upon his disbelief.' So the verse was revealed." It was said to them: The distinguishing is inevitable, but Allah did not make you aware of the unseen concerning who will believe or who will remain a disbeliever. But this is a chosen Messenger, so believe in him. If you believe, you will be saved and you will have a reward.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj and the people of the first opinion, their interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "Wa mā kāna Allāhu liyuṭli'akum 'alā al-ghayb," is that it concerns the affair of Uḥud, meaning: Allah would not make you aware that you would be defeated, so you would be hit in the face (tukʿawna), and similar to this. Also, He would not make you aware of the hypocrites by explicit identification and naming them, but this would be through the indications of their deeds and words in such a situation.

"Ḥattā" in His saying "ḥattā yamīza" is an absolute limit (ghāyah mujarradah), because the speech before it means: Allah purifies what is among you by testing and examining you, until He distinguishes.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi', Abū 'Amr, Ibn 'Āmir and 'Āṣim read "ḥattā yamīza" with a fatḥa on the yā', a kasra on the mīm and a light (unshaddah) yā'. Likewise "liyamīza." Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "ḥattā yumayyiza" and "liyumayyiza Allāhu" with a ḍammah on the yā' and a shaddah.

Ya'qūb ibn al-Sikkīt said: Mizt and mayyiztu are two dialects with one meaning. Abū 'Alī said: Mayyiztu is not derived by transitivity (naql) from mizt, as evidence that mayyiztu does not take two objects but takes one object, like mizt. Just as "alqaytu" is not derived by transitivity from "laqiya," but has the meaning of "asqaṭtu" (I dropped).

Al-ghayb here means what is hidden from mankind of what is in Allah's knowledge, such as the events that will happen, and the secrets that are in the hearts of the hypocrites, and the statements they make when they are away from people. Al-Zajjāj and others said: It is narrated that some of the disbelievers said: "Why should not all of us be prophets?" So this verse was revealed. "Yajtabī" means: He chooses and selects. It is from jabaytu al-mā' and al-māl (I collected the water and the wealth). The rest of the verse is clear, and Allah is the One sought for help.

(p. 427) "Yumlī" means: We grant respite and prolong the life span. Al-Milāwah is a period of time, and al-Malawān are the night and the day. One says: "Mallāka Allāh al-ni'mah," meaning He granted you the blessing for a long life.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 180–181:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is evil for them. What they were niggardly with will be hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Certainly has Allah heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾

The readings of His saying, ﴿Let not those who are niggardly think﴾, are the same as those mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Let not those who disbelieve think﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

As-Suddi and a group of the interpreters (al-mutawwilin) said: The verse was revealed concerning withholding wealth, not spending in the way of Allah, not paying the obligatory zakat, and similar matters. They said: The meaning of ﴿what they were niggardly with will be hung around their necks﴾ is what has come in the hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no kinsman who comes to his kinsman, asks him about some of what he has, and he is niggardly with it toward him, except that on the Day of Resurrection there will come out for him a bald poisonous snake among the people, which will keep licking until it coils around him." The hadiths on this kind of thing, concerning the withholding of zakat and the hoarding of wealth, are many and sound. Ibn 'Abbas said: The verse was only revealed concerning the People of the Book and their niggardliness in making clear what Allah had taught them about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Mujahid and a group of the people of tafsir said the same.

His saying, may He be exalted, "will be hung around their necks" — according to this interpretation, its meaning is: they will bear the punishment for what they were niggardly with. It is from ṭāqa (capacity), as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it [a ransom]﴾ [al-Baqara: 184], and it is not from taṭwīq (encircling). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "sayuṭawwaqūn" means a collar of fire will be made for them on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This accords with the first interpretation that I mentioned, attributed to as-Suddi and others.

Mujahid said: The meaning of "sayuṭawwaqūn" is: they will be burdened to bring the like of what they were niggardly with on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is inconsistent with his statement that the niggardliness is with the knowledge which Allah graciously bestowed upon them by teaching it to them.

As for the grammatical analysis of His saying, "those who are niggardly": it is in the nominative case according to the reading of the one who reads "yahsabanna" with the yā' from below. The first object is implied by the relative clause, its estimated form being: "Let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think their niggardliness to be good for them." "Huwa" is a separator pronoun (fāṣilat al-'imād) according to the Kufans. His saying "yabkhalūn" indicates this implied niggardliness, just as the word "al-safīh" (the foolish one) indicates folly in the words of the poet:

؎ When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, and the foolish one turns to opposition.

Thus the meaning is: he rushes toward folly. As for the one who reads "tahsabanna" with the tā' from above, there is an omitted genitive construction in the speech which constitutes the first object. Its estimated form is: "And do not think, O Muhammad, that the niggardliness of those who are niggardly is good for them." Al-Zajjaj said: This is like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens﴾ is an address in accordance with what human beings do, indicating the perishing of all, and that no owner remains except Allah, may He be exalted, although His ownership over everything has never ceased.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "wa-Allāhu bimā ya'malūn" with the yā' from below, referring to those who are niggardly and are encircled. The rest read with the tā' from above, and this is a turning from the third person to the second person address, since it has previously been mentioned: "And if you believe and are mindful of Allah."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Certainly has Allah heard﴾... the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Finhas the Jew, because "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, to the house of study (bayt al-midras) to invite them. He found in it a group of Jews who had gathered around Finhas, who was their rabbi (ḥabr). Abu Bakr said to him: 'O Finhas, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; he has come to you with the truth from Allah; you find it written with you in the Torah.' Finhas said: 'By Allah, O Abu Bakr, we have no need of Allah; rather, He is in need of us, and we are free of Him. If He were rich, He would not have borrowed our wealth as your companion claims,' in a lengthy speech, at which Abu Bakr became angry. He raised his hand and slapped Finhas's face, cursed him, and intended to kill him, but the Prophet (ﷺ) prevented him from that, saying to him: 'Do not do anything until you return to me.' Then Finhas went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained of Abu Bakr's action. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr: 'What prompted you to do what you did?' Then the verse was revealed concerning that."

Qatada said: The verse was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, because when ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqara: 245] was revealed, he said: "Our Lord asks us for a loan? It is only the poor who borrow from the rich." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ma'mar, Qatada also, and others said: When ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqara: 245] was revealed... the verse, the Jews said: "It is only the poor who borrow from the rich."

Without doubt, this is a statement that first issued from Finhas, Huyayy, and their like among the rabbis, and then the Jews repeated it. It is a statement by which followers and those without knowledge of the purposes of speech are misled, and this is the Jews' distortion of interpretation, in the manner of what they did with their Torah.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿the statement of those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Tawba: 30] indicates that they were a group.

As for the grammatical analysis of His saying, "those who are niggardly": it is in the nominative case according to the reading of the one who reads "yahsabanna" with the yā' from below. The first object is implied by the relative clause, its estimated form being: "Let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think their niggardliness to be good for them." "Huwa" is a separator pronoun (fāṣilat al-'imād) according to the Kufans. His saying "yabkhalūn" indicates this implied niggardliness, just as the word "al-safīh" (the foolish one) indicates folly in the words of the poet:

؎ When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, and the foolish one turns to opposition.

Thus the meaning is: he rushes toward folly. As for the one who reads "tahsabanna" with the tā' from above, there is an omitted genitive construction in the speech which constitutes the first object. Its estimated form is: "And do not think, O Muhammad, that the niggardliness of those who are niggardly is good for them." Al-Zajjaj said: This is like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens﴾ is an address in accordance with what human beings do, indicating the perishing of all, and that no owner remains except Allah, may He be exalted, although His ownership over everything has never ceased.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "wa-Allāhu bimā ya'malūn" with the yā' from below, referring to those who are niggardly and are encircled. The rest read with the tā' from above, and this is a turning from the third person to the second person address, since it has previously been mentioned: "And if you believe and are mindful of Allah."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Certainly has Allah heard﴾... the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Finhas the Jew, because "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, to the house of study (bayt al-midras) to invite them. He found in it a group of Jews who had gathered around Finhas, who was their rabbi (ḥabr). Abu Bakr said to him: 'O Finhas, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; he has come to you with the truth from Allah; you find it written with you in the Torah.' Finhas said: 'By Allah, O Abu Bakr, we have no need of Allah; rather, He is in need of us, and we are free of Him. If He were rich, He would not have borrowed our wealth as your companion claims,' in a lengthy speech, at which Abu Bakr became angry. He raised his hand and slapped Finhas's face, cursed him, and intended to kill him, but the Prophet (ﷺ) prevented him from that, saying to him: 'Do not do anything until you return to me.' Then Finhas went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained of Abu Bakr's action. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr: 'What prompted you to do what you did?' Then the verse was revealed concerning that."

Qatada said: The verse was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, because when ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqara: 245] was revealed, he said: "Our Lord asks us for a loan? It is only the poor who borrow from the rich." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ma'mar, Qatada also, and others said: When ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqara: 245] was revealed... the verse, the Jews said: "It is only the poor who borrow from the rich."

Without doubt, this is a statement that first issued from Finhas, Huyayy, and their like among the rabbis, and then the Jews repeated it. It is a statement by which followers and those without knowledge of the purposes of speech are misled, and this is the Jews' distortion of interpretation, in the manner of what they did with their Torah.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿the statement of those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Tawba: 30] indicates that they were a group.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 182–183:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿We shall record what they have said, and their killing of the prophets without right, and We shall say: Taste the punishment of the burning.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181] ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth, and because Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ ﴿Those who said: Indeed Allah has taken our covenant that we not believe in a messenger until he brings us an offering which the fire consumes.﴾

Hamzah alone recited: "sa-yuktabu" (سَيُكْتَبُ) with the yā' from below, in the passive form of the verb; and "qatluhum" (قَتْلُهُمْ) with a raised lām, in coordination with the subject that has not been named as agent; and "yaqulu" (يَقُولُ) with the yā' from below. The rest recited with the nūn of plurality. So it is either the nūn of majesty (nūn al-'azamah), or it refers to the angels. On this recitation, "mā" (ما) is the object, and "qatlahum" (قَتْلَهُمْ) with a fatḥah on the lām, in coordination with "mā"; and "wa-naqulu" (وَنَقُولُ) with the nūn, in the pattern of "sanaktubu". The meaning in these two recitations is close, one part to another. Al-Kisa'i said: In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "wa-yuqalu dhuqu" (وَيُقالُ ذُوقُوا). Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said regarding the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "sanaktubu ma yaqulun" (سَنَكْتُبُ ما يَقُولُونَ) "wa-yuqalu lahum dhuqu" (وَيُقالُ لَهم ذُوقُوا). Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "sanaktubu ma yaqulun" (سَنَكْتُبُ ما يَقُولُونَ), and Abu 'Amr also related from him that he recited: "satuktabu" (سَتُكْتَبُ) with a raised tā', "ma qalu" (ما قالُوا), meaning: their saying will be recorded.

This verse is a threat to them, that is: He will count their words against them. The writing, as many scholars have related, is in scrolls in which the angels record it; those written scrolls are the ones that are weighed, and in them Allah creates heaviness and lightness according to the deed written in them. Some people held that "writing" is an expression for enumeration and non-neglect, so it is expressed by what the Arabs understand as the utmost precision and recording. The meaning of the verse, then: their sayings are written down and their deeds, and this connects with the deeds of their fathers, such as killing the prophets without right and the like; then it is said to all of them: "Taste the punishment of the burning." The verse mixes the fathers with the sons in the pronouns, since the fathers are those who paved the way for their sons to disbelieve, and the sons are content with the deeds of the fathers and follow them.

"Tasting" (dhawq) with punishment is a metaphor, an expression for direct contact, since tasting is among its most intense kinds, and the sense of taste is highly discerning. "Al-Harīq" (الحَرِيقُ) means: that which burns; it is a form of fa'īl in the sense of mufʿil. It was also said: al-Harīq is one of the levels of Jahannam.

As for His, the Exalted, saying:

﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ is a rebuke and a reproach, included in what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. It is possible that it is an address to the contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ on the day this verse was revealed. He attributed this sending forth to the hand, since it is the hand that acquires deeds in most of a person's affairs, so every acquisition is ascribed to it. Then He, the Exalted, explained that He does this with justice from Him toward them, and placing a thing in its proper place. The implied sense is: "and because Allah is not ever unjust to the servants." He pluralized "'abd" (servant) in this verse as "'ibad" (عِبَدِ/عَبِيدٍ), because it is a place of compassion and deliverance from injustice.

(p-435) And His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Those who said: Indeed Allah has taken our covenant﴾ is an attribute referring back to His saying: ﴿Those who said: Indeed Allah is poor﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181]. Al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) is an attribute of "al-'abid" (the servants), and this corrupts the meaning and the construction. This statement was made by the rabbis of the Jews, opposing the command of the Prophet ﷺ, that is: "You do not bring a fire, so we have been charged that we not believe in you." "'Ahida" (عَهِدَ) means: commanded; and "al-'ahd" (the covenant) is more specific than "al-amr" (command), since it is in whatever its matter is lasting and remains through the passage of time. The verb "amina" (أَمِنَ) in this verse is transitive with lām and bā' within this sense. "Qurban" (قُرْبانٌ) is a verbal noun used as the name of the thing that is brought near, like "rahn" (pledge). The matter of the offering was an ancient ruling among the prophets. Do you not see that the two sons of Adam offered an offering? That is because when they wished to know whether Allah the Exalted accepted a person's charity, deed, or truthfulness of speech, he would bring near an offering, a sheep or a cow, slaughtered, or part of that, and place it in an open place for the air, and wait a while with it; then a fire would descend from the sky and burn that thing. This was the sign of acceptance, and if the fire did not descend, that deed was not accepted. Then this ruling continued among the prophets of the Children of Israel. This fire also used to descend upon spoils of war and burn them, until spoils were made lawful for Muhammad ﷺ, according to the hadith.

It is related from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he used to recite "biqurubanin" (بِقُرُبانٍ) with a ḍammah on the rā', on the basis of assimilation to the ḍammah of the qāf; but it is not a dialect form, because there is no fu'lān in speech with a ḍammah on the fā' and the 'ayn. Sibawayh related: "al-sulṭān" (السُلُطانُ) with a ḍammah on the lām, and said that this is by assimilation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 184:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Already there have come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you speak of. So why did you kill them, if you are truthful?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183] ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied who came with clear proofs and the Scriptures and the illuminating Book.﴾

This is a response to them in their statement and a clarification of its falsehood. That is: messengers have already come to you with the magnificent, clear signs, and among them is what you mention regarding the matter of the offering. "So why did you kill them, O Children of Israel?" The meaning: rather, this from you is a pretext and obstinacy. Even if I had brought you the offering, you would have made some other pretext. Demands have no limit, and not every one who makes a demand is answered. Allah did not answer a demander except that He intended to punish him and not grant him respite, like the people of Salih and others. Likewise it was said to Muhammad concerning the demand of Quraysh, and he refused and said: "Rather, I will call them and treat them."

Then Allah, the Exalted, consoled His Prophet with the example and model of the prophets who preceded him. That is: let that not weigh heavily upon you.

Ibn 'Amir recited: "wa-bil-zuburi" with the repetition of the preposition bi', and its omission in the recitation of the majority is also well-founded, because the conjunction (wa) joined "al-zubur" with the first bi', so the repetition of the bi' was dispensed with; its repetition is also well-founded for the sake of emphasis. Likewise it is attested in the codices of the people of Syria. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he repeated the bi' in his saying: "wa-bil-Kitabi al-Munir."

"Al-zubur" (the written scriptures): the written book. It is said: zabartu al-kitab when I wrote it, and zabartuhu when I read it. The evidence that it means a book is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Whose abode is this that I saw, and it stirred my longing, like the writing of a scribe on a palm-frond of Yemen?

Al-Zajjaj said: zabartu means I wrote, and dhabartu with the dhal means I read. "Al-munir" (illuminating): its form is mufil from the light (nur), meaning its light shone forth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 185:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Every soul shall taste death; and you will only be paid your full wages on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has indeed triumphed. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾

This is an admonishing report, containing consolation for the Prophet (peace be upon him) and his community concerning the affair of this world and its people, and a promise concerning the Hereafter. Through reflection on death, the matter of the disbelievers and their denial becomes easy to bear. The meaning is: every created soul (nafs) is living, and the "tasting" here is a metaphor (isti'arah). The word "innama" (only/indeed) is restrictive (hasirah) upon the "tawfiyah" (full payment), which is complete, because whoever has been decreed the Garden, while he has not yet entered it, is not yet fully paid. God, exalted is He, singled out the mention of the wages (ujur) for their nobility, and as an indication of His knowledge of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community. There is no doubt that the meaning is: on the Day of Resurrection the wages occur and the full recompense of punishment takes place. "Zuhzih" means: was distanced, and a "zahzah" place is a far place. "Faza" means: he was saved from its danger and fear. "Ghurur" means deception and false hope with vanity, and the life of this world and everything in it of wealth is a little enjoyment that deceives a person and fills him with falsehoods.

Upon this interpretation of the verse, a majority of the exegetes agreed. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: "Matá' al-ghurur is like the provision of a shepherd, who is given a handful of dates or some flour with which he drinks milk." Al-Tabari said: he meant that the enjoyment of this world is little, not sufficient for the one who enjoys it, nor does it carry him to his journey's end.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

"Ghurur" in this sense is used in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is their proverb: "Live, but do not be deceived" (ashshi wa la taghtarr), meaning: do not be content with what does not suffice you.

'Ikrimah said: "Matá' al-ghurur" is the glass vessels, meaning: they must inevitably break and decay, and so is the entire matter of the life of this world.

This is a simile from 'Ikrimah.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar read "al-Gharur" with a fatha on the ghayn. Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read "dha'iqatun" with tanwin and "al-mawta" in the accusative. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The place of a whip of one of you in the Garden is better than this world and whatever is in it," and then he recited this verse..

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 186–187:

(p-438) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and in your selves, and you will surely hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associated others with Allah. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed among the steadfast matters.﴾ ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. How evil is what they buy.﴾

This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. The meaning: you will surely be tested and examined in your possessions by calamities and misfortunes, and by spending in the way of Allah and in the rest of the obligations of the Shari'ah; and in your selves by death, illnesses, and the loss of loved ones through death.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you﴾. 'Ikrimah and others said: the occasion of it was the saying of Finhas: "Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich," and His saying: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and so on. al-Zuhri and others said: this verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, for he used to satirize the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions and composed amorous verses about the women of the Muslims, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone who killed him, the well-known killing mentioned in the Sirah.

Al-adha (harm) is a comprehensive noun meaning injury, and here it includes their words concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, by way of reviling them, and their words concerning Allah Exalted and His prophets. Allah Exalted urged His servants to patience and God-consciousness (taqwa), and informed that it is among the steadfast matters, that is, among the most firm and the best of matters. Al-'azm: carrying out a matter after deliberation and refinement. Undertaking a matter without deliberation is not 'azm, except in the manner of the reckless among the fierce Arabs, as he said:

(p-439)

When he resolves, he places his determination between his eyes, and turns aside from mention of misfortunes.

al-Naqqash said: 'azm and hazm have one meaning; the ḥāʾ is substituted for the ʿayn.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error. Hazm is soundness of judgment in matters, refining it, and guarding against error in it; 'azm is the intention to carry out. Allah Exalted says: ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have resolved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. So consultation and what is in its meaning is hazm, and the Arabs say: "I may exercise hazm, if I exercise 'azm."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ ... the verse, it is a rebuke to the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ), and yet it is also a general statement for them and for others. The governing element in "idh" (when) is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember," and He took this covenant through the tongues of the prophets, nation after nation. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: the verse concerns the Jews specifically; Allah took the covenant from them concerning the matter of Muhammad, but they concealed it and cast it aside.

Muslim al-Bateen said: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf asked his companions about the interpretation of this verse, and a man rose to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, asked him, and he said: it was revealed concerning the Jews; the covenant was taken from them concerning the matter of Muhammad, and they concealed it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: You must make it clear..." so that His saying "but they cast it" refers to the people to whom the prophets had made it clear. Some exegetes said: the verse concerns the Jews and the Christians. The majority of scholars said: the verse is general for everyone whom Allah has taught knowledge, and the scholars of this Community are included in this covenant. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." Abu Hurayrah said: "Indeed I narrate to you a hadith, and were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated it to you," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174].

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read: "la-yubayyinannahu lil-nasi wa la yaktumunahu," with the ya' from below in both, and the rest, with Hafs and 'Asim, read with the ta' from above in both. Both readings are sound, and the pronoun in both verbs refers to the Book. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "la-tubayyinunahu," without the heavy nun. Sibawayh said that this nun is not necessarily required with the lam of oath. Al-nabdh: throwing away. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿behind their backs﴾ is a metaphor for what is utterly discarded; and from it is ﴿and you have taken it behind your backs as something cast away﴾ [Hud: 92]. And from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Tamim ibn Murr, let not my need be behind a back, so that its answer will not be difficult for me.

And from it in meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not make me like the bowl of the rider." He, peace be upon him, meant: do not put my remembrance and obedience behind you, which is the place of the bowl. And from it is the saying of Hassan:

... what hangs behind the rider, the single bowl.

The comparison to the bowl is only in its form, not in its meaning, because the rider needs it, and its place among the rider's possessions is significant. "The small price" is the worldly gain. The remainder of the verse is clear.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

The apparent meaning of this verse is that it was revealed concerning the Jews, and they are the ones intended; then, every concealer from this Community takes his share of this blame and is characterized by it.
