But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed among the steadfast matters.﴾ ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and exchanged it for a small price. How evil is what they buy.﴾

This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. The meaning: you will surely be tested and examined in your possessions by calamities and misfortunes, and by spending in the way of Allah and in the rest of the obligations of the Shari'ah; and in your selves by death, illnesses, and the loss of loved ones through death.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you﴾. 'Ikrimah and others said: the occasion of it was the saying of Finhas: "Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich," and His saying: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and so on. al-Zuhri and others said: this verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, for he used to satirize the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions and composed amorous verses about the women of the Muslims, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone who killed him, the well-known killing mentioned in the Sirah.

Al-adha (harm) is a comprehensive noun meaning injury, and here it includes their words concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, by way of reviling them, and their words concerning Allah Exalted and His prophets. Allah Exalted urged His servants to patience and God-consciousness (taqwa), and informed that it is among the steadfast matters, that is, among the most firm and the best of matters. Al-'azm: carrying out a matter after deliberation and refinement. Undertaking a matter without deliberation is not 'azm, except in the manner of the reckless among the fierce Arabs, as he said:

(p-439)

When he resolves, he places his determination between his eyes, and turns aside from mention of misfortunes.

al-Naqqash said: 'azm and hazm have one meaning; the ḥāʾ is substituted for the ʿayn.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error. Hazm is soundness of judgment in matters, refining it, and guarding against error in it; 'azm is the intention to carry out. Allah Exalted says: ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have resolved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. So consultation and what is in its meaning is hazm, and the Arabs say: "I may exercise hazm, if I exercise 'azm."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ ... the verse, it is a rebuke to the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ), and yet it is also a general statement for them and for others. The governing element in "idh" (when) is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember," and He took this covenant through the tongues of the prophets, nation after nation. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj said: the verse concerns the Jews specifically; Allah took the covenant from them concerning the matter of Muhammad, but they concealed it and cast it aside.

Muslim al-Bateen said: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf asked his companions about the interpretation of this verse, and a man rose to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, asked him, and he said: it was revealed concerning the Jews; the covenant was taken from them concerning the matter of Muhammad, and they concealed it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: You must make it clear..." so that His saying "but they cast it" refers to the people to whom the prophets had made it clear. Some exegetes said: the verse concerns the Jews and the Christians. The majority of scholars said: the verse is general for everyone whom Allah has taught knowledge, and the scholars of this Community are included in this covenant. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." Abu Hurayrah said: "Indeed I narrate to you a hadith, and were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated it to you," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174].

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read: "la-yubayyinannahu lil-nasi wa la yaktumunahu," with the ya' from below in both, and the rest, with Hafs and 'Asim, read with the ta' from above in both. Both readings are sound, and the pronoun in both verbs refers to the Book. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "la-tubayyinunahu," without the heavy nun. Sibawayh said that this nun is not necessarily required with the lam of oath. Al-nabdh: throwing away. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿behind their backs﴾ is a metaphor for what is utterly discarded; and from it is ﴿and you have taken it behind your backs as something cast away﴾ [Hud: 92]. And from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Tamim ibn Murr, let not my need be behind a back, so that its answer will not be difficult for me.

And from it in meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not make me like the bowl of the rider." He, peace be upon him, meant: do not put my remembrance and obedience behind you, which is the place of the bowl. And from it is the saying of Hassan:

... what hangs behind the rider, the single bowl.

The comparison to the bowl is only in its form, not in its meaning, because the rider needs it, and its place among the rider's possessions is significant. "The small price" is the worldly gain. The remainder of the verse is clear.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

The apparent meaning of this verse is that it was revealed concerning the Jews, and they are the ones intended; then, every concealer from this Community takes his share of this blame and is characterized by it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 188–190:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they did not do, will be safe from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Able over all things.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding.﴾

The exegetes (mufassirun) differed over the meaning of His saying ﴿those who rejoice﴾. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Zayd and a group said: the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, because whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) went out for a military expedition (ghazw), they would stay behind from him. When he returned, they would make excuses to him and say: "We had pressing tasks," and the like. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would show acceptance and ask forgiveness for them. So Allah exposed them with this verse. They used to rejoice in what they had done by way of staying behind and making excuses, and they loved to be told that they were in the position of those who strive (mujahidun), but that an excuse had held them back.

A large group of exegetes said: the verse was revealed only concerning the People of the Book, the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews. Then they differed over what it was that they had done, and how they came to love praise. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they had misled their followers away from belief in Muhammad, and they rejoiced at this because their worldly leadership would endure, and they loved to be described as scholars of the Book of Allah and of the earlier messages. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Dahhak and al-Suddi: they had made pacts and written letters to one another from every region, binding themselves to deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and to strike at the core of his prophethood. They loved to be described as people of prayer and fasting [p. 442] and worship, and they themselves claimed that about themselves. Mujahid said: they rejoiced at their followers' admiration for them because of their altering the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved their followers' praise of them for that, while in reality they had done nothing beneficial or sound, for the truth is clear.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse concerns the Jews. They rejoiced in what Allah had given the family of Abraham of prophethood and the Book, so they would say: "We are upon their way," and they loved to be praised for this, though they were not upon their way.

The reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr is "utu" (أُوتُوا), meaning "were given," with a dammah on the hamzah and the taa'. According to his reading, the meaning he stated is sound.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: the verse was revealed concerning a people whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked about something, and they concealed the truth from him and told him otherwise. They rejoiced at what they had done and loved to be praised for the answer they had given, and they thought that this had been accepted and that its correctness had been believed.

Qatada said: the verse concerns the Jews of Khaybar, who once showed hypocrisy toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. They said: "We are with you, upon your opinion, and a support for you," while they believed otherwise. So they loved the praise for what they displayed and rejoiced at it.

Al-Zajjaj said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of Jews who entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), spoke with him about various matters, and then left. They said to the Muslims they met: "The Prophet informed us of things that we already knew." The Muslims praised them for this and hoped for their conversion to Islam. They had concealed the opposite of what they displayed to the Muslims and persisted in their disbelief, so the verse was revealed about them.

[p. 443] The majority of people recited "ataw" (أَتَوْا) with the meaning "did," as you say: "I came upon (ataytu) such a matter." Marwan ibn al-Hakam and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "ataw" (آتَوْا) with the long vowel, meaning "gave," with a fathah on the hamzah and the taa'.

Abu Muhammad (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

This is a reading that is sound according to some of the meanings mentioned earlier.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited "utu" (أُوتُوا) with the meaning "were given," and its meaning has already been mentioned. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ) and ﴿so let them not think﴾ (فَلا يَحْسِبُنَّهُمْ) with the ya' (يَ) at the beginning in both, with a kasrah on the sin (سين) and a dammah on the ba' in "yahsibunnahum." Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: "alladhina" is raised as the subject (fa'il) of "yahsab," and "yahsabanna" did not take an object. These verbs may come as lagw, that is, not in the sense of complete propositions, as in the words of the poet:

"And I did not think there remained between us any affection,
except the broad-chested fine steeds and the she-camels that are ridden."

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say: "I did not see him say that except Zayd, and I did not think him to say that except Zayd." So the reading is consistent with the words ﴿so let them not think﴾ being a substitute (badal) for the first. The verb has been extended to its two objects, namely the pronoun and the phrase "bimafaza," so the verb's extension to them is dispensed with in the first, as in the words of the poet:

"By what Book, or by what Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

So the extension of one of the two verbs has been dispensed with in the other. The fa' in His saying ﴿so let them not think﴾ is superfluous, and that is why the substitution is good, for it cannot be a conjunctive fa' (fa' al-'atf) or a fa' of consequence (fa' al-jaza'). So nothing remains but that it is superfluous, whose presence does not spoil the relation between the substitute and what it substitutes. His saying according to this reading, ﴿so let Him not think﴾ (فَلا يَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ), involves the agent's action extending to his own self, as in: "I thought myself his brother," "I saw myself at the Ka'bah last night," and "I found myself hungry from listening." This is because these verbs and what carries their meaning, when they enter upon the subject and predicate, resemble inna and its sisters. Just as you say "Innani dhahibun" (I am indeed going), so you say "zanantuni dhahiban" (I thought myself going). If you said "azunnu nafsi af'alu kadha" (I think myself doing such-and-such), it would not be as good as "azunnuni fa'ilan" (I think myself doing it).

[p. 444] Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ) with the ya' at the beginning and a fathah on the ba'. Nafi' kasrahed the sin and Ibn 'Amir made it fathah. ﴿so do not think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ) is with the taa' at the beginning and a fathah on the ba'. The two objects required by His saying ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ are omitted because of what is mentioned after it, and the discussion of this is as stated earlier in the reading of Ibn Kathir, except that the substitution mentioned in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr is not permitted here, because the two verbs differ and their subjects differ. Hamzah recited ﴿Do not let them think﴾ (لا تَحْسِبَنَّ) with the taa' at the beginning and a kasrah on the sin, and ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسِبَنَّهُمْ) with the taa' at the beginning, a kasrah on the sin and a fathah on the ba'. According to this reading, "alladhina" is the first object of "tahsibanna," and the second object is omitted because of what follows it, as was said just above concerning the two objects. Repeating the verb in His saying ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ is good because of the length of the speech, and this is the habit of the Arabs, as it brings the matter closer to the mind of the addressee. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim recited ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسُبُنَّهُمْ) with the taa' at the beginning, a fathah on the sin, and a dammah on the ba'.

Al-mafaza (المَفازَة) is a noun of place (maf'alah) from faza, yafuzu, meaning "he was saved," so it means a place of salvation. The place of danger was called "mafaza" by way of optimism (tafa'ul). This was said by al-Asma'i. It was also said: it is so called because it is a place of destruction (taf wiz) and a likely place of ruin. The Arabs say: "fawwaza al-rajul" when a man dies. Tha'lab said: I related to Ibn al-A'rabi the statement of al-Asma'i, and he said: "He was wrong." Abu al-Makarim said to me: it is only called mafaza because whoever crosses it is saved. Al-Asma'i also said: the stung one is called "salim" (the safe one) by way of optimism. Ibn al-A'rabi said: rather, it is because he submits to what has afflicted him.

After forbidding them to think themselves saved, He informed them that for them is a punishment. Then He opened the speech by mentioning Allah's power and dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾... to the end of the verse. Some exegetes said: the verse is a rebuttal of those who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181].

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and Allah is Able over all things﴾, al-Qadi Ibn al-Tayyib and others said: its outward form is generality, but its meaning is particularity, because Allah the Exalted is not described as being able over impossibilities. And "shay'" (thing) in the language of the Arabs means that which exists.

Then the Exalted indicated the places of reflection and lesson, where inference to the Maker (al-Sani') is made through the existence of the heavens and the earths. Created things indicate knowledge, and it is impossible that the originator of a world, a willing one, be non-living. Thus through reflection on this verse the greatness of the attributes is established.

﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾: this is their succession, since Allah made them alternate (khilfah). Included in the word "ikhtilaf" (alternation) is that one of them shortens while the other lengthens, and vice versa, and included in it is their difference in light and darkness. "Ayat" means signs. And "al-albab" (those of understanding) in this verse refers to the minds of obligation (albab al-taklif), not the minds of experience (albab al-tajriba), because everyone who has necessary knowledge perceives it, and so he knows necessarily what we have said about the attributes of Allah the Exalted.

When he returned, they would make excuses to him and say: "We had pressing tasks," and the like. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would show acceptance and ask forgiveness for them. So Allah exposed them with this verse. They used to rejoice in what they had done by way of staying behind and making excuses, and they loved to be told that they were in the position of those who strive (mujahidun), but that an excuse had held them back.

A large group of exegetes said: the verse was revealed only concerning the People of the Book, the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews. Then they differed over what it was that they had done, and how they came to love praise. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they had misled their followers away from belief in Muhammad, and they rejoiced at this because their worldly leadership would endure, and they loved to be described as scholars of the Book of Allah and of the earlier messages. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Dahhak and al-Suddi: they had made pacts and written letters to one another from every region, binding themselves to deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and to strike at the core of his prophethood. They loved to be described as people of prayer and fasting [p. 442] and worship, and they themselves claimed that about themselves. Mujahid said: they rejoiced at their followers' admiration for them because of their altering the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved their followers' praise of them for that, while in reality they had done nothing beneficial or sound, for the truth is clear.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse concerns the Jews. They rejoiced in what Allah had given the family of Abraham of prophethood and the Book, so they would say: "We are upon their way," and they loved to be praised for this, though they were not upon their way.

The reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr is "utu" (أُوتُوا), meaning "were given," with a dammah on the hamzah and the taa'. According to his reading, the meaning he stated is sound.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: the verse was revealed concerning a people whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked about something, and they concealed the truth from him and told him otherwise. They rejoiced at what they had done and loved to be praised for the answer they had given, and they thought that this had been accepted and that its correctness had been believed.

Qatada said: the verse concerns the Jews of Khaybar, who once showed hypocrisy toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. They said: "We are with you, upon your opinion, and a support for you," while they believed otherwise. So they loved the praise for what they displayed and rejoiced at it.

Al-Zajjaj said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of Jews who entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), spoke with him about various matters, and then left. They said to the Muslims they met: "The Prophet informed us of things that we already knew." The Muslims praised them for this and hoped for their conversion to Islam. They had concealed the opposite of what they displayed to the Muslims and persisted in their disbelief, so the verse was revealed about them.

[p. 443] The majority of people recited "ataw" (أَتَوْا) with the meaning "did," as you say: "I came upon (ataytu) such a matter." Marwan ibn al-Hakam and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited "ataw" (آتَوْا) with the long vowel, meaning "gave," with a fathah on the hamzah and the taa'.

Abu Muhammad (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

This is a reading that is sound according to some of the meanings mentioned earlier.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited "utu" (أُوتُوا) with the meaning "were given," and its meaning has already been mentioned. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ) and ﴿so let them not think﴾ (فَلا يَحْسِبُنَّهُمْ) with the ya' (يَ) at the beginning in both, with a kasrah on the sin (سين) and a dammah on the ba' in "yahsibunnahum." Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: "alladhina" is raised as the subject (fa'il) of "yahsab," and "yahsabanna" did not take an object. These verbs may come as lagw, that is, not in the sense of complete propositions, as in the words of the poet:

"And I did not think there remained between us any affection,
except the broad-chested fine steeds and the she-camels that are ridden."

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say: "I did not see him say that except Zayd, and I did not think him to say that except Zayd." So the reading is consistent with the words ﴿so let them not think﴾ being a substitute (badal) for the first. The verb has been extended to its two objects, namely the pronoun and the phrase "bimafaza," so the verb's extension to them is dispensed with in the first, as in the words of the poet:

"By what Book, or by what Sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

So the extension of one of the two verbs has been dispensed with in the other. The fa' in His saying ﴿so let them not think﴾ is superfluous, and that is why the substitution is good, for it cannot be a conjunctive fa' (fa' al-'atf) or a fa' of consequence (fa' al-jaza'). So nothing remains but that it is superfluous, whose presence does not spoil the relation between the substitute and what it substitutes. His saying according to this reading, ﴿so let Him not think﴾ (فَلا يَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ), involves the agent's action extending to his own self, as in: "I thought myself his brother," "I saw myself at the Ka'bah last night," and "I found myself hungry from listening." This is because these verbs and what carries their meaning, when they enter upon the subject and predicate, resemble inna and its sisters. Just as you say "Innani dhahibun" (I am indeed going), so you say "zanantuni dhahiban" (I thought myself going). If you said "azunnu nafsi af'alu kadha" (I think myself doing such-and-such), it would not be as good as "azunnuni fa'ilan" (I think myself doing it).

[p. 444] Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ) with the ya' at the beginning and a fathah on the ba'. Nafi' kasrahed the sin and Ibn 'Amir made it fathah. ﴿so do not think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ) is with the taa' at the beginning and a fathah on the ba'. The two objects required by His saying ﴿Let not those who rejoice think﴾ are omitted because of what is mentioned after it, and the discussion of this is as stated earlier in the reading of Ibn Kathir, except that the substitution mentioned in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr is not permitted here, because the two verbs differ and their subjects differ. Hamzah recited ﴿Do not let them think﴾ (لا تَحْسِبَنَّ) with the taa' at the beginning and a kasrah on the sin, and ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسِبَنَّهُمْ) with the taa' at the beginning, a kasrah on the sin and a fathah on the ba'. According to this reading, "alladhina" is the first object of "tahsibanna," and the second object is omitted because of what follows it, as was said just above concerning the two objects. Repeating the verb in His saying ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ is good because of the length of the speech, and this is the habit of the Arabs, as it brings the matter closer to the mind of the addressee. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim recited ﴿so do not let them think them﴾ (فَلا تَحْسُبُنَّهُمْ) with the taa' at the beginning, a fathah on the sin, and a dammah on the ba'.

Al-mafaza (المَفازَة) is a noun of place (maf'alah) from faza, yafuzu, meaning "he was saved," so it means a place of salvation. The place of danger was called "mafaza" by way of optimism (tafa'ul). This was said by al-Asma'i. It was also said: it is so called because it is a place of destruction (taf wiz) and a likely place of ruin. The Arabs say: "fawwaza al-rajul" when a man dies. Tha'lab said: I related to Ibn al-A'rabi the statement of al-Asma'i, and he said: "He was wrong." Abu al-Makarim said to me: it is only called mafaza because whoever crosses it is saved. Al-Asma'i also said: the stung one is called "salim" (the safe one) by way of optimism. Ibn al-A'rabi said: rather, it is because he submits to what has afflicted him.

After forbidding them to think themselves saved, He informed them that for them is a punishment. Then He opened the speech by mentioning Allah's power and dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾... to the end of the verse. Some exegetes said: the verse is a rebuttal of those who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181].

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and Allah is Able over all things﴾, al-Qadi Ibn al-Tayyib and others said: its outward form is generality, but its meaning is particularity, because Allah the Exalted is not described as being able over impossibilities. And "shay'" (thing) in the language of the Arabs means that which exists.

Then the Exalted indicated the places of reflection and lesson, where inference to the Maker (al-Sani') is made through the existence of the heavens and the earths. Created things indicate knowledge, and it is impossible that the originator of a world, a willing one, be non-living. Thus through reflection on this verse the greatness of the attributes is established.

﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾: this is their succession, since Allah made them alternate (khilfah). Included in the word "ikhtilaf" (alternation) is that one of them shortens while the other lengthens, and vice versa, and included in it is their difference in light and darkness. "Ayat" means signs. And "al-albab" (those of understanding) in this verse refers to the minds of obligation (albab al-taklif), not the minds of experience (albab al-tajriba), because everyone who has necessary knowledge perceives it, and so he knows necessarily what we have said about the attributes of Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 191–192:

His Exalted Majesty said:

﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire." "Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾

"Alladhina" (those who) is in the genitive position as an attribute of "li-ulil-albab" (for people of understanding). This description apparently refers to the use of tahmid (saying "al-hamdu lillah"), tahlil (saying "la ilaha illa Allah"), takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") and similar remembrance of Allah, and that the heart should keep the tongue company. This is among the greatest forms of worship, and the hadiths on this are numerous. The son of Adam moves through these three states and at most times of his affairs he is not free of them, so they are as if they encompass his time. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, similarly extended the encompassing of time in her saying: «The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to remember Allah at all his times,» so that included his being in the lavatory and other than that.

A group of exegetes went to the view that His saying: ﴿those who remember Allah﴾ is merely an expression for the prayer, meaning: they do not neglect it, so in a state of excuse they pray it sitting and on their sides. Some of them said: this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 103]... the verse, according to the interpretation of one who interprets "qadaytum" there as meaning "you performed," because some people say "qadaytum" there means "you finished them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If this verse concerns the prayer, its jurisprudence is that a person prays standing; if he is unable, then sitting. The apparent position of al-Mudawwana is sitting cross-legged. It is narrated from Malik and some of his companions that he prays as he sits between the two prostrations. If he is unable to sit, he prays on his side or his back, with choice. This is the position of al-Mudawwana.

Ibn Habib related from Ibn al-Qasim: he prays on his back; if he cannot, then on his right side, then on his left. In the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz: he prays on his right side, otherwise on his left, otherwise on his back. Sahnun said: he prays on his right side as he is placed in his grave, otherwise on his back, otherwise on his left.

The conjunction of His saying "and on their sides" to His saying "standing and sitting" is fine, because it has the meaning of lying down. Then He linked to this worship, which is remembrance of Allah by the tongue or the prayer, obligatory and recommended, another great act of worship, which is reflection upon the power of Allah Exalted and His creations, and the lessons He has scattered:

"And in everything there is a sign indicating that He is One."

It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a people who were reflecting about Allah, so he said: "Reflect upon the creation and do not reflect upon the Creator, for you cannot measure His measure." This is the intent of the verse: ﴿and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Some scholars said: the one who reflects on the Essence of Allah Exalted is like one who looks at the sun's disc, because He Exalted is "not like Him is anything"; rather, reflection and the expansion of the mind is upon the creatures and upon the frights of the Hereafter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no worship like reflection." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: reflection is the mirror of the believer, in which he looks at his good deeds and his bad deeds.

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Darda' said: "An hour's reflection is better than a night's standing in prayer." Sari al-Saqati said: "An hour's reflection is better than a year's worship," meaning only that you loosen the ropes of your tent and set it up in the Hereafter. Abu Sulayman al-Darani took a cup of water to perform ablution for the night prayer while he had a guest; the guest saw him, when he put his finger into the rim of the cup, remain thus reflecting until dawn broke. He said to him: "What is this, Abu Sulayman?" He said: "When I placed my finger in the rim of the cup, I remembered the saying of Allah, Majestic and Exalted: ﴿when the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71], so I reflected on my own state, and how I would bear the shackle if it were placed on my neck on the Day of Resurrection. I remained in that until morning."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the extreme of fear, and the best of matters is their middle course. The scholars of the Community, who are the proof, are not on this method; and the study of the knowledge of the Book of Allah and the meanings of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for one who understands and whose benefit is hoped for is better than this; but it is good that the lands are not empty of the like of this.

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me from some scholars of the East, who said: I was spending the night in the Masjid al-Aqdam in Egypt. I prayed the 'atama and saw a man who had lain down in a cloak, wrapped in his garment, until morning. We prayed that night and stayed awake. When the Subh prayer was called, that man rose, faced the qibla and prayed with the people. I was astonished at his boldness in praying without wudu'. When the prayer finished he went out, and I followed him to admonish him. When I drew near to him I heard him reciting:

"Body dissolved, absent yet present; heart alert, silent yet remembering."

"Contracted amid the hidden, expanded; so is one who knows and remembers."

"He spends his night as a man of thought, and all night long he is standing and wakeful."

He said: I knew that he was among those who worship through reflection, and I turned away from him.

His saying, Exalted is He: "Our Lord" means: they say "Our Lord" as a call (nida'). ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾ means: not for an unappointed purpose; rather You created it and created mankind so that it be considered, whereupon You are made one and worshipped. So whoever does this, You bless him, and whoever strays from that, You punish him for his disbelief and for his saying about You what is not fitting for You. For this meaning which the strength of the wording gives, their saying "Glory be to You" is apt, meaning: a declaration of Your transcendence above what the falsifiers say. And their saying "protect us from the punishment of the Fire" is apt, since we are those who glorify and declare You transcendent, who affirm Your oneness.

As for their saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, it is a plea for protection and refuge, meaning: so do not do that to us, and do not make us among those who do its deeds. Al-khizy is the disgrace that shames and destroys a person's standing: "khaziya al-rajul yakhza khizyan" when he is exposed, and "khaza'a" when he feels shame; the verb is one but the verbal noun differs.

Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and others said: this refers to whoever abides eternally in the Fire; whoever leaves it through intercession and faith is not disgraced. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and others said: everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced, even if he leaves it, and that in what is less than that there is indeed disgrace.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Indeed it is a lesser disgrace than another disgrace; the disgrace of one who leaves it is not the exposure that destroys his standing. The complete disgrace belongs only to the disbelievers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ is from the words of those who supplicate, and by this the description of the verse is coherent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 193–194:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not break the promise.﴾

These verses relate the words of those endowed with minds (ulu al-albab), that they say: "Our Lord, our Lord." Abu al-Darda' said: May Allah have mercy on the believers; they continued saying "Our Lord, our Lord" until it was answered for them.

The commentators differed concerning the caller (al-munadi). Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others said: the caller is Muhammad (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: the caller is the Book of Allah, and not all of them saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and heard him. Since "yunadi" (calls) holds the position of "yad'u" (invites), its construction with "li" (to) is fine, in the sense of "ila al-iman" (to faith).

As for His saying "an amanu" (that believe): "an" is explanatory (mufassira) and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The forgiveness of sins and the expiation of misdeeds are close to one another, but it was repeated for emphasis, and because both are kinds of covering (satr) and removal of the ruling of sin after it has occurred. "Al-abrar" is the plural of barr; its origin is "barara" on the pattern of "fa'ala," and the letter ra' was assimilated into the ra'. It was also said that it is the plural of bar, like sahib and ashab. The meaning is: cause us to die along with them in all their rulings and actions.

His saying: ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ means: upon the tongues of Your messengers. Al-A'mash recited "rusulika" with a sukun on the sin. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to fulfil the promise, and He is one from whom breaking the promise is not permissible. In their request there is a desire that they be among those who deserve it; so the seeking and the fear lie on their side, not on the side of Allah, exalted is He, because this supplication is in this world. Thus the meaning of a person's saying "O Allah, fulfil Your promise to me" is only: make me among those who deserve the fulfilment of the promise. It was also said that the meaning of their supplication is seeking speed, along with their confidence that the promise will be fulfilled. Al-Tabari and others said: the meaning of the verse is what You promised us through the tongues of Your messengers of victory over the enemies; so the supplication is in the sense of worldly matters.

Their saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection, indeed You do not break the promise﴾ is an allusion to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. This is His promise, exalted is He, and it indicates that disgrace is only with eternal abiding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verses 193–194:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not break the promise.﴾

These verses relate the words of those endowed with minds (ulu al-albab), that they say: "Our Lord, our Lord." Abu al-Darda' said: May Allah have mercy on the believers; they continued saying "Our Lord, our Lord" until it was answered for them.

The commentators differed concerning the caller (al-munadi). Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others said: the caller is Muhammad (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: the caller is the Book of Allah, and not all of them saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and heard him. Since "yunadi" (calls) holds the position of "yad'u" (invites), its construction with "li" (to) is fine, in the sense of "ila al-iman" (to faith).

As for His saying "an amanu" (that believe): "an" is explanatory (mufassira) and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The forgiveness of sins and the expiation of misdeeds are close to one another, but it was repeated for emphasis, and because both are kinds of covering (satr) and removal of the ruling of sin after it has occurred. "Al-abrar" is the plural of barr; its origin is "barara" on the pattern of "fa'ala," and the letter ra' was assimilated into the ra'. It was also said that it is the plural of bar, like sahib and ashab. The meaning is: cause us to die along with them in all their rulings and actions.

His saying: ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ means: upon the tongues of Your messengers. Al-A'mash recited "rusulika" with a sukun on the sin. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to fulfil the promise, and He is one from whom breaking the promise is not permissible. In their request there is a desire that they be among those who deserve it; so the seeking and the fear lie on their side, not on the side of Allah, exalted is He, because this supplication is in this world. Thus the meaning of a person's saying "O Allah, fulfil Your promise to me" is only: make me among those who deserve the fulfilment of the promise. It was also said that the meaning of their supplication is seeking speed, along with their confidence that the promise will be fulfilled. Al-Tabari and others said: the meaning of the verse is what You promised us through the tongues of Your messengers of victory over the enemies; so the supplication is in the sense of worldly matters.

Their saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection, indeed You do not break the promise﴾ is an allusion to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. This is His promise, exalted is He, and it indicates that disgrace is only with eternal abiding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 195:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿So their Lord answered them: "Never will I allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another. So those who emigrated, were driven out of their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed—I will surely remove from them their misdeeds and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah. And with Allah is the best reward."﴾

"Istajaba" (is a form of) istaf'ala (the Form X pattern) in the sense of ajaba (to answer). So istaf'ala here is not on its own pattern of seeking something; rather, it is as the poet said:

A caller called, "O you who answers to generosity," but no answerer answered him at that time.

That is, he did not answer him. His saying "anni" may be that "anna" is explanatory (mufassira), and it is possible that it means "ay" (that is). 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "inni" with a kasra on the hamza. This is a verse of promise from Allah, Exalted, meaning: this is His action toward those who possess the qualities mentioned.

It is narrated that Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has mentioned the men in emigration and has not mentioned the women in anything of that, so the verse was revealed." And verses were revealed with a similar meaning in which women are mentioned.

His saying "min dhakarin" is a specification of the category of the worker. Some people said: "min" is extra (za'ida), because negation precedes it in the speech.

His Exalted saying: ﴿you are of one another﴾ means in reward and the acceptance of deeds; that is, men and women are on one equal footing in this. Allah, Exalted, described the state of the emigrants; then the verse afterwards extends to everyone who is harmed for the sake of Allah, Exalted, and who also emigrates to Allah, Exalted. Although the name of emigration and its specific merit has ceased after the Conquest, the meaning remains until the Day of Resurrection, because the one who abandons his homeland and kin for Allah's sake, it is as though the homeland and kin also abandon him; so it is an emigration.

His Exalted saying: ﴿and were driven out of their homes﴾ is an expression of attributing blame to the disbelievers. The emigrants were driven out only by bad companionship and ugly deeds, so they left by their own choice. When the speech is in the context of attributing blame to the disbelievers, it is said: "They were driven out of their homes," and ﴿the expulsion of its people from it is greater in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and other examples. When the speech is in the context of boasting and strength against enemies, the other aspect is adopted, that they left by their own opinion. Among this is the Prophet's ﷺ disapproval of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith when he recited to him:

"..............  And he who I drove out of every place drove me back to Allah."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "You drove me out of every place?" as a rebuke to him.

Among this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"In a band of Quraysh, one of them said, in the valley of Makkah, when they embraced Islam: 'Depart!'
They departed, and there was no retreat, nor any uncovering, at the meeting, nor a deviation of those who had been abandoned."

Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read "wa qatalu wa qutilu" with the taa' lightened and the qaf vowelled with a damma; the meaning of this reading is clear. Ibn Kathir read "wa qatalu wa quttilu" with the taa' doubled, and in meaning it is like the first in emphasis on killing. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa qutilu wa qatalu," beginning with the verb in the passive form, and likewise their disagreement in Surah al-Tawbah, except that Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir double it in al-Tawbah.

The meaning of Hamza's reading is: not giving the waw a rank, because what is conjoined by waw may be first in meaning, and that is not so with the conjunction by fa'. It may also mean: "and they were killed, and those remaining among them fought." The verse then resembles His Exalted saying: ﴿So they did not weaken for what befell them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], according to the interpretation of one who holds that the killing occurred among the Rabbiyyun.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "wa qatalu" with a fatha on the qaf and the ta', without an alif, and "qutilu" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the ta', lightened. This is a reading of good meaning, fulfilling both merits in the commonly known order. Muharib ibn Dithar read "wa qatalu" with a fatha on the qaf, "wa qatalu" (with alif). Talha ibn Musarrif read "qutthilu" with a damma on the qaf and a doubled ta', "wa qatalu." This reading involves either abandoning the rank of the waw, or that he fought those who remained.

The lam in His saying "la-ukaffiranna" is the lam of oath. "Thawaban" is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the sense, like His saying "sun'a Allah" and ﴿the Book of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 3, verse 196–198:

His Exalted and Majestic Word:

﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ ﴿A little enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place.﴾ ﴿But those who fear their Lord—for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a welcome from Allah. And what is with Allah is best for the righteous.﴾

The phrase "yaghurrannaka" (let not deceive you) is revealed in this verse with the meaning: do not suppose that the state of the disbelievers is good, so that you should be concerned about it. This is because the one who is deceived rejoices in the thing by which he is deceived. The disbelievers are deceived by their going to and fro, while the believers are concerned with it. However, it may occur to a believer that this granting of respite to the disbelievers is for their own good, so this thought becomes an inclination towards their condition and a kind of being deceived. Therefore "lā yaghurrannaka" is apt.

A parallel to this is the statement of 'Umar to Hafsah: "Let not deceive you that your neighbour is more beautiful than you and more beloved to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The meaning: do not be deceived by the pride that this neighbour displays, lest you fall into it and the Prophet (ﷺ) divorce you. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community, and the disbelievers have a share in it; that is, let not their going to and fro deceive them.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read "lā yaghurrankа" with the nun of emphasis unstressed (lightened), and likewise "lā yaṣuddannaka", "lā yaṣuddannakum", and "lā yaḍurrannakum", and similar forms.

Al-taqallub (going to and fro) means engaging in trade, profit, wars and all other pursuits. Then God, Exalted, informed of the paucity of that enjoyment, because it is transient, leading to humiliation, scarcity and punishment.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "lakinna alladhina" with the nun stressed, and on this reading "alladhina" is in the accusative position as the noun of "lakinna". "Nuzulan" means honour (takrima), and its accusative is as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid).

Al-Hasan read "nuzlan" with the zay unvowelled (sakin).

His Exalted word: ﴿And what is with Allah is best for the righteous﴾ may mean: better than what these people have of going to and fro and luxury; and it may mean: better than what they have in this world. Ibn Mas'ud took this view, for he said: "There is no believer or disbeliever but that death is better for him: as for the disbeliever, so that he may not increase in sin; as for the believer, because what is with Allah is best for the righteous."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." Qadi Ibn al-Tayyib said: This is only in relation to what each of them will attain in the Hereafter: the world is a prison for the believer who is blessed, in relation to Paradise, and the world is a paradise for the poor disbeliever who is constrained in his state and health, in relation to Hell. It was also said: the meaning is that it is the prison of the believer because it is a place of obligation in acts of obedience, in his fasting and his standing in prayer; so he is in it like one who is troubled and restrained, awaiting reward in the other life, which is his paradise. And the world is the paradise of the disbeliever because it is the place of his reward for whatever good he may do, and he does not await any reward in the Hereafter; so this is his paradise. This statement, in my view, is like an explanation and elaboration of the first.

(p-٤٥٥)His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the signs of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, be steadfast, endure together, stay on guard, and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

The commentators differed about who is meant by this verse. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and others said: "It was revealed concerning Ash'amah al-Najashi, the ruler of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). He believed in Allah and in Muhammad (ﷺ). When he died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) learned of it on that same day, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: 'Go out and pray over a brother of yours.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led the people in the funeral prayer over him and said the takbir four times. And in some narrations: the bier of the Negus was uncovered for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the hour when he was about to be buried, so he could see it from his place in Medina. When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed over him, the hypocrites said: 'Look at this man praying over a foreign Christian (ʿilj) whom he has never seen!' So this verse was revealed." Ash'amah al-Najashi was a Christian, and Ash'amah in Arabic means "ʿaṭiyyah" (gift). This was stated by Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and others. It is also narrated that after this the hypocrites said: "Indeed, he did not pray toward the qiblah," so there was revealed: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. Others said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning all of the People of the Book who believed.

(p-٤٥٦)"Khāshiʿīn" (humbling themselves; "khāshiʿīn" is in the accusative) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a grammatical term meaning the state in which the subject is) from the pronoun in "yu'minu" (believes). He made "khāshiʿīn" agree with the meaning of "man" (those who), because it is plural, not with the wording of "man," because the wording is singular.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not exchange the signs of Allah for a small price﴾ is praise for them and a censure of the rest of the disbelievers among the People of the Book, for their substitution and their preference of worldly gain, which is a small price, over their Hereafter and over the signs of Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ — it was said that its meaning is: swift in bringing the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day of Reckoning, so the reckoning is swift, since everything that is coming is near. Others said: "Swift in reckoning" means the counting of the deeds of the servants and their rewards and their sins, since all of that in His doing does not need counting, deliberation and consideration, as humans need.

Then Allah, exalted is He, concluded the sūrah with this charge, which combines victory over enemies in this world and success with the bliss of the Hereafter. He urged patience in obedience and patience against desires, and He commanded "muṣābarah" (enduring together). It was said: its meaning is enduring against the enemies; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. It was also said: its meaning is enduring the promise of Allah regarding victory; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, meaning: do not grow weary, and wait for relief. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Waiting for relief through patience is an act of worship."

Likewise, the commentators differed about the meaning of His saying "wa-rābiṭū" (and stay on guard, or stand ready at the frontier). The majority of the Ummah said: its meaning is: "stand guard against your enemies with horses," i.e., keep horses stationed as your enemies keep theirs. From this is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿and from the mounting of horses﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]... the verse.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah, who had written to him mentioning the armies of the Romans. 'Umar wrote to him: "As to what follows: whenever hardship befalls a believing servant, Allah makes relief after it, and hardship will never overcome two eases (cf. al-Sharh: 5–6). Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says in His Book: ﴿O you who believe, be steadfast, endure together, and stay on guard﴾... the verse."

(p-٤٥٧)Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: this verse refers to waiting for the prayer after the prayer, and there was no military campaign in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in which one would stand guard. He argued with the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not guide you to that by which Allah erases sins and raises ranks? Completing the wudu' in difficult conditions, frequent walking to the mosques, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer; that is ribāṭ, that is ribāṭ, that is ribāṭ."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that ribāṭ is constant presence in the way of Allah. Its origin is from tying horses (rabṭ al-khayl). Then every person who remains stationed at one of the frontiers (thughūr) of Islam was called "murābiṭ" (one who stands guard), whether mounted or on foot. The word is derived from "rabṭ" (tying). The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "that is ribāṭ," is only a comparison to ribāṭ in the way of Allah, since waiting for the prayer is only one of the paths that bring salvation. The linguistic ribāṭ is the first meaning. This is like his saying (ﷺ): "The strong man is not the one who overcomes others in wrestling," and his saying: "The poor man is not this one who goes around (for alms)," and other examples besides these.

(p-٤٥٨)The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to the jurists, the murābiṭ in the way of Allah is the one who travels to one of the frontiers in order to stand guard there for a period of time. This was stated and narrated by Ibn al-Mawwaz. As for the residents of the frontiers who live there permanently with their families, earning their living there, although they are defenders, they are not murābiṭūn.

His saying: ﴿that you may be successful﴾ is an expression of hope regarding human beings.

The commentary on Sūrat Āl ʿImrān is complete, and all praise is due to Allah for that, abundantly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ — it was said that its meaning is: swift in bringing the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day of Reckoning, so the reckoning is swift, since everything that is coming is near. Others said: "Swift in reckoning" means the counting of the deeds of the servants and their rewards and their sins, since all of that in His doing does not need counting, deliberation and consideration, as humans need.

Then Allah, exalted is He, concluded the sūrah with this charge, which combines victory over enemies in this world and success with the bliss of the Hereafter. He urged patience in obedience and patience against desires, and He commanded "muṣābarah" (enduring together). It was said: its meaning is enduring against the enemies; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. It was also said: its meaning is enduring the promise of Allah regarding victory; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, meaning: do not grow weary, and wait for relief. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Waiting for relief through patience is an act of worship."

Likewise, the commentators differed about the meaning of His saying "wa-rābiṭū" (and stay on guard, or stand ready at the frontier). The majority of the Ummah said: its meaning is: "stand guard against your enemies with horses," i.e., keep horses stationed as your enemies keep theirs. From this is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿and from the mounting of horses﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]... the verse.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah, who had written to him mentioning the armies of the Romans. 'Umar wrote to him: "As to what follows: whenever hardship befalls a believing servant, Allah makes relief after it, and hardship will never overcome two eases (cf. al-Sharh: 5–6). Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says in His Book: ﴿O you who believe, be steadfast, endure together, and stay on guard﴾... the verse."

(p-٤٥٧)Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: this verse refers to waiting for the prayer after the prayer, and there was no military campaign in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in which one would stand guard. He argued with the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not guide you to that by which Allah erases sins and raises ranks? Completing the wudu' in difficult conditions, frequent walking to the mosques, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer; that is ribāṭ, that is ribāṭ, that is ribāṭ."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that ribāṭ is constant presence in the way of Allah. Its origin is from tying horses (rabṭ al-khayl). Then every person who remains stationed at one of the frontiers (thughūr) of Islam was called "murābiṭ" (one who stands guard), whether mounted or on foot. The word is derived from "rabṭ" (tying). The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "that is ribāṭ," is only a comparison to ribāṭ in the way of Allah, since waiting for the prayer is only one of the paths that bring salvation. The linguistic ribāṭ is the first meaning. This is like his saying (ﷺ): "The strong man is not the one who overcomes others in wrestling," and his saying: "The poor man is not this one who goes around (for alms)," and other examples besides these.

(p-٤٥٨)The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to the jurists, the murābiṭ in the way of Allah is the one who travels to one of the frontiers in order to stand guard there for a period of time. This was stated and narrated by Ibn al-Mawwaz. As for the residents of the frontiers who live there permanently with their families, earning their living there, although they are defenders, they are not murābiṭūn.

His saying: ﴿that you may be successful﴾ is an expression of hope regarding human beings.

The commentary on Sūrat Āl ʿImrān is complete, and all praise is due to Allah for that, abundantly.
